docs.title: Задание: проверка и унификация статистик распределения
docs.text:
Замени <distribution> на нужное распределение.

Приведи тестовые статистики распределения <distribution> к общей архитектуре проекта, проверь их математическую корректность, оптимизируй и дополни документацию. Выполни работу полностью, включая код, тесты и документацию.

docs.title: 1. Архитектура и автогенерация
docs.text:
• Изучи continuous/uniform и weibull/weibull_statistics.py.
  • Убери supported_hypotheses из базового класса распределения. Каждый конкретный критерий должен самостоятельно объявлять поддерживаемые гипотезы; для генерируемых классов укажи их в спецификациях.
  • Удали ручные реализации критериев, алгоритмы которых уже есть в edf.py и frequency.py. Подключи их через общие фабрики по образцу Weibull.
  • Обнови публичные экспорты и устаревшие импорты, связанные с изменениями. Не создавай дубли критериев в реестре.

docs.title: 2. Структура пакета и типизация
docs.text:
Организуй пакет по образцу continuous/uniform:

continuous/<distribution>/
├── __init__.py
├── __init__.pyi
└── <distribution>_statistics.py
  • В __init__.py явно экспортируй публичные классы.
  • Сохрани существующие публичные пути импорта и совместимость pickle, где это возможно. Необходимые изменения API явно опиши.
  • Создай или обнови генератор __init__.pyi с режимом --check. Stub должен покрывать все публичные классы и соответствовать их сигнатурам.

docs.title: 3. Математическая проверка
docs.text:
• Проверь все конкретные критерии, включая автоматически генерируемые.
  • Сопоставь формулы с научными статьями: коэффициенты, нормировки, индексы, оценивание параметров и направление критической области.
  • Проверь ограничения выборки, границы носителя, повторы, постоянные выборки, пустые интервалы, экстремальные значения и численную устойчивость.
  • Различай полностью заданные и составные гипотезы. Проверь применимость калибровки, зависимость от неизвестных параметров и необходимость повторного оценивания при моделировании.
  • Добавь независимые проверки: аналитические формулы, SciPy, численное интегрирование, высокую точность или точную арифметику — по необходимости. Сравнение с тем же общим ядром не заменяет независимую проверку.
  • Исправь найденные ошибки. Если реализация является адаптацией или первоисточник недоступен, явно зафиксируй это, не приписывая ей неподтверждённые свойства.

docs.title: 4. Оптимизация Numba
docs.text:
• По образцу uniform_statistics.py вынеси численные вычисления в статические методы классов с @jit(nopython=True, cache=True).
  • Используй уже скомпилированные общие ядра EDF и частотных критериев.
  • Не создавай вспомогательные функции вне классов. Нужные методы размещай внутри соответствующего класса.
  • Сохрани точность, обработку границ и валидацию входа. Если необходим точный Python-fallback, сохрани его и объясни назначение.
  • Проверь, что публичный путь выполнения действительно вызывает nopython-ядра. Измерь скорость после прогрева отдельно от времени компиляции.

docs.title: 5. Документация
docs.text:
• Для каждого конкретного критерия создай отдельную страницу с гипотезой, формулой, ограничениями, направлением отклонения, особенностями калибровки, рабочим примером и научными ссылками.
  • Создай общую страницу index.md со всеми критериями, публичными классами, кодами и ссылками на отдельные страницы.
  • Добавь страницы в навигацию MkDocs.
  • По образцу отчёта Uniform и отчёта Pareto создай docs/criteria/goodness-of-fit/<distribution>/mathematical-validation.md: проверенные формулы, источники, найденные исправления, ограничения, результаты тестов и оптимизации.
  • Обнови docstrings. Проверь выполнение примеров, полноту каталога и корректность локальных ссылок.

docs.title: 6. Итоговая проверка
docs.text:
• Запусти профильные тесты, Ruff, проверку актуальности stub и сборку документации.
  • Проверь регистрацию критериев, уникальность кодов, экспорты и совместимость pickle.
  • Сохрани посторонние изменения в рабочем дереве.
  • Если обычный запуск блокируют существующие ошибки проекта, явно укажи причину. Изолированный запуск обозначай как изолированный.
  • В результате кратко перечисли изменения, математические выводы, исправления, результаты проверок и оставшиеся ограничения.

docs.title: Frequency statistics and binning
docs.text:
For the public user guide, comparison table and method examples, see Binning for frequency goodness-of-fit tests.

Frequency kernels in continuous/frequency.py take observed and expected arrays. They do not choose bins, estimate distribution parameters, or calculate p-values. The power-divergence family underlying these kernels is described by Cressie and Read (1984). Five frequency criteria are available for uniformity:

Class Code Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic CHI2_PEARSON FreemanTukeyUniformGofStatistic FREEMAN_TUKEY ModifiedLogLikelihoodUniformGofStatistic MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD NeymanChi2UniformGofStatistic CHI2_NEYMAN CressieReadUniformGofStatistic CRESSIE_READ

The old bins and lambda_ constructor arguments have been removed. Select an algorithm by class and a grouping policy with binning:

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import (
    EqualProbabilityBins,
    SturgesCount,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    CressieReadUniformGofStatistic,
)

criterion = CressieReadUniformGofStatistic(
    Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1}),
    binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=SturgesCount(), min_expected=5),
)

Both Uniform bounds must be fixed. The criterion validates and binds the null distribution on each execution, builds a frequency table, then calls the kernel. Strategies are retained as configuration; tables are never cached across samples. This also applies to Monte Carlo calibration.

docs.title: Number of bins
docs.text:
All count rules implement resolve(sample_size):

Rule Requested count Source / status Integer or FixedCount(k) k, an integer >= 2 User-selected configuration. SturgesCount() max(2, ceil(1 + log2(n))) Sturges (1926); rounding and the minimum of two are implementation choices. SqrtCount() max(2, ceil(sqrt(n))) Convenience heuristic; no claim of an optimal GoF rule or attribution to a specific paper. PowerCount(coefficient=2, exponent=0.4) max(2, ceil(coefficient * n**exponent)) Default heuristic documented in NIST §7.2.1.1; NIST is a handbook, not a research paper.

The default is EqualProbabilityBins(PowerCount()), with max_bins=1000 and min_expected=None. PowerCount is an explicit heuristic, not a claim of optimal power or an implementation of a specific Mann–Wald formula. Counts are recomputed for each sample size. max_bins caps the requested count, including fixed counts. For the historical problem of choosing the number of chi-square classes, see Mann and Wald (1942). This reference is background, not the source of the exact default coefficient or rounding policy.

min_expected=None permits sparse tables for simulation-based calibration. A positive value, such as 5, is an explicit minimum expected count policy; it does not by itself establish the validity of a chi-square approximation. Insufficient sample sizes raise an error instead of silently reducing the table to one cell. For a discussion of expected counts and chi-square calibration, see Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora, preprint §2.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
Equal-probability and equal-width binning are discussed in Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora, preprint §5.1. Their equation (3) also gives the interpolation of the two sets of boundaries. Our tail handling, endpoint delegation and numerical CDF inversion are explicit implementation policies described below, rather than a verbatim implementation of the paper.

  • EqualProbabilityBins(count=..., min_expected=None, max_bins=1000) transforms the observations with the continuous null CDF and uses equal-width probability cells. Expected counts are n/k. With min_expected, k is capped by floor(n/min_expected) before building the table.
  • ExplicitBins(edges=(...), min_expected=None) uses full-support boundaries. Continuous cells follow NumPy's [left, right) convention, with the last right endpoint included. Bounds must include all null probability and all sample values. Use infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions.
  • EqualWidthBins(lower, upper, count=..., min_expected=None, max_bins=1000) uses fixed finite central bounds and adds separate lower/upper tail categories when they have positive null probability. Count and max_bins apply to central cells; there may be two additional tail cells. Bounds must be specified independently of the tested sample.
  • InterpolatedBins(lower, upper, count=..., kappa=0.5, ...) interpolates interior boundaries between null quantiles and equal-width boundaries, keeping full coverage. Null quantiles are obtained by numerical CDF inversion because the distribution evaluation protocol has no PPF. Failure to bracket a quantile raises a clear error. For 0 < kappa < 1, equal-probability quantiles use the total count including tails. At exactly 0 it delegates to EqualProbabilityBins; at exactly 1 it delegates to EqualWidthBins. Thus the endpoint strategies can have different cell counts when tails are present.
  • DiscreteCategoryBins(cut_points=(...), min_expected=None) uses right-closed groups (-inf, c1], (c1, c2], ..., (cm, inf). Null probabilities are actual CDF differences, not 1/k. Integer counts, real-valued atoms, and grouped discrete support all use the same convention. Uniform rejects this strategy.

For explicit, width-based and discrete strategies, min_expected merges the smallest expected cell with its right neighbor (or left neighbor at the end) until the requirement is met. Selection depends only on null expectations, not the observed discrepancies. Zero-probability cells with zero observations are removed. An observed value in a zero-probability category raises an error. The result must contain at least two categories. This particular adjacent-cell merging algorithm is a library policy; it is not attributed to the cited papers.

Interval probabilities use survival-function differences in the upper tail to avoid cancellation. FrequencyTable validates positive expectations, aligned one-dimensional arrays, finite nonnegative observations and equal totals; it owns read-only copies of both arrays.

docs.title: Selection for a specified alternative
docs.text:
AlternativeOptimizedBins.select(...) performs a reproducible Monte Carlo search across explicit candidates. Supply a bound null distribution, null and alternative samplers (n, rng) -> sample, a frequency kernel, sample size, seed, repetition count and significance level. Each candidate is scored using synthetic null critical values and its estimated rejection rate on alternative samples.

The returned strategy freezes the winning candidate and sample size. It never selects bins from the tested observations. Ties keep the first candidate. Rebuild it for another sample size, null model, or kernel; the caller must use the same model and kernel as during selection. Power scores are selection estimates, not unbiased performance estimates. Calibrate the selected test on fresh null simulations. The idea of selecting bins for a specified alternative is discussed by Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora (2021), with an open preprint, §5.3. Our Monte Carlo candidate search is not an implementation of their exact selection algorithm.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
code() identifies the algorithm, hypothesis() describes the null hypothesis, and configuration() describes computation settings. Storage keys include the canonical JSON configuration hash alongside the code hash, hypothesis parameter hash and sample size. Both limit distributions and critical values use this key. Different binning policies therefore have independent calibrations.

Create new calibration records with LimitDistributionModel.from_statistic(criterion, sample_size, values) after simulation. StorageLimitDistributionResolver constructs the matching key through DistributionKey.from_statistic. Direct model construction without a configuration denotes legacy/unspecified data, not the current defaults.

Built-in binning policies expose to_config(), including defaults and policy versions. Integer counts and FixedCount serialize identically. JSON keys are sorted, equivalent numeric values are normalized, and infinite explicit edges use "-inf" and "+inf". Update the corresponding version whenever mathematical behavior changes. Custom policies and count rules need a stable to_config() dictionary for storage; Monte Carlo alone does not require it. AlternativeOptimizedBins records its selected policy and sample size; estimated powers and search provenance do not participate in calibration identity.

Use a new database for the configuration-aware schema. AlchemyDatabase.init() rejects incompatible existing tables; it does not alter their schema or transfer old calibration records.

See the uniformity catalog for criterion descriptions, formulas, and usage examples.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Pearson, K. (1900). On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling. Philosophical Magazine, 50, 157–175. DOI. Original Pearson chi-square statistic.
  2. Cressie, N., and Read, T. R. C. (1984). Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 46(3), 440–464. DOI, publisher page. Power-divergence family used by the frequency kernels.
  3. Sturges, H. A. (1926). The Choice of a Class Interval. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 21(153), 65–66. DOI, article scan. Basis for the logarithmic count rule, not a universal GoF power guarantee.
  4. Mann, H. B., and Wald, A. (1942). On the Choice of the Number of Class Intervals in the Application of the Chi Square Test. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 13(3), 306–317. DOI. Historical reference on choosing chi-square class intervals.
  5. Rolke, W., and Gutierrez Gongora, C. (2021). A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for continuous distributions against a known alternative. Computational Statistics, 36, 1885–1900. DOI, open 2020 preprint. Binning types, interpolation and selection against a specified alternative. Section and equation links above refer to preprint version 1.

Additional practical guidance: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, §7.2.1.1, Chi-square goodness-of-fit test. This handbook supplies the 2 * n**0.4 starting heuristic used by the default count rule; it is listed separately from the research articles.

docs.title: Universal goodness-of-fit statistics
docs.text:
Universal statistics implement an algorithm once and bind it to distributions at runtime. The first built-in template is UniversalKolmogorovSmirnov. Adding a continuous distribution descriptor with a vectorized CDF makes KS available through the existing utils functions without writing a KS class.

For frequency-based statistics, see Binning: the shared counting pipeline, all available grouping methods, and calibration requirements.

docs.title: Using an automatically generated KS
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion import DistributionType
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.utils.statistic import (
    get_available_criteria,
    get_available_criteria_codes,
    get_criterion_by_code,
)

assert "KS" in get_available_criteria_codes(DistributionType.WEIBULL)
KS = get_criterion_by_code("KS_UNIVERSAL_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT")
assert KS in get_available_criteria(DistributionType.WEIBULL)
parameters = WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"shape": 2, "scale": 3})
statistic = KS(parameters)
distance = statistic.execute_statistic([0, 0.5, 1, 1, 3, 5])

The returned object is a concrete subclass of AbstractGoodnessOfFitStatistic and, when available, the distribution's abstract GoF family class. Repeated lookups return the same class. Weibull KS accepts fixed shape and scale; existing fitted Weibull criteria continue to accept unknown parameters.

docs.title: Adding a distribution
docs.text:
A descriptor remains the source of parameter metadata. It can now also expose mathematical functions as class or static methods with the signature function(x, parameters) -> array. x is a NumPy array, and parameters is an explicit ParameterValues object. A function returns one value per input and must not fill missing parameters implicitly.

Here is a complete extension for the existing RAYLEIGH enum member, which has no built-in descriptor. Importing the module containing this class is sufficient:

import numpy as np
from numpy.typing import NDArray
from scipy import stats

from pysatl_criterion import DistributionType
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import ContinuousDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.distribution.parameters import (
    ParameterizationDescriptor,
    ParameterSpec,
    ParameterValues,
)
from pysatl_criterion.distribution.validator import PositiveNumberValidator


class RayleighDistributionDescriptor(ContinuousDistributionDescriptor):
    SCALE = ParameterSpec("rayleigh.scale", "scale", "σ", validator=PositiveNumberValidator())
    DEFAULT = ParameterizationDescriptor("rayleigh.scale", DistributionType.RAYLEIGH, (SCALE,))

    @staticmethod
    def type() -> DistributionType:
        return DistributionType.RAYLEIGH

    @classmethod
    def parameters(cls) -> list[ParameterSpec]:
        return list(cls.DEFAULT.parameters)

    @classmethod
    def parameterizations(cls) -> tuple[ParameterizationDescriptor, ...]:
        return (cls.DEFAULT,)

    @classmethod
    def cdf(cls, x: NDArray[np.float64], parameters: ParameterValues) -> NDArray[np.float64]:
        return stats.rayleigh.cdf(x, scale=parameters[cls.SCALE])

from pysatl_criterion.utils.statistic import get_criterion_by_code

KS = get_criterion_by_code("KS_UNIVERSAL_RAYLEIGH_GOODNESS_OF_FIT")
parameters = RayleighDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"scale": 2})
assert KS.distribution() is RayleighDistributionDescriptor
assert 0 <= KS(parameters).execute_statistic([0, 1, 2, 4]) <= 1

An entirely new distribution identifier still requires an entry in DistributionType, as before. There must be only one concrete descriptor for an identifier. A separate family-specific abstract statistic is optional. If an extension provides one, it can explicitly bind it before the first lookup:

from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.registry import criterion_registry

# AbstractRayleighGofStatistic is an optional existing extension class.
criterion_registry.register_distribution(
    RayleighDistributionDescriptor,
    family_base=AbstractRayleighGofStatistic,
)

Direct abstract GoF family subclasses from the existing library are discovered automatically. Parameter validation belongs to the descriptor's parameter schema and mathematical functions. Generated algorithms initialize the shared ParameterValues contract; they do not run arbitrary family-specific constructors.

docs.title: Mathematical capabilities
docs.text:
DistributionDescriptor.mathematical_functions() discovers callable cdf, pdf, ppf, sf, logcdf, and logsf methods. Abstract or missing methods are not capabilities. Override this mapping to expose additional named functions. All entries use the same (x, parameters) contract. Function names alone do not supply numerical implementations.

A universal algorithm declares its requirements:

required_capabilities = frozenset({"cdf"})

Compatibility also requires a concrete continuous descriptor with a declared default parameterization. The initial generic hypothesis contract fixes every parameter in the calculation parameterization. A discrete CDF is deliberately insufficient for this continuous-KS implementation.

CDF methods were added to Normal, Beta, Uniform, LogNormal, Weibull and Exponentiated Weibull descriptors, using existing core functions or SciPy. Other existing KS classes retain family-specific CDF hooks, including stable transformations and numerical checks. Additional descriptors can opt in by implementing the same CDF contract; no registry table of distribution names needs to be edited.

docs.title: Registering another universal algorithm
docs.text:
The base UniversalGoodnessOfFitStatistic supplies the fixed-parameter hypothesis contract. For example, the following Cramér–von Mises template reuses the existing numerical kernel. It is an extension example, not a second algorithm registered by the library by default.

from abc import ABC

import numpy as np

from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.edf import AbstractCrammerVonMisesStatistic
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.registry import criterion_registry
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.universal import (
    UniversalGoodnessOfFitStatistic,
)


class UniversalCramerVonMises(
    UniversalGoodnessOfFitStatistic, AbstractCrammerVonMisesStatistic, ABC
):
    required_capabilities = frozenset({"cdf"})

    @staticmethod
    def short_code() -> str:
        return "CVM"

    def execute_statistic(self, rvs, **kwargs) -> float:
        raw = np.asarray(rvs)
        if raw.ndim != 1 or raw.size == 0 or raw.dtype.kind not in "iuf":
            raise ValueError("Expected a nonempty one-dimensional real sample")
        if np.ma.isMaskedArray(rvs) and np.any(np.ma.getmaskarray(rvs)):
            raise ValueError("Masked observations are not supported")
        x = np.sort(np.asarray(raw, dtype=float))
        if not np.all(np.isfinite(x)):
            raise ValueError("Observations must be finite")
        cdf = self.distribution().mathematical_functions()["cdf"]
        u = np.asarray(cdf(x, self._parameters), dtype=float)
        if (
            u.shape != x.shape
            or not np.all(np.isfinite(u))
            or np.any((u < 0) | (u > 1))
            or np.any(np.diff(u) < 0)
        ):
            raise FloatingPointError("Invalid CDF values")
        return float(self.do_execute_statistic(x, u))


criterion_registry.register_algorithm(UniversalCramerVonMises)

The template must leave distribution() abstract. Registering the same template again is harmless; registering a different template with the same short code raises an error. Special-purpose algorithms may override is_compatible() and supported_hypotheses() to impose narrower requirements.

docs.title: Initialization, factory and discovery
docs.text:
All three utility functions use the same registry. At lookup time it:

  1. Imports the built-in GoF modules.
  2. Recursively discovers concrete distribution descriptors and statistic classes.
  3. Finds specialized implementations for each universal algorithm.
  4. Generates missing compatible classes using type(), with the universal template before the optional family base in the MRO.
  5. Walks the statistic inheritance tree and returns the selected concrete classes.

The registry owns strong references, serializes initialization with a reentrant lock, and caches classes by (distribution_type, algorithm.short_code()). Generated class names combine the template name without Universal, the descriptor name without DistributionDescriptor, and GofStatistic. Generated codes insert UNIVERSAL before the existing family prefix, or before the uppercase distribution value when there is no family base. For example: KS_UNIVERSAL_RAYLEIGH_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. This prevents reusing retired identifiers and their calibrations: KS_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT remains unavailable, while the new fixed-parameter Weibull KS is KS_UNIVERSAL_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. All existing public class names and full codes are retained.

Results are sorted by full code, module and qualified name. Built-in import order and whether code lookup or family lookup happens first do not change discovery. External modules must first be imported or registered; the registry does not search the filesystem for unloaded extensions. Fetch generated classes through utils, rather than assuming a new symbol is exported from a family module.

docs.title: Specialized implementations and migration
docs.text:
A specialized class has priority over an automatically generated class with the same distribution and universal algorithm short code. A specialization imported after generation takes priority on the next lookup as well. Existing instances of the generated class remain valid; its presence in __subclasses__() cannot be removed, so the public catalogue filters it out. Two competing specializations raise a clear error instead of choosing whichever was imported first. Unrelated legacy algorithms retain their existing discovery behavior.

All 13 existing public KS classes inherit the shared execute_statistic(). Their constructors, hypotheses, full codes and public imports are retained. Family-specific sample validation, stable CDF evaluation, supported execution settings and calibration checks remain in place. Beta and Hyperbolic retain their accelerated numerical kernels. Other classes use AbstractKSStatistic's existing kernel. The universal execution method checks CDF shape, finite probabilities, range and monotonicity before evaluating the statistic.

docs.title: Calibration limitations
docs.text:
KS generation supplies a statistic only. It does not automatically provide a sampler, a p-value, stored calibration, or critical values for a new distribution. Existing resolvers remain responsible for those operations. For example, the existing Weibull generator can calibrate a generated fixed-parameter Weibull KS, whereas a new Rayleigh descriptor also needs a compatible sampling/calibration integration before Monte Carlo hypothesis testing is available.

Unknown parameters are rejected by generated KS rather than fitted implicitly. A fitted null requires an explicit estimator and suitable calibration. Do not reuse fixed-null critical values for such a procedure.

alternative_type selects D+, D-, or max(D+, D-); every variant rejects for large distances. Generated KS rejects one-sided storage lookup because the current storage key does not encode this setting. The legacy mode option is retained but does not calculate a p-value or change the statistic.

docs.title: Beta goodness-of-fit criteria
docs.text: The package pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta exports 23 concrete criteria: 13 EDF, 5 frequency, Neyman smooth and 4 fitted-Beta tests. Every criterion has a page below. See the mathematical verification report for formula checks, numerical regressions and the limits of the scientific attribution.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text:
The layout follows continuous/uniform:

continuous/beta/
├── __init__.py          # public exports and stable class module paths
├── __init__.pyi         # generated public type declarations
└── beta_statistics.py  # implementations and dynamic EDF/frequency catalogs

Existing imports from continuous.beta remain valid. The public module paths are preserved for discovery and previously serialized class references. Regenerate the stub with python scripts/generate_beta_stub.py; use --check to detect drift. The generator reads the implementation without importing the package and uses the project's Ruff formatter.

docs.title: Hypotheses and calibration
docs.text:
The support is fixed at \([0,1]\), with positive finite shapes \(a,b\). For the 19 specified-null criteria use Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}). Both shapes must be chosen independently of the tested sample; there are no default shape values. For Ebner–Liebenberg, Raschke, Riad–Abd El Mabood and Kullback–Leibler use Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}); both shapes are estimated by maximum likelihood for every sample. Partially specified shapes are not supported by these 23 classes.

All criteria return scalar statistics and reject large values. Executing a statistic does not compute a p-value. Fixed-null EDF and smooth statistics use the probability integral transform; fitted-Beta tests require a parametric bootstrap with refitting.

docs.title: Complete catalog
docs.text:
Full identifiers append _BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT to the short codes below. CrammerVonMisesBetaGofStatistic is the exported spelling; no alternative alias is supplied. KS D+ and D− are separate classes. Frequency settings use binning, not lambda_; Watson's short code is WATSON.

docs.title: Anderson–Darling for a specified Beta distribution
docs.text:
All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

Class: AndersonDarlingBetaGofStatistic. Code: AD_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Both shape parameters a > 0 and b > 0 are finite and fixed independently of the sample. Pass Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}); omitted shapes are unknown and are rejected by this class. The support is fixed at \([0,1]\).

For sorted observations, let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\) and \(W^2=1/(12n)+\sum_i(u_i-(i-1/2)/n)^2\).

\[ A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})] \]

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample in \([0,1]\). Ties and constants are allowed; masked observations and complex values are rejected. It returns a scalar and leaves the sample unchanged. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

For a continuous fully specified null, the probability integral transform makes this EDF statistic's null law independent of both shapes. Calibrate at the same sample size. No parameter is fitted, and no p-value is returned. AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang use separate log-CDF and log-survival probabilities; the other kernels use the CDF. Underflowed interior tails have a hypergeometric logarithmic fallback; unrepresentable tail evaluation raises ValueError. True endpoints give infinity for AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang. Other EDF statistics remain finite. The data are never clipped.

docs.title: Pearson chi-squared for a specified Beta distribution
docs.text:
All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

Class: Chi2PearsonBetaGofStatistic. Code: CHI2_PEARSON_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Both shape parameters a > 0 and b > 0 are finite and fixed independently of the sample. Pass Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}); omitted shapes are unknown and are rejected by this class. The support is fixed at \([0,1]\).

For bins \(j=1,\ldots,J\), write \(O_j\) for the observed count and \(E_j=np_j>0\) for the expected count under the specified Beta law.

\[ X^2=\sum_j\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{E_j} \]

With an empty observed cell and positive expected count, Pearson contributes \(E_j\), Freeman–Tukey \(4E_j\), modified log-likelihood and Neyman infinity, and Cressie–Read zero.

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample in \([0,1]\). Ties and constants are allowed; masked observations and complex values are rejected. It returns a scalar and leaves the sample unchanged. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

The constructor accepts binning: BinningStrategy; the default is EqualProbabilityBins() with PowerCount(coefficient=2, exponent=0.4), a maximum of 1000 bins and no minimum expected-count pooling. CDF-space boundaries belong to the cell on their right; 1 belongs to the last cell. See binning strategies. Each of the five divergences has its own class; lambda_ is not a supported constructor argument.

For fixed deterministic bins with positive probabilities the usual asymptotic null is chi-square with \(J-1\) degrees of freedom, with no fitted-shape deduction. That statement does not justify a fixed-degree limit for a growing number of bins or data-dependent boundaries. Calibrate using the same binning rule and sample size. Storage identity includes the serialized binning configuration.

docs.title: Ebner–Liebenberg test for the Beta distribution
docs.text: All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The criterion tests the composite null hypothesis

\[ H_0: X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \operatorname{Beta}(a,b), \qquad a,b>0, \]

against general alternatives on the fixed support \([0,1]\). Both shape parameters are unknown and fitted by maximum likelihood on each sample; location and scale remain fixed at 0 and 1.

The test is based on the conditional-moment characterization of the Beta family in Ebner and Liebenberg. Large values of the statistic provide evidence against the null hypothesis. This is the new statistic proposed in the paper, not the fitted Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic used there as a competitor.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import EbnerLiebenbergBetaGofStatistic

statistic = EbnerLiebenbergBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}))
sample = [0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57]
value = statistic.execute_statistic(sample)
print(value)

docs.title: Arguments and return value
docs.text:
Argument Meaning parameters Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}): neither shape is fixed. Supplying either shape is unsupported. rvs One-dimensional sample of at least two finite real observations strictly inside (0, 1). The sample must be nonconstant. **kwargs Reserved for interface compatibility; ignored.

execute_statistic returns a nonnegative Python float. The class computes only the statistic, without a p-value or a hypothesis decision. Fitted shapes are local to each call and do not change hypothesis().parameters(), which remains {}. The input sample is not modified.

Invalid samples, including endpoints, masked observations and constant samples, raise ValueError. Failures of the maximum-likelihood solver propagate to the caller. Nonfinite numerical results or materially negative residuals also raise ValueError; negative residuals within the implementation's roundoff tolerance are set to zero.

The short identifier is EL. alternative() returns RightAlternative.

docs.title: Test statistic
docs.text:
Let \(\hat a,\hat b\) be the maximum-likelihood estimates and define \(c_j=(\hat a+\hat b)x_j-\hat a\). The integral definition is

\[ T_n=n\int_0^1\left[ \frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\mathbf1\{x_j\ge t\} -\frac{t^{\hat a}(1-t)^{\hat b}}{B(\hat a,\hat b)} \right]^2dt. \]

Here \(B\) is the beta function. Equation (3) of the source gives

\[ \begin{aligned} T_n={}&\frac1n\sum_{j,k=1}^n c_jc_k\min(x_j,x_k)\\ &-2\frac{B(\hat a+1,\hat b+1)}{B(\hat a,\hat b)} \sum_{j=1}^n c_j F_{\hat a+1,\hat b+1}(x_j)\\ &+n\frac{B(2\hat a+1,2\hat b+1)}{B(\hat a,\hat b)^2}, \end{aligned} \]

where \(F_{a,b}\) is the Beta CDF.

For sorted observations, set \(x_{(0)}=0\) and \(S_i=\sum_{j=i}^n c_{(j)}\). The implementation evaluates the first term as

\[ \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{(i)}-x_{(i-1)})S_i^2. \]

This avoids an \(n\times n\) matrix. After parameter fitting, evaluating the statistic requires \(O(n\log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory. The last beta-function ratio uses logarithms, and the cross-term ratio uses the identity \(B(a+1,b+1)/B(a,b)=ab/[(a+b)(a+b+1)]\).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The null distribution depends on the unknown shapes. Section 2 of the paper uses a parametric bootstrap:

  1. Fit both shapes to the observed sample and calculate its statistic.
  2. Generate bootstrap samples of the same size from the fitted Beta law.
  3. Calculate the statistic on every bootstrap sample, refitting both shapes each time.
  4. Reject when the observed statistic exceeds the empirical upper critical quantile at the chosen significance level.

The hypothesis-testing layer implements this procedure with reproducible RNG:

from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.beta_bootstrap import parametric_bootstrap_beta
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta import (
    EbnerLiebenbergBetaGofStatistic,
)

statistic = EbnerLiebenbergBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}))
sample = [0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57]
result = parametric_bootstrap_beta(
    statistic, sample, significance_level=0.05, n_resamples=1999, random_state=2026
)
print(result.statistic, result.critical_value, result.p_value, result.rejected)

The function uses the inverse empirical CDF for the upper critical quantile. rejected means strictly greater than that quantile, following the paper. The reported p-value is \((1+\#\{T_b^*\ge T_n\})/(B+1)\), where \(B\) is n_resamples; its decision can differ from the critical-value decision at finite \(B\). Every replicate is refitted. Fit failures propagate; simulated endpoints caused by floating-point rounding are neither clipped nor dropped.

The p-value is a bootstrap approximation; the correction does not make a composite-null bootstrap exact in finite samples. More replicates reduce simulation error. Universal critical values or arbitrary Beta(1, 1) calibration are inappropriate. An empty composite hypothesis alone does not specify the generating shapes; calibration needs the observed sample.

docs.title: Null limit, consistency and implementation
docs.text:
The null limit is \(\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j(a,b)Z_j^2\), with independent standard normal \(Z_j\) and eigenvalues of the fitted-process covariance operator (Corollary 2.2). The weights depend on both shapes. Section 3 proves consistency against alternatives for which the shape estimators converge to finite positive limits, as assumed in equation (6). This is an omnibus characterization under those conditions, not an unconditional assertion for all possible samples or endpoint-contaminated distributions.

Statistic implementation and bootstrap implementation. The full identifier is EL_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
B. Ebner and S. C. Liebenberg, On a new test of fit to the beta distribution (2020 preprint), Corollary 1.2, equation (3), and Section 2.

Ebner, B., Liebenberg, S. C. (2021). On a new test of fit to the beta distribution. Stat, 10, e341. DOI: 10.1002/sta4.341.

docs.text: StorageLimitDistributionResolver rejects this composite hypothesis because the storage key lacks fitted shapes. Use parametric_bootstrap_beta with the observed sample; a stored law indexed only by code and sample size is invalid.

docs.title: Vasicek–Kullback–Leibler Beta criterion
docs.text: KullbackLeiblerBetaGofStatistic, code KL_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT, estimates KL divergence from a Beta density with both shapes fitted by maximum likelihood. The support is fixed at \([0,1]\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the ordered sample \(X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(n)}\), use repeated endpoints: \(X_{(j)}=X_{(1)}\) for \(j<1\) and \(X_{(j)}=X_{(n)}\) for \(j>n\). For an integer window \(1\le m<n/2\), the Vasicek entropy estimate is

\[H_{m,n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left[ \frac{n}{2m}(X_{(i+m)}-X_{(i-m)})\right].\]

For the maximum-likelihood estimates \(\hat a,\hat b\) the returned statistic is

\[I_{m,n}=-H_{m,n}+\log B(\hat a,\hat b) -(\hat a-1)\frac1n\sum_i\log X_i -(\hat b-1)\frac1n\sum_i\log(1-X_i).\]

This estimates \(D(f\Vert f_{a,b})=-H(f)-E_f\log f_{a,b}(X)\). There is no factor \(n\) or exponentiation. Finite-sample estimates can be negative and are not clipped. Log spacings are evaluated before adding the logarithm of the scale factor, avoiding avoidable underflow. Sorting takes \(O(n\log n)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory, in addition to fitting.

docs.title: Parameters and calibration
docs.text:
Use Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}). Set the entropy window in the constructor with window=.... With window=None, the local default is \(\min(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor,\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor)\); this is an explicit implementation choice, not a claimed optimal rule from the article. Booleans and noninteger windows are rejected. The bound \(2m<n\) is checked for each sample.

Require at least three finite, real observations strictly inside \((0,1)\) in a nonconstant one-dimensional sample. Masked observations are rejected. Ties with positive window gaps are accepted; zero gaps raise ValueError. Input arrays are unchanged and fitted shapes are not retained.

Large values reject. Use parametric_bootstrap_beta to simulate the fitted Beta and refit both shapes for each replicate while preserving the entropy-window setting. Zero gaps are rejected before bootstrap calibration. It gives approximate calibration, not exact finite-sample size. Do not reuse fixed-shape tables or silently optimize the window over the data. Generic stored calibration is disabled for fitted Beta tests.

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta import (
    KullbackLeiblerBetaGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.beta_bootstrap import parametric_bootstrap_beta

sample = [0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57]
test = KullbackLeiblerBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}), window=2)
print(test.execute_statistic(sample))
# Small resample count for illustration; use more for actual inference.
result = parametric_bootstrap_beta(test, sample, n_resamples=99, random_state=42)
print(result.p_value)

  • O. Vasicek (1976), A test for normality based on sample entropy, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 38(1), 54–59. Entropy estimator.

The 2013 article describes the general Vasicek/KL method and its Beta application. Its full text was unavailable during implementation. Exact agreement with its Beta normalization, window selection and numerical tables is not verified. The explicit raw-KL formula above follows directly from the Beta log density. Tests compare it with SciPy's independent Vasicek estimator and an explicit log-likelihood reference. See the mathematical verification report.

docs.title: Mathematical verification of Beta statistics
docs.text: Audit date: 2026-10-14. Scope: all 23 concrete classes exported by continuous/beta/beta_statistics.py, including their shared EDF/frequency kernels and hypothesis_testing/beta_bootstrap.py. See the complete catalog for every class, short code and individual page.

docs.title: Conclusion and scope of the claims
docs.text:
The implemented definitions were checked algebraically and against independent numerical references. The current catalog contains 18 generated criteria, Neyman smooth and four fitted-Beta procedures: Ebner–Liebenberg, Raschke, Riad–Abd El Mabood and Vasicek–Kullback–Leibler. References identify published functionals or Beta-specific procedures; their critical values cannot automatically be reused after fitting parameters.

Passing formula checks does not establish exact finite-sample significance, uniform power, or numerical accuracy for every representable positive shape.

docs.title: Null hypotheses and estimation
docs.text:
\[ f_{a,b}(x)=\frac{x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)},\qquad 0<x<1,\quad a,b>0. \] Criteria Hypothesis Estimation 13 EDF, 5 frequency, Neyman smooth Both shapes fixed independently of the sample None Ebner–Liebenberg Both shapes unknown; support fixed Beta MLE on each call Raschke Both shapes unknown; support fixed Beta MLE, normal quantile transform, normal location/scale MLE on each call Riad–Abd El Mabood; Vasicek–KL Both shapes unknown; support fixed Beta MLE; same weight/window in each bootstrap replicate

Specified criteria use Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}); fitted criteria use Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}). No default or partially fixed shapes are accepted. All critical regions are right-tailed. Samples must be finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected rather than dropped.

The Beta EDF regression integrates the Beta density to obtain CDF values, then checks all thirteen statistics at five shape pairs. KS additionally uses SciPy's one-sided and two-sided tests; CvM, Watson and AD use piecewise numerical EDF integrals. Zhang and Liao–Shimokawa use explicit rank formulas, independently of production kernels. The shared-kernel suite adds high-precision Zhang references and true endpoint limits. The five frequency implementations are checked against SciPy power divergences with independently constructed bins.

With fixed shapes the continuous probability integral transform makes EDF null laws shape-free. Ties can be evaluated, but rounding or discrete observations change the continuous-null calibration. For fixed deterministic bins and positive probabilities the usual frequency limit is \(\chi^2_{J-1}\). The default EqualProbabilityBins() uses a sample-size-dependent count; a fixed-degree chi-square claim is not made for that rule. Empty observed cells give infinity for modified log-likelihood and Neyman, which is mathematically intentional. Calibration must preserve binning settings; storage keys serialize them.

docs.title: Neyman smooth
docs.text:
For fixed positive integer \(k\) and \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_i)\),

\[T_k=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^k\left(\sum_i\sqrt{2j+1}P_j(2u_i-1)\right)^2.\]

Shifted normalized Legendre polynomials have zero means and identity covariance under a uniform null, yielding a \(\chi^2_k\) limit for fixed \(k\). The recurrence is checked against explicit polynomials of orders 1–4 and endpoint identities at higher order. The result is shape-free under a fully specified Beta null, but fixed \(k\) does not give omnibus consistency. This applies Neyman (1937) through the PIT. k != 4 is rejected by the storage-calibration guard; use matching Monte Carlo simulation. The class does not fit unknown shapes.

docs.title: Ebner–Liebenberg
docs.text: With both shapes estimated by MLE and \(c_j=(\hat a+\hat b)X_j-\hat a\), the statistic is \(n\int_0^1[n^{-1}\sum_j c_j1\{X_j\ge t\} -t^{\hat a}(1-t)^{\hat b}/B(\hat a,\hat b)]^2dt\). The sorted cumulative implementation matches equation (3) of the full preprint, independently checked by quadrature and a quadratic pairwise sum. Beta-function ratios preserve the cross and constant terms. Require at least two distinct observations strictly inside the support. Refitting occurs on each bootstrap replicate; no fitted state is retained. The paper's bootstrap and consistency statements have regularity conditions, not an exact finite-sample distribution-free law.

docs.title: Raschke
docs.text: The author manuscript's sections 4–5 prescribe Beta MLE, normal quantile transformation, normal MLE and corrected AD. The implementation uses normal variance divisor \(n\) and correction \(1+0.75/n+2.25/n^2\). A separate weighted EDF integral checks the resulting value. At least three nonconstant interior observations are required; with two, normal standardization makes the scores \((-1,1)\) and the statistic constant. Separate Beta tails avoid 1-CDF cancellation; unrepresentable normal transforms raise an error. The paper's normal critical values are approximate. The supplied Beta bootstrap repeats both fits and is a different calibration; its validity is not implied by the Ebner–Liebenberg theorem. See Raschke's page and author manuscript.

docs.title: Numerical boundaries
docs.text: EDF underflow is handled with the DLMF 8.17.8 identity; a failed hypergeometric evaluation raises an error. True endpoints can legitimately yield infinity. The fitted criteria require interior, nonconstant samples and propagate fitting failures. Calibration must preserve the hypothesis and any binning/order settings.

docs.title: Package layout and import compatibility
docs.text: Beta follows the uniform package layout: beta/beta_statistics.py contains implementations, beta/__init__.py explicitly re-exports the public classes, and beta/__init__.pyi declares their types. The former beta.py and beta.pyi are replaced by these package files. All 25 public classes (23 concrete and two abstract) retain the module path pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta. Regression checks cover identity between the package and implementation, old pickle references, round trips and unique criterion discovery. Private catalogs live in the implementation module and are not re-exported from the package.

docs.title: Type declarations
docs.text: src/pysatl_criterion/statistics/goodness_of_fit/continuous/beta/__init__.pyi declares all 23 concrete criteria and both abstract bases, including generated EDF and frequency classes. Constructor options weight, window, k and binning, scalar results, NumPy array arguments and class-level numerical helpers are typed. tests/distributions/test_beta_stub.py checks exports, inheritance, method parameter names and keyword-only defaults against runtime definitions. The generated stub is maintained with python scripts/generate_beta_stub.py; python scripts/generate_beta_stub.py --check verifies that it is current without importing the package. Generation helpers are methods of BetaStubGenerator, and type annotations are preserved through formatting. A focused mypy check of the stub and usage examples passed with --follow-imports=skip to isolate unrelated package typing issues.

docs.title: Numba execution and optimization
docs.text:
All 23 criteria execute numerical reductions through class methods decorated with @jit(nopython=True, cache=True), without fastmath. This does not mean that SciPy distribution transforms or maximum-likelihood fitting are JIT compiled.

Criteria Compiled computation Work retained in Python/SciPy 13 EDF Shared EDF and log-tail reduction kernels Validation, sorting and Beta log tails 5 frequency Shared frequency divergence kernels Binning and expected probabilities Ebner–Liebenberg Tail sums and statistic reduction MLE, sorting and incomplete Beta functions Neyman smooth Legendre recurrence and squared-component sums Validation and Beta CDF Riad–Abd El Mabood Residual coefficients, compensated pair sum and fallback integrand MLE and adaptive quadrature controller Vasicek–KL Fused entropy/log-density reduction MLE, sorting and scalar betaln Raschke Two-pass normal standardization and AD reduction Beta MLE and Beta/normal distribution functions

KL now computes window gaps, log spacings and log densities in a single loop, without materializing those arrays. The Laplace fallback computes the minimum and shifted sample once, and calls a compiled integrand through quad(args=...). Raschke standardizes in a compiled two-pass calculation using the MLE variance with denominator n. All new helpers are class methods; the EDF log-probability callback was also moved into AbstractSpecifiedBetaGofStatistic.

tests/distributions/test_beta_numba.py checks that every concrete criterion executes a nopython kernel, compares the new reductions with independent SciPy references, and covers degenerate transformations and input preservation. The existing integral, tail-underflow, negative-KL and quadrature-fallback regressions remain in the complete run below.

Local timing on 2026-10-14: median of seven batches of ten complete execute_statistic calls, after JIT warm-up, on Beta(2,5) samples generated with np.random.default_rng(234) separately for each n. Times include fitting.

Criterion n Before, microseconds After, microseconds Vasicek–KL 100 137.2 58.4 Vasicek–KL 1000 214.3 94.0 Raschke 100 288.1 264.1 Raschke 1000 913.7 832.3 Riad–Abd El Mabood 100 71.3 68.1 Riad–Abd El Mabood 1000 2013.8 1933.6

These are local measurements, not portable performance guarantees. Small Laplace differences may reflect timing variability; its dominant pairwise kernel was already compiled. First-call compilation cost is excluded. Observed KL differences were below 6e-15; the other recorded values agreed at float64 precision for these benchmark samples.

docs.title: Riad–Abd El Mabood (2018)
docs.text:
See the Laplace criterion for the complete formula and original DOI. The implementation uses MLE shapes in the Kummer residual with weight \(e^{-\rho t}\). Integrating each pair uses \(\int_0^\infty t^k e^{-st}dt=k!/s^{k+1}\). Tests compare the resulting sum with independent numerical integration of \(L_n,L_n',L_n''\), for multiple weights, shapes and sample sizes.

Source discrepancy: the expanded RF expression in Section 4 of Ebner–Liebenberg (published text) prints \(\hat\alpha^2\) in the cross-term denominator. From \(A_i=x_i(x_i-1)/\hat\alpha\) and \(B_i=1-x_i/\hat\mu\), the cross term \(A_iB_j+A_jB_i\) contains one factor \(1/\hat\alpha\), not two. We implement the squared differential-equation residual, independently verified by quadrature; the printed expansion is not used verbatim. Here \(\hat\mu=\hat\alpha/(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta)\), as defined in that published comparison. It is generally different from the sample mean. The original 2018 full text was unavailable; exact replication of its tables is not claimed. Default weight 2 is documented and included in configuration.

docs.title: Alizadeh Noughabi–Arghami (2013)
docs.text:
See the KL criterion and original DOI. The original full text was unavailable. The general Vasicek/MLE formula was verified in Section 2 of the same author's later paper. Substituting the Beta log density yields the documented statistic. This is not the previously removed difference between theoretical and sample entropy. Tests use SciPy's explicit Vasicek estimator and independent Beta log-density calculation, including boundary window indices, reflection and negative values. The library window default is explicit and is not attributed to the 2013 paper. Zero window spacings raise an error; finite negative estimates remain unchanged. Bootstrap preserves settings and refits both shapes in every draw.

Both new criteria reject large values. Their tests cover configuration, invalid settings/samples, no input mutation, permutation invariance and reproduction of bootstrap p-values. This validates definitions and computation, not published power tables or exact finite-sample significance.

docs.title: Verification and reproducibility
docs.text:
The audit runs all Beta suites plus the shared EDF/frequency suites: tests/distributions/test_beta*.py, tests/statistics/test_beta_dynamic.py, test_beta_mathematical_validation.py, test_beta_published.py, test_edf.py, and test_frequency.py. These cover formula references, sample constraints, hypotheses, endpoints, small and large shapes, unchanged inputs, fitting and bootstrap reproduction.

The documentation audit compares runtime concrete classes with all 23 pages, checks scientific URLs, Python examples, overview/navigation coverage and local links, then executes every page example. MkDocs checks HTML generation and math markup; it does not prove browser-side MathJax rendering.

Historical source access is not uniform: the Ebner–Liebenberg full preprint and Raschke author manuscript were accessible. DOI access to Zhang, Liao–Shimokawa, Cressie–Read, Lemeshko and Neyman failed through the web tool. Their links and shared definitions are documented, but this report does not claim fresh full-text verification of those articles.

Normal package initialization currently fails on stale imports of AbstractChi2Statistic and AbstractCrammerVonMisesStatistic from edf.py in the common initializer and unrelated distribution modules. The tests and examples therefore use an isolated continuous namespace, without introducing compatibility aliases into production. This limitation applies to the public import path and is not concealed by the numerical results.

Reproduce the isolated test run from the repository root:

.venv/bin/python - <<'PYCODE'
import sys
import types
from pathlib import Path
import pytest
name = "pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous"
package = types.ModuleType(name)
package.__path__ = [str(Path("src/pysatl_criterion/statistics/goodness_of_fit/continuous").resolve())]
sys.modules[name] = package
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import beta
for export in beta.__all__:
    setattr(package, export, getattr(beta, export))
raise SystemExit(pytest.main([
    *map(str, sorted(Path("tests/distributions").glob("test_beta*.py"))),
    "tests/statistics/test_beta_dynamic.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_beta_mathematical_validation.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_beta_documentation.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_beta_published.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_edf.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_frequency.py", "-q", "--tb=short",
]))
PYCODE

Measured results for the extended catalog:

  • 680 tests passed in the isolated run described above, including the independent formula suites and the Numba execution regressions.
  • 23/23 criteria have a dedicated page, scientific reference, Python example, overview entry and navigation entry.
  • 25 Python example blocks executed successfully, each in a fresh namespace.
  • All Beta Markdown local links resolve.
  • MkDocs built successfully. Existing warnings concern other documentation sections.
  • Ruff passed for the implementation and both new numerical test suites.

Ordinary package imports remain blocked by the unrelated obsolete imports listed above. No compatibility aliases were added.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood for a specified Beta distribution
docs.text:
All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

Class: ModifiedLogLikelihoodBetaGofStatistic. Code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Both shape parameters a > 0 and b > 0 are finite and fixed independently of the sample. Pass Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}); omitted shapes are unknown and are rejected by this class. The support is fixed at \([0,1]\).

For bins \(j=1,\ldots,J\), write \(O_j\) for the observed count and \(E_j=np_j>0\) for the expected count under the specified Beta law.

\[ MLL=2\sum_j E_j\log(E_j/O_j) \]

With an empty observed cell and positive expected count, Pearson contributes \(E_j\), Freeman–Tukey \(4E_j\), modified log-likelihood and Neyman infinity, and Cressie–Read zero.

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample in \([0,1]\). Ties and constants are allowed; masked observations and complex values are rejected. It returns a scalar and leaves the sample unchanged. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

The constructor accepts binning: BinningStrategy; the default is EqualProbabilityBins() with PowerCount(coefficient=2, exponent=0.4), a maximum of 1000 bins and no minimum expected-count pooling. CDF-space boundaries belong to the cell on their right; 1 belongs to the last cell. See binning strategies. Each of the five divergences has its own class; lambda_ is not a supported constructor argument.

For fixed deterministic bins with positive probabilities the usual asymptotic null is chi-square with \(J-1\) degrees of freedom, with no fitted-shape deduction. That statement does not justify a fixed-degree limit for a growing number of bins or data-dependent boundaries. Calibrate using the same binning rule and sample size. Storage identity includes the serialized binning configuration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodBetaGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins, FixedCount

statistic = ModifiedLogLikelihoodBetaGofStatistic(
    Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}), binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=FixedCount(3))
)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57])
print(value)

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, \(\lambda=-1\).

The source identifies the shared statistical functional; applying it through the specified Beta distribution does not constitute a new Beta-specific test.

docs.title: Neyman smooth test for the Beta distribution
docs.text: All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tests the simple hypothesis of iid observations from \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) on \([0,1]\), with specified \(a,b>0\). Both shapes must be fixed independently of the observations. This is Neyman's uniform smooth test after the probability integral transform, not a new Beta-specific polynomial construction.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import NeymanSmoothBetaGofStatistic

statistic = NeymanSmoothBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}), k=4)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57])

docs.title: Arguments and statistic
docs.text:
parameters specifies both positive finite shapes; partial hypotheses are rejected. k is a positive integer (default 4), chosen before examining the sample. rvs is a nonempty one-dimensional finite real sample in \([0,1]\); masked observations are rejected. A single observation and endpoints are valid. Invalid inputs raise ValueError (invalid parameter types may raise TypeError). The result is a scalar; larger values are significant. Identifiers are NEYMAN and NEYMAN_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

Let \(n\) be sample size, \(u_i=F_{a,b}(x_i)\), and \(P_j\) the degree-\(j\) Legendre polynomial, normalized by \(P_j(1)=1\). Then

\[ N_k=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left[\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sqrt{2j+1}\,P_j(2u_i-1)\right]^2. \]

docs.title: Calibration and limitations
docs.text:
For fixed \(k\), the null limit is \(\chi^2_k\). The finite-sample distribution depends on \(n,k\) but not on \(a,b\), because the \(u_i\) are iid uniform under the simple null. Monte Carlo from independent uniforms gives finite-sample critical values; the chi-square limit can be inaccurate for small \(n\). For fixed \(k\) the test is consistent against alternatives with a nonzero selected component, but not omnibus: other distributions can match all \(k\) component means. No adaptive order selection is implemented.

Plugging sample estimates into this class does not produce a calibrated composite test. Such a procedure requires refitting in every bootstrap sample and must not use the stated simple-null chi-square or uniform calibration.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: NeymanSmoothBetaGofStatistic uses NeymanSmoothTestUniformGofStatistic to validate the order and evaluates the shifted Legendre recurrence in its own cached Numba kernel. Unit references integrate the Beta density and use explicit polynomials independently of the implementation.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Neyman, J. (1937). Smooth test for goodness of fit. Skandinavisk Aktuarietidskrift, 20, 149–199. DOI: 10.1080/03461238.1937.10404821.

docs.title: Stored calibration
docs.text: The Beta storage guard currently permits only the default order. Stored calibration is allowed only for k=4. Other settings raise ValueError before storage lookup; use MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver instead. Existing stored results generated with other options under the same key must be regenerated.

docs.title: Raschke biased-transformation test for Beta
docs.text: All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Tests the composite hypothesis of iid \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) observations, \(a,b>0\), on fixed support \([0,1]\). Both shapes are unknown. Sections 4–5 of Raschke (2009) prescribe Beta maximum likelihood, transformation to normal quantiles, normal maximum likelihood and corrected Anderson–Darling.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import RaschkeBetaGofStatistic
from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.beta_bootstrap import parametric_bootstrap_beta

statistic = RaschkeBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}))
sample = [0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57]
value = statistic.execute_statistic(sample)
result = parametric_bootstrap_beta(statistic, sample, n_resamples=1999, random_state=2026)

docs.title: Arguments and statistic
docs.text:
parameters must leave both shapes unknown. rvs must contain at least three finite real observations strictly in \((0,1)\) and be nonconstant. Endpoints, masked data, and out-of-support observations raise ValueError. MLE failures propagate. Shapes are fitted with fixed location 0 and scale 1 on every call. The two-observation case is excluded because standardizing two distinct normal scores always produces \((-1,1)\) and hence a constant statistic.

Let \(F_{a,b}\) be the Beta CDF, \(\Phi\) the standard normal CDF, and \((\hat a,\hat b)\) the Beta MLE. Set

\[ y_i=\Phi^{-1}(F_{\hat a,\hat b}(x_i)),\quad \hat\mu=\frac1n\sum_i y_i,\quad \hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu)^2,\quad z_i=(y_i-\hat\mu)/\hat\sigma. \]

The normal scale uses the MLE divisor \(n\). For ordered \(z_{(i)}\), compute

\[ A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1) \{\log\Phi(z_{(i)})+\log[1-\Phi(z_{(n+1-i)})]\}, \qquad A^{*2}=A^2(1+0.75/n+2.25/n^2). \]

The result is \(A^{*2}\), a scalar with right critical region. Identifiers are RASCHKE and RASCHKE_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Calibration and limitations
docs.text:
The original paper transfers fitted-normal critical values approximately, with simulation evidence for selected shapes and sample sizes. This does not establish a parameter-free Beta null law or universal omnibus consistency. The transformed observations share estimated parameters and are not an iid normal sample. Finite-sample calibration must account for the Beta shapes; no universal limiting law is used here.

The supplied bootstrap is an explicitly different calibration from the paper's normal tables: simulate from the observed Beta MLE, then repeat both fits, the transformation, and the AD correction for every replicate. It returns an approximate p-value \((1+\#\{T_b^*\ge T\})/(B+1)\) and empirical upper critical quantile (inverted_cdf). rejected follows the strict critical-value comparison; the corrected p-value decision can differ for finite \(B\). significance_level is in \((0,1)\), n_resamples=B is a positive integer, and an integer random_state ensures reproducibility. Bootstrap validity for this transformed test is not established by the Ebner–Liebenberg theorem; no exact finite-sample level or blanket consistency claim is made.

Both Beta tails are evaluated to avoid subtracting a CDF rounded to 1. Normal log-CDF/log-SF keep the AD sum stable. Unrepresentable transforms or failed fits raise errors, including in bootstrap; no clipping or selective removal of failed replicates occurs. Very small shape parameters can yield machine-rounded endpoints in simulated samples.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: RaschkeBetaGofStatistic reuses the shared AbstractAndersonDarlingStatistic kernel. Bootstrap calibration lives in the hypothesis-testing layer and requires the observed sample.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Raschke, M. (2009). The Biased Transformation and Its Application in Goodness-of-Fit Tests for the Beta and Gamma Distribution. Communications in Statistics – Simulation and Computation, 38, 1870–1890. DOI: 10.1080/03610910903152631. Author manuscript, Sections 4–5.

docs.title: Stored calibration
docs.text: StorageLimitDistributionResolver rejects this composite hypothesis because the storage key lacks fitted shapes. Use parametric_bootstrap_beta with the observed sample; a stored law indexed only by code and sample size is invalid.

docs.title: Riad–Abd El Mabood Beta criterion
docs.text: RiadAbdElMaboodBetaGofStatistic (RF_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT) tests the Beta family on the fixed support \([0,1]\). Both shapes are unknown and fitted by maximum likelihood. Reject large statistic values. See the catalog and verification report.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For fitted shapes \(\hat\alpha,\hat\beta\), define

\[ L_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_i e^{-tx_i},\qquad D_n(t)=\frac{t}{\hat\alpha}L_n''(t) +\left(1+\frac{\hat\beta}{\hat\alpha}+\frac{t}{\hat\alpha}\right)L_n'(t)+L_n(t). \]

The statistic, with weight \(\rho>0\), is

\[ T_{n,\rho}=n\int_0^\infty D_n(t)^2e^{-\rho t}\,dt. \]

Put \(A_i=x_i(x_i-1)/\hat\alpha\), \(B_i=1-(1+\hat\beta/\hat\alpha)x_i\) and \(s_{ij}=x_i+x_j+\rho\). Exact integration gives

\[ T_{n,\rho}=\frac1n\sum_{i,j}\left[ \frac{2A_iA_j}{s_{ij}^3}+\frac{A_iB_j+A_jB_i}{s_{ij}^2} +\frac{B_iB_j}{s_{ij}}\right]. \]

weight=2.0 is the library default, one of the values studied by Ebner and Liebenberg. Fix it before examining the sample. The fitted mean is \(\hat\alpha/(\hat\alpha+\hat\beta)\), not the arithmetic sample mean. The printed expanded RF formula in their Section 4 has an apparent extra factor \(\hat\alpha\) in the cross-term denominator. This implementation follows the defining differential equation above; it does not reproduce that factor.

Samples require at least two distinct finite observations strictly inside \((0,1)\). Invalid weights and samples raise ValueError. Analytic evaluation uses compensated summation in \(O(n^2)\) time and \(O(n)\) memory; severe cancellation triggers scaled quadrature of the nonnegative integrand. Numerical failures raise errors rather than yielding a negative squared norm.

docs.title: Scientific sources
docs.text:
• Riad, M.; Abd El Mabood, O. F. (2018). A new goodness of fit test for the beta distribution based on the empirical Laplace transform. Advances and Applications in Statistics 53(2), 165–177. DOI.
  • Ebner, B.; Liebenberg, S. C. (2021). On a new test of fit to the beta distribution, Section 4. DOI, open published text.

The original 2018 full text was not accessible during this audit. The characterization and MLE convention were checked against the published 2021 comparison; the integral was expanded independently.

docs.title: Example and calibration
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta import (
    RiadAbdElMaboodBetaGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.beta_bootstrap import parametric_bootstrap_beta

sample = [0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57]
criterion = RiadAbdElMaboodBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({}), weight=2.0)
value = criterion.execute_statistic(sample)
result = parametric_bootstrap_beta(
    criterion,
    sample,
    n_resamples=99,
    random_state=42,
)
print(value, result.p_value)

The small bootstrap count keeps this example fast. Use more replicates for inference. Calibration is approximate and shape-dependent: every replicate refits both shapes and retains the same settings. execute_statistic returns only the statistic; stored universal critical values are unsupported.

docs.title: Watson for a specified Beta distribution
docs.text:
All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

Class: WatsonBetaGofStatistic. Code: WATSON_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Both shape parameters a > 0 and b > 0 are finite and fixed independently of the sample. Pass Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}); omitted shapes are unknown and are rejected by this class. The support is fixed at \([0,1]\).

For sorted observations, let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\) and \(W^2=1/(12n)+\sum_i(u_i-(i-1/2)/n)^2\).

\[ U^2=W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2,\quad W^2=\frac1{12n}+\sum_i[u_i-(i-1/2)/n]^2 \]

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample in \([0,1]\). Ties and constants are allowed; masked observations and complex values are rejected. It returns a scalar and leaves the sample unchanged. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

For a continuous fully specified null, the probability integral transform makes this EDF statistic's null law independent of both shapes. Calibrate at the same sample size. No parameter is fitted, and no p-value is returned. AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang use separate log-CDF and log-survival probabilities; the other kernels use the CDF. Underflowed interior tails have a hypergeometric logarithmic fallback; unrepresentable tail evaluation raises ValueError. True endpoints give infinity for AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang. Other EDF statistics remain finite. The data are never clipped.

value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57])
print(value)

The source identifies the shared statistical functional; applying it through the specified Beta distribution does not constitute a new Beta-specific test.

docs.title: Zhang Z_C for a specified Beta distribution
docs.text:
All Beta criteria · Mathematical verification

Class: ZhangCBetaGofStatistic. Code: ZHANG_ZC_BETA_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Both shape parameters a > 0 and b > 0 are finite and fixed independently of the sample. Pass Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}); omitted shapes are unknown and are rejected by this class. The support is fixed at \([0,1]\).

For sorted observations, let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\) and \(W^2=1/(12n)+\sum_i(u_i-(i-1/2)/n)^2\).

\[ Z_C=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\log\frac{1-u_i}{u_i}-\log\frac{n-i+1/4}{i-3/4}\right]^2 \]

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample in \([0,1]\). Ties and constants are allowed; masked observations and complex values are rejected. It returns a scalar and leaves the sample unchanged. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

For a continuous fully specified null, the probability integral transform makes this EDF statistic's null law independent of both shapes. Calibrate at the same sample size. No parameter is fitted, and no p-value is returned. AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang use separate log-CDF and log-survival probabilities; the other kernels use the CDF. Underflowed interior tails have a hypergeometric logarithmic fallback; unrepresentable tail evaluation raises ValueError. True endpoints give infinity for AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang. Other EDF statistics remain finite. The data are never clipped.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import BetaDistributionDescriptor as Beta
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.beta import ZhangCBetaGofStatistic

statistic = ZhangCBetaGofStatistic(Beta.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 2, "b": 5}))
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.08, 0.14, 0.22, 0.31, 0.38, 0.46, 0.57])
print(value)
