docs.title: Binning for frequency goodness-of-fit tests
docs.text: Binning converts a sample and a fully specified null distribution into observed and expected category counts. A frequency statistic then measures the discrepancy between those counts. Changing bins changes the test, even when its statistic formula stays the same.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
sample + fixed null parameters
              |
              v
count rule -> binning strategy -> observed / expected -> frequency statistic

For categories \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) and a sample of size \(n\):

\[ O_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{x_j\in C_i\},\qquad E_i = n\,P_{H_0}(X\in C_i). \]

A strategy's build(sample, distribution) returns a FrequencyTable with observed and expected arrays. The arrays are read-only, have at least two entries, and have matching totals. Observations must be a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample. Expected counts must be strictly positive.

The criterion validates its family-specific sample support, binds the null parameters, builds a fresh table, and calls the frequency kernel. Binning does not fit missing parameters or calculate p-values.

docs.title: All available methods
docs.text:
Choose one count rule and one compatible binning strategy. Explicit and discrete strategies take boundaries directly and do not need a count rule.

Method Role Rule or mechanism Applicable input FixedCount Count A specified integer \(k\ge2\) Strategies accepting a count SturgesCount Count \(\max(2,\lceil1+\log_2 n\rceil)\) Strategies accepting a count SqrtCount Count \(\max(2,\lceil\sqrt n\rceil)\) Strategies accepting a count PowerCount Count \(\max(2,\lceil c n^p\rceil)\); default \(c=2\), \(p=0.4\) Strategies accepting a count EqualProbabilityBins Strategy Equal null probability; \(E_i=n/k\) Continuous null ExplicitBins Strategy User-specified full-support edges Continuous null EqualWidthBins Strategy Equal central widths plus nonempty null tails Continuous null InterpolatedBins Strategy Interpolation of null-quantile and equal-width boundaries Continuous null DiscreteCategoryBins Strategy Right-closed categories with actual null masses Discrete null AlternativeOptimizedBins Selection Monte Carlo search over candidate strategies before testing Compatible candidates and a specified alternative

FixedCount and SqrtCount are configuration/heuristic choices, not claims of optimal GoF power. Statistical sources and differences from published methods are given on the individual pages.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import (
    EqualProbabilityBins,
    SturgesCount,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
criterion = Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic(
    parameters,
    binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=SturgesCount()),
)
value = criterion.execute_statistic([0.1, 0.15, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9])
assert value >= 0

The same binning argument is available on FreemanTukeyUniformGofStatistic, ModifiedLogLikelihoodUniformGofStatistic, NeymanChi2UniformGofStatistic, and CressieReadUniformGofStatistic. Choose the class for the desired formula; the former bins and lambda_ constructor arguments have been removed.

All strategies and count rules are imported from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning. Standalone examples on method pages use SciPy frozen distributions, which provide the required CDF/SF methods; a descriptor's bind(parameters) result can be used as well.

docs.title: Defaults and small expected counts
docs.text:
The default is EqualProbabilityBins(count=PowerCount(), max_bins=1000, min_expected=None). It permits sparse tables for simulation-based calibration. Counts are resolved again for every sample size. max_bins caps even an explicit fixed count; width-based methods can add up to two extra tail categories.

Set min_expected=5, for example, to request a minimum expected-count policy. For equal-probability bins, the count is capped by \(\lfloor n/5\rfloor\). Other strategies repeatedly merge the smallest expected category with its right neighbor, or its left neighbor when last. Merging uses null expectations only. If fewer than two valid categories remain, an error is raised.

A zero-probability category with no observations is removed. Observations in a zero-probability category raise an error. No sample observations or tail mass may be silently dropped. Minimum expected counts do not by themselves guarantee an accurate asymptotic calibration.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The Uniform criteria support fully fixed bounds. Parameters are never estimated implicitly. Continuous equal-probability binning must not be applied to a discrete CDF; use discrete category probabilities instead.

Use MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver to calibrate the configured criterion. Every simulation rebuilds its bins. StorageLimitDistributionResolver retrieves only an exact configuration match, including binning parameters. Legacy records with unknown configuration do not match implicitly. See saving and retrieving calibrations for examples and schema requirements. A statistic value alone is not a p-value.

Selection for a specified alternative uses synthetic data before observing the tested sample. Calibrate the selected strategy using fresh null simulations; its reported selection power is not an unbiased performance estimate.

docs.title: Sources and related documentation
docs.text:
The frequency-kernel family is described in Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests. Binning choices and alternative-specific selection are discussed in Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora (2021), A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for continuous distributions against a known alternative (open preprint, §5.1). These sources motivate the methods; count caps, tail policies, merging rules and the Monte Carlo candidate search are library choices.

See frequency binning guide and universal goodness-of-fit statistics.

docs.title: Binning selected for a specified alternative
docs.text: AlternativeOptimizedBins.select(...) chooses from an explicit list of candidate strategies using synthetic null and alternative samples. Selection happens before the tested observations are processed.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Supply a bound null distribution, a matching null sampler, an alternative sampler, the frequency kernel, sample size and candidate strategies.
  2. Generate repetitions null and alternative samples with a seeded NumPy RNG. Each sampler receives (sample_size, rng). Candidates share these samples.
  3. Evaluate every candidate/kernel combination on the generated samples.
  4. For each candidate, sort its null values and select zero-based rank ceil((1-alpha) * (repetitions-1)) as a simulated critical value.
  5. Score the candidate by the fraction of alternative values strictly above its critical value. Choose the largest score; ties retain the first candidate.
  6. Freeze the winning strategy, sample size and all estimated_powers.

Defaults are repetitions=1000, alpha=0.05, and seed=0; at least 20 repetitions and 0 < alpha < 1 are required. Candidate errors are propagated. NaN statistics are rejected; infinite statistics can occur for some kernels.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import (
    AlternativeOptimizedBins,
    EqualProbabilityBins,
)


def pearson(observed, expected):
    return float(np.sum((observed - expected) ** 2 / expected))


selected = AlternativeOptimizedBins.select(
    [EqualProbabilityBins(2), EqualProbabilityBins(4)],
    distribution=stats.uniform(),
    null_sampler=lambda n, rng: rng.uniform(size=n),
    alternative_sampler=lambda n, rng: rng.beta(1, 4, size=n),
    kernel=pearson,
    sample_size=40,
    repetitions=100,  # Small demonstration budget, not a precision recommendation.
    seed=19,
)

# New observations, not the synthetic selection samples.
sample = np.random.default_rng(100).uniform(size=40)
table = selected.build(sample, stats.uniform())
assert table.observed.sum() == 40
assert len(selected.estimated_powers) == 2

Pass the resulting strategy as binning=selected to the criterion using that same kernel and null model. A different sample size is rejected. The caller must also repeat selection when changing the null model or kernel; only sample size is checked automatically.

The returned power scores are selection estimates, not unbiased performance estimates. Calibrate the selected test on fresh null simulations. Do not choose candidates by maximizing the statistic on the actual tested observations.

docs.title: Scientific context and differences
docs.text:
Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora (2021), A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for continuous distributions against a known alternative studies selection against a known alternative; see the open preprint, §5.3. Our implementation is a Monte Carlo candidate search, not a reproduction of their exact selection algorithm, and it provides no universal optimality claim.

All binning methods

docs.title: Saving and retrieving calibrations
docs.text: Binning affects the null distribution. A calibration for four bins cannot be reused for eight bins. Storage identity now includes the criterion code, null-hypothesis parameters, criterion configuration, and sample size. Simulation count still determines which calibration is newer for that identity. The critical-value cache uses the same configuration and checks the source's simulation count, significance level and alternative.

docs.title: Save and retrieve
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.limit_distribution.base import (
    MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver,
    StorageLimitDistributionResolver,
)
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.models.distribution_key import DistributionKey
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.models.limit_distribution import LimitDistributionModel
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.database import AlchemyDatabase
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.stores.limit_distribution import (
    AlchemyLimitDistributionStorage,
)

criterion = Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic(
    Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1}),
    binning=EqualProbabilityBins(8, min_expected=5),
)
values = MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver(1000).resolve(criterion, 100)
record = LimitDistributionModel.from_statistic(criterion, 100, values)

database = AlchemyDatabase("sqlite:///:memory:")
database.init()
with database.session_factory.begin() as session:
    store = AlchemyLimitDistributionStorage(session)
    store.insert(record)
    saved = store.get(DistributionKey.from_statistic(criterion, 100))
    assert saved is not None
    resolved = StorageLimitDistributionResolver(store).resolve(criterion, 100)
    assert resolved is not None
database.dispose()

StorageLimitDistributionResolver returns None if that configuration is absent. Place it before MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver in a CompositeLimitDistributionResolver to simulate on a miss. The composite does not automatically save simulations; use from_statistic to persist them.

docs.title: Configuration and filters
docs.text:
criterion.code() remains unchanged. criterion.configuration() includes schema_version, statistic_version and binning. Built-in policies expose to_config() with a stable type name, version and explicit defaults: count rule, merging threshold, maximum bins and other policy parameters. An optimized policy records the selected strategy and sample size; selection scores are excluded.

Both tables store canonical JSON in criterion_configuration and SHA-256 in criterion_configuration_hash. The hash participates in primary keys and the critical-value foreign key. Callers do not calculate hashes themselves. Dictionary order does not affect identity; equivalent numbers such as 4 and 4.0 match. Infinite explicit edges use "-inf" and "+inf"; other non-finite numbers are rejected.

Custom policies and count rules must implement a stable to_config() dictionary for storage. Monte Carlo does not require this method. Include every option that affects computation, and increment the policy or statistic version when its meaning changes.

from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.limit_distribution import (
    CriterionFilter,
    LimitDistributionFilter,
)

all_variants = LimitDistributionFilter(
    criteria=[CriterionFilter(criterion.code())],
)
exact_variant = LimitDistributionFilter(
    criteria=[
        CriterionFilter(
            criterion.code(),
            criterion.hypothesis().parameters(),
            criterion.configuration(),
        )
    ],
)
legacy_only = LimitDistributionFilter(
    criteria=[CriterionFilter(criterion.code(), legacy_only=True)],
)
# Within a session:
# rows = store.get_batch(exact_variant, batch_size=100)
# next_rows = store.get_batch(exact_variant, batch_size=100, after=rows[-1].key)

Configuration None in a filter means all variants. Configuration None in a DistributionKey means unknown legacy settings. {} is an explicit empty configuration and is distinct from None.

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text:
database.init() rejects incompatible existing tables: create_all cannot change their primary and foreign keys. Use a new database for configuration-aware calibrations and recalibrate to populate it. No schema migration or transfer of old records is provided.

Unknown settings are represented by JSON null and never match a newly configured criterion, including defaults. Do not infer missing settings from current defaults.

docs.title: Discrete category bins
docs.text: DiscreteCategoryBins(cut_points, min_expected=None) groups a discrete null using ordered cut points. It uses actual category masses, not equal probabilities.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
For finite increasing cuts \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\), form

\[ (-\infty,c_1],\ (c_1,c_2],\ \ldots,\ (c_m,\infty). \]
  1. Assign each observation to its right-closed category. An atom exactly at a cut belongs to the category on its left.
  2. Calculate null masses using CDF differences, with stable SF differences in the upper tail; multiply by \(n\) for expected counts.
  3. Remove zero-probability empty categories and optionally merge adjacent small expected categories using the shared policy.

Cuts need not be integers. The distribution defines the masses; the caller is responsible for valid sample support when using this strategy directly. At least two positive-probability categories must remain. This strategy declares compatibility with discrete distributions and is rejected by Uniform criteria.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import DiscreteCategoryBins

# Geometric here counts trials including the first success: 1, 2, ...
table = DiscreteCategoryBins((1, 3)).build([1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], stats.geom(0.5))
np.testing.assert_array_equal(table.observed, [2, 2, 2])
np.testing.assert_allclose(table.expected, 6 * np.array([0.5, 0.375, 0.125]))

docs.title: Scientific context
docs.text:
Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, section 1, treats exhaustive categories through multinomial probabilities. Right-closed cut points and this library's deterministic merging policy are implementation choices rather than an algorithm claimed from the paper.

All binning methods

docs.title: Equal-probability bins
docs.text: EqualProbabilityBins(count=PowerCount(), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000) constructs cells with equal probability under a continuous null distribution.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Resolve \(k\) from the sample size and cap it by max_bins.
  2. If min_expected=m is supplied, also cap it by \(\lfloor n/m\rfloor\). Reject the request if fewer than two bins remain.
  3. Transform each observation to \(u_j=F_0(x_j)\).
  4. Count these values in \(k\) equal intervals over \([0,1]\).
  5. Set every expected count to \(n/k\).

This avoids evaluating an inverse CDF. The probability-space bins use NumPy's left-closed convention; the final bin includes 1. The CDF must return finite values in \([0,1]\) aligned with the sample.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins

null = stats.norm(loc=2, scale=3)
sample = null.ppf([0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9])
table = EqualProbabilityBins(count=4).build(sample, null)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(table.observed, [2, 1, 1, 2])
np.testing.assert_allclose(table.expected, [1.5] * 4)

A descriptor-bound distribution can replace the SciPy frozen distribution. The null parameters must already be specified; they are not fitted here. Uniform criteria additionally reject observations outside their fixed support.

Do not apply this strategy to a discrete CDF: jumps prevent the equal-probability assumption. Use DiscreteCategoryBins instead.

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora (2021), A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for continuous distributions against a known alternative, open preprint, §5.1, discusses equal-probability grouping. Our count resolution, probability-space boundary convention and limits are implementation policies.

All binning methods

docs.title: Equal-width bins with tails
docs.text: EqualWidthBins(lower, upper, count=PowerCount(), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000) creates equal-width central intervals and preserves nonempty null tails.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Require fixed finite bounds lower < upper with finite width.
  2. Resolve and cap the number \(k\) of central bins.
  3. Place \(k+1\) equally spaced edges between the bounds.
  4. Add -inf if the null assigns probability below lower; add inf if it assigns probability above upper.
  5. Build an explicit frequency table, including optional merging.

The final count can be \(k\), \(k+1\), or \(k+2\) before merging. Expected counts are computed from the null CDF and generally differ across bins. max_bins limits central bins, not the additional tails.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualWidthBins

null = stats.norm()
table = EqualWidthBins(-1, 1, count=2).build([-3, -0.5, 0.5, 3], null)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(table.observed, [1, 1, 1, 1])
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    table.expected,
    4 * np.diff(null.cdf([-np.inf, -1, 0, 1, np.inf])),
)

Set central bounds before testing. Selecting them from sample extrema introduces another data-dependent step which this class does not implement.

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora (2021), A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for continuous distributions against a known alternative, open preprint, §5.1, discusses equal-width grouping. The separate tail categories and finite central-bound API are our implementation policies, not a claim to reproduce every boundary convention in the paper.

All binning methods

docs.title: Explicit bin edges
docs.text: ExplicitBins(edges, min_expected=None) uses supplied continuous bin boundaries. They must cover the full null probability and all observations.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Require at least three strictly increasing edges, without NaNs.
  2. Verify that the null probability below the first edge and above the last is zero.
  3. Count observations using [left, right) cells; include the final right endpoint.
  4. Calculate \(E_i=n(F_0(b_{i+1})-F_0(b_i))\).
  5. Remove empty zero-probability categories and apply optional expected-count merging.

Upper-tail probabilities use survival-function differences to avoid subtracting CDF values near one. A positive observation count in a zero-probability category is an error. At least two categories must remain.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import ExplicitBins

strategy = ExplicitBins((-np.inf, 0, np.inf))
table = strategy.build([-2, -0.5, 0.5, 2], stats.norm())
np.testing.assert_array_equal(table.observed, [2, 2])
np.testing.assert_allclose(table.expected, [2, 2])

Choose boundaries independently of the tested observations, or calibrate any additional boundary-selection procedure explicitly. Finite edges are appropriate when they cover a bounded null support.

docs.title: Scientific context
docs.text:
Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, section 1, supplies the multinomial-category framework. The explicit boundary API and the adjacent-cell merging algorithm are library policies, not a bin-selection algorithm attributed to this paper.

All binning methods

docs.title: Fixed number of bins
docs.text: FixedCount(count) returns a user-selected integer independently of sample size. It is a count rule, not a partition of the sample.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Require an integer count >= 2; booleans are rejected.
  2. Require a positive integer sample size.
  3. Return the configured count.

A consuming strategy can reduce it because of max_bins or min_expected. Passing an integer to a strategy is shorthand for FixedCount.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import FixedCount, EqualProbabilityBins

rule = FixedCount(4)
assert rule.resolve(100) == 4
strategy = EqualProbabilityBins(count=rule)
table = strategy.build([0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9], stats.uniform())
assert len(table.expected) == 4

Choose this when a study specifies the grouping in advance. Increasing the sample size does not increase the number of bins automatically.

docs.title: Scientific context
docs.text:
Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests treats observations as counts in specified categories. This provides the multinomial context, not a formula for choosing this class's count. The fixed-count setting is a user decision and is not attributed to an optimal selection algorithm in that paper.

All binning methods

docs.title: Interpolated bins
docs.text: InterpolatedBins(lower, upper, count=PowerCount(), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000, kappa=0.5) blends equal-probability and equal-width boundaries.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
For 0 < kappa < 1:

  1. Construct equal-width central edges and any required tail cells.
  2. Let \(K\) be the total number of cells, including tails.
  3. Find the null quantiles \(q_i=F_0^{-1}(i/K)\) for interior indices.
  4. Replace each interior equal-width edge \(w_i\) by \(b_i=(1-\kappa)q_i+\kappa w_i\); keep the outer coverage edges.
  5. Count observations and compute actual expected probabilities, then apply optional merging.

Null quantiles are found by numerical CDF inversion. The supplied finite bounds seed a bracket that is expanded if needed. Failure to bracket a finite quantile or obtain valid ordered edges raises an error.

At kappa=0 the implementation delegates to EqualProbabilityBins; at kappa=1 it delegates to EqualWidthBins. The number of cells can therefore change at the zero endpoint when width-based grouping has extra tails. This is a library policy, not a continuous fixed-cell-count interpolation across that endpoint.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import InterpolatedBins

strategy = InterpolatedBins(0, 4, count=2, kappa=0.5)
table = strategy.build([0.1, 0.5, 1.5, 3, 10], stats.expon())
assert len(table.expected) == 3  # Two central bins and an upper tail.
assert table.observed.sum() == 5
np.testing.assert_allclose(table.expected.sum(), 5)

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
Rolke and Gutierrez Gongora (2021), A chi-square goodness-of-fit test for continuous distributions against a known alternative, open preprint, §5.1, equation (3), gives the boundary interpolation formula. Numerical inversion, tail handling and endpoint delegation described above are specific to this implementation.

All binning methods

docs.title: Power count rule
docs.text: PowerCount(coefficient=2.0, exponent=0.4) provides an explicit sample-size heuristic whose parameters can be changed.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
Require positive finite \(c\) and \(p\) and a positive integer sample size \(n\):

\[ k=\max(2,\lceil c n^p\rceil). \]

The default is \(\lceil2n^{2/5}\rceil\) with a minimum of two. The consuming strategy applies its caps. For example, min_expected=5 in equal-probability binning restricts \(k\le\lfloor n/5\rfloor\).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import PowerCount, EqualProbabilityBins

rule = PowerCount()
assert rule.resolve(100) == 13
table = EqualProbabilityBins(count=rule, min_expected=5).build(

)

docs.title: Sources and scope
docs.text:
NIST/SEMATECH handbook, §7.2.1.1 gives \(2n^{2/5}\) as a practical starting heuristic. It is a handbook, not a research paper. Rounding and caps are implementation choices.

Mann and Wald (1942), On the Choice of the Number of Class Intervals in the Application of the Chi Square Test is historical scientific background on choosing class intervals. This class does not implement a particular Mann–Wald optimality formula. Its general coefficient/exponent API does not establish optimality for arbitrary settings.

All binning methods

docs.title: Square-root count rule
docs.text: SqrtCount() is a convenience heuristic based only on sample size.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
For a positive integer \(n\), return

\[ k=\max(2,\lceil\sqrt n\rceil). \]

The strategy then applies max_bins and, where applicable, min_expected. The rule neither inspects the sample's dispersion nor constructs boundaries.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import SqrtCount, EqualProbabilityBins

rule = SqrtCount()
assert rule.resolve(100) == 10
table = EqualProbabilityBins(count=rule).build([0.2, 0.8] * 50, stats.uniform())
assert len(table.expected) == 10

docs.title: Scientific context
docs.text:
This heuristic is not attributed to a specific research article and does not carry a GoF optimality claim. For research on the separate problem of choosing chi-square class intervals, see Mann and Wald (1942), On the Choice of the Number of Class Intervals in the Application of the Chi Square Test. That reference is background, not the source of the square-root formula.

docs.title: Sturges count rule
docs.text: SturgesCount() chooses a logarithmically growing number of bins.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
For a positive integer sample size \(n\), return

\[ k=\max(2,\lceil1+\log_2 n\rceil). \]

Ceiling and the minimum of two are library policies. A binning strategy applies its own count cap and expected-count policy afterward. No sample values enter the formula.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from scipy import stats
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import SturgesCount, EqualProbabilityBins

rule = SturgesCount()
assert rule.resolve(100) == 8
strategy = EqualProbabilityBins(count=rule, min_expected=5)
table = strategy.build([0.25, 0.75] * 50, stats.uniform())
assert len(table.expected) == 8

The rule offers a simple grouping convention; it does not guarantee maximum power against a particular alternative.

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
Sturges (1926), The Choice of a Class Interval. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 21(153), 65–66. Open article scan. The original work motivates the logarithmic class-count relationship.

docs.title: Exponential goodness-of-fit criteria
docs.text: continuous/exponent exports 50 concrete criteria: 14 generated EDF classes (including fitted-rate Lilliefors), 5 generated frequency classes and 31 specialized classes. Every criterion is linked below with its class name, short code, hypothesis and example. See mathematical verification for formulas, evidence and explicit provenance limitations, including the scientific bibliography with article links.

docs.title: Model and use
docs.text:
The origin is zero; lam is the positive rate, not the scale. The mean is 1/lam. Pass ExponentialDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({'lam': 2}) for a specified rate or parse({}) for an unknown rate where supported. The latter is fitted within each generated criterion call. KS D+/D−/D accept only a fixed rate; Lilliefors accepts only an unknown rate. Other generated criteria accept both. Specialized criteria accept the unknown-rate model.

Full codes append _EXPONENTIALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT to the short code. Class prefixes in the tables append ExponentialityGofStatistic. fixed means a specified rate, unknown means a composite hypothesis. Right-tail discrepancies reject large values; both-tail rules use both extremes. Not all named legacy classes are established omnibus tests: Six graph criteria are local constructions. WE uses the published normalization \(G-1/n\), where \(G\) is Greenwood. Several historical conventions remain qualified in the report. Hollander–Proschan uses the left tail against NBU alternatives.

docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import ExponentialDistributionDescriptor as E
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.exponent import (
    AndersonDarlingExponentialityGofStatistic,
)

result = monte_carlo_exponential(
    criterion,
    [0.12, 0.30, 0.55, 0.90, 1.40, 2.10, 3.20, 4.80],
    n_resamples=199,
    random_state=20261015,
)

Every replicate repeats fitting and preserves settings. Rank p-values retain infinite boundary penalties and include ties. binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=5) reproduces the old Pearson bin count; its current code is CHI2_PEARSON. Use the separate D+ and D− classes in place of alternative_type on KS.

docs.title: Ahsanullah exponentiality criterion
docs.text:
AhsanullahExponentialityGofStatistic — short code AHS; right tail.

All exponential criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
The model is \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\) for \(x\ge0\), with known origin zero and \(\lambda>0\). Unknown rate only: pass E.DEFAULT.parse({}). Omitted parameters remain unknown. Where fitting is needed, \(\widehat\lambda=1/\bar x\) is recomputed for each sample; no fitted state is retained.

Write \(y_i=x_i/\bar x\), \(u_i=1-\exp(-\lambda x_{(i)})\) with the specified or fitted rate, \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\). For spacing statistics, \(d_i=(n-i+1)(x_{(i)}-x_{(i-1)})\) and \(x_{(0)}=0\). For frequency statistics, \(O_j\) and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are aligned counts.

\[ n^{-3}\sum_{i,j,k}\left[\mathbf1\{|x_i-x_j|<x_k\}-\mathbf1\{2\min(x_i,x_j)<x_k\}\right] \]

Repeated indices are included (V-statistic convention), with strict inequalities. Right-tail directional test. The characterization requires distributional regularity; it does not prove omnibus consistency of this signed integral. Exact finite-sample agreement with published tables was not established.

docs.title: Input and calibration
docs.text:
Observations must be finite, real, nonnegative and one-dimensional. Masked observations are rejected. Fixed-rate generated criteria accept \(n\ge1\); unknown-rate EDF/frequency criteria require \(n\ge2\) and positive total. Specialized criteria may require more observations, distinct spacings or a nonconstant sample, as stated above and in the class contract. Ties are not silently jittered. Infinite mathematical boundary penalties are retained.

execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. Use monte_carlo_exponential with the same sample size and constructor settings. It refits each simulated sample for a composite hypothesis. Rescaling to Exp(1) is justified only for a scale-invariant statistic. A continuous-null calibration does not model rounding, censoring or dependence.

    AhsanullahExponentialityGofStatistic,
)

criterion = AhsanullahExponentialityGofStatistic(E.DEFAULT.parse({}))
value = criterion.execute_statistic(sample)
print(value)

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula

docs.text:
GreenwoodExponentialityGofStatistic — short code GREENWOOD; both tails.

All exponential criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
The model is \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\) for \(x\ge0\), with known origin zero and \(\lambda>0\). Unknown rate only: pass E.DEFAULT.parse({}). Omitted parameters remain unknown. Where fitting is needed, \(\widehat\lambda=1/\bar x\) is recomputed for each sample; no fitted state is retained.

HarrisExponentialityGofStatistic — short code HM; both tails.

All exponential criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
The model is \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\) for \(x\ge0\), with known origin zero and \(\lambda>0\). Unknown rate only: pass E.DEFAULT.parse({}). Omitted parameters remain unknown. Where fitting is needed, \(\widehat\lambda=1/\bar x\) is recomputed for each sample; no fitted state is retained.

\[ \frac{(2r)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}d_i+\sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}d_i\right)}{(n-2r)^{-1}\sum_{i=r+1}^{n-r}d_i} \]

Rescaling to Exp(1) is justified only for a scale-invariant statistic. A continuous-null calibration does not model rounding, censoring or dependence.

docs.title: Lorenz ordinate exponentiality criterion
docs.text:
LorenzExponentialityGofStatistic — short code LZ; right tail.

All exponential criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
The model is \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\) for \(x\ge0\), with known origin zero and \(\lambda>0\). Unknown rate only: pass E.DEFAULT.parse({}). Omitted parameters remain unknown. Where fitting is needed, \(\widehat\lambda=1/\bar x\) is recomputed for each sample; no fitted state is retained.

Write \(y_i=x_i/\bar x\), \(u_i=1-\exp(-\lambda x_{(i)})\) with the specified or fitted rate, \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\). For spacing statistics, \(d_i=(n-i+1)(x_{(i)}-x_{(i-1)})\) and \(x_{(0)}=0\). For frequency statistics, \(O_j\) and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are aligned counts.

\[ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor np\rfloor}x_{(i)}}{\sum_i x_i} \]

Constructor 0<p<1, default 0.5; floor(np) must be at least one. Uses a step ordinate, without fractional interpolation. The API uses only the upper tail; population null center p+(1-p)log(1-p).

docs.title: Input and calibration
docs.text:
Observations must be finite, real, nonnegative and one-dimensional. Masked observations are rejected. Fixed-rate generated criteria accept \(n\ge1\); unknown-rate EDF/frequency criteria require \(n\ge2\) and positive total. Specialized criteria may require more observations, distinct spacings or a nonconstant sample, as stated above and in the class contract. Ties are not silently jittered. Infinite mathematical boundary penalties are retained.

docs.title: Hypotheses, fitting and invariance
docs.text:
The null family is \(F_\lambda(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\ge0\), \(\lambda>0\), with known origin zero. lam is a rate, with scale \(1/\lambda\). For unknown rate, \(\widehat\lambda=1/\bar x\) and \(y_i=x_i/\bar x\).

Classes Accepted parameters Fitting/calibration KS D+, D− and D Fixed lam No fit; continuous fixed-null probability transform Lilliefors Empty schema Fit rate on every sample, including every replicate Other 10 generated EDF classes Fixed lam or empty schema Fixed CDF or per-sample MLE Five frequency classes Fixed lam or empty schema Bind specified/fitted distribution; preserve binning 31 specialized classes Empty schema Scale-invariant definition; no fitted parameters stored

Every concrete class declares its supported hypotheses. Omitted parameters are not filled with defaults. The family base supplies no support declaration. For fitted criteria, Exp(1) simulation is justified by positive-scale invariance, not by treating the fitted sample as independent uniform observations.

EqualProbabilityBins() uses a sample-size-dependent count. Explicit counts, count rules and binning strategies belong to the criterion configuration. Fitted-rate frequency calibration with an arbitrary fixed set of raw-unit edges is not scale invariant; the built-in helper rejects it. A known-rate criterion may use those edges because simulation uses that specified rate.

docs.title: EDF and frequency definitions
docs.text:
KS and its one-sided variants were checked against SciPy's continuous fixed-CDF test; Lilliefors was checked against KS evaluated at the fitted exponential CDF. Cramér–von Mises was compared with SciPy and with integration of the squared step-CDF discrepancy. Anderson–Darling and Watson were independently integrated on each probability interval, including both support tails. Kuiper and its two multipliers were compared with independently computed one-sided deviations.

The shared Zhang definitions match equations (3.1)–(3.3) of Zhang (2002); independent high-precision fixtures and direct scalar logarithms check rank offsets and normalization. Exponential log-survival is \(-\lambda x\), avoiding loss of the upper tail when the CDF rounds to one. Liao–Shimokawa's functional is checked by direct summation, but its original estimated-Weibull critical values do not apply to fitted exponential observations. Finite-sample Kuiper multipliers do not constitute an exact fitted-null p-value.

For frequencies, the five kernels agree with the power-divergence family at parameters \(1,-1/2,-1,-2,2/3\), independently evaluated by SciPy from histogram counts. Empty-cell contributions are, respectively, \(E_j\), \(4E_j\), \(+\infty\), \(+\infty\), and zero. Known-rate Pearson has an asymptotic chi-square(k-1) limit under suitable cell conditions; fitting by ungrouped MLE with moving cells does not justify automatically subtracting another degree of freedom.

docs.title: Scores, moments and spacings
docs.text:
Differentiating the profiled Weibull log likelihood at shape 1 gives \(n+\sum_i(1-y_i)\log y_i\), verifying the Cox–Oakes sign and factor. The test compares that analytic score with a central finite difference of the likelihood. Its raw value is not standardized; a conventional asymptotic standardization multiplies it by \(\sqrt{6/n}/\pi\).

Atkinson uses an absolute power-mean contrast. The accepted computational range \(p>-1\) is broader than the usual finite-variance asymptotic range \(p>-1/2\). Near zero its geometric-mean limit is used; \(p=1\) is excluded as degenerate. Normal calibration of an unstandardized raw value is unjustified. The Mimoto–Zitikis paper is linked for provenance; full-text verification was unavailable in this audit.

Under an exponential sample, \(P_i=X_i/\sum_jX_j\) has Dirichlet(1,...,1) distribution. Direct Dirichlet moment calculations give

\[ E(G)=\frac2{n+1},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G)=\frac{4(n-1)}{(n+1)^2(n+2)(n+3)}. \]

They also give Moran's exact mean \(\log n-\psi(n)\) and variance \(\psi_1(1)/n-\psi_1(n)\) for the centered value used here. Integrating a Beta(1,n-1) marginal gives the exact Pietra mean \((1-1/n)^n\), rather than its asymptotic center \(1/e\). Gini uses denominator \(n-1\), with exact null mean \(1/2\) and variance \(1/[12(n-1)]\). WE is exactly

\[ WE=G-\frac1n. \]

For normalized ordered spacings, independence and exponentiality imply that sums over disjoint groups are independent gamma variables. Their ratios of means yield F(2r,2(n-r)) for Gnedenko and F(4r,2(n-2r)) for Harris. These identities validate the scalar ratios independently of historical attribution. Both criteria now use TwoSidedAlternative, with equal probabilities in the lower and upper tails. Regression checks construct samples from prescribed spacings and verify rejection for both small and large ratios, and acceptance for a ratio of one, through Monte Carlo calibration. Epstein's logarithmic spacing contrast and correction were checked algebraically, but its attribution and purported finite-sample approximation are not certified.

docs.title: Characterizations, direction and graph limitations
docs.text:
For independent continuous observations, the raw Hollander–Proschan statistic estimates \(P(X>Y+Z)\). Under NBU, \(\bar F(y+z)\le\bar F(y)\bar F(z)\), hence

\[ P(X>Y+Z)\le\left[\int\bar F(y)\,dF(y)\right]^2=\frac14. \]

Thus the original NBU procedure rejects small values. The API now uses LeftAlternative. Uniform(1,2) supplies a concrete regression case: its statistic is zero. A deterministic sample in (1,2) checks the scalar and rejection through lower-tail Monte Carlo calibration. The former upper-tail rule missed this NBU departure. Deshpande's raw expectation \(1/(1+b)\) follows by integrating \(P(X>bY)\); its upper-tail choice is compatible with the IFRA alternative.

Ahsanullah and Rossberg were checked against exhaustive indicator enumeration, including repeated-index versus distinct-index conventions and strict ties. Characterization identities alone do not establish consistency of a particular signed integral against every alternative. Their exact original finite-sample conventions remain qualified, rather than assigning unverified normal laws.

The six graph algorithms were compared with explicit NetworkX graphs, maximal cliques and complement cliques. Their proximity threshold is data range/10. Translation leaves every edge unchanged. Shapiro–Wilk W also cancels a shift in both numerator and denominator, as discussed by Spinelli and Stephens (1987), §3. Neither construction can consistently detect a positive location shift while the declared origin is fixed at zero. The graph reference on each page is background, not evidence for this exact exponentiality procedure.

docs.title: Transform criteria
docs.text: The ELT definition was compared with the normalized differential-equation construction in Baringhaus and Henze (1991), pp. 552–553. Independent numerical quadrature verifies the implemented pair sum. For the mean-residual-life family, direct integration and the independent pair representation in Ebner (2023), equations (4)–(5) verify the piecewise implementation. Both keep tuning fixed; they refit the mean for every sample. The accepted \(0<a\le100\) range is an implementation constraint, not a statement of the entire theoretical domain.

docs.title: Scientific provenance: what was and was not verified
docs.text:
Full text was available for the Baringhaus–Henze ELT, Ebner residual-life, Zhang and Spinelli–Stephens comparisons above. Other linked originals were checked at bibliographic/abstract level where accessible; this is not claimed to be equation-by-equation verification of every paywalled article. Original links for Deshpande, Gini, Lorenz, Kimber–Michael, Kochar, Wong–Wong, Ahsanullah and Rossberg are recorded on their individual pages. No claim is made that all external hosts are currently reachable or that their tables match this API.

The exponential HG1 and HG2 tests are described by Ushakov and Ushakov in the scientific article cited below. Their scientific attribution is established; they are not listed as tests with unconfirmed provenance. Calibrate under the fitted exponential null. Historical publication priority is separate from verification of the implemented formula and calibration. See Ushakov and Ushakov, On sensitivity of exponentiality tests to data rounding: a Monte Carlo simulation study.

Frozini's original reference is a book chapter; a scientific comparison article is linked as context, not misrepresented as its first publication. Cox–Oakes similarly has a historical book source, with an independent likelihood derivation here. WE is a published test name associated with Ascher (1990), not an invented local name. The later rounding study cited below gives the definition

\[ WE_{\mathrm{published}}=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}{(\sum_i x_i)^2}=G-\frac1n. \]

The implementation now returns this published formula. The former extra factor \((n-1)/n\) has been removed. WE is an increasing affine function of Greenwood for fixed sample size, but this class currently uses the right tail while Greenwood uses both tails. The full text of Ascher was not accessible during this follow-up; the formula comparison uses the later article, which explicitly cites Ascher for WE. The historical rejection-tail convention has not been verified here.

Sources: Ascher (1990), A survey of tests for exponentiality, 19(5), 1811–1825; On sensitivity of exponentiality tests to data rounding: a Monte Carlo simulation study.

The six graph classes still have no identified primary publication for their exact range/10 tests.

docs.title: Numerical and Monte Carlo evidence
docs.text:
The combined isolated run passed 837 tests (one upstream SciPy deprecation warning). All 51 documentation examples executed. Ruff and generated-stub synchronization checks passed. MkDocs built successfully with no warnings for exponentiality/; existing broken-link warnings remain in other families.

The audit runs the existing exponential correctness, numerical-boundary, verification and generated-class suites, plus:

  • test_exponent_mathematical_audit.py: all 50 scalar definitions, every supported rate mode, profile-likelihood score, infinity/NaN rank behavior, and an explicit Hollander–Proschan lower-tail rejection regression.
  • test_exponent_documentation.py: one page per concrete class, complete catalog and MkDocs navigation, scientific links, local-link existence and execution of all 51 page/catalog examples.
  • test_edf.py: shared-kernel reference integrals and high-precision Zhang values, including endpoint behavior.

The opt-in test_exponential_validation.py run passed 3 statistical tests. It checks signed-contrast normal approximations, exact spacing F laws, known-rate KS/Pearson laws, Baringhaus–Henze null behavior, held-out power diagnostics and legacy-class level diagnostics. Seeds are 20261008, 19461991 and 31082026; the null-law stage uses up to 5000 replicates. These simulations do not replace formula proofs, do not certify every alternative, and are not an all-50 uniform-power study. Discrete graph tests can be conservative.

The Monte Carlo helper now retains positive/negative infinity in comparisons. It rejects NaNs instead of dropping replicates. For the upper tail, \(p=(1+\#\{T_b\ge T_{obs}\})/(B+1)\); two-tail values double the smaller corrected tail probability, capped at one. Empirical inverse-CDF quantiles use order statistics rather than interpolating infinity. Rejection is based on the rank p-value, not on strict comparison with the displayed quantile. The rank denominator, inclusive ties and use of the specified simulation rate are separately tested. No claim is made that rounded or censored observations follow the continuous-null calibration.

docs.title: Reproducing the isolated run
docs.text:
Normal pytest currently fails during collection because the aggregate continuous/__init__.py imports removed legacy names from edf.py. This pre-existing issue is outside the exponential formula/doc audit. To reproduce this audit without replacing algorithms or mocking results, create only the parent package namespace and load the real modules from disk:

.venv/bin/python - <<'PYTEST'
import sys
import types
from pathlib import Path
import pytest

root = Path.cwd()
sys.path.insert(0, str(root))
sys.path.insert(0, str(root / "src"))
name = "pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous"
package = types.ModuleType(name)
package.__path__ = [str(root / "src/pysatl_criterion/statistics/goodness_of_fit/continuous")]
sys.modules[name] = package
raise SystemExit(pytest.main([
    "tests/distributions/test_exponent.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_exponent_correctness.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_exponent_numerics.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_exponential_verification.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_exponent_dynamic.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_exponent_mathematical_audit.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_exponent_documentation.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_edf.py", "-q",
]))
PYTEST

For the statistical run, set PYSATL_STATISTICAL=1 and use tests/statistical/test_exponential_validation.py in the same runner. An isolated pass verifies the target modules and examples, not package-wide importability. A normal package-level regression run remains necessary after the aggregate import migration is complete.

docs.title: Documentation coverage and migration
docs.text:
There are 50 criterion pages, one overview and this report, all registered in MkDocs. Twelve missing generated-criterion pages were added; the other pages were updated to current ParameterValues, fitting and tail contracts. Each page has a scientific link, with background-only and unverified attribution explicitly labelled. Broken references to absent root-level exponential audits were removed from these pages.

The current API uses separate KS D+/D− classes, binning rather than bins, and Pearson code CHI2_PEARSON. Old critical values must match the statistic, hypothesis, sample size, selected tail and settings; a label alone is not enough. The Monte Carlo infinity fix additionally changes behavior for previously rejected sparse-cell simulations. Historical scientific alternatives were not silently replaced during this audit.

docs.title: Scientific bibliography
docs.text:
The formula tables above link each criterion to the relevant article(s). The following list collects their full titles and DOI or article links. A citation is not by itself confirmation of every implementation convention: review articles, related models and background-only sources are explicitly qualified in the tables and in the findings above. In particular, no primary source has been identified for the six range/10 graph tests. WE has a published name; its normalization correction is documented above.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood exponentiality criterion
docs.text:
ModifiedLogLikelihoodExponentialityGofStatistic — short code MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD; right tail.

All exponential criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
The model is \(F(x)=1-\exp(-\lambda x)\) for \(x\ge0\), with known origin zero and \(\lambda>0\). Fixed or unknown rate: pass E.DEFAULT.parse({"lam": rate}) or E.DEFAULT.parse({}), respectively. Omitted parameters remain unknown. Where fitting is needed, \(\widehat\lambda=1/\bar x\) is recomputed for each sample; no fitted state is retained.

Write \(y_i=x_i/\bar x\), \(u_i=1-\exp(-\lambda x_{(i)})\) with the specified or fitted rate, \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\). For spacing statistics, \(d_i=(n-i+1)(x_{(i)}-x_{(i-1)})\) and \(x_{(0)}=0\). For frequency statistics, \(O_j\) and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are aligned counts.

\[ 2\sum_j E_j\log(E_j/O_j) \]

Power-divergence parameter -1; an empty observed cell gives positive infinity, retained in Monte Carlo ranks.

docs.title: Input and calibration
docs.text:
Observations must be finite, real, nonnegative and one-dimensional. Masked observations are rejected. Fixed-rate generated criteria accept \(n\ge1\); unknown-rate EDF/frequency criteria require \(n\ge2\) and positive total. Specialized criteria may require more observations, distinct spacings or a nonconstant sample, as stated above and in the class contract. Ties are not silently jittered. Infinite mathematical boundary penalties are retained.

execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. Use monte_carlo_exponential with the same sample size and constructor settings. It refits each simulated sample for a composite hypothesis. Rescaling to Exp(1) is justified only for a scale-invariant statistic. A continuous-null calibration does not model rounding, censoring or dependence.

The binning keyword accepts a BinningStrategy. Default EqualProbabilityBins() chooses the count from sample size; it is not fixed at five. With unknown rate, built-in Monte Carlo requires this strategy; other bins need external calibration at an explicit rate. Known-rate Pearson has an asymptotic chi-square(k-1) law with suitable expected counts. After fitting from ungrouped observations and moving bins, chi-square(k-2) is not asserted. Empty-cell infinities are valid outcomes for Neyman and modified log-likelihood; ties at infinity make rank calibration conservative.

docs.text:

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=\left[1-\exp\left(-(x/s)^k\right)\right]^a,\quad x\ge0, \qquad a,k,s>0. \]

Criterion Public class Short code Pearson chi-squared Chi2PearsonExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic CHI2_PEARSON Freeman–Tukey FreemanTukeyExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic FREEMAN_TUKEY Modified log-likelihood ModifiedLogLikelihoodExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD Neyman modified chi-squared NeymanChi2ExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic CHI2_NEYMAN Cressie–Read CressieReadExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic CRESSIE_READ

All rejection regions are right-tailed, including D+ and D−. The three Kuiper normalizations have different critical values. The Liao–Shimokawa criterion uses the shared EDF kernel.

Here \(O_j\) and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are observed and expected counts in exhaustive, mutually exclusive cells, with \(\sum_jO_j=\sum_jE_j=n\). The constructor accepts keyword-only binning. The default is EqualProbabilityBins(PowerCount(2.0, 0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000): \(B=\min(1000,\max(2,\lceil2n^{0.4}\rceil))\), and \(p_j=1/B\). Thus the default has two cells even for a singleton sample. The old \(\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\) rule and its one-cell singleton result no longer apply.

The example chooses three equal-probability cells explicitly. You can instead use ExplicitBins((0, b1, b2, float("inf"))) for fixed full-support edges; then \(p_j=F(b_{j+1})-F(b_j)\). See binning strategies.

The full identifier appends _EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT to the short code. Frequency configuration() includes the binning strategy. Historical square-root-bin calibrations and the old Watson W identifier are incompatible with the current catalog. Storage loading remains explicitly blocked by this family.

For EDF statistics and fixed equal-probability cells the continuous fixed null is distribution-free through the probability integral transform. Fitting any parameter from the same observations changes the null distribution and is outside this API contract.

docs.title: Anderson–Darling for exponentiated Weibull
docs.text:
AndersonDarlingExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic

Short code: AD. Full code: AD_EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text:
The null is fully specified:

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=\left[1-\exp\left(-(x/s)^k\right)\right]^a,\quad x\ge0, \qquad a,k,s>0. \]

Fix exponent=a, shape=k, scale=s in ExponentiatedWeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse(...); location is zero. All three parameters are required and are never estimated from the observations. execute_statistic accepts a nonempty one-dimensional finite nonnegative sample; ties and constant samples are allowed. It returns a scalar statistic, not a p-value, and leaves the sample and parameters unchanged.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Write \(u_i=F_{a,k,s}(x_{(i)})\) for the sorted observations, \(i=1,\ldots,n\).

\[ A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)\{\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})\}. \]

No fitted-parameter or finite-sample correction is applied. Logarithmic CDF and survival values prevent premature rounding to 0 or 1.

An exact zero observation gives positive infinity. Finite tail penalties are retained using log probabilities when the CDF rounds to one; the statistic may still overflow when its true magnitude exceeds float64.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Reject for large values (right tail). Use the same sample size and statistic normalization when calibrating the fixed null. The probability integral transform gives a Uniform(0,1) null in exact arithmetic. Critical values from tests that estimate Weibull parameters are unsuitable. The family currently rejects stored unversioned calibrations; regenerate them and do not assume storage loading is enabled.

docs.title: Freeman–Tukey for exponentiated Weibull
docs.text:
FreemanTukeyExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic

Short code: FREEMAN_TUKEY. Full code: FREEMAN_TUKEY_EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text:
The null is fully specified:

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=\left[1-\exp\left(-(x/s)^k\right)\right]^a,\quad x\ge0, \qquad a,k,s>0. \]

Fix exponent=a, shape=k, scale=s in ExponentiatedWeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse(...); location is zero. All three parameters are required and are never estimated from the observations. execute_statistic accepts a nonempty one-dimensional finite nonnegative sample; ties and constant samples are allowed. It returns a scalar statistic, not a p-value, and leaves the sample and parameters unchanged.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Here \(O_j\) and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are observed and expected counts in exhaustive, mutually exclusive cells, with \(\sum_jO_j=\sum_jE_j=n\). The constructor accepts keyword-only binning. The default is EqualProbabilityBins(PowerCount(2.0, 0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000): \(B=\min(1000,\max(2,\lceil2n^{0.4}\rceil))\), and \(p_j=1/B\). Thus the default has two cells even for a singleton sample. The old \(\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\) rule and its one-cell singleton result no longer apply.

The example chooses three equal-probability cells explicitly. You can instead use ExplicitBins((0, b1, b2, float("inf"))) for fixed full-support edges; then \(p_j=F(b_{j+1})-F(b_j)\). See binning strategies.

\[ T_{FT}=4\sum_{j=1}^B(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j})^2. \]

Power divergence at lambda=−½. The factor 4 is required. A zero observed count contributes 4E_j.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Reject for large values (right tail). Use the same sample size and statistic normalization when calibrating the fixed null. For fixed B and sufficiently large expected counts the usual reference is chi-squared with B−1 degrees of freedom; no parameters are fitted. Small or empty cells and a sample-size-dependent B require appropriate calibration, preferably Monte Carlo. Repeat the chosen binning procedure in every replicate. The family currently rejects stored unversioned calibrations; regenerate them and do not assume storage loading is enabled.

Short code: LS. Full code: LS_EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.text:

docs.title: Mathematical verification of exponentiated Weibull statistics
docs.text: The 18 public criteria were audited: 13 EDF statistics and five frequency statistics. This report follows the structure of the uniformity audit.

docs.title: Hypothesis and scope
docs.text:
The independent observations have the fully specified null

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=[1-\exp(-(x/s)^k)]^a,\quad x\ge0,\qquad a,k,s>0. \]

The location is zero. exponent, shape and scale must all be fixed before observing the data; partial parameter sets are rejected. The exponent is not the ordinary Weibull shape. At \(a=1\) this distribution reduces to ordinary Weibull. The parameterization agrees with SciPy's exponweib (a=exponent, c=shape, scale=scale, loc=0).

Write \(u_i=F_{a,k,s}(x_{(i)})\), \(r_i=i-1/2\), and \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\). The probability integral transform supplies the fixed uniform null. All classes return statistics, not p-values; all use right-tail rejection, including D+ and D−. No parameter fitting or fitted-Weibull critical-value correction is performed.

docs.title: Formula checks
docs.text:
Criterion Verified definition or normalization Scientific source Kolmogorov–Smirnov D+ \(D^+\); no square or \(\sqrt n\) factor Zhang (2002), §2.1 Kolmogorov–Smirnov D− \(D^-\); right-tail rejection Zhang (2002), §2.1 Kolmogorov–Smirnov \(\max(D^+,D^-)\); legacy direction options select the same directional statistics Zhang (2002), §2.1 Anderson–Darling \(-n-n^{-1}\sum_i(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})]\) Zhang (2002), §2.2 Cramér–von Mises \(1/(12n)+\sum_i(u_i-r_i/n)^2\) Zhang (2002), §2.3 Liao–Shimokawa \(n^{-1/2}\sum_i\max(i/n-u_i,u_i-(i-1)/n)/\sqrt{u_i(1-u_i)}\) Liao and Shimokawa (1999); cross-check in Al-Zahrani (2012), eq. (13) Watson \(W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2\), computed as centered squared deviations Lemeshko et al. (2014), eq. (6); Watson (1961) Kuiper \(V=D^++D^-\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), eq. (1) Scaled Kuiper \(\sqrt n V\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), discussion before eq. (2) Corrected Kuiper \((\sqrt n+0.155+0.24/\sqrt n)V\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), eq. (3) Zhang K \(\max_i[r_i\log(r_i/(nu_i))+(n-r_i)\log((n-r_i)/(n(1-u_i)))]\) Zhang (2002), eq. (3.1) Zhang A \(-\sum_i[\log u_i/(n-r_i)+\log(1-u_i)/r_i]\) Zhang (2002), eq. (3.2) Zhang C \(\sum_i[\log((1-u_i)/u_i)-\log((n-i+1/4)/(i-3/4))]^2\) Zhang (2002), eq. (3.3) Pearson \(\sum_j(O_j-E_j)^2/E_j\), power divergence \(\lambda=1\) Cressie and Read (1984) Freeman–Tukey \(4\sum_j(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j})^2\), \(\lambda=-1/2\) Cressie and Read (1984) Modified log-likelihood \(2\sum_jE_j\log(E_j/O_j)\), \(\lambda=-1\) Cressie and Read (1984) Neyman modified chi-squared \(\sum_j(O_j-E_j)^2/O_j\), \(\lambda=-2\) Cressie and Read (1984) Cressie–Read \((9/5)\sum_jO_j[(O_j/E_j)^{2/3}-1]\), \(\lambda=2/3\) Cressie and Read (1984)

The shared EDF and divergence kernels match these definitions. The audit found numerical errors in the family probability calculations, rather than incorrect normalizations in these kernels; the corrections are described below.

docs.title: Sources and verification limits
docs.text:
• Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, full text.
  • Lemeshko et al. (2014), Solving Problems of Using Some Nonparametric Goodness-of-Fit Tests, authors' university copy.
  • Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, full text.
  • Liao and Shimokawa (1999), A new goodness-of-fit test for type-I extreme-value and 2-parameter Weibull distributions with estimated parameters.
  • Al-Zahrani (2012), Goodness-of-Fit for the Topp-Leone Distribution with Unknown Parameters, eq. (13).
  • Watson (1961), Goodness-of-fit tests on a circle.

Zhang and Lemeshko were checked in accessible full texts. The power-divergence family and its parameter correspondences were checked against the accessible text of Cressie and Read. The original Liao–Shimokawa full text was unavailable: its bibliographic record and abstract were checked, and the implemented weighted EDF expression was cross-checked in Al-Zahrani's application. That latter paper is not used as a reference for the other EDF formulas or for exponentiated Weibull critical values.

The original Liao–Shimokawa procedure estimates parameters, whereas this family uses a specified CDF. Its fitted-null tables are therefore unsuitable here. Zhang C implements the published quarter-rank approximation in eq. (3.3), not the preceding integrated statistic with its constants. Corrected Kuiper uses an empirical normalization, not an exact finite-sample distribution.

docs.title: Numerical corrections
docs.text:
1. False infinite logarithmic penalties for tiny exponents. For exponent=1e-320, shape=scale=1 and sample [1, 2, 10], the old Anderson–Darling calculation returned infinity. An 800-digit Decimal evaluation gives approximately 2214.0422443729744. Multiplication by the exponent rounded \(\log F\) to a subnormal value or zero before computing \(\log(1-F)\). The family probability kernel now computes \(\log q=\log a+\log[-\log(1-e^{-t})]\), where \(t=(x/s)^k\) and \(q=-\log F\), and uses \(\log(1-e^{-q})\simeq\log q\) for tiny \(q\). The regression also covers Liao–Shimokawa and all three Zhang statistics.
  2. Overflow before a compensating exponent. For shape=1e308, exponent=1e-308, scale=1 and positive observations below one, \(k\log(x/s)\) can overflow negatively even though \(ak\log(x/s)\) is finite. The lower-tail branch now evaluates the latter product directly. The limiting CDF in the regression is \(F(x)\simeq x\); KS is checked against an independent uniform reference.
  3. Frequency cells computed from an underflowed intermediate CDF. At shape=1000, exponent=0.001, scale=1, directly evaluating the ordinary Weibull CDF before exponentiation can round it to zero. For sample [0.01, 0.1, 0.4, 0.8], the correct two-cell Pearson value is 1. Frequency binning now uses the same stable CDF and logarithmic tails as EDF evaluation. Both equal-probability and explicit-edge bins are checked.

These are floating-point corrections to the specified mathematical model. Exact zero observations still give infinite logarithmic EDF penalties. Statistics whose true magnitudes exceed float64 can still be infinite. Extreme parameter combinations may also be unsuitable for sampling with the SciPy-backed generator; this audit does not certify that generator across the entire floating-point parameter range.

docs.title: Frequency bins and calibration
docs.text:
The current default is EqualProbabilityBins(PowerCount(2.0, 0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000):

\[ B=\min(1000,\max(2,\lceil2n^{0.4}\rceil)),\qquad E_j=n/B. \]

The previous Pearson documentation incorrectly retained \(\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\) and a one-cell singleton. The pages now describe the actual default, its cap, and explicit binning options. At \(n=1\) the default has two cells: Pearson is 1, not 0. Zero observed cells produce infinity for modified log-likelihood and Neyman; Freeman–Tukey, Pearson and Cressie–Read have finite limits.

For fixed exhaustive cells with positive probabilities, the large-sample chi-squared reference has \(B-1\) degrees of freedom because no parameters are estimated. This does not establish accuracy with small expected counts or sample-size-dependent bins. Monte Carlo must reproduce the chosen statistic, sample size and binning. The family still rejects stored unversioned critical values. Changing the binning or statistic identifier requires recalibration; the current Watson short code is WATSON, not the historical W.

docs.title: Package and type declarations
docs.text:
The public package follows the uniform family layout:

continuous/exponentiated_weibull/
    __init__.py
    __init__.pyi
    exponentiated_weibull_statistics.py

__init__.py re-exports all 19 public classes (one abstract family base and 18 criteria). The public import paths and class module identifiers remain unchanged, including compatibility with existing pickle references. __init__.pyi describes the generated classes, per-criterion hypotheses, frequency binning arguments, and the legacy KS direction and mode options. Regenerate and check it without importing the package:

python scripts/generate_exponentiated_weibull_stub.py
python scripts/generate_exponentiated_weibull_stub.py --check

docs.title: Numba implementation
docs.text:
All 18 criteria use the compiled shared EDF or frequency statistic kernels. AbstractExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic.do_log_probabilities additionally uses @jit(nopython=True, cache=True) to evaluate the family probabilities in one pass. It avoids intermediate masks and arrays, and computes survival logs only when required. EDF criteria without logarithmic kernels and frequency CDF binning use the CDF-only path. Validation, sorting, strategy selection and parameter objects remain outside the compiled kernel, as in the uniform family.

All family callbacks are class methods; the module has no module-level function definitions. No fastmath is enabled: NaNs, infinities and the tail safeguards above retain their intended meaning. Compilation has a first-call cost; timings of repeated evaluations must exclude compilation. Tests check nopython dispatch for every criterion and compare compiled results with the Python kernel at ordinary and extreme parameter values.

docs.title: Numerical verification and documentation coverage
docs.text:
The dedicated suite is tests/statistics/test_exponentiated_weibull_mathematical_validation.py. It checks all 18 formulas using independent EDF quadrature, SciPy KS and multinomial power divergences, direct rank formulas, and 800-digit Decimal references. It includes zero observations, ties, singletons, empty cells, legacy KS directions, extreme exponents, intermediate overflow, and the probability adapter's scalar/array and support contracts.

Every criterion has a dedicated page, explicit formula, scientific links and an executable example. The coverage test matches pages against the actual runtime catalog, checks the index and MkDocs navigation, and executes all 18 examples. Public class docstrings also contain examples and scientific links.

The focused isolated run passed 275 tests, including execution of all 18 page examples and all 72 docstring example steps. Ruff passed for the changed Python files. MkDocs built successfully; existing warnings concern other sections, with no warnings for exponentiated Weibull pages.

The ordinary pytest invocation is currently blocked during package import by an unrelated obsolete AbstractChi2Statistic import in inverse_gamma.py. The focused run bypasses only the eager continuous/__init__.py imports; it loads the real family, factories, kernels, distributions and binning code. Consequently the results verify these calculations and documentation, but do not establish that ordinary package initialization works.

A reproducible isolated invocation from the repository root is:

import sys
import types
from pathlib import Path
import pytest

name = "pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous"
package = types.ModuleType(name)
package.__path__ = [
    str(Path("src/pysatl_criterion/statistics/goodness_of_fit/continuous").resolve())
]
sys.modules[name] = package
raise SystemExit(
    pytest.main(
        [
            "tests/statistics/test_exponentiated_weibull_mathematical_validation.py",
            "tests/statistics/test_exponentiated_weibull_dynamic.py",
            "tests/distributions/test_weibull_families.py",
            "tests/statistics/test_exponentiated_weibull_numba.py",
            "-q",
        ]
    )
)

The checks establish agreement with the stated formulas on the tested cases. They are not a proof of exact rejection probabilities, a power study, or a certification of all possible float64 parameter combinations.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood for exponentiated Weibull
docs.text:
ModifiedLogLikelihoodExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic

Short code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD. Full code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text:
The null is fully specified:

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=\left[1-\exp\left(-(x/s)^k\right)\right]^a,\quad x\ge0, \qquad a,k,s>0. \]

Fix exponent=a, shape=k, scale=s in ExponentiatedWeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse(...); location is zero. All three parameters are required and are never estimated from the observations. execute_statistic accepts a nonempty one-dimensional finite nonnegative sample; ties and constant samples are allowed. It returns a scalar statistic, not a p-value, and leaves the sample and parameters unchanged.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Here \(O_j\) and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are observed and expected counts in exhaustive, mutually exclusive cells, with \(\sum_jO_j=\sum_jE_j=n\). The constructor accepts keyword-only binning. The default is EqualProbabilityBins(PowerCount(2.0, 0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000): \(B=\min(1000,\max(2,\lceil2n^{0.4}\rceil))\), and \(p_j=1/B\). Thus the default has two cells even for a singleton sample. The old \(\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\) rule and its one-cell singleton result no longer apply.

The example chooses three equal-probability cells explicitly. You can instead use ExplicitBins((0, b1, b2, float("inf"))) for fixed full-support edges; then \(p_j=F(b_{j+1})-F(b_j)\). See binning strategies.

\[ T_{ML}=2\sum_{j=1}^B E_j\log\frac{E_j}{O_j}. \]

Power divergence at lambda=−1. This reverses the usual likelihood-ratio divergence. Any zero O_j with E_j>0 gives positive infinity.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Reject for large values (right tail). Use the same sample size and statistic normalization when calibrating the fixed null. For fixed B and sufficiently large expected counts the usual reference is chi-squared with B−1 degrees of freedom; no parameters are fitted. Small or empty cells and a sample-size-dependent B require appropriate calibration, preferably Monte Carlo. Repeat the chosen binning procedure in every replicate. The family currently rejects stored unversioned calibrations; regenerate them and do not assume storage loading is enabled.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import ExponentiatedWeibullDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.exponentiated_weibull import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins

parameters = Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"exponent": 1, "shape": 2, "scale": 1})
test = ModifiedLogLikelihoodExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic(
    parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=3)
)
value = test.execute_statistic([0.1, 0.25, 0.4, 0.55, 0.7, 0.9, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0])
print(value)

docs.text:
WatsonExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic

Short code: WATSON. Full code: WATSON_EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text:
The null is fully specified:

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=\left[1-\exp\left(-(x/s)^k\right)\right]^a,\quad x\ge0, \qquad a,k,s>0. \]

Fix exponent=a, shape=k, scale=s in ExponentiatedWeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse(...); location is zero. All three parameters are required and are never estimated from the observations. execute_statistic accepts a nonempty one-dimensional finite nonnegative sample; ties and constant samples are allowed. It returns a scalar statistic, not a p-value, and leaves the sample and parameters unchanged.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Write \(u_i=F_{a,k,s}(x_{(i)})\) for the sorted observations, \(i=1,\ldots,n\).

\[ U^2=W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2=\frac1{12n}+\sum_{i=1}^n(d_i-\bar d)^2,\quad d_i=u_i-\frac{i-1/2}{n}. \]

The implementation centers deviations before squaring to avoid cancellation. No finite-sample correction is used. The current short code is WATSON; historical W calibrations must not be reused.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Reject for large values (right tail). Use the same sample size and statistic normalization when calibrating the fixed null. The probability integral transform gives a Uniform(0,1) null in exact arithmetic. Critical values from tests that estimate Weibull parameters are unsuitable. The family currently rejects stored unversioned calibrations; regenerate them and do not assume storage loading is enabled.

ZhangAExponentiatedWeibullGofStatistic

Short code: ZHANG_ZA. Full code: ZHANG_ZA_EXPONENTIATED_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text:

\[ F_{a,k,s}(x)=\left[1-\exp\left(-(x/s)^k\right)\right]^a,\quad x\ge0, \qquad a,k,s>0. \]

docs.title: Gamma goodness-of-fit statistics
docs.text:
The module exposes 28 concrete classes: 13 generated EDF criteria, five generated frequency criteria, and 10 local criteria. Liao–Shimokawa is generated by the shared EDF factory.

The null is Gamma with fixed shape alfa > 0, rate beta > 0 and origin zero:

\[ f(x)=\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x},\qquad x>0. \]

Supply both parameters via GammaDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse(...). beta is a rate, not a scale. Estimating parameters from the tested sample changes the null law and is outside these criteria's supported hypotheses.
