H0: independent observations follow Laplace(t, s) for some unknown t and s > 0. Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}). Fixed or partially fixed parameters are rejected.

DLO_Z = Z(Knet), signed kurtosis component. Requires n >= 4.

Composite Laplace null: both location and scale are unknown. Use Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}); refit on every simulated sample. Rejection direction: two-sided. Constant samples are invalid.

The exact mathematical definitions and notation are in fitted definitions.

docs.title: Options and limitations
docs.text:
The implementation uses the parity-dependent finite-sample corrections in equations (7)–(9) of the comparison paper. It requires n >= 4, since the odd-n kurtosis variance correction is negative at n=3. Asymptotic normal/chi-square approximations are discussed for n >= 20; use simulated calibration for small samples. The full formula is in fitted definitions.

Input must be a finite, real, one-dimensional nonconstant sample with n >= 3 (n >= 4 for DLO). Sorting does not modify the caller's sample. Extreme floating point shifts can erase differences before execution; no implementation can recover those differences. These methods return a statistic, not a p-value.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Use the statistic's declared rejection direction. Simulate independent Laplace(0,1) samples of the same size and call execute_statistic on every replicate, preserving all constructor settings. Location and scale are re-estimated on each call. get_hypothesis_generator selects the standard representative while the public hypothesis retains both parameters as unknown. Fixed-parameter EDF critical values are not applicable.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import (
    DesgagneLafayeDeMicheauxOuimetZLaplaceGofStatistic,
)

criterion = DesgagneLafayeDeMicheauxOuimetZLaplaceGofStatistic(Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}))
value = criterion.execute_statistic([-3.2, -1.4, -0.8, -0.1, 0.05, 0.5, 0.9, 1.7, 4.1])
assert np.isfinite(value)

docs.title: Fitted Laplace: definitions and conventions
docs.text: All statistics on this page test the composite family Laplace(t, s), s > 0. Write n for sample size, μ̂ for the sample median (average of the two middle observations for even n), b̂ = mean|x−μ̂|, and z_i=(x_i−μ̂)/b̂. Let x̄ be the sample mean and s_n²=mean(x−x̄)², with divisor n throughout. Order-statistic subscripts outside 1,…,n are clamped to the nearest endpoint. The implementation works on standardized observations to avoid scale overflow. Constant samples have no admissible fitted scale.

docs.title: Characteristic-function tests
docs.text:
For j=1,2,

\[ T_{n,a}^{(j)}=n\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left|(1+t^2)n^{-1}\sum_i e^{it z_i}-1\right|^2w_j(t,a)\,dt, \quad w_1=e^{-a|t|},\quad w_2=e^{-at^2}. \]

The default is MLE standardization. With estimator="mom", replace z by (x−x̄)/(s_n/√2). Both statistics reject for large values. The closed forms in Meintanis (2004) are evaluated without allocating an n×n matrix. Default a values are 2 and 0.5, respectively. The defining integral provides both an independent test and a cancellation fallback.

docs.title: Choi–Kim entropy tests
docs.text:
Choose integer 1 ≤ m < n/2 and define Δ_i=z_(i+m)−z_(i−m).

\[ H_v=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log\frac{n\Delta_i}{2m},\qquad H_{\mathrm{vanEs}}=\frac1{n-m}\sum_{i=1}^{n-m}\log(z_{i+m}-z_i) +\sum_{k=m}^{n}\frac1k. \]

For Correa, let z̄_i be the average of the 2m+1 clamped observations indexed j=i−m,…,i+m. The rank j itself is not clamped:

\[ H_c=-\frac1n\sum_i\log \frac{\sum_{j=i-m}^{i+m}(j-i)(z_j-\bar z_i)/n} {\sum_{j=i-m}^{i+m}(z_j-\bar z_i)^2}. \]

CK_v=exp(H_v), CK_c=exp(H_c), CK_e=exp(H_vanEs) on standardized data; in original units these are exp(H)/b̂. No extra 2e divisor is applied. Small values reject. See Choi–Kim (2006).

docs.title: AP entropy tests and corrected scales
docs.text:
Alizadeh Noughabi–Park (2016) use AP_r=log(2θ_r)+1−H_r. Their H_e is the Ebrahimi estimate, not van Es. For r=v,e,a,z,

\[ H_r=\frac1n\sum_i\log\frac{n\Delta_i}{m c_{r,i}}, \]

where c_v,i=2; c_e,i=1+min(i−1,m,n−i)/m; c_a,i=1 at i≤m or i≥n−m+1 and 2 otherwise; c_z,i=i/m for i≤m, (n−i+1)/m for i≥n−m+1, and 2 otherwise.

For AP_y, define B=(n−1)/(n(n+1)) and the smoothed empirical CDF values

\[ F_1=B\left(\frac n{n-1}+\frac n{2n-1}\right),\quad F_n=B\left(\frac{(n-1)^2+1}{n-1}+1+\frac{n-1}{2n-1}\right), \] \[ F_i=B\left(\frac{i(n-1)+1}{n-1}+ \frac{z_i-z_{i-1}}{z_{i+1}-z_{i-1}}\right),\quad 2\le i\le n-1. \]

Set d_i=F_(i+m)−F_(i−m), C=Σd_i and H_y=Σ(d_i/C)log(Δ_i/d_i). The implementation uses the strictly increasing sample branch of this definition: AP_y rejects tied observations explicitly.

The corrected scale is the integral of absolute deviation of a piecewise-linear quantile Q with knots β_i at (i−1)/n, i=1,…,n+1:

\[ \theta(\beta)=\int_0^1|Q(u)-Q(1/2)|\,du. \]

Define ξ_i=(2m)⁻¹Σ_{k=i−m}^{i+m−1}z_k. For v use β=ξ, and for y use β_i=2mξ_i/C. For e,a,z, interior knots m+1≤i≤n−m+1 equal ξ_i; replace tails by

\[ \beta_i=\xi_{m+1}-\sum_{k=i}^{m}\frac{z_{m+k}-z_1}{d_{L,k}} \quad(i\le m),\qquad \beta_i=\xi_{n-m+1}+\sum_{k=n-m+2}^{i}\frac{z_n-z_{k-m-1}}{d_{R,k}} \quad(i\ge n-m+2). \] Variant d_L,k d_R,k e m+k−1 n+m−k+1 a m m z k n−k+2

The integral uses trapezoids on each side of ½, splitting the central interval for odd n. scale_estimator="mle" substitutes θ=1 on standardized data, providing the corresponding MLE-scale variants. Large values reject.

docs.title: Moment and smooth components
docs.text:
Let g_1=mean((x−x̄)/s_n)³ and g_2=mean((x−x̄)/s_n)⁴. The signed rescaled components are

\[ \widetilde V_3=\sqrt{n/63}\,g_1,\qquad \widetilde V_4=\sqrt{n/1188}\,(g_2-6). \]

The moment components reported in Batsidis et al., Section 3.3 use denominators 54 and 1072.8 and have asymptotic variances 7/6 and 165/149. Rescaling gives 54·7/6=63 and 1072.8·165/149=1188. This is a reconstruction of the unit-variance versions motivated by Best–Rayner–Thas (2008). It can also be checked directly from Laplace moments: for standardized variance-one Y, E(Y^(2k))=(2k)!/2^k. The influence functions are Y³−3Y and Y⁴−12Y²+6, with variances 63 and 1188. Both components have two-sided rejection.

For Gel (2010), put q_j=mean((x−x̄)/(√2 b̂))^j, j=3,4:

\[ Ge=nq_3^2/60+n(q_4-6)^2/1200. \]

Large values reject. The constants are the recommended small/moderate-sample choice, not a fitted estimate of asymptotic variances.

The signed González-Estrada–Villaseñor (2016) statistic is

\[ GV=2\sqrt n\left\{\frac{s_n}{\sqrt2\,\mathrm{mean}|x-\bar x|}-1\right\}. \]

The absolute deviations here are about the sample mean. Rejection is two-sided.

docs.title: Density likelihood and informational energy
docs.text:
For Alizadeh Noughabi (2016),

\[ A_{rat}=\min_{1\le m<\min(n^\delta,n/2)} \prod_{i=1}^n\frac{2m}{n\Delta_i f_{0,1}(z_i)},\qquad \delta=0.5. \]

Only integer windows are considered. The extra n/2 bound follows the comparison paper, Section 3.3. The calculation sums log factors and minimizes before exponentiating. log_scale=True returns the log of the minimum. Large values reject.

For Alizadeh Noughabi–Jarrahiferiz (2019),

\[ AJ=\frac1n\sum_i\frac{2m}{n\{F_{0,1}(z_{i+m})-F_{0,1}(z_{i-m})\}}. \]

Large values reject. Tail differences use exponential identities with expm1.

docs.title: DLO finite-sample scores
docs.text:
The λ=1 specialization of Desgagné–Lafaye de Micheaux–Ouimet is implemented with the finite-sample corrections in equations (7)–(9) of the comparison paper. Define

\[ S=\mathrm{mean}(z),\quad K=\mathrm{mean}(|z|\log|z|),\quad K_{net}=\max(0,K-S^2/2),\quad c=1-\gamma. \]

Use 0·log0=0 and Euler's constant γ. Then

\[ Z_S=\frac{\sqrt n S}{\sqrt{v_S}},\qquad Z_K=\frac{\sqrt n(K_{net}^{1/4}-c^{1/4}b_K)} {\sqrt{c^{-3/2}(\pi^2/3-3)v_K/16}}. \] n v_S b_K v_K even 1−1.856/n^1.06 1−0.422/n^1.01 1−1.950/n^0.92+39.349/n^2.3 odd 1−0.281/n^1.03 1−0.198/n^0.86 1−3.827/n^1.04

DLO_X=Z_S²+Z_K² rejects on the right; DLO_Z=Z_K is signed and two-sided. Require n≥4. Normal/chi-square asymptotic approximations are not substituted for finite-sample calibration.

docs.title: Data-driven smooth adaptation
docs.text:
This class specializes the general efficient-score construction and Schwarz selection rule of Janic–Ledwina, Sections 2–2.1 to the Laplace MLE. It is not a verified implementation of the DD comparator in Best–Rayner–Thas.

Let φ_j(u)=√(2j+1)P_j(2u−1) for Legendre polynomials P_j. The standardized Laplace nuisance score is s(z)=(sign z, |z|−1)', with E(ss')=I₂. Let A_j=E[φ_j(F(Z))s(Z)'] under Z∼Laplace(0,1), and v=mean φ(F(z))−A mean s(z). For each k=1,…,d,

\[ W_k=n v_{1:k}'(I_k-A_{1:k}A_{1:k}')^{-1}v_{1:k},\qquad \hat k=\min\arg\max_k\{W_k-k\log n\}. \]

The statistic is W_k̂ and rejects on the right. Default d=4; integer 1≤d≤10. Population integrals are computed at construction, not estimated from the sample. A fixed d does not give an omnibus-consistency guarantee.

docs.title: Shared calibration and implementation settings
docs.text:
Constructor settings enter configuration(). Use identical sample size, window, weight, estimation mode, score dimension and log/product convention when calibrating. The built-in generator uses Laplace(0,1) for these invariant composite tests. Every execution fits anew and leaves the hypothesis parameters unknown.

All spacing windows default to m=1. This explicit choice does not reproduce the size-dependent power-optimized tables in the comparison paper. Ties are permitted except in AP_y; zero required spacings yield limiting zero CK or infinite AP/AJ/A_rat. Neither known-parameter EDF tables nor critical values for a different window apply.

docs.title: Freeman–Tukey test for the Laplace distribution
Description
docs.text: FreemanTukeyLaplaceGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim \operatorname{Laplace}(t,s)\). Its algorithm code is FREEMAN_TUKEY_LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor as Laplace
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import (
    FreemanTukeyLaplaceGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Laplace.DEFAULT.parse({"t": 0, "s": 1})
criterion = FreemanTukeyLaplaceGofStatistic(parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=3))
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([-2.0, -1.0, -0.2, 0.2, 1.0, 2.0])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with finite location t and positive finite scale s, both fixed before observing the sample. Missing parameters are unsupported. No parameters are estimated by this criterion.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

binning — keyword-only strategy, default EqualProbabilityBins(): PowerCount(coefficient=2.0, exponent=0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000. The support is the entire real line. Ties and constant samples are accepted. Bins must cover the full support; expected counts are obtained from the fixed Laplace null. No minimum expected count is imposed by default.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The default equal-probability bins are built in Laplace probability space, not as equal-width intervals on the real line. With \(m\) such bins, \(p_j=1/m\). Other strategies use their actual null bin probabilities. Unknown or sample-fitted parameters are not supported. A fitted extension would need refitting and rebuilding bins in every Monte Carlo replicate.

For observed bin counts \(O_j\) and positive expected counts \(E_j=np_j\), where \(p_j\) is the bin probability under the specified Laplace null:

\[ T_{FT}=4\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j}\right)^2. \]

The power-divergence parameter is \(\lambda=-1/2\). An empty observed bin contributes \(4E_j\), so zero observed counts do not make this statistic infinite.

Large values form the right-tail rejection region. Binning is reapplied for every sample. Calibrate with the same rule and sample size; a statistic value alone is not a p-value. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. See binning strategies and calibration storage. configuration() includes the binning policy, while code() identifies the algorithm.

docs.title: Greenwood statistic for the Laplace distribution
docs.text: GreenwoodLaplaceGofStatistic tests independent observations from Laplace(t, s) with both parameters fixed in advance. Its support is the real line. No parameters are fitted by execute_statistic.

docs.title: Parameters and usage
docs.text:
t=0.0 is a finite real scalar location; s=1.0 is a finite positive real scalar scale. rvs must be a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real numbers. A single observation, ties, and constant samples are accepted. Invalid inputs raise ValueError. The sample and model are not modified. execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) returns a scalar; extra keywords are ignored.

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import (
    GreenwoodLaplaceGofStatistic,
)

statistic = GreenwoodLaplaceGofStatistic(
    LaplaceDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"t": 0.0, "s": 1.0})
)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0])

docs.title: Formula and calibration
docs.text:
Let u_i = F_(t,s)(x_(i)), for sorted observations, i=1,...,n. The Laplace CDF is exp((x-t)/s)/2 for x<t and 1-exp(-(x-t)/s)/2 otherwise.

G = sum((u_i-u_(i-1))**2), i = 1, ..., n+1,
with u_0=0 and u_(n+1)=1. Both endpoint spacings are included;
repeated observations yield zero spacings. The result is unscaled.
This right-tail spacing test detects clustering; it is not asserted
to be consistent against every nonuniform alternative.

Large values reject the null. These are exact definitions of the statistics, without asymptotic rescaling. Under the fixed continuous null the transformed observations are independent uniforms, so the null distribution depends on sample size, but not on t or s. hypothesis() nevertheless retains both fixed parameters. Monte Carlo calibration generates Laplace(t,s) samples and calls execute_statistic for each. Fitting parameters to the tested sample is outside this API and requires calibration accounting for fitting.

CDF rounding can erase very small tail spacings. AD evaluates analytic log probabilities, avoiding exponential underflow. Standardization avoids an intermediate overflow in x-t when the quotient is representable. Float64 range limitations still apply; a mathematically finite AD value can overflow. No observations or probabilities are clipped.

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
R. J. M. M. Does, R. Helmers and C. A. J. Klaassen (1988), "Approximating the distribution of Greenwood's statistic", Statistica Neerlandica 42, 153-162, Section 1, equations (1)-(2). https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/1694/1694D.pdf

This source describes the general statistic. Here it is applied to the known Laplace CDF, not to a model fitted to the observations.

docs.title: Kolmogorov–Smirnov D− test for the Laplace distribution
Description
docs.text: KolmogorovSmirnovDMinusLaplaceGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim \operatorname{Laplace}(t,s)\). Its algorithm code is KS_MINUS_LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor as Laplace
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovDMinusLaplaceGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Laplace.DEFAULT.parse({"t": 0, "s": 1})
criterion = KolmogorovSmirnovDMinusLaplaceGofStatistic(parameters)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([-2.0, -1.0, -0.2, 0.2, 1.0, 2.0])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with finite location t and positive finite scale s, both fixed before observing the sample. Missing parameters are unsupported. No parameters are estimated by this criterion.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

The support is the entire real line. Singletons, ties and constant samples are accepted. Empty, nonfinite, complex and multidimensional samples are rejected.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Writing \(z=(x-t)/s\), the Laplace CDF is \(F_{t,s}(x)=e^z/2\) for \(z<0\) and \(F_{t,s}(x)=1-e^{-z}/2\) otherwise. For a fixed continuous null the probability integral transform gives independent uniforms. Its null law depends on sample size, not the known location or scale. Parameters estimated from the sample require a different test and calibration with refitting in every replicate. Rounding-induced ties require a matching observation model during calibration.

Let \(u_i=F_{t,s}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ D_n^- = \max_{1\le i\le n}\left(u_i-\frac{i-1}{n}\right). \]

This is the unscaled negative EDF deviation. Large values indicate an empirical CDF below the null CDF, corresponding to observations tending toward larger values. The statistic uses a right-tail rejection region even though the EDF deviation is one-sided.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

docs.text:
Let u_i = F_(t,s)(x_(i)), for sorted observations, i=1,...,n. The Laplace CDF is exp((x-t)/s)/2 for x<t and 1-exp(-(x-t)/s)/2 otherwise.

D+ = max(i/n - u_i), D- = max(u_i - (i-1)/n), and
D = max(D+, D-), for i = 1, ..., n. RIGHT selects D+; LEFT
selects D-; TWO_TAILED selects D. All reject for large values.

Large values reject the null. These are exact definitions of the statistics, without asymptotic rescaling. Under the fixed continuous null the transformed observations are independent uniforms, so the null distribution depends on sample size, but not on t or s. hypothesis() nevertheless retains both fixed parameters. Monte Carlo calibration generates Laplace(t,s) samples and calls execute_statistic for each. Fitting parameters to the tested sample is outside this API and requires calibration accounting for fitting.

CDF rounding can erase very small tail spacings. AD evaluates analytic log probabilities, avoiding exponential underflow. Standardization avoids an intermediate overflow in x-t when the quotient is representable. Float64 range limitations still apply; a mathematically finite AD value can overflow. No observations or probabilities are clipped.

alternative_type=AlternativeType.TWO_TAILED selects D; RIGHT selects D+ and LEFT selects D-. All three use a right-tailed rejection region. mode accepts auto, exact, asymp, or approx for compatibility and has no effect on the statistic. No p-value is calculated here. Writing \(z=(x-t)/s\), the Laplace CDF is \(F_{t,s}(x)=e^z/2\) for \(z<0\) and \(F_{t,s}(x)=1-e^{-z}/2\) otherwise. docs.text:
Writing \(z=(x-t)/s\), the Laplace CDF is \(F_{t,s}(x)=e^z/2\) for \(z<0\) and \(F_{t,s}(x)=1-e^{-z}/2\) otherwise. docs.title: Scope and sources
docs.text:
The catalog contains 38 concrete criteria, each with a separate page: 13 generated EDF criteria, five generated frequency criteria, Greenwood and 19 fitted specialist criteria. The original 19 use a fully specified Laplace(t, s) null. The added 19 use a composite location-scale null; see the fitted-test audit below. The checks below distinguish independent numerical validation from bibliographic attribution. No Laplace-specific power or optimality claim is made.

The definitions of D, W², A², V and U² follow Section 2 and Case 0 of Stephens (1974), EDF Statistics for Goodness of Fit and Some Comparisons. Greenwood uses the n+1 spacings, including both endpoints, in equations (1)–(2) of Does, Helmers and Klaassen (1988). These sources concern continuous, fully specified null distributions. No Laplace-specific power or optimality claim is made.

docs.title: Formulas and independent checks
docs.text:
Let z=(x-t)/s, F(x)=exp(z)/2 for z<0 and F(x)=1-exp(-z)/2 otherwise. Let u_i=F(x_(i)), i=1,…,n, with u_0=0, u_(n+1)=1. The original six statistics use the unmodified, unscaled definitions below. Scaled and corrected Kuiper variants are listed separately.

Code Formula Independent verification KS D=max(D+,D−), D+=max(i/n−u_i), D−=max(u_i−(i−1)/n) SciPy CDF and direct maxima; all three directions CVM W²=1/(12n)+Σ(u_i−(2i−1)/(2n))² SciPy probabilities and numerical integration of n(F_n(u)−u)² AD A²=−n−Σ((2i−1)/n)(log u_i+log(1−u_(n+1−i))) SciPy log probabilities, weighted numerical integration, analytic extreme-tail limits KUI V=D++D− Direct maxima using SciPy probabilities WAT U²=W²−n(mean(u)−½)² Direct formula and integration of centered EDF discrepancy GRW G=Σ(u_i−u_(i−1))², i=1,…,n+1 Direct spacings including endpoints and exact tied-sample example G=¼

docs.text:
Use the same sorted probabilities and define r_i=i−½. Each short code below has the suffix _LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT in the registry.

The added pages retain the shared algorithms' scientific references: Smirnov for directional KS, Stephens/Lemeshko for Kuiper scaling, Zhang (2002), equations (3.1)–(3.3), for Z_K/Z_A/Z_C, and Liao–Shimokawa (1999). The latter is an adaptation to the fixed Laplace null; fitted-Weibull tables from that paper do not apply. The additional references are inherited from the shared algorithms' documentation; their full texts were not independently reverified during this documentation update (the DOI retrievals were unavailable). The direct-formula tests verify implementation, not published power claims.

docs.title: Frequency criteria
docs.text:
Let O_j be observed counts and E_j=np_j>0 expected counts for exhaustive bins. With equal-probability bins E_j=n/m. Explicit or adaptive strategies can have unequal expected counts. For each of the five classes, independent counts (2,3,4,5) and equal expected counts are compared with SciPy power_divergence.

Code and page Formula SciPy λ Empty observed bin CHI2_PEARSON Σ(O_j−E_j)²/E_j 1 contributes E_j FREEMAN_TUKEY 4Σ(√O_j−√E_j)² −½ contributes 4E_j MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD 2Σ E_j log(E_j/O_j) −1 +infinity CHI2_NEYMAN Σ(O_j−E_j)²/O_j −2 +infinity CRESSIE_READ (9/5)Σ O_j[(O_j/E_j)^(⅔)−1] ⅔ zero contribution in this expression

These are the shared power-divergence definitions documented with the Pearson and Cressie–Read references on the criterion pages. Cressie–Read fixes λ=⅔; there is no lambda_ constructor option. Modified log likelihood uses E_j in the weight and differs from the ordinary G statistic (λ=0).

docs.title: Extreme-value checks for the original six criteria
docs.text: For (-a,0,a), A² approaches 2a/3+8log(2)/3−3 as a grows. At a=10^308 the result remains representable. This detects premature overflow when tail logs are added before normalization. Watson at n=1 equals 1/12 for every observation; equally spaced midpoint probabilities give 1/(12n). Location-scale transformations are checked independently for all six criteria.

docs.title: Changes and compatibility
docs.text:
• Converted continuous/laplace.py into a package with explicit exports and a generated __init__.pyi; generator supports --check without importing the package.
  • Preserved all six public class names, short codes and the continuous.laplace module identity used by pickle. The abstract family no longer declares hypotheses; concrete classes and factory specifications declare both parameters fixed.
  • All 13 EDF and five frequency criteria use shared factories and kernels. Greenwood is the only manually declared concrete class. Generated KS retains its existing constructor through the factory compatibility option; its former call to the removed multi-argument KS interface is corrected.
  • do_execute_statistic(sample) remains an observation-based compatibility entry point. Private _calculate_statistic helpers were removed; benchmark scripts now use the public execute_statistic API. mode remains a compatibility setting.
  • Analytic CDF and log probabilities and Greenwood spacings are static cached Numba methods. No numerical helpers remain outside classes.
  • Shared AD log evaluation now weights each tail before adding, avoiding intermediate overflow. The mathematical definition and calibration scale are unchanged.
  • A factory validation callback retains Laplace's rejection of strings and other nonnumeric inputs. Masked observations are now rejected instead of silently used.

docs.title: Input and calibration limits
docs.text:
Nonempty one-dimensional finite real samples are required. Singletons, ties, constant samples and gaps of any width are allowed. The support is the entire real line. EDF and Greenwood require no binning; ties give zero spacings. Frequency criteria use a configurable binning strategy and positive expected counts. Empty observed bins are handled as specified in the table above. The exact continuous null calibration assumes continuous observations; rounding-induced ties require a matching observation model in simulation.

For EDF and Greenwood, the PIT gives a parameter-free null law at fixed n when both parameters are known. Frequency calibration must also match binning, including adaptive bin selection; arbitrary binning is not parameter-free. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. See binning calibration. Monte Carlo must call the same statistic, including the KS direction. Stored KS calibration is rejected for LEFT/RIGHT because its key does not encode direction. Fitting t or s outside this API does not justify using the known-parameter null law; a fitted test would need a separately supported hypothesis and refitting in every simulation. All 19 criteria use the right rejection tail. Greenwood's right-tail form detects clustering; universal consistency is not asserted.

CDF rounding can erase tiny tail spacings. AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang K/A/C use analytic log tails instead of reconstructing rounded tail probabilities. Standardization avoids overflow in x−t when the quotient is representable; a result beyond float64 range is still +infinity. No clipping or Python high-precision fallback is used. Warm timing includes validation, sorting, CDF evaluation and the shared kernel.

docs.text:
• 478 tests passed in an isolated run covering Laplace, shared EDF kernels and Uniform/Pareto factory regressions. Checks include independent formulas, integrals, SciPy power divergences, extreme tails, input validation, KS options, pickle, registry uniqueness, nopython dispatch, stub and catalog coverage.

The following measurements cover the original six criteria only. No timing claim is made for the 13 additional variants. Measured on the local Python 3.11 environment, n=10,000, seed 42, best of three batches of 200 calls. Both paths include sorting; the reference uses SciPy CDFs and independent NumPy formulas. docs.title: Documentation coverage
docs.text: All 19 concrete classes have individual pages linked from the catalog and MkDocs navigation. Each page states the fixed null, formula, input limits, rejection direction, calibration requirements, an executable example and scientific sources. mathematical-validation.md summarizes verification; it does not replace those pages.

docs.title: Fitted-test audit
docs.text:
The added formulas follow the original article citations in each class and Desgagné–Lafaye de Micheaux–Ouimet, comparison, Section 3. Exact definitions record all estimator and normalization choices.

Independent checks in tests/statistics/test_laplace_published.py cover:

  • Meintanis: numerical integration of the squared empirical-characteristic-function discrepancy, both weights and both parameter estimators.
  • Choi–Kim: direct spacings, van Es harmonic correction and independent regression slopes for Correa.
  • AP: entropy spacings and numerical integration of the absolute deviation of the reconstructed piecewise-linear quantile; corrected and MLE variants.
  • Gel, GV and rescaled V3/V4: direct sample central moments and the correct centering of absolute deviations.
  • A_rat: direct products over every admissible integer window; optional log transform checked separately.
  • AJ: independent SciPy fitted CDF differences.
  • DLO: even/odd corrections checked at n=4, 5, 20, 21, including the zero-log-zero convention.
  • Data-driven smooth: independent population integrals in observation coordinates, covariance solve and Schwarz selection.
  • All added classes: hypothesis capabilities, registry/pickle, affine invariance, permutation invariance, finite-real input validation, no sample mutation and calibration sampler resolution.

docs.title: Explicit adaptations and limits
docs.text:
Entropy windows default to m=1 rather than silently extrapolating power-optimal tables. AP_y rejects ties; other spacing tests use their limiting zero/infinite statistic when a required spacing vanishes. A_rat uses the additional n/2 upper window bound from the comparison, and offers an explicit log-scale option. DLO starts at n=4 because its finite-sample odd-n variance correction is invalid at n=3.

The smooth moment components are rescaled to asymptotic unit variance (63 and 1188). Their reconstruction uses the moment components and variances reported in Batsidis, Economou and Bar-Lev (2022), Section 3.3, and is independently checked using Laplace moments. The original Best et al. full text was unavailable; no unverified DD formula is attributed to it. The data-driven class is explicitly a Laplace specialization of the general Janic–Ledwina score construction, not a replication of the DD comparator in Best et al.

Most arithmetic runs in cached nopython kernels. Meintanis has a quadrature fallback for cancellation/extreme weights. Data-driven population matrices are computed once per instance with SciPy, outside the sample kernel. Fitting/validation remains NumPy.

docs.title: ME1: fitted Laplace statistic
docs.text: Public class: Meintanis1LaplaceGofStatistic. Registry code: ME1_LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and definition
docs.text:
H0: independent observations follow Laplace(t, s) for some unknown t and s > 0. Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}). Fixed or partially fixed parameters are rejected.

T_(n,a)^(1): n integral |(1+t^2) mean exp(it*z)-1|^2 w_a(t) dt.

Composite Laplace null: both location and scale are unknown. Use Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}); refit on every simulated sample. Rejection direction: right. Constant samples are invalid.

The exact mathematical definitions and notation are in fitted definitions.

docs.title: Options and limitations
docs.text:
a > 0 selects the weight; defaults are 2 for ME1 and 0.5 for ME2. estimator="mle" uses median/MAD, while "mom" uses mean and sqrt(variance/2). Closed-form kernels use O(n²) time and O(n) memory. For cancellation or weights outside [0.01, 10], adaptive quadrature evaluates the defining integral; failure to converge raises ArithmeticError.

Input must be a finite, real, one-dimensional nonconstant sample with n >= 3 (n >= 4 for DLO). Sorting does not modify the caller's sample. Extreme floating point shifts can erase differences before execution; no implementation can recover those differences. These methods return a statistic, not a p-value.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Use the statistic's declared rejection direction. Simulate independent Laplace(0,1) samples of the same size and call execute_statistic on every replicate, preserving all constructor settings. Location and scale are re-estimated on each call. get_hypothesis_generator selects the standard representative while the public hypothesis retains both parameters as unknown. Fixed-parameter EDF critical values are not applicable.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:

docs.title: ME2: fitted Laplace statistic
docs.text: Public class: Meintanis2LaplaceGofStatistic. Registry code: ME2_LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and definition
docs.text:
H0: independent observations follow Laplace(t, s) for some unknown t and s > 0. Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}). Fixed or partially fixed parameters are rejected.

T_(n,a)^(2): n integral |(1+t^2) mean exp(it*z)-1|^2 w_a(t) dt.

Composite Laplace null: both location and scale are unknown. Use Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}); refit on every simulated sample. Rejection direction: right. Constant samples are invalid.

The exact mathematical definitions and notation are in fitted definitions.

docs.title: Options and limitations
docs.text:
a > 0 selects the weight; defaults are 2 for ME1 and 0.5 for ME2. estimator="mle" uses median/MAD, while "mom" uses mean and sqrt(variance/2). Closed-form kernels use O(n²) time and O(n) memory. For cancellation or weights outside [0.01, 10], adaptive quadrature evaluates the defining integral; failure to converge raises ArithmeticError.

Input must be a finite, real, one-dimensional nonconstant sample with n >= 3 (n >= 4 for DLO). Sorting does not modify the caller's sample. Extreme floating point shifts can erase differences before execution; no implementation can recover those differences. These methods return a statistic, not a p-value.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Use the statistic's declared rejection direction. Simulate independent Laplace(0,1) samples of the same size and call execute_statistic on every replicate, preserving all constructor settings. Location and scale are re-estimated on each call. get_hypothesis_generator selects the standard representative while the public hypothesis retains both parameters as unknown. Fixed-parameter EDF critical values are not applicable.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood test for the Laplace distribution
Description
docs.text: ModifiedLogLikelihoodLaplaceGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim \operatorname{Laplace}(t,s)\). Its algorithm code is MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor as Laplace
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodLaplaceGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Laplace.DEFAULT.parse({"t": 0, "s": 1})
criterion = ModifiedLogLikelihoodLaplaceGofStatistic(
    parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=3)
)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([-2.0, -1.0, -0.2, 0.2, 1.0, 2.0])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with finite location t and positive finite scale s, both fixed before observing the sample. Missing parameters are unsupported. No parameters are estimated by this criterion.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

binning — keyword-only strategy, default EqualProbabilityBins(): PowerCount(coefficient=2.0, exponent=0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000. The support is the entire real line. Ties and constant samples are accepted. Bins must cover the full support; expected counts are obtained from the fixed Laplace null. No minimum expected count is imposed by default.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The default equal-probability bins are built in Laplace probability space, not as equal-width intervals on the real line. With \(m\) such bins, \(p_j=1/m\). Other strategies use their actual null bin probabilities. Unknown or sample-fitted parameters are not supported. A fitted extension would need refitting and rebuilding bins in every Monte Carlo replicate.

For observed bin counts \(O_j\) and positive expected counts \(E_j=np_j\), where \(p_j\) is the bin probability under the specified Laplace null:

\[ T_{ML}=2\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_j\log\frac{E_j}{O_j}. \]

This is the \(\lambda=-1\) power divergence, with expected counts multiplying the log ratio. It differs from the ordinary likelihood-ratio G statistic (\(\lambda=0\)). Any zero observed count produces positive infinity.

Large values form the right-tail rejection region. Binning is reapplied for every sample. Calibrate with the same rule and sample size; a statistic value alone is not a p-value. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. See binning strategies and calibration storage. configuration() includes the binning policy, while code() identifies the algorithm.

docs.title: Watson statistic for the Laplace distribution
docs.text: WatsonLaplaceGofStatistic tests independent observations from Laplace(t, s) with both parameters fixed in advance. Its support is the real line. No parameters are fitted by execute_statistic.

docs.title: Parameters and usage
docs.text:
t=0.0 is a finite real scalar location; s=1.0 is a finite positive real scalar scale. rvs must be a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real numbers. A single observation, ties, and constant samples are accepted. Invalid inputs raise ValueError. The sample and model are not modified. execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) returns a scalar; extra keywords are ignored.

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import WatsonLaplaceGofStatistic

statistic = WatsonLaplaceGofStatistic(
    LaplaceDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"t": 0.0, "s": 1.0})
)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0])

docs.title: Formula and calibration
docs.text:
Let u_i = F_(t,s)(x_(i)), for sorted observations, i=1,...,n. The Laplace CDF is exp((x-t)/s)/2 for x<t and 1-exp(-(x-t)/s)/2 otherwise.

U² = W² - n*(mean(u)-1/2)**2, where
W² = 1/(12*n) + sum((u_i - (2*i-1)/(2*n))**2).
Computation uses the equivalent centered sum of squares of
u_i - (2*i-1)/(2*n) to avoid subtracting two large totals.
No finite-sample correction is applied. For n=1, U²=1/12
for every observation, so the statistic cannot discriminate.

Large values reject the null. These are exact definitions of the statistics, without asymptotic rescaling. Under the fixed continuous null the transformed observations are independent uniforms, so the null distribution depends on sample size, but not on t or s. hypothesis() nevertheless retains both fixed parameters. Monte Carlo calibration generates Laplace(t,s) samples and calls execute_statistic for each. Fitting parameters to the tested sample is outside this API and requires calibration accounting for fitting.

CDF rounding can erase very small tail spacings. AD evaluates analytic log probabilities, avoiding exponential underflow. Standardization avoids an intermediate overflow in x-t when the quotient is representable. Float64 range limitations still apply; a mathematically finite AD value can overflow. No observations or probabilities are clipped.

docs.title: Scientific source
docs.text:
M. A. Stephens (1974), "EDF Statistics for Goodness of Fit and Some Comparisons", JASA 69, 730-737, Section 2 (definitions and computation), Case 0 (fully specified continuous distribution). https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1974.10480196 Full text: https://www.math.utah.edu/~morris/Courses/6010/p1/writeup/ks.pdf

This source describes the general statistic. Here it is applied to the known Laplace CDF, not to a model fitted to the observations.

docs.title: Zhang Z_A test for the Laplace distribution
Description
docs.text: ZhangALaplaceGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim \operatorname{Laplace}(t,s)\). Its algorithm code is ZHANG_ZA_LAPLACE_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LaplaceDistributionDescriptor as Laplace
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.laplace import (
    ZhangALaplaceGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Laplace.DEFAULT.parse({"t": 0, "s": 1})
criterion = ZhangALaplaceGofStatistic(parameters)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([-2.0, -1.0, -0.2, 0.2, 1.0, 2.0])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with finite location t and positive finite scale s, both fixed before observing the sample. Missing parameters are unsupported. No parameters are estimated by this criterion.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

The support is the entire real line. Singletons, ties and constant samples are accepted. Empty, nonfinite, complex and multidimensional samples are rejected.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Writing \(z=(x-t)/s\), the Laplace CDF is \(F_{t,s}(x)=e^z/2\) for \(z<0\) and \(F_{t,s}(x)=1-e^{-z}/2\) otherwise. For a fixed continuous null the probability integral transform gives independent uniforms. Its null law depends on sample size, not the known location or scale. Parameters estimated from the sample require a different test and calibration with refitting in every replicate. Rounding-induced ties require a matching observation model during calibration.

Let \(u_i=F_{t,s}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ Z_A=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{\log u_i}{n-i+1/2}+\frac{\log(1-u_i)}{i-1/2}\right]. \]

This is Zhang (2002), equation (3.2). Analytic Laplace log-CDF and log-survival values avoid infinities caused solely by rounded CDF probabilities. Extreme statistics can still exceed float64 range.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

docs.title: Log-logistic goodness-of-fit statistics
docs.text:
The family has 20 concrete criteria: 13 EDF, 5 frequency and 2 fitted-model statistics. Mathematical verification records the formula audit, numerical checks, corrections and calibration limitations.

For \(x>0\) the distribution is

\[ F_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\frac1{1+(\alpha/x)^\beta},\qquad \alpha>0,\quad\beta>0. \]

Equivalently, \(\log X\) is logistic with location \(\log\alpha\) and scale \(1/\beta\). CDF and logarithmic tails are evaluated through logarithms to avoid overflow of \(x/\alpha\). All criteria reject for large values. Their output is a statistic, not a calibrated p-value.

docs.title: Parameters and examples
docs.text:
There are no implicit unit-scale/unit-shape defaults in the criterion constructor. The 18 generated criteria require both parameters; Nikulin and Mirvaliev require an empty parameter set. Each individual page contains a runnable example and scientific references. For example:

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_logistic import (
    AndersonDarlingLogLogisticGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": 1.0, "beta": 2.0})
statistic = AndersonDarlingLogLogisticGofStatistic(parameters)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.4, 2.5])
assert value >= 0

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For fixed parameters, the probability integral transform gives a uniform null for EDF statistics. Equal-probability frequency cells give multinomial counts with equal probabilities. Preserve sample size, the exact statistic normalization and the binning configuration in simulation. General binning strategies need calibration under the actual distribution. The default frequency interface is binning=EqualProbabilityBins(); the former bins keyword is not supported.

For Mirvaliev, refit log-moments in every replicate. For Nikulin, reproduce the censoring and observation scheme, refit the likelihood and recompute exposure intervals. Event flag 1 means failure. No built-in log-logistic generator is registered, so simulation is external. Critical values for fitted Weibull tests or fixed-parameter KS tests cannot be reused for these fitted criteria.

See binning and the verification report for sources and limitations.

docs.title: AndersonDarlingLogLogisticGofStatistic
docs.text:
Anderson–Darling for a fully specified log-logistic distribution.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": alpha, "beta": beta}) as parameters. Both scale alpha and shape beta must be fixed, finite and strictly positive. Neither parameter is estimated. The sample must be a nonempty, finite, strictly positive one-dimensional array; ties and a single observation are accepted. Censored samples are not supported. The returned value is a scalar statistic; large values reject the null (right tail).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For ordered observations, \(u_i=F_{\alpha,\beta}(x_{(i)})\), \(F_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=1/[1+(\alpha/x)^\beta]\) for \(x>0\). Write \(r_i=i-1/2\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\).

\[ A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})] \]

Logarithmic tails are evaluated directly from \(z=\beta(\log x-\log\alpha)\), without clipping probabilities. A result beyond float64 range can be positive infinity.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For a fixed continuous null, EDF statistics and equal-probability cell counts can be calibrated through independent Uniform(0,1) samples. Other binning rules require the actual null and the same rule in every replicate. A rounded-data null must reproduce rounding. Passing parameters estimated from this sample as fixed values does not account for fitting.

The library currently has no built-in log-logistic random generator: use external simulation (for example scipy.stats.fisk). This class computes a statistic, not a p-value. For frequency statistics, the chi-square law with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom is an asymptotic approximation for fixed cells with adequate expected counts, not an exact small-sample calibration. Binning is included in the frequency criterion's storage configuration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_logistic import (
    AndersonDarlingLogLogisticGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": 1.0, "beta": 1.0})
statistic = AndersonDarlingLogLogisticGofStatistic(parameters)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0])
assert value >= 0

docs.text: Zhang (2002), §§2–3 (full text); Anderson and Darling (1952)

The summand for \(O_j=0\) is zero by continuity.

docs.title: CramerVonMisesLogLogisticGofStatistic
docs.text:
Cramér–von Mises for a fully specified log-logistic distribution.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": alpha, "beta": beta}) as parameters. Both scale alpha and shape beta must be fixed, finite and strictly positive. Neither parameter is estimated. The sample must be a nonempty, finite, strictly positive one-dimensional array; ties and a single observation are accepted. Censored samples are not supported. The returned value is a scalar statistic; large values reject the null (right tail).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For ordered observations, \(u_i=F_{\alpha,\beta}(x_{(i)})\), \(F_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=1/[1+(\alpha/x)^\beta]\) for \(x>0\). Write \(r_i=i-1/2\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\).

\[ W^2=\frac1{12n}+\sum_{i=1}^n\left(u_i-\frac{i-1/2}{n}\right)^2 \]

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For a fixed continuous null, EDF statistics and equal-probability cell counts can be calibrated through independent Uniform(0,1) samples. Other binning rules require the actual null and the same rule in every replicate. A rounded-data null must reproduce rounding. Passing parameters estimated from this sample as fixed values does not account for fitting.

The library currently has no built-in log-logistic random generator: use external simulation (for example scipy.stats.fisk). This class computes a statistic, not a p-value. For frequency statistics, the chi-square law with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom is an asymptotic approximation for fixed cells with adequate expected counts, not an exact small-sample calibration. Binning is included in the frequency criterion's storage configuration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_logistic import (
    CramerVonMisesLogLogisticGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": 1.0, "beta": 1.0})
statistic = CramerVonMisesLogLogisticGofStatistic(parameters)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0])
assert value >= 0

Freeman–Tukey for a fully specified log-logistic distribution.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": alpha, "beta": beta}) as parameters. Both scale alpha and shape beta must be fixed, finite and strictly positive. Neither parameter is estimated. \[ T=4\sum_j(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j})^2 \]

Here \(O_j\) are observed cell counts and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are null expected counts, with equal totals. The keyword binning accepts a BinningStrategy. The default EqualProbabilityBins() uses PowerCount() (at least two cells, approximately \(2n^{0.4}\), rounded up, subject to max_bins). To fix the number, use EqualProbabilityBins(5). Internal boundaries belong to the cell on the right. The default does not merge small expected counts. See binning strategies.

An empty observed cell contributes \(4E_j\).

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": alpha, "beta": beta}) as parameters. Both scale alpha and shape beta must be fixed, finite and strictly positive. Neither parameter is estimated. docs.title: Mathematical verification of log-logistic statistics
docs.text: Audit date: 2026-10-17. All 20 concrete criteria in log_logistic/log_logistic_statistics.py were reviewed: 13 generated EDF statistics, 5 generated frequency statistics and the 2 fitted-model statistics Nikulin and Mirvaliev. The report follows the uniformity verification report. The catalog links to an individual page for every criterion.

docs.title: Formula checks
docs.text:
Write \(u_i=F_{\alpha,\beta}(x_{(i)})\) and \(r_i=i-1/2\). For positive observations,

\[ z_i=\beta(\log x_i-\log\alpha),\qquad F(x_i)=\operatorname{expit}(z_i),\quad \log F(x_i)=-\log(1+e^{-z_i}),\quad \log S(x_i)=-\log(1+e^{z_i}). \]

The implementation uses logaddexp for the last two expressions. The generated criteria require both parameters fixed. The two bespoke criteria require both unknown; hypothesis support is declared separately by each concrete criterion.

Criteria (number) Checked definition Scientific source KS D+, D−, D (3) \(D^+=\max(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max(u_i-(i-1)/n)\), \(D=\max(D^+,D^-)\); no square or scaling Zhang (2002), §2.1 Anderson–Darling (1) Weighted logarithmic sum, factor \(1/n\), subtraction of \(n\) Anderson and Darling (1952); Zhang (2002), §2.2 Cramér–von Mises (1) \(1/(12n)+\sum(u_i-r_i/n)^2\) Zhang (2002), §2.3 Watson (1) \(W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2\), evaluated with centered deviations Watson (1961); Lemeshko et al. (2014), eq. (6) Kuiper, scaled, corrected (3) \(V=D^++D^-\), \(\sqrt nV\), \((\sqrt n+0.155+0.24/\sqrt n)V\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), eqs. (1)–(3) Zhang K, A, C (3) Half-rank likelihood ratios and quarter-rank log-odds correction Zhang (2002), eqs. (3.1)–(3.3) Liao–Shimokawa (1) \(n^{-1/2}\sum_i\max(i/n-u_i,u_i-(i-1)/n)/\sqrt{u_i(1-u_i)}\) Liao and Shimokawa (1999); Al-Zahrani (2012), eq. (13) Pearson, Freeman–Tukey, modified log-likelihood, Neyman, Cressie–Read (5) Power-divergence family at \(\lambda=1,-1/2,-1,-2,2/3\); zero-count limits checked explicitly Cressie and Read (1984) Bagdonavicius–Nikulin (1) Exposure residuals and information correction with an observed-count denominator Bagdonavicius and Nikulin (2011), §§3–5 Mirvaliev (1) Moment-fitted logistic quadratic form applied to \(\log X\) Pya (2004), pp. 70–71, eqs. (8)–(15)

No algebraic changes were needed to the statistic kernels checked here. All criteria reject in the right tail; directional KS refers to CDF deviation, not to the rejection tail of the returned nonnegative statistic.

docs.title: Bagdonavicius–Nikulin derivation
docs.text:
With \(z=(\log t-\mu)/s\), the hazard is \(h(t)=F(t)/(st)\) and cumulative hazard is \(H(t)=\log(1+e^z)\). The implemented hazard-score coordinates are \((-S,-1-zS)\), an invertible rescaling of the location/log-scale score at the fit. Consequently the quadratic form is unchanged by this coordinate choice.

Boundaries equalize \(\sum_i\min(H(t_i),H(a_j))\). With event counts \(U_j\), exposures \(e_j\), \(Z=(U-e)/\sqrt n\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(U/n)\), cell score sums \(C\) divided by \(n\), and event score outer products \(I\) divided by \(n\), the implementation returns

\[ Z^TA^{-1}Z+(CA^{-1}Z)^T(I-CA^{-1}C^T)^{-1}(CA^{-1}Z). \]

Within-cell centering computes the latter matrix without cancellation. An independent reference uses SciPy's censored logistic likelihood fit, numerically integrates exposure over the risk sets, and inverts \(A-C^TI^{-1}C\) directly. Agreement verifies both the coordinate change and Woodbury rearrangement. Empty event cells return infinity; singular or ill-conditioned correction matrices raise an error instead of being regularized.

docs.title: Mirvaliev derivation
docs.text:
Standardized logs use the sample variance with divisor \(n\). For the unit-variance logistic null, \(E[Y^4]=21/5\), hence \(V=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^2-1)=\operatorname{diag}(1,16/5)\) and \(K=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\). The implemented matrices give

\[ A=I-qq^T+C(V-C^TC)^{-1}C^T,\quad D=C-BK^{-1}V,\quad L=V+D^TAD, \]

and \(v^TAv-(D^TAv)^TL^{-1}(D^TAv)\) for standardized cell residuals \(v\). This reproduces Pya's moment-based correction in standardized coordinates. An independent check constructs the covariance of fitted cell residuals from integrals of the mean/standard-deviation influence functions and evaluates its pseudoinverse quadratic form. No normal-distribution fourth moment is substituted.

docs.title: Numerical correction found during the audit
docs.text:
The shared distribution adapter previously delegated log-logistic probabilities to SciPy's Fisk evaluator, which could underflow the ratio \(x/\alpha\) before applying a small shape exponent. For alpha=1e250, beta=0.001, sample [1e-40, 1e-60, 1e-100, 1e-250] and ten equal-probability cells, Pearson returned 16 instead of 21. Freeman–Tukey and Cressie–Read were also affected. The problem was in cell assignment, not their discrepancy formulas.

The log-logistic bound distribution now evaluates CDF, SF, log-CDF and log-SF from log odds. It retains support limits and NaN propagation. This also repairs premature infinite log probabilities: at alpha=1, beta=2, x=1e-250, logcdf is approximately −1151.292546497, not negative infinity. EDF kernels already used stable log odds and did not require this correction. Old calibrations or results computed in the affected numerical regimes should be regenerated; ordinary-range definitions and normalizations are unchanged.

docs.title: Sources and qualifications
docs.text:
Full text was inspected for Zhang, Lemeshko et al., Bagdonavicius–Nikulin and Pya. Cressie–Read's publisher summary identifies the five divergence parameters; their formulas and limiting zero-count contributions were additionally checked algebraically and against SciPy.

The original Liao–Shimokawa full text was inaccessible in this audit. Its bibliography and fitted-model scope were checked, and the expression was compared with its use in Al-Zahrani's published study. The implementation uses a local maximum of two deviations at each observation. This is a fixed-null log-logistic adaptation; original fitted-Weibull critical values do not apply. The original Mirvaliev (2001) paper was not inspected: the logistic application is checked against Pya (2004), then transferred through the logarithm.

These checks establish agreement of the calculations with the stated definitions on the tested domains. They do not prove finite-sample significance levels, omnibus consistency of every discrepancy, or power against every alternative. Ties are computable but continuous-null critical values are not automatically valid for rounded data. Frequency chi-square approximations require appropriate cell counts and assumptions. Neither default bin count nor Kuiper correction makes an asymptotic reference exact.

Nikulin uses the sample maximum as the observation horizon. The source assumes an observation scheme and regularity conditions; no exact finite-sample law for this random horizon is asserted. External calibration must reproduce censoring, observation/stopping, fitting and grouping. Mirvaliev supports only complete data and must refit moments in simulation. The package has no registered log-logistic random generator; the generic Monte Carlo resolver is therefore unavailable.

docs.title: Numerical verification and documentation coverage
docs.text:
The focused suite passed 230 tests across:

  • tests/distributions/test_log_logistic.py;
  • tests/distributions/test_log_logistic_correctness.py;
  • tests/distributions/test_log_logistic_mathematical_validation.py.

References include EDF integrals (AD, CvM, Watson), SciPy KS and multinomial power divergences, 250-digit Decimal tail calculations, independent fitted-model covariance expressions, censored likelihood fits and risk integrals. Checks cover all 20 criteria, fixed/unknown parameter contracts, transformations, unsorted input, ties, singletons, invalid data, empty cells, extreme scales, nonmutation and calibration restrictions.

The documentation check finds exactly one page per concrete class, verifies its catalog and navigation entry and scientific URL, and executes every individual page's Python example. Generated class docstrings also have executable examples. There are 20 criterion pages, one catalog and this report; six existing criterion URLs are preserved. Formula, hypothesis, input, rejection direction, binning and calibration information are included.

Ordinary test collection is currently blocked by an unrelated pre-existing NameError: AbstractCrammerVonMisesStatistic in continuous/log_normal.py. The focused run supplies the continuous package path without executing its aggregate __init__.py; the actual log-logistic module, factories, kernels and probability adapter execute normally. Thus these results do not certify that ordinary package initialization succeeds in the current working tree.

The shared probability-evaluation suite additionally passed 50 tests after the adapter correction. Ruff and whitespace checks passed for the changed code. MkDocs built the site successfully; its six broken-link warnings concern pre-existing Weibull audit links, not the log-logistic section.

To reproduce the isolated focused run from the repository root:

import types

]

docs.title: Numba optimization follow-up
docs.text:
The 18 generated criteria retain the compiled shared EDF/frequency kernels. Local numerical work now uses @jit(nopython=True, cache=True) for CDF and log probabilities, Nikulin likelihood terms and exposure/information accumulation, and Mirvaliev moment integrands, fitted cell residuals and the final quadratic form. Validation, SciPy optimization/quadrature and checked matrix solves remain Python orchestration. All helpers in log_logistic/log_logistic_statistics.py are class methods.

Mirvaliev caches only distribution-dependent edges, derivatives and integrals by interval count (LRU bound: 32 entries); cached arrays are read-only. Sample moments and residuals are recomputed for every call. Nikulin reduces likelihood terms with NumPy to preserve its pairwise summation and optimizer convergence. No fast-math mode or relaxed optimizer tolerance is used.

A local warm-cache measurement used 1,000 observations from exp(default_rng(13).logistic(size=1000)), default criterion settings, and the minimum of three batches of 20 calls. Compilation was excluded:

Criterion Before After Approximate speedup Anderson–Darling 0.054 ms 0.053 ms No material change Nikulin 2.20 ms 1.90 ms 1.16× Mirvaliev 0.478 ms 0.111 ms 4.3×

These timings describe this machine and sample, not a universal performance bound. First-call compilation and uncached quadrature cost extra. Values agree with the original implementation within floating-point precision on this sample. The expanded focused suite passes 237 tests, including independent likelihood/finite-difference gradient checks, nopython compilation of every local numerical kernel and all generated criteria, bounded/read-only cache behavior, and absence of module-level helper functions. The ordinary-import limitation noted above still applies.

docs.title: MirvalievLogLogisticGofStatistic
docs.text:
Mirvaliev moment-fitted statistic on log-transformed complete data.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameters: pass LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). Both alpha and beta are unknown and are fitted anew on every execution. Partially or fully fixed parameters are unsupported.

n_intervals : int, optional Number of equiprobable cells, at least 2; default 8.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return a scalar discrepancy. hypothesis() Return the fixed parameters; omitted parameters are unknown.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Apply equations (8)-(10) of [1] to log(X), a logistic location-scale family. Fit its mean and standard deviation with divisor n, per call. Both log-logistic parameters are unknown. In unit-variance coordinates, cell residuals are v_j=(N_j-n/r)/sqrt(n/r), q_j=1/sqrt®. B contains fixed-boundary probability derivatives divided by sqrt(p). C contains cell integrals of (Y, Y²-1) divided by sqrt(p), V=diag(1,16/5), K=diag(1,2). Set A=I-qq'+C(V-C'C)^-1 C', D=C-B K^-1 V, L=V+D' A D. Return v' A v-v' A D L^-1 D' A v. Integrals are evaluated by adaptive quadrature. These are logistic moments, not normal moments. No MLE or survival-hazard correction is used. Reject large values. Log-location/scale invariance justifies simulation at alpha=beta=1 with refitting. Preserve n and r. The asymptotic chi-square(r-1) statement in [1] is not an exact finite-sample law. No built-in log-logistic generator exists; Monte Carlo is external. Storage omits r and is blocked; discard old MIRVALIEV calibrations. The cited paper treats logistic data; logarithms give the log-logistic application. A source for the former censored version was not found; censored observations now raise ValueError. No fitted state is retained.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] N. Pya (2004), "Goodness-of-fit tests for the logistic distribution", Mathematical Journal 4(2), 68-75, equations (8)-(10). Source

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_logistic import (
    MirvalievLogLogisticGofStatistic,
)

statistic = MirvalievLogLogisticGofStatistic(LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}))
value = statistic.execute_statistic(np.exp(np.linspace(-2, 2, 100)))
bool(np.isfinite(value))

docs.title: Input and result
docs.text: Compute the statistic independently for the supplied sample.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: rvs : array_like Positive finite 1D times (at least three, not constant), or (times, delta) with matching binary indicators, 1 for events. All indicators must be one; censoring is unsupported. **kwargs : dict Accepted for the common interface; unused.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: statistic : float or numpy.float64 Nonnegative discrepancy; larger values reject the null.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ValueError Invalid sample or singular correction matrix. RuntimeError Numerical failure produces a negative quadratic form.

docs.title: Calibration and interpretation
docs.text: The moment fit is to \(\log X\), not to \(X\): with \(m=\overline{\log X}\) and \(s^2=n^{-1}\sum(\log X_i-m)^2\), the implied parameters are \(\hat\alpha=e^m\) and \(\hat\beta=\pi/(\sqrt3s)\). Computation uses standardized logs and need not form these possibly overflowing parameters. This applies the logistic statistic in Pya (2004) after the invertible logarithm transformation. It is not a censored-data extension. At a fixed number of cells, the source's limiting law is \(\chi^2_{r-1}\) under its assumptions; calibrate finite samples externally with moment fitting repeated in every replicate.

docs.title: ModifiedLogLikelihoodLogLogisticGofStatistic
docs.text:
Modified log-likelihood for a fully specified log-logistic distribution.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": alpha, "beta": beta}) as parameters. Both scale alpha and shape beta must be fixed, finite and strictly positive. Neither parameter is estimated. The sample must be a nonempty, finite, strictly positive one-dimensional array; ties and a single observation are accepted. Censored samples are not supported. The returned value is a scalar statistic; large values reject the null (right tail).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For ordered observations, \(u_i=F_{\alpha,\beta}(x_{(i)})\), \(F_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=1/[1+(\alpha/x)^\beta]\) for \(x>0\). Write \(r_i=i-1/2\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\).

\[ T=2\sum_j E_j\log(E_j/O_j) \]

Here \(O_j\) are observed cell counts and \(E_j=np_j>0\) are null expected counts, with equal totals. The keyword binning accepts a BinningStrategy. The default EqualProbabilityBins() uses PowerCount() (at least two cells, approximately \(2n^{0.4}\), rounded up, subject to max_bins). To fix the number, use EqualProbabilityBins(5). Internal boundaries belong to the cell on the right. The default does not merge small expected counts. See binning strategies.

An empty observed cell with positive expectation returns positive infinity.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For a fixed continuous null, EDF statistics and equal-probability cell counts can be calibrated through independent Uniform(0,1) samples. Other binning rules require the actual null and the same rule in every replicate. A rounded-data null must reproduce rounding. Passing parameters estimated from this sample as fixed values does not account for fitting.

The library currently has no built-in log-logistic random generator: use external simulation (for example scipy.stats.fisk). This class computes a statistic, not a p-value. For frequency statistics, the chi-square law with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom is an asymptotic approximation for fixed cells with adequate expected counts, not an exact small-sample calibration. Binning is included in the frequency criterion's storage configuration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_logistic import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodLogLogisticGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins

parameters = Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": 1.0, "beta": 1.0})
statistic = ModifiedLogLikelihoodLogLogisticGofStatistic(
    parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(4)
)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0])
assert value >= 0

docs.text: Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests

docs.title: NikulinLogLogisticGofStatistic
docs.text:
Bagdonavicius-Nikulin statistic with fitted log-logistic survival.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameters: pass LogLogisticDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). Both alpha and beta are unknown and are fitted anew on every execution. Partially or fully fixed parameters are unsupported.

n_intervals : int, optional Number of equal-exposure intervals, at least 2; default 5.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return a scalar discrepancy. hypothesis() Return the fixed parameters; omitted parameters are unknown.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Both alpha and beta are unknown. Each call fits the right-censored likelihood in standardized log-time location and log-scale coordinates. Non-informative right censoring is assumed; delta=1 denotes an event. H(t)=logaddexp(0, betalog(t/alpha)); hence h(t)=betaF(t)/t. Section 5 of [1] chooses boundaries with sum_i min(H(t_i), H(a_j)) equal to j/k times total exposure, so all e_j equal total/k. In Sections 3-4, Z=(U-e)/sqrt(n), A=diag(U/n), C contains cell sums of event hazard scores divided by n, and I their outer-product mean. Return Z'A^-1 Z + W'G^-1 W, W=C A^-1 Z, G=I-C A^-1 C'. Scores use equivalent location/log-scale coordinates. G is calculated by within-cell centering, without a ridge or pseudoinverse. Empty event cells have positive exposure and return infinity. Singular or ill-conditioned G is rejected. Small samples need fewer intervals. Reject large values. The paper gives an asymptotic chi-square result under regularity conditions; finite-sample calibration must reproduce censoring, interval count and refitting. Generic Monte Carlo and storage are blocked: they cannot express the censoring plan. Old BN_GOF calibration values must be discarded. No estimates are retained.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] V. Bagdonavicius and M. Nikulin (2011), "Chi-squared tests for general composite hypotheses from censored samples", Sections 3-5. Source Source

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: rvs : array_like Positive finite 1D times (at least three, not constant), or (times, delta) with matching binary indicators, 1 for events. Nikulin requires at least three events at two distinct times. **kwargs : dict Accepted for the common interface; unused.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: statistic : float or numpy.float64 Nonnegative discrepancy; larger values reject the null. Positive infinity when any event cell is empty.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ValueError Invalid sample or singular correction matrix. RuntimeError No finite MLE converges.

docs.title: Calibration and interpretation
docs.text: This is the Bagdonavicius–Nikulin survival statistic, not the complete-data Nikulin–Rao–Robson multinomial statistic. An event flag of 1 means observed failure, and 0 means right censoring. Without flags all observations are events. The risk integral includes censored exposure. Intervals are \((a_{j-1},a_j]\), so an event on an internal boundary belongs to the preceding interval. The implementation uses the last observed time as its observation horizon. The article's asymptotic result requires regularity and an appropriate observation scheme; this implementation does not establish an exact null law for a random sample-maximum horizon. Use external calibration reproducing censoring, stopping, grouping and parameter fitting.

\[ Z_C=\sum_i\left[\log\frac{1-u_i}{u_i}-\log\frac{n-i+1/4}{i-3/4}\right]^2 \]

Logarithmic tails are evaluated directly from \(z=\beta(\log x-\log\alpha)\), without clipping probabilities. A result beyond float64 range can be positive infinity.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For a fixed continuous null, EDF statistics and equal-probability cell counts can be calibrated through independent Uniform(0,1) samples. Other binning rules require the actual null and the same rule in every replicate. A rounded-data null must reproduce rounding. Passing parameters estimated from this sample as fixed values does not account for fitting.

The library currently has no built-in log-logistic random generator: use external simulation (for example scipy.stats.fisk). This class computes a statistic, not a p-value. For frequency statistics, the chi-square law with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom is an asymptotic approximation for fixed cells with adequate expected counts, not an exact small-sample calibration. Binning is included in the frequency criterion's storage configuration.

)

parameters = Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": 1.0, "beta": 1.0})
statistic = ZhangCLogLogisticGofStatistic(parameters)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0])
assert value >= 0

docs.title: ZhangKLogLogisticGofStatistic
docs.text:
Zhang K for a fully specified log-logistic distribution.

All log-logistic criteria · Mathematical verification

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({"alpha": alpha, "beta": beta}) as parameters. Both scale alpha and shape beta must be fixed, finite and strictly positive. Neither parameter is estimated. The sample must be a nonempty, finite, strictly positive one-dimensional array; ties and a single observation are accepted. Censored samples are not supported. The returned value is a scalar statistic; large values reject the null (right tail).

docs.title: Log-normal goodness-of-fit statistics
docs.text: All 55 concrete statistics exported by continuous.log_normal are listed below. There are 15 EDF variants, 5 frequency statistics, one spacing statistic, 32 logarithmic normality wrappers and two KL functionals. The abstract base is not itself a test. Every row links to a formula, executable example and scientific sources; the mathematical verification distinguishes verified definitions from unresolved historical attribution.

docs.title: Choosing the hypothesis
docs.text:
• Fixed: LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({"mu": 0.4, "s": 0.8}) or LogNormal.SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": 0.8, "scale": exp(0.4)}). These 21 criteria test a specified CDF; s is log standard deviation, mu is log mean and scale is the median. The mean of X is exp(mu+s²/2).
  • Family: LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({}). The 34 shape criteria remove log-location and log-scale. Fully fixed schemas remain accepted for API compatibility, but their values are ignored by the shape statistic. These criteria cannot distinguish log-normal laws with different parameters.
  • Omitted parameters are never silently filled into a hypothesis. Both coordinate schemas are supported, partial schemas are rejected, and hypothesis() preserves the input. Family calibration explicitly chooses mu=0,s=1 for sampling; it does not change the hypothesis.

All inputs must be finite, real, one-dimensional and unmasked. Logarithmic statistics additionally require strictly positive observations and sufficient nonconstant log data; individual pages state their minimum sizes. EDF statistics may assign a finite discrepancy to out-of-support data. Frequency zero-count limits may legitimately be infinite. Undefined input raises ValueError.

import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogNormalDistributionDescriptor as LogNormal
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_normal import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovLogNormalGofStatistic,
    ShapiroWilkLogNormalGofStatistic,
)
from pysatl_criterion.utils.generator import get_hypothesis_generator

sample = np.exp([-1.3, -0.8, -0.4, -0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9, 1.4, 2.0])
fixed = KolmogorovSmirnovLogNormalGofStatistic(LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({"mu": 0, "s": 1}))
family = ShapiroWilkLogNormalGofStatistic(LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({}))
assert np.isfinite(fixed.execute_statistic(sample))
assert np.isfinite(family.execute_statistic(sample))
assert family.hypothesis().parameters() == {}
assert get_hypothesis_generator(family).parameters() == {"mu": 0, "s": 1}

docs.title: Calibration and limitations
docs.text: Fixed-CDF EDF formulas use u=F(X); fitted-normal tables do not apply. Family statistics reuse the normality functional on log observations. Their normality approximations and qualifications remain applicable: particularly Hosking 1–4, GLB, Coin and finite-order moment tests. KL uses a finite r window; its legacy critical-value regressions are not certified. The report explains what was independently checked and what remains unverified. Recalibrate changed statistics; old unversioned stored values are not evidence of correct size.

docs.title: Anderson-Darling test for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: AndersonDarlingLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: AD_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
Both parameters must be supplied before observing the sample: mu is the mean of log(X), s > 0 is its standard deviation. The alternative coordinates are s and scale = exp(mu), the median, not the mean of X. Use LOG_LOCATION_SCALE.parse({"mu": ..., "s": ...}) or SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": ..., "scale": ...}). Partial and empty hypotheses are rejected. No parameters are fitted to the sample.

The sample must be nonempty, finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected. Ties are permitted. EDF/spacing formulas use the null CDF, which is zero at nonpositive observations; finite penalties are possible. This is not the same policy as logarithmic family statistics, which reject such input.

docs.title: Statistic
docs.text:
Set \(u_i=\Phi((\log x_{(i)}-\mu)/s)\) for positive observations. The following general EDF definition is evaluated at these fixed-null probabilities.

Anderson-Darling A² statistic.

Computes -n-sum((2i-1)(log(u_i)+log(1-u_(n+1-i))))/n. Endpoints give positive infinity; no finite-sample correction is applied.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Anderson, T. W., and Darling, D. A. (1952). Asymptotic Theory of Certain Goodness of Fit Criteria Based on Stochastic Processes. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 23(2), 193-212. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177729437 Computational form: Zhang (2002), Section 2.2. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00337

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. Use the fixed null and the same sample size, settings and binning for calibration. Do not substitute fitted-normality tables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogNormalDistributionDescriptor as LogNormal
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_normal import (
    AndersonDarlingLogNormalGofStatistic,
)

parameters = LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({"mu": 0.4, "s": 0.8})
statistic = AndersonDarlingLogNormalGofStatistic(parameters)
sample = np.exp([-1.7, -1.2, -0.9, -0.6, -0.3, -0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.1])
value = statistic.execute_statistic(sample)
assert np.isfinite(value)
