docs.title: Bonett-Seier test for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: BonettSeierLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: BS_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Logarithmic reduction
docs.text: The implementation computes BonettSeierNormalityGofStatistic on y = log(rvs) with an empty normal-family hypothesis. Thus its formula, sample-size limits, normalization and rejection tail are exactly those of the normality statistic at its default settings. Constructor-specific normality options are not exposed by this wrapper. The identity was checked on normal, nonnormal and tied logarithmic samples and under transformations X -> exp(a) * X**b, b > 0.

docs.title: Underlying normality definition
docs.text:
In this section, x denotes y = log(X), not the original positive sample. The normal-family hypothesis and dispersion conventions below concern these log observations. See also the normality source page.

H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Both tails of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

The factor sqrt(n+2), the population sample variance (ddof=0), and the two-sided rejection rule agree with equations (5)–(6) of the original article.

Let d=mean(abs(x-mean(x))) and omega=13.29log(s0/d). Return sqrt(n+2)(omega-3)/3.54, a signed kurtosis transform. The constants are rounded approximations; use finite-sample simulation.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] Bonett, D. G. and Seier, E. (2002). A test of normality with high uniform power. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 40(3), 435-445. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-9473(02)00074-9

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: two_tailed. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. For the composite null, simulation can use log-normal mu=0, s=1 because log-location and log-scale are removed by the statistic. Every replicate must call execute_statistic again. This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

docs.text:

    BonettSeierLogNormalGofStatistic,

statistic = BonettSeierLogNormalGofStatistic(parameters)
sample = np.exp([-1.7, -1.2, -0.9, -0.6, -0.3, -0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.1])

docs.text:
Class: CabanaCabana1LogNormalGofStatistic

Code: CC1_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Logarithmic reduction
docs.text: The implementation computes CabanaCabana1NormalityGofStatistic on y = log(rvs) with an empty normal-family hypothesis. Thus its formula, sample-size limits, normalization and rejection tail are exactly those of the normality statistic at its default settings. Constructor-specific normality options are not exposed by this wrapper. The identity was checked on normal, nonnormal and tied logarithmic samples and under transformations X -> exp(a) * X**b, b > 0.

docs.title: Underlying normality definition
docs.text:
In this section, x denotes y = log(X), not the original positive sample. The normal-family hypothesis and dispersion conventions below concern these log observations. See also the normality source page.

H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Use the l=5 process in Cabana and Cabana, equation (7). For z=(x-mean(x))/s1, h_j=He_j/sqrt(j!), H_j=sum(h_j(z))/sqrt(n), P(t)=sum_{j=1..5}(h_(j-1)(t)H_(j+3)/sqrt(j)). Return sup_t abs(Phi(t)H_3-phi(t)P(t)). Evaluate every real stationary point (roots of H_3+tP-P') and both limits at infinity. This is the supremum of the truncated process, not the untruncated infinite series. Polynomial root solving is subject to float64 accuracy.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] Cabaña, A. and Cabaña, E. M. (2003). Tests of Normality Based on Transformed Empirical Processes. Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability, 5, 309-335. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1026235220018

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. For the composite null, simulation can use log-normal mu=0, s=1 because log-location and log-scale are removed by the statistic. Every replicate must call execute_statistic again. This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

docs.title: Pearson chi-squared for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: Chi2PearsonLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: CHI2_PEARSON_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
Both parameters must be supplied before observing the sample: mu is the mean of log(X), s > 0 is its standard deviation. The alternative coordinates are s and scale = exp(mu), the median, not the mean of X. Use LOG_LOCATION_SCALE.parse({"mu": ..., "s": ...}) or SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": ..., "scale": ...}). Partial and empty hypotheses are rejected. No parameters are fitted to the sample.

The sample must be nonempty, finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected. Ties are permitted. EDF/spacing formulas use the null CDF, which is zero at nonpositive observations; finite penalties are possible. This is not the same policy as logarithmic family statistics, which reject such input.

docs.title: Statistic and binning
docs.text: Pearson chi-square: sum((observed - expected)**2 / expected).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Pearson, K. (1900). On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling. Philosophical Magazine, 50(302), 157-175. https://doi.org/10.1080/14786440009463897

The constructor accepts binning: BinningStrategy; its default is EqualProbabilityBins(). Bins use the fixed log-normal distribution in the original sample units. Define observed counts O_j and expected counts E_j = n * P(X in cell j). The zero-count limits are part of the definition; Neyman and modified log-likelihood can return positive infinity when O_j=0<E_j. A positive observed count in a zero-probability cell gives infinity. For a fixed partition with k positive-probability cells, the usual multinomial asymptotic reference has k-1 degrees of freedom. Adaptive bins require calibration of the entire bin-building procedure; no automatic k-3 correction is justified.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. Use the fixed null and the same sample size, settings and binning for calibration. Do not substitute fitted-normality tables.

docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Logarithmic reduction
docs.text: The implementation computes DAPNormalityGofStatistic on y = log(rvs) with an empty normal-family hypothesis. Thus its formula, sample-size limits, normalization and rejection tail are exactly those of the normality statistic at its default settings. Constructor-specific normality options are not exposed by this wrapper. The identity was checked on normal, nonnormal and tied logarithmic samples and under transformations X -> exp(a) * X**b, b > 0.

docs.title: Underlying normality definition
docs.text:
In this section, x denotes y = log(X), not the original positive sample. The normal-family hypothesis and dispersion conventions below concern these log observations. See also the normality source page.

H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. The upper tail of the statistic defines rejection. Use at least 8 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

K2 = Z_skew2 + Z_kurtosis2 using the signed transforms implemented by SkewNormalityGofStatistic and KurtosisNormalityGofStatistic. The resulting nonnegative discrepancy uses the upper tail.

docs.title: References
docs.text: .. [1] D'Agostino, R. B. and Pearson, E. S. (1973). Tests for departure from normality. Empirical results for the distributions of b2 and sqrt(b1). Biometrika, 60(3), 613-622. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/60.3.613

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. For the composite null, simulation can use log-normal mu=0, s=1 because log-location and log-scale are removed by the statistic. Every replicate must call execute_statistic again. This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogNormalDistributionDescriptor as LogNormal
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_normal import (
    DAPLogNormalGofStatistic,
)

parameters = LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({})
statistic = DAPLogNormalGofStatistic(parameters)
sample = np.exp([-1.7, -1.2, -0.9, -0.6, -0.3, -0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.1])
value = statistic.execute_statistic(sample)

docs.title: Freeman–Tukey for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: FreemanTukeyLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: FREEMAN_TUKEY_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
Both parameters must be supplied before observing the sample: mu is the mean of log(X), s > 0 is its standard deviation. The alternative coordinates are s and scale = exp(mu), the median, not the mean of X. Use LOG_LOCATION_SCALE.parse({"mu": ..., "s": ...}) or SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": ..., "scale": ...}). Partial and empty hypotheses are rejected. No parameters are fitted to the sample.

The sample must be nonempty, finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected. Ties are permitted. EDF/spacing formulas use the null CDF, which is zero at nonpositive observations; finite penalties are possible. This is not the same policy as logarithmic family statistics, which reject such input.

docs.title: Statistic and binning
docs.text:
Freeman-Tukey: 4 * sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))**2).

Zero observed counts contribute 4 * expected to the statistic.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Cressie, N. and Read, T. R. C. (1984). Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests. JRSS B, 46(3), 440-464; power divergence with lambda = -½. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1984.tb01318.x

The constructor accepts binning: BinningStrategy; its default is EqualProbabilityBins(). Bins use the fixed log-normal distribution in the original sample units. Define observed counts O_j and expected counts E_j = n * P(X in cell j). The zero-count limits are part of the definition; Neyman and modified log-likelihood can return positive infinity when O_j=0<E_j. A positive observed count in a zero-probability cell gives infinity. For a fixed partition with k positive-probability cells, the usual multinomial asymptotic reference has k-1 degrees of freedom. Adaptive bins require calibration of the entire bin-building procedure; no automatic k-3 correction is justified.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. Use the fixed null and the same sample size, settings and binning for calibration. Do not substitute fitted-normality tables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogNormalDistributionDescriptor as LogNormal
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_normal import (
    FreemanTukeyLogNormalGofStatistic,
)

parameters = LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({"mu": 0.4, "s": 0.8})
statistic = FreemanTukeyLogNormalGofStatistic(parameters)

docs.text:
Class: KLIntegralLogNormalGoFStatistic

Code: KL_INT_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Statistic
docs.text:
At least two positive, nonconstant observations are required. Set \(y_i=\log x_i\), \(z_i=(y_i-\bar y)/s_0\) with \(s_0^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\). Define

\[K(r)=\log\left(n^{-1}\sum_i e^{r z_i}\right),\qquad D(r)=2K(r)-rK'(r),$$ $$\sigma^2(r)=e^{r^2}(r^4-3r^2+4)-(4+r^2),\qquad R(r)=D(r)/\sigma(r).\]

The returned value is \(n\int_{-5}^5 R(r)^2\,dr\), computed with adaptive quadrature split at zero (absolute and relative tolerance 1e-9). It is a truncated integral; no bound on the omitted infinite tails is asserted.

Centering cancels from D exactly. The implementation avoids forming powers of X and uses log-sum-exp. Near zero it uses cumulants through order 10 and a positive-coefficient variance series. If m3 = mean(z**3), \(\lim_{r\downarrow0}R(r)=-m_3/\sqrt6\) and \(\lim_{r\to0}R(r)^2=m_3^2/6\). This removes the spurious 0/0 singularity.

docs.title: Critical values and source limitations
docs.text: calculate_critical_value(n, alpha) retains the historical numerical regressions at alpha=0.01 and 0.05. These are not verified finite-sample quantiles. Their published validity range and compatibility with this truncated implementation have not been established from accessible full text. Do not use them as a certified significance rule. Invalid n/alpha and nonpositive or nonfinite regression outputs are rejected; other significance levels raise NotImplementedError, because the old generic formula could produce negative critical values. Prefer Monte Carlo simulation of this exact implementation at the actual sample size.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Batsidis, Economou and Tzavelas (2016), Tests of fit for a lognormal distribution, Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation 86(2), 215–235. The publisher abstract verifies the KL size-bias symmetry motivation; full text was inaccessible. The formulas above were checked independently with 70-digit arithmetic and quadrature, not certified as an exact reproduction of every normalization and integration domain in that paper.

If m3 = mean(z**3), \(\lim_{r\downarrow0}R(r)=-m_3/\sqrt6\) and \(\lim_{r\to0}R(r)^2=m_3^2/6\). This removes the spurious 0/0 singularity.

docs.title: Critical values and source limitations
docs.text: calculate_critical_value(n, alpha) retains the historical numerical regressions at alpha=0.01 and 0.05. These are not verified finite-sample quantiles. Their published validity range and compatibility with this truncated implementation have not been established from accessible full text. Do not use them as a certified significance rule. Invalid n/alpha and nonpositive or nonfinite regression outputs are rejected; other significance levels raise NotImplementedError, because the old generic formula could produce negative critical values. Prefer Monte Carlo simulation of this exact implementation at the actual sample size.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Batsidis, Economou and Tzavelas (2016), Tests of fit for a lognormal distribution, Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation 86(2), 215–235. The publisher abstract verifies the KL size-bias symmetry motivation; full text was inaccessible. The formulas above were checked independently with 70-digit arithmetic and quadrature, not certified as an exact reproduction of every normalization and integration domain in that paper.

docs.text:
Class: KurtosisLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: KURTOSIS_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Logarithmic reduction
docs.text: The implementation computes KurtosisNormalityGofStatistic on y = log(rvs) with an empty normal-family hypothesis. Thus its formula, sample-size limits, normalization and rejection tail are exactly those of the normality statistic at its default settings. Constructor-specific normality options are not exposed by this wrapper. The identity was checked on normal, nonnormal and tied logarithmic samples and under transformations X -> exp(a) * X**b, b > 0.

docs.title: Underlying normality definition
docs.text:
In this section, x denotes y = log(X), not the original positive sample. The normal-family hypothesis and dispersion conventions below concern these log observations. See also the normality source page.

H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Both tails of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 5 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Return the signed Anscombe-Glynn transform of g2=m4/m2**2, using the finite-n expectation, variance and skewness of g2. A real cube root is used. A zero transformation denominator is undefined. Both light and heavy tails matter; the normal approximation is particularly inaccurate for small samples.

docs.text: [1] Anscombe, F. J. and Glynn, W. J. (1983). Distribution of the kurtosis statistic b2 for normal samples. Biometrika, 70(1), 227-234. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/70.1.227

This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Let M=median(x), A=median(abs(x-M)), u=(x-M)/(9A), and I={i: abs(u_i)<1}. Define B=nsum_I((x_i-M)2* (1-u_i2)4)/(sum_I((1-u_i2)(1-5u_i2)))2. Return sum((x-M)*2)/((n-1)B). Contributions with abs(u)>=1 are zero in both biweight sums. Zero MAD or a zero biweight denominator makes the estimator undefined and raises ValueError.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. For the composite null, simulation can use log-normal mu=0, s=1 because log-location and log-scale are removed by the statistic. Every replicate must call execute_statistic again. This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

docs.title: Mathematical verification of log-normal statistics
docs.text: Audit date: 2026-10-17. Scope: all 55 concrete classes exported by statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.log_normal: 15 EDF variants, five frequency statistics, one spacing statistic, 32 logarithmic normality wrappers and two KL functionals. The catalog lists every class, full code, hypothesis, rejection tail and individual documentation page.

docs.title: Findings and corrections
docs.text:
1. Shape tests were presented as tests of fixed parameter values. Normality statistics on logs and both KL statistics eliminate log-location and log-scale. They now accept an empty hypothesis in either coordinate system; Monte Carlo sampling explicitly selects mu=0,s=1. Fully fixed schemas remain accepted for compatibility and remain in hypothesis(), but these shape statistics are invariant to those values. They cannot distinguish two log-normal distributions with different parameters. The 21 fixed-CDF/spacing/frequency tests continue to require both parameters. This is an explicit contract distinction, not implicit parameter filling or a claim that every shape test is omnibus.
  2. Invalid logarithmic data could become a rejection-tail error. A universal +inf penalty is inappropriate for lower-tail tests such as Shapiro–Wilk and Filliben. Logarithmic wrappers and KL now raise ValueError for nonpositive input. Empty, multidimensional, nonfinite, complex and actively masked data are rejected before conversion. Quesenberry–Miller now validates its input too. EDF and frequency behavior follows their mathematical support/zero-count limits.
  3. KL powers and cancellations were unstable. Forming X**(1/sigma_hat) could overflow solely because the measurement unit changed. KL now uses centered, standardized logs, log-sum-exp and a near-zero cumulant series. The former near-zero expression used uncentered log moments and the wrong coefficient; the squared limiting integrand is m3²/6, not its former expression. No integration warnings are suppressed, and zero dispersion is rejected.
  4. The general-alpha KL threshold regression could return impossible negative thresholds. For example, the old supremum expression at n=50, alpha=0.025 gave approximately -103.91 although the statistic is nonnegative. That branch now raises NotImplementedError. The historical alpha=0.01/0.05 formulas remain available for compatibility, explicitly labelled unverified regressions. Their finite-sample level and published domain are not certified by this audit. Nonpositive or nonfinite regression results now raise ValueError too.
  5. Documentation coverage was incomplete. There were 40 pages for 55 classes, without a complete catalog or a log-normal validation report. The pages now state formulas, hypotheses, tails, input restrictions, executable examples and scientific references; all 15 missing pages and MkDocs entries were added. References to the implementation itself were replaced by scientific sources.
  6. Shared kernels and normality definitions were retained. Direct CDF evaluation, KS directions, Zhang–Wu's 10*Z_A-32 normalization and frequency zero-count limits passed independent comparisons. Qualifications for Hosking, GLB and approximate normal-score methods are retained, not silently certified.

docs.title: Mathematical reduction and hypothesis conventions
docs.text:
For X>0, log(X) ~ N(mu,s²) if and only if X is log-normal. There is no density Jacobian in a test statistic evaluated on transformed observations: the normality functional is simply T(log(X_1),...,log(X_n)). For location-scale-invariant T, T(a+b*log(X))=T(log(X)) for b>0. This proves the transfer of the implemented functional and its null distribution, but does not prove consistency or verify the scientific provenance of a legacy T.

For a fully specified null set u_i=Phi((log(x_(i))-mu)/s). The probability integral transform reduces fixed-CDF EDF and spacing criteria to their uniform functionals. No mean/variance is fitted. In shape statistics the normality functional may use s0 (ddof=0), s1 (ddof=1), robust scales or other estimates; those individual conventions are preserved. They must not be confused with the specified log-normal shape parameter s. scale=exp(mu) is the median; the arithmetic mean of X is exp(mu+s²/2).

All statistics reject in the tail listed in the catalog. Signed two-tail statistics need two simulated quantiles; symmetry is not assumed. D+ and D− are directional CDF discrepancies but both reject large values. Frequency statistics use O_j and E_j=n*p_j in original sample units; only fixed positive cell probabilities justify the ordinary multinomial k-1 asymptotic reference. Adaptive partitions require calibration of the whole binning procedure.

docs.title: KL derivation, numerical definition and limits of verification
docs.text:
Let z_i be centered log observations standardized with ddof=0, K® the empirical log moment-generating function and kappa_k its cumulants. With D®=2K®-rK'®, its power series begins

\[D(r)=-\frac{\kappa_3r^3}{6}-\frac{\kappa_4r^4}{12}+O(r^5).\]

The denominator satisfies

\[\sigma^2(r)=e^{r^2}(r^4-3r^2+4)-(4+r^2) =r^6\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(j+1)^2r^{2j}}{(j+3)!}.\]

Thus R®=D®/sigma® has opposite one-sided limits when skewness is nonzero, but its absolute value and square have continuous extensions. In particular, R(0+)=-kappa3/sqrt(6), R(0+)²=kappa3²/6. The implementation uses these extensions, not a denominator floor. Centering cancels algebraically: replacing log data by log data+c adds cr to K and c to K', cancelling the explicit r*mean term in the uncentered formula. Positive rescaling cancels through the fitted log SD.

KL_SUP retains the legacy 1000-point equally spaced grid on [-5,5]; this is only a grid approximation to a finite-window supremum. KL_INT integrates nR®² on [-5,5] with adaptive quadrature, split at zero and absolute/relative tolerance 1e-9. No error bound for omitted infinite tails or missed grid maxima is asserted. Decimal 70-digit direct expressions independently check both signs of r, including ±1e-6, plus the integral; scale tests shift log data by ±600. The cumulant expansion is used through order 10 when |r|max|z|<=0.05.

Batsidis, Economou and Tzavelas (2016) provides the KL size-weighted symmetry motivation. The publisher abstract and author bibliography were available; the primary full text was not. Consequently this audit verifies the documented truncated functionals, not the exact paper's domain, normalization, critical-value regressions or reported power. The old test comments calling two data values “from the article” cannot serve as independent provenance without a pinpoint source. Those rounded regressions are retained as compatibility checks, not used as the mathematical proof.

docs.title: Scientific sources and inherited qualifications
docs.text:
The accessible Zhang (2002) paper, §§2–3 provides the fixed-null EDF expressions and likelihood-ratio ranks. The noncyclic Quesenberry–Miller definition is available in the authors' comparative study, Sreedevi and Kattumannil, §4.1. Original bibliographic links appear in every page. A bibliography entry or an accessible abstract is not claimed to be a full-text formula check.

For the 32 wrappers, the detailed scientific-source audit and independent functional constructions are in the normality report. Their numerical verification was rerun; inherited limitations remain:

  • Hosking 1–4: L-moments agree with exhaustive order-statistic combinations. The three local rows of centering/variance constants have no established primary-source calibration here and do not shrink as an asymptotic variance sequence. They define local discrepancies; simulate at the actual n.
  • GLB: the fitted beta/order-probability transformation and reversed log weights agree with the documented local expression. Equality to the original Glen–Leemis–Barr test remains unconfirmed; do not use its tables by name alone.
  • Coin, SW, SF, SWRG, correlations and spacings: normal order scores or their covariance are approximated. Coin retains its 4<=n<=2000 restriction. These are not exact finite-sample normal covariance inversions.
  • Hermite/moment and directed shape tests: finite-order moments and directed alternatives do not guarantee power against every nonnormal log distribution.
  • Zhang–Wu variants: historical normalization is retained; the log-normal versions use a fixed CDF rather than fitted normality probabilities.
  • Liao–Shimokawa: a fixed-log-normal application of the general EDF functional; the original extreme-value-family calibration is not transferred.

docs.title: Numerical checks and reproducibility
docs.text:
Result: 1576 tests passed with ordinary imports. Ruff and stub freshness checks passed. MkDocs built successfully; its existing broken-link warnings concern other families, not the log-normal pages. This count includes the normality reference suite and hypothesis-generator checks listed below.

The focused checks exercise all 55 public statistics and both coordinate systems. They include independent normal-density and EDF quadrature, rank sums, SciPy multinomial power divergences, hand-calculated spacing sums, 70-digit KL expressions, normality functional references, log-affine invariance, invalid samples, unchanged input, hypothesis preservation and composite-null sampling.

Typical checked tolerances are rel=2e-9, abs=2e-10 for EDF identities; rel=3e-8, abs=2e-9 for log-transform composition at large log offsets; rel=2e-7, abs=2e-9 for KL pointwise comparisons, and rel=2e-8 for KL integration. These bound the tested cases, not a global error or exact significance level. No Monte Carlo level/power study was performed. In particular, the legacy KL threshold regressions and unresolved historical calibrations are not certified.

Run from the repository root using ordinary package imports (no isolation shim):

PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/distributions/test_log_normal.py \
  tests/distributions/test_log_normal_parameters.py \
  tests/distributions/test_log_normal_mathematical_validation.py \
  tests/distributions/test_log_normal_documentation.py \
  tests/statistics/test_log_normal_factory.py \
  tests/distributions/test_normal_correctness.py \
  tests/distributions/test_normal_mathematical_validation.py \
  tests/utils/test_hypothesis_generator.py -q
.venv/bin/python scripts/generate_log_normal_stub.py --check
.venv/bin/python -m mkdocs build --site-dir /tmp/pysatl-log-normal-audit

docs.text: The catalog, report, navigation and 55 individual pages are checked against runtime exports. Every page names its exact Python class and code, supplies an executable example and scientific links, and links back to this report. Python examples and public-class docstring examples execute in tests; local Markdown links are checked. log_normal/__init__.pyi is regenerated and checked with --check.

docs.title: Numba optimization verification
docs.text:
Optimization checked on 2026-10-23. All 55 public criteria reach numerical kernels compiled with @jit(nopython=True, cache=True). EDF, frequency and normality wrappers reuse their existing compiled kernels. Quesenberry–Miller now compiles sorting and the spacing sum; KL compiles cumulant coefficients, the stable ratio, the entire 1000-point supremum loop and the squared integrand. SciPy retains CDF/log-tail evaluation and adaptive quadrature with the same window, tolerance and split at zero. No fast-math reassociation is enabled. The public call is therefore not claimed to be wholly compiled.

All implementation helpers, including validation, class generation and factory adapters, are methods inside classes in log_normal/log_normal_statistics.py. There are no module-level function definitions. The public import path and statistic names are unchanged; the package stub describes the class methods.

The 117 tests in tests/distributions/test_log_normal_numba.py verify actual nopython signatures, disk-cache configuration, compiled/Python kernel agreement, unchanged input and execution through every public criterion on continuous and tied samples. Together with the mathematical, documentation and generator suites listed above, 1693 tests passed. Ruff and stub freshness checks also passed.

A local comparison against the saved pre-optimization implementation used n=200, seed 123 and the minimum of three batches of ten warmed public calls. All 55 values agreed (rtol=2e-8, atol=2e-9). Measured results for the changed numerical paths were:

Statistic Before, microseconds After, microseconds Speedup KL supremum 42886.4 1491.3 28.76x KL integral 6543.8 619.8 10.56x Quesenberry–Miller 38.0 30.2 1.26x

These are local warmed timings, not performance guarantees. Existing shared kernels were already compiled. First-call timings include compilation or disk cache loading and are reported separately by the benchmark:

PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_log_normal_pipeline.py --size 200 --number 10
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/distributions/test_log_normal_numba.py -q

The benchmark's optional --baseline /path/to/saved/log_normal.py compares against a saved prior module and checks values before reporting speedups.

docs.title: Modified log likelihood for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: ModifiedLogLikelihoodLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
Both parameters must be supplied before observing the sample: mu is the mean of log(X), s > 0 is its standard deviation. The alternative coordinates are s and scale = exp(mu), the median, not the mean of X. Use LOG_LOCATION_SCALE.parse({"mu": ..., "s": ...}) or SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": ..., "scale": ...}). Partial and empty hypotheses are rejected. No parameters are fitted to the sample.

The sample must be nonempty, finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected. Ties are permitted. EDF/spacing formulas use the null CDF, which is zero at nonpositive observations; finite penalties are possible. This is not the same policy as logarithmic family statistics, which reject such input.

docs.title: Statistic and binning
docs.text:
Modified log likelihood: 2 * sum(expected * log(expected / observed)).

Returns positive infinity if any observed count is zero.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Cressie, N. and Read, T. R. C. (1984). Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests. JRSS B, 46(3), 440-464; power divergence with lambda = -1. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1984.tb01318.x

The constructor accepts binning: BinningStrategy; its default is EqualProbabilityBins(). Bins use the fixed log-normal distribution in the original sample units. Define observed counts O_j and expected counts E_j = n * P(X in cell j). The zero-count limits are part of the definition; Neyman and modified log-likelihood can return positive infinity when O_j=0<E_j. A positive observed count in a zero-probability cell gives infinity. For a fixed partition with k positive-probability cells, the usual multinomial asymptotic reference has k-1 degrees of freedom. Adaptive bins require calibration of the entire bin-building procedure; no automatic k-3 correction is justified.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. Use the fixed null and the same sample size, settings and binning for calibration. Do not substitute fitted-normality tables.

docs.text:

    ModifiedLogLikelihoodLogNormalGofStatistic,

docs.text:
Class: QuesenberryMillerLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: QUESENBERRY_MILLER_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
Both parameters must be supplied before observing the sample: mu is the mean of log(X), s > 0 is its standard deviation. The alternative coordinates are s and scale = exp(mu), the median, not the mean of X. Use LOG_LOCATION_SCALE.parse({"mu": ..., "s": ...}) or SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": ..., "scale": ...}). Partial and empty hypotheses are rejected. No parameters are fitted to the sample.

The sample must be nonempty, finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected. Ties are permitted. EDF/spacing formulas use the null CDF, which is zero at nonpositive observations; finite penalties are possible. This is not the same policy as logarithmic family statistics, which reject such input.

docs.title: Statistic
docs.text:
Set \(u_i=F_{\mu,s}(x_{(i)})\), \(u_0=0\), \(u_{n+1}=1\) and \(D_i=u_i-u_{i-1}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n+1\). Then

\[Q=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}D_i^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_iD_{i+1}.\]

There is no cyclic term \(D_{n+1}D_1\). All n+1 spacings, including both boundary gaps, are present. Uniform quantile samples provide an exact hand-calculated reference. The null CDF must be specified in advance.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Quesenberry and Miller (1977), Power studies of some tests for uniformity.
  • The explicit noncyclic formula is also given in the authors' comparative study, Sreedevi and Kattumannil, §4.1.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. Use the fixed null and the same sample size, settings and binning for calibration. Do not substitute fitted-normality tables.

docs.text:

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import LogNormalDistributionDescriptor as LogNormal

    QuesenberryMillerLogNormalGofStatistic,
)

parameters = LogNormal.DEFAULT.parse({"mu": 0.4, "s": 0.8})
statistic = QuesenberryMillerLogNormalGofStatistic(parameters)
sample = np.exp([-1.7, -1.2, -0.9, -0.6, -0.3, -0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.1])

docs.title: Robust Jarque-Bera test for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: RobustJarqueBeraLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: RJB_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Logarithmic reduction
docs.text: The implementation computes RobustJarqueBeraNormalityGofStatistic on y = log(rvs) with an empty normal-family hypothesis. Thus its formula, sample-size limits, normalization and rejection tail are exactly those of the normality statistic at its default settings. Constructor-specific normality options are not exposed by this wrapper. The identity was checked on normal, nonnormal and tied logarithmic samples and under transformations X -> exp(a) * X**b, b > 0.

docs.title: Underlying normality definition
docs.text:
In this section, x denotes y = log(X), not the original positive sample. The normal-family hypothesis and dispersion conventions below concern these log observations. See also the normality source page.

H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Let J=sqrt(pi/2)mean(abs(x-median(x))). Return n(m3/J3)2/6 + n(m4/J4-3)*2/64. Moments are centered at the sample mean, whereas J uses the median. The reference identifies this robust-scale modification; small-sample chi-square calibration is not justified.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] Gel, Y. R. and Gastwirth, J. L. (2008). A robust modification of the Jarque-Bera test of normality. Economics Letters, 99(1), 30-32. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2007.05.022

docs.title: Rejection and calibration

For the composite null, simulation can use log-normal mu=0, s=1 because log-location and log-scale are removed by the statistic. Every replicate must call execute_statistic again. This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

docs.text:
Class: WatsonLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: WATSON_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
Both parameters must be supplied before observing the sample: mu is the mean of log(X), s > 0 is its standard deviation. The alternative coordinates are s and scale = exp(mu), the median, not the mean of X. Use LOG_LOCATION_SCALE.parse({"mu": ..., "s": ...}) or SHAPE_SCALE.parse({"s": ..., "scale": ...}). Partial and empty hypotheses are rejected. No parameters are fitted to the sample.

The sample must be nonempty, finite, real and one-dimensional; masked values are rejected. Ties are permitted. EDF/spacing formulas use the null CDF, which is zero at nonpositive observations; finite penalties are possible. This is not the same policy as logarithmic family statistics, which reject such input.

docs.title: Statistic
docs.text:
Set \(u_i=\Phi((\log x_{(i)}-\mu)/s)\) for positive observations. The following general EDF definition is evaluated at these fixed-null probabilities.

Watson U² statistic for CDF values of a sorted sample.

Returns W²-n(mean(u)-½)2, evaluated as a centered sum of squares plus 1/(12n) to avoid cancellation. No finite-sample correction is used.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Lemeshko et al. (2014), Eq. (6). https://doi.org/10.3103/S875669901401004X Watson (1961), https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/48.1-2.109; sorted CDF input.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: right. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. Use the fixed null and the same sample size, settings and binning for calibration. Do not substitute fitted-normality tables.

docs.title: Zhang Q test for log-normal data
docs.text:
Class: ZhangQLogNormalGofStatistic

Code: ZQ_LOGNORMAL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and inputs
docs.text:
This is a log-normal family/shape statistic: log(X) is normal with unknown location and positive scale. Use LogNormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). An empty SHAPE_SCALE schema is also accepted. All observations must be finite, real, strictly positive and one-dimensional. Active masks and undefined constant-sample contrasts raise ValueError; minimum sizes are specified below.

For compatibility, fully specified mu, s or s, scale coordinates are also accepted and preserved by hypothesis(). They do not enter this shape statistic: it cannot detect a wrong location/scale within the log-normal family. Use a fixed-CDF EDF or frequency criterion when those particular values are part of the hypothesis. Partial parameter sets are rejected.

docs.title: Logarithmic reduction
docs.text: The implementation computes ZhangQNormalityGofStatistic on y = log(rvs) with an empty normal-family hypothesis. Thus its formula, sample-size limits, normalization and rejection tail are exactly those of the normality statistic at its default settings. Constructor-specific normality options are not exposed by this wrapper. The identity was checked on normal, nonnormal and tied logarithmic samples and under transformations X -> exp(a) * X**b, b > 0.

docs.title: Underlying normality definition
docs.text:
In this section, x denotes y = log(X), not the original positive sample. The normal-family hypothesis and dispersion conventions below concern these log observations. See also the normality source page.

H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Both tails of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 8 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

The publication was identified, but the exact finite-sample implementation is not fully certified against its primary text.

For u_i=Phi*-1((i-⅜)/(n+¼)), set q1=mean_{i=2..n}((x_(i)-x_(1))/(u_i-u_1)), q2=mean_{i=1..n-4}((x_(i+4)-x_(i))/(u_(i+4)-u_i)). Return log(q1)-log(q2). The four-spacing construction and Blom approximation are explicit implementation choices. Both contrasts must be positive. Both critical tails are used for the signed log ratio; this is the Q component, not a combined Q/Q p-value procedure.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] Zhang, P. (1999). Omnibus test of normality using the Q statistic. Journal of Applied Statistics, 26(4), 519-528. https://doi.org/10.1080/02664769922395

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text: Rejection tail: two_tailed. A statistic value alone is not a p-value. For the composite null, simulation can use log-normal mu=0, s=1 because log-location and log-scale are removed by the statistic. Every replicate must call execute_statistic again. This does not make every directed shape test omnibus. Signed two-tail tests require both null quantiles, without assuming symmetry. Legacy attribution qualifications carry over from normality.

docs.title: Normality statistics
docs.text:
The module pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.normal exports 60 concrete statistics: 16 generated EDF statistics, 5 generated frequency statistics and 39 explicit statistics, including six graph functionals. Every entry below links to a separate page with its formula, runnable example, scientific references and the qualifications on its interpretation.

Read the mathematical verification report before reusing a published table or interpreting a legacy name as a certified test.

docs.title: Hypotheses and calibration
docs.text:
• Fixed: KS and CVM require {'mean': mu, 'var': sigma_squared}. They accept a singleton or a constant sample. Variance is not standard deviation.
  • Family: 52 statistics take {}. For generated EDF/frequency statistics, mean and unbiased variance are fitted on every call. Other tests use the estimators stated on their individual pages. Calibrate by simulating N(0,1) and repeating the complete computation; fitted CDF values are dependent.
  • Graph: six statistics take {'var': sigma_squared} with unknown mean. Their radius is translation invariant but not scale invariant. Simulate at the specified variance; a standard-normal table cannot be reused arbitrarily.

Lower-tail tests reject for small values, upper-tail tests for large values. Two-tail statistics require both quantiles; they need not have a symmetric null law. Directional KS deviations still have an upper-tail rejection rule. None of these classes returns a p-value. Small samples, ties/rounding and algorithm options must be reproduced in calibration. Default frequency bins are equal-probability bins; user-specified boundaries can destroy scale invariance.

docs.title: Anderson-Darling test for normality
docs.text:
Class: AndersonDarlingNormalityGofStatistic

Code: AD_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Anderson-Darling statistic for the normal location-scale family.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 2 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

A2 = -n - sum((2i-1)(log(Phi(z_(i))) + log(1-Phi(z_(n+1-i)))))/n, where z=(x-mean(x))/s1. This is the unadjusted fitted-normal statistic. Log-CDF and log-survival functions avoid rounding probabilities to zero or one.

Brys-Hubert-Struyf MC-LR statistic for the normal family.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Return nv.TV-1v with v=(MC, LMC-0.198828, RMC-0.198828), V=[[1.24581,0.322918,-0.322918],[0.322918,2.62068,-0.0123455], [-0.322918,-0.0123455,2.62068]]. LMC=-MC(xmedian(x)); median observations belong to neither half. MC is the median of (upper+lower-2median)/(upper-lower) over lower<=median<=upper, with antisymmetric rank values for zero ties. At least two observations must remain in each strict half. Constant halves have MC=0. The exact kernel median uses O(n2) time and memory, unlike the fast selection algorithm in the paper. Constants agree with the rounded normal row in Table 1; simulate for finite n.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:

Code: CC1_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Cabaña-Cabaña normality statistic focused on skewness departures.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Use the l=5 process in Cabana and Cabana, equation (7). For z=(x-mean(x))/s1, h_j=He_j/sqrt(j!), H_j=sum(h_j(z))/sqrt(n), P(t)=sum_{j=1..5}(h_(j-1)(t)H_(j+3)/sqrt(j)). docs.title: Pearson chi-squared for normality
docs.text:
Class: Chi2PearsonNormalityGofStatistic

Code: CHI2_PEARSON_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: H0 is the normal family with unknown mean and positive variance. Pass NormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). Both parameters are fitted on every sample; the variance estimator uses ddof=1. At least two real, finite, unmasked, one-dimensional observations with nonzero dispersion are required. Ties are accepted. The sample is not modified and no fit is retained. Large values reject H0. Calibration repeats fitting on each simulated sample.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Let O_j be the observed count and E_j=n*p_j>0 the fitted expected count.

Σ (O_j-E_j)²/E_j. A zero observed count contributes E_j.

docs.title: Binning and calibration
docs.text: The optional binning keyword accepts a BinningStrategy; the default is EqualProbabilityBins(). ExplicitBins boundaries are in the original data units. Fit mean and unbiased variance on each replicate, then rebuild the same bins. Do not assume a universal chi-square distribution with k-3 degrees of freedom: raw-data estimates, adaptive boundaries and the bin-count rule affect calibration. Zero-probability categories and any configured minimum-expected-count merging follow the shared binning contract.

docs.title: References

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.text:

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,var), with unknown mu and fixed var; hypothesis() reports var. Calibrate at this variance; setting the simulation mean to zero is valid. Both tails of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 2 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. This local construction is translation invariant but not scale invariant. var selects the null law for calibration; it is not inserted in the radius. docs.title: Hosking1 test for normality
docs.text:
Class: Hosking1NormalityGofStatistic

Code: HOSKING1_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Hosking L-moment normality statistic without trimming.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Local quadratic discrepancy of L-moment ratios with trim t=0. For r=2,3,4, L_r=sum_i x_(i)sum_{k=0..r-1}((-1)k C(r-1,k)C(i-1,r+t-1-k)C(n-i,t+k))/(rC(n,r+2t)). Return (L3/L2)2/v3+(L4/L2-mu4)2/v4. The constants (mu4,v3,v4) are the three historical rows in the implementation for n<=25, 25<n<=50 and n>50. They are not a consistent asymptotic covariance sequence. A primary source for this exact omnibus formula and these rows was not located; the L-moment papers alone do not validate this test. Treat it as a local statistic and simulate its null law at the actual n. L2 must be positive.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Hosking, J. R. M. (1990). L-moments: analysis and estimation of distributions using linear combinations of order statistics. JRSS B, 52(1), 105–124. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1990.tb01775.x

Hosking, J. R. M. (2007). Some theory and practical uses of trimmed L-moments. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference, 137(9), 3024–3039. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jspi.2006.12.002

These articles justify the L-moment construction, not the three local rows of calibration constants used here.

docs.title: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for normality
docs.text:
Class: KolmogorovSmirnovNormalityGofStatistic

Code: KS_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

One-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic for a specified normal law.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameters : ParameterValues
    Values with mean, var fixed; omitted parameters are unknown.
alternative_type : AlternativeType, optional
    ``TWO_TAILED`` computes ``max(D_plus, D_minus)``; ``RIGHT`` computes
    ``D_plus = sup(F_n - F_0)`` and ``LEFT`` computes
    ``D_minus = sup(F_0 - F_n)``. Defaults to ``TWO_TAILED``.
mode : str, optional
    Setting retained by the shared KS implementation. ``"auto"`` is
    stored as ``"exact"``. It does not affect the statistic and this
    class does not calculate a p-value.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mean,var) with both parameters fixed; hypothesis() reports both. Constant samples are valid. Simulate the specified normal law. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 1 finite real observations in one dimension. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

D+ = max(i/n - F0(x_(i))) and D- = max(F0(x_(i)) - (i-1)/n). Return D+, D-, or max(D+, D-) according to alternative_type. F0 is the normal CDF with the fixed mean and variance. All three distances use the upper critical tail; mode does not compute a p-value.

Class: KurtosisNormalityGofStatistic

Code: KURTOSIS_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Anscombe-Glynn transformed-kurtosis statistic for the normal family.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Both tails of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 5 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Return the signed Anscombe-Glynn transform of g2=m4/m2**2, using the finite-n expectation, variance and skewness of g2. A real cube root is used. A zero transformation denominator is undefined. Both light and heavy tails matter; the normal approximation is particularly inaccurate for small samples.

Code: MI_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Martinez-Iglewicz statistic comparing two estimates of dispersion.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Let M=median(x), A=median(abs(x-M)), u=(x-M)/(9A), and I={i: abs(u_i)<1}. Define B=nsum_I((x_i-M)2* (1-u_i2)4)/(sum_I((1-u_i2)(1-5u_i2)))2. Return sum((x-M)*2)/((n-1)B). Contributions with abs(u)>=1 are zero in both biweight sums. Zero MAD or a zero biweight denominator makes the estimator undefined and raises ValueError.

docs.title: Mathematical verification of normality statistics
docs.text:
Audit date: 2026-10-17. Scope: all 60 concrete classes exported by statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.normal, including the generated EDF and frequency classes. The catalog lists the exact Python names, storage codes, hypotheses and rejection tails.

The audit checks implemented mathematical functionals, numerical behavior, hypothesis contracts and documentation. It does not certify exact finite-sample p-values, universal power or every historical author attribution. In particular, eleven legacy classes (four Hosking, six graph and GLB) have qualifications described below. They remain available under their existing names.

docs.title: Findings and changes
docs.text:
• No discrepancy was found between the implemented formulas and the independent numerical definitions on the tested cases. For some legacy classes the independently checked definition is the library's documented functional, rather than a fully verified reconstruction of the original publication.
  • Masked observations were silently converted to ordinary arrays by most normal statistics, exposing the hidden values to the calculation. _normal_sample now rejects observations with an active mask, consistent with frequency tests.
  • The D’Agostino–Pearson page incorrectly documented SkewNormalityGofStatistic, a signed skewness test. It now documents DAPNormalityGofStatistic, the sum of squared skewness and kurtosis transforms, and its upper rejection tail.
  • Fifteen generated criteria had no page. They now have separate pages with formulas, examples, sources and fitted-normal calibration instructions.
  • Scientific context was missing for Hosking, GLB and graph pages. References have been added without claiming that related theory establishes their exact local normality tests. Broken links to normal-statistics-review.md were replaced by links to this report and the catalog.
  • Generated class docstrings now distinguish fixed and fitted hypotheses and include executable examples. Existing finite-sample normalizations, including 10*Z_A-32, have been retained.
  • Storage lookup tests were updated to expect the configuration already included by the current DistributionKey implementation; no storage algorithm changed.

docs.title: Hypothesis and scale conventions
docs.text:
Write m_r = mean((x-mean(x))**r), s0=sqrt(m2), s1=sqrt(n*m2/(n-1)), and z0=(x-mean(x))/s0, z1=(x-mean(x))/s1. Changing ddof changes a finite-sample statistic, even if the difference vanishes asymptotically. The tests explicitly retain these distinctions.

Only KS and CVM test a fully specified normal law; their mean and var must be supplied, and var means variance. The other generated EDF and all frequency criteria estimate the mean and unbiased variance on each sample. Thus D+ and D− generated classes have a fitted hypothesis, whereas legacy two-sided KS has a fixed hypothesis. Lilliefors is the fitted two-sided KS statistic.

Fifty-two classes have a family hypothesis {}. For location-scale-invariant settings their null can be simulated with N(0,1), repeating all fits. This representative distribution does not fix parameters in the hypothesis. Six graph classes instead fix variance and leave mean unknown. User-supplied frequency bin edges are in original units and can break scale invariance.

For fitted normal EDF tests, independent uniform CDF values cannot replace refitted normal samples. Neither the known-CDF EDF tables nor the familiar multinomial chi-square law can be transferred automatically. In particular, chi-square(k-3) is not asserted for raw-data estimates with adaptive bins. For two-tail tests simulate both quantiles; a signed statistic's null need not be symmetric. Directional KS deviations are nonnegative and reject in the upper tail.

docs.title: Sources and level of verification
docs.text:
The following primary texts were inspected where accessible:

  • Zhang (2002), §§2–3: EDF functionals, including half-rank and quarter-rank corrections. KS here is D, not the squared distance printed in §2.1.
  • Doornik and Hansen, author manuscript, appendix p.7: skewness and conditional-kurtosis transformations; rounded printed examples provide an external numerical check. The journal version is Doornik–Hansen (2008).
  • Bonett and Seier (2002), equations (5)–(6): ddof=0, the factor sqrt(n+2) and the two-sided rule. This is the individual Geary-kurtosis transform, not the paper's further combined test.
  • Bontemps and Meddahi (2005), §§2–3: orthonormal Hermite moments. This implementation uses iid weighting and s1; it does not implement the paper's HAC extension to dependent data.
  • Brys, Hubert and Struyf, author manuscript, §3 and Table 1: the MC-LR quadratic form. The library uses more digits in the constants than the table prints; exact agreement with those additional digits is not claimed.
  • Cabaña and Cabaña (2003), author-posted full text: truncated Hermite processes, fixed truncation five and continuous supremum.
  • Desgagné, Lafaye de Micheaux and Leblanc (2013), author copy: fitted-score approach. Independent quadrature verifies the implemented score means and covariance projection, within the precision of rounded constants.
  • Lemeshko et al. (2014), equations (1)–(3), (6): Kuiper normalizations and Watson centering. These equations alone do not validate calibration after normal parameter fitting.

Direct scientific references for all 60 statistics appear in the coverage table below; their individual pages provide further bibliographic detail. A bibliographic link alone is not evidence of a line-by-line formula check. Original full texts for several older methods were inaccessible; those methods were checked against independent mathematical constructions or external software, with approximations stated explicitly below.

External software checks use the official SciPy definitions of Shapiro–Wilk, skewness, kurtosis and Filliben plotting positions. Agreement with a numerical implementation complements, but does not replace, scientific attribution.
