docs.title: Legacy definitions and unresolved scientific attribution
docs.text:
Hosking 1–4. The L-moment and trimmed L-moment calculations agree with exhaustive averaging of order-statistic combinations. The three historical rows (mu4,v3,v4) for n<=25, 25<n<=50 and n>50 are not an asymptotically shrinking covariance sequence. Neither Hosking (1990) nor Hosking (2007) is claimed to justify these exact rows. These are local discrepancies: simulate at the actual sample size. No unsupported replacement constants were introduced.

Graph statistics. Exhaustive small-graph checks establish their combinatorial values. The sample-dependent radius range/(10*m2) changes as inverse scale, while interpoint distances change as scale. Hence location invariance holds, but scale invariance does not. Mean can be set to zero for simulation; variance must match the hypothesis. No paper establishing this exact normality procedure was located. Ebner, Nestmann and Schulte is explicitly cited as related graph-testing research about uniformity, not as provenance for these six normality tests.

GLB. The fitted beta transformation and reversed logarithmic weights are reproduced using binomial probabilities. This does not make the expression the ordinary Anderson–Darling statistic. The Glen–Leemis–Barr paper was identified, but the primary full text was inaccessible. Its exact equality to this fitted-normal implementation remains unconfirmed. Use simulation of the implemented functional, not an assumed GLB table.

Approximations and directed tests. Coin's regression is checked against quadrature of expected normal order statistics, with tolerance reflecting its nscor2 approximation. Bonett–Seier is a kurtosis component; GMG is directed against heavy tails. Fixed-order Hermite and moment tests are not proved consistent against every nonnormal alternative by this audit. A finite value or Monte Carlo calibration alone does not establish omnibus power.

docs.title: Numerical verification and reproducibility
docs.text:
Result: 1495 tests passed in the isolated focused run. Ruff checks passed. mkdocs build --site-dir /tmp/pysatl-normal-docs-audit succeeded; its warnings concern existing broken links outside the normality section. All normality pages, examples, catalog entries and local links passed the dedicated checks.

The focused suite consists of:

  • tests/distributions/test_normal.py
  • tests/distributions/test_normal_parameters.py
  • tests/distributions/test_normal_hypotheses.py
  • tests/distributions/test_normal_correctness.py
  • tests/distributions/test_normal_mathematical_validation.py
  • tests/distributions/test_normal_documentation.py
  • tests/statistics/test_normal_dynamic.py
  • tests/statistics/test_normal_numba.py
  • tests/statistics/test_normal_stub.py

The new numerical references do not call the production EDF/frequency kernels. They integrate the normal density and EDF discrepancies, use SciPy multinomial power divergences, calculate score correlations and robust scales, invert a quantile covariance matrix, and integrate order-statistic densities. Existing checks independently optimize the Cabaña supremum, enumerate trimmed L-moments, check all six graph functionals and integrate the fitted-score covariance.

Cases include normal and skewed samples, repeated values, symmetric samples, small-size boundaries, refitting across calls, nonmutation, invalid and masked data, signed tails, and positive affine transformations. Location-scale-invariant family cases are tested at scales 1e-250 and 1e250; graph statistics and fixed-boundary binning are not incorrectly required to have this invariance. Neyman and modified likelihood legitimately return infinity at empty observed cells with positive expected probability. Extremely small probabilities may still be limited by floating-point representability.

EDF comparisons use rel=2e-9, abs=2e-10; SciPy Shapiro comparisons use abs=2e-8; the Coin approximation uses rel=3e-3, abs=1e-6; the rounded Desgagné covariance comparison uses rel=2e-4. These are bounds for the checked cases, not global error guarantees.

Ordinary pytest collection is currently blocked by the pre-existing import of AbstractChi2Statistic from edf.py in inverse_gamma.py. Focused verification loads the real normal, EDF, frequency, distribution and binning modules while bypassing only the unrelated continuous/__init__.py import aggregator. This is not evidence that package initialization is healthy. To reproduce that run from the repository root:

.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import sys
import types
from pathlib import Path
import pytest

name = "pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous"
package = types.ModuleType(name)
package.__path__ = [str(Path("src/pysatl_criterion/statistics/goodness_of_fit/continuous").resolve())]
sys.modules[name] = package
raise SystemExit(pytest.main([
    "tests/distributions/test_normal.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_normal_parameters.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_normal_hypotheses.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_normal_correctness.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_normal_mathematical_validation.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_normal_documentation.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_normal_dynamic.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_normal_numba.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_normal_stub.py", "-q",
]))
PY

docs.title: Numba optimization verification
docs.text:
Numerical kernels use static class methods decorated with @jit(nopython=True, cache=True), without fast-math reassociation. The public entry points retain input validation and stable rescaling. All 60 criteria reach compiled kernels; generated EDF and frequency criteria reuse their existing common kernels. Normal quantiles and beta/log-tail functions remain in SciPy, and Cabaña polynomial root finding remains in NumPy. Compiling a reduction does not mean the entire public call is compiled.

The 128 additional checks in test_normal_numba.py exercise every public path on continuous and tied data, require actual nopython signatures and disk-cache configuration, and compare compiled results with the Python kernel bodies. They also check large Hosking combination weights and strict graph-radius boundaries against explicit graph calculations. Independent formula checks listed above remain the mathematical reference. Baseline comparisons before and after optimization also passed on normal samples of sizes 12, 100 and 1000 for all 39 explicitly implemented statistics (rtol=2e-8, atol=2e-9).

Graph statistics now use sorted scans instead of constructing adjacency lists; the strict edge condition remains abs(x_i-x_j) < radius. BHS uses one flat medcouple-kernel array instead of multiple broadcast matrices, preserving its tie convention. Hosking uses floating-point low-order combination products to avoid fixed-width integer overflow. Coin and Shapiro–Wilk evaluate quantiles in batches, and Cabaña reuses its fixed polynomial basis.

A local warmed benchmark used the public API, n=200, seed 123 and the minimum of three batches of ten calls, comparing against the pre-optimization source. Observed speedups were approximately 9× for Epps–Pulley, 13–15× for Hosking 2–4, 15× for Jarque–Bera, 41× for Coin and 89× for Shapiro–Wilk. The four graph statistics that previously built adjacency lists improved by about 186–222×. GLB was essentially unchanged (0.98×), since SciPy beta tails dominate it. These are local measurements, not performance guarantees; compilation/cache loading is excluded from these speedup ratios.

To measure first-call and warmed execution separately for all 60 criteria:

PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_normal_pipeline.py --isolated-imports

The explicit isolation flag bypasses the unrelated package-import failure described above. Once that failure is fixed, omit the flag. First-call timings include compilation or disk-cache loading, depending on the cache state.

docs.title: Package layout and compatibility
docs.text:
Like continuous/uniform, the normality implementation is a package:

  • continuous/normal/normal_statistics.py contains the statistics and factories.
  • continuous/normal/__init__.py explicitly re-exports the 60 concrete classes and two abstract bases, retaining their public continuous.normal identities.
  • continuous/normal/__init__.pyi describes the complete public interface.

Existing from ...continuous.normal import ... imports and pickle references retain their paths. The 65 stub/package checks cover exports, method signatures, class identity, old pickle references and unique criterion discovery. Generate and verify the package stub with scripts/generate_normal_stub.py and its --check option; generation reads the source without importing the package. Mypy checking of the stub passed with --follow-imports=silent.

docs.title: Documentation coverage
docs.text:
The catalog and navigation contain all 60 classes, with exactly one individual page per class, plus the catalog and this report. Tests compare class names, codes and exports with documentation, require examples and scientific links, execute every Python example and check local Markdown links. This catches a page accidentally documenting a different criterion, as happened with DAP. All concrete class docstrings include references and executable examples.

An available related scientific link is explicitly distinguished from a source that validates the exact implementation. The unresolved attribution of the legacy methods above is part of the result, not concealed by coverage checks.

docs.title: Modified log likelihood for normality
docs.text:
Class: ModifiedLogLikelihoodNormalityGofStatistic

Code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

docs.title: Hypothesis and input
docs.text: H0 is the normal family with unknown mean and positive variance. Pass NormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). Both parameters are fitted on every sample; the variance estimator uses ddof=1. At least two real, finite, unmasked, one-dimensional observations with nonzero dispersion are required. Ties are accepted. The sample is not modified and no fit is retained. Large values reject H0. Calibration repeats fitting on each simulated sample.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Let O_j be the observed count and E_j=n*p_j>0 the fitted expected count.

2 Σ E_j log(E_j/O_j). If O_j=0<E_j, the statistic is positive infinity.

docs.title: Binning and calibration
docs.text: The optional binning keyword accepts a BinningStrategy; the default is EqualProbabilityBins(). ExplicitBins boundaries are in the original data units. Fit mean and unbiased variance on each replicate, then rebuild the same bins. Do not assume a universal chi-square distribution with k-3 degrees of freedom: raw-data estimates, adaptive boundaries and the bin-count rule affect calibration. Zero-probability categories and any configured minimum-expected-count merging follow the shared binning contract.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import NormalDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.normal import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodNormalityGofStatistic,
)
import numpy as np

statistic = ModifiedLogLikelihoodNormalityGofStatistic(
    NormalDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({})
)
sample = [-1.7, -1.2, -0.9, -0.6, -0.3, -0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.1]
value = statistic.execute_statistic(sample)
assert np.isfinite(value)
assert statistic.hypothesis().parameters() == {}

docs.title: Robust Jarque-Bera test for normality
docs.text:
Class: RobustJarqueBeraNormalityGofStatistic

Code: RJB_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Gel-Gastwirth robust Jarque-Bera normality statistic.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. Large values of the statistic define rejection. Use at least 4 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Let J=sqrt(pi/2)mean(abs(x-median(x))). Return n(m3/J3)2/6 + n(m4/J4-3)*2/64. Moments are centered at the sample mean, whereas J uses the median. The reference identifies this robust-scale modification; small-sample chi-square calibration is not justified.

docs.text: [1] Gel, Y. R. and Gastwirth, J. L. (2008). A robust modification of the Jarque-Bera test of normality. Economics Letters, 99(1), 30-32. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2007.05.022

docs.title: Ryan-Joiner test for normality
docs.text:
Class: RyanJoinerNormalityGofStatistic

Code: RJ_NORMALITY_GOODNESS_OF_FIT

Ryan-Joiner probability-plot correlation statistic for normality.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameters : ParameterValues
    An empty distribution schema; all distribution parameters are unknown.
weighted : bool, optional
    If True, average the plotting probabilities within each group of
    tied observations before applying the normal quantile function.
    Default is False.
cte_alpha : {'3/8', '1/2', '0'}, optional
    Plotting-position constant ``a`` in ``(i-a)/(n-2*a+1)`` for one-based
    ranks. Default is ``'3/8'``. Unrecognized values currently fall back
    to ``3/8``.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) Return one scalar statistic. hypothesis() Report fixed null parameters only. alternative() Report the critical tail.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
H0 is N(mu,sigma**2), with unknown real mu and sigma>0; hypothesis() reports {}. Location and positive scale cancel, allowing N(0,1) null simulation. Every simulated sample must go through execute_statistic again. The lower tail of the statistic defines rejection. Use at least 3 finite real observations in one dimension. Nonzero dispersion is required. Ties are accepted unless a scale or contrast becomes undefined. Write x_(i) for ascending observations (i=1,...,n), Phi and phi for the standard normal CDF and density, s0=std(x,ddof=0), and s1=std(x,ddof=1). Calculations do not modify the sample or retain fits.

Return corr(x_(i), Phi*-1(p_i)), p_i=(i-alpha)/(n+1-2alpha). cte_alpha selects alpha=0, ⅜, or ½. If weighted=True, replace positions of tied observations by their group mean before taking normal quantiles. This tie convention and nondefault positions need separate calibration; they are not fixed distribution parameters.

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] Ryan, T. A., Jr. and Joiner, B. L. (1976). Normal Probability Plots and Tests for Normality. Technical report, Statistics Department, The Pennsylvania State University. Original report: https://www.additive-net.de/en/component/jdownloads/send/70-support/236-normal-probability-plots-and-tests-for-normality-thomas-a-ryan-jr-bryan-l-joiner

docs.title: Calibration and interpretation
docs.text:
The full code appends _PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT to each short code. Built-in Pareto simulation is unavailable. Fixed-null EDF statistics can be calibrated through independent uniforms; frequency calibration must preserve bin probabilities and binning policy. Composite criteria have different null laws. Greenwood and Obradović eliminate the nuisance shape under continuous IID sampling; KL retains finite-sample shape dependence and requires refitting with the same window on each replicate. Plug-in parametric bootstrap is approximate.

The Greenwood Pareto formula is a library adaptation of the Greenwood concentration functional. Liao–Shimokawa uses the shared EDF functional on a fixed CDF. Neither is asserted to reproduce a published fitted-Pareto test with supplied critical values. KL implements the raw fixed-window estimate, not the adaptive, bias-corrected procedure of vsgoftest.

docs.title: Anderson–Darling for Pareto I
docs.text: Public class: AndersonDarlingParetoGofStatistic. Full code: AD_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both \(a=\mathrm{shape}>0\) and \(s=\mathrm{scale}>0\) are fixed before observing the sample. Location is zero; \(F(x)=1-(s/x)^a\) for \(x\ge s\). No parameters are estimated.

For sorted data set \(u_i=F(x_{(i)})\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\).

\[ A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})]. \]

No finite-sample correction is applied. An observation at the lower endpoint gives positive infinity. Log probabilities preserve finite upper-tail contributions when the CDF rounds to one.

Input is a finite real one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge1\) and \(x_i\ge s\). Masked observations and data below scale are rejected. The method returns one scalar statistic; large values reject. Ties are accepted computationally, but continuous-null calibration does not account for rounding or discrete data.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The probability integral transform gives the same finite-sample statistic law as independent uniform observations when both Pareto parameters are truly fixed. Do not substitute estimates from this sample and then use the fixed-null tables. Use critical values for this precise normalization and sample size.

Built-in Pareto Monte Carlo generation is unavailable; calibration is external.

docs.text: Public class: Chi2PearsonParetoGofStatistic. Full code: CHI2_PEARSON_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both \(a=\mathrm{shape}>0\) and \(s=\mathrm{scale}>0\) are fixed before observing the sample. Location is zero; \(F(x)=1-(s/x)^a\) for \(x\ge s\). No parameters are estimated.

For full-support edges \(b_0,\ldots,b_k\), let \(O_j\) be the observed counts and \(E_j=n[F(b_j)-F(b_{j-1})]\). Expected counts must be positive and totals must agree.

\[ X^2=\sum_j\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{E_j}. \]

Power-divergence parameter \(\lambda=1\). A zero observed count contributes \(E_j\).

Input is a finite real one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge1\) and \(x_i\ge s\). Masked observations and data below scale are rejected. The method returns one scalar statistic; large values reject. docs.title: Binning and calibration
docs.text:

For fixed cells and large expected counts, the usual asymptotic reference is \(\chi^2_{k-1}\); this is not an exact small-sample calibration. docs.title: Greenwood logarithmic residual ratio for Pareto I
docs.text: Public class: GreenwoodParetoGofStatistic. Full code: Greenwood_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both shape and scale are unknown. For positive observations define

\[ y_i=\log(x_i/x_{(1)}),\qquad G=\frac{\sum_i y_i^2}{(\sum_i y_i)^2}. \]

The sample must be finite, real, unmasked, one-dimensional, nonconstant and have \(n\ge3\) observations. At \(n=2\) the ratio is identically one, so this case is rejected. Ties are accepted if the sample remains nonconstant. Small and large values reject; the method returns the statistic, not a p-value.

docs.title: Derivation and calibration
docs.text:
Under Pareto I, \(\log(X/s)\) is exponential with rate \(a\). After subtracting the minimum, one residual is zero and the other \(n-1\) residuals, before ordering, have the exponential memoryless law. Their normalized proportions follow \(\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1)\) with \(n-1\) components. Thus, by direct derivation,

\[ \frac1{n-1}\le G\le1,\qquad \mathbb E G=\frac2n,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G)=\frac{4(n-2)}{n^2(n+1)(n+2)}. \]

Scale cancels in the logarithmic ratios and shape cancels when normalizing. The continuous IID null law is parameter-free. Calibrate both tails using this \(n-1\)-component law or externally simulated Pareto samples. Ordinary Greenwood CDF spacings from \(n\) observations have \(n+1\) components and different calibration. Rounding and ties change the continuous-null law. Built-in Pareto simulation is unavailable.

docs.text:
Does, Helmers and Klaassen (1988), Approximating the distribution of Greenwood's statistic, eqs. (1)–(2) describes the squared spacing concentration functional. The logarithmic residual construction above is a library adaptation with the direct derivation given here. An original paper establishing this exact fitted-Pareto implementation was not located; the source is not presented as such a claim.

docs.title: Vasicek–Song fixed-window KL statistic for Pareto I
docs.text: Public class: LequesneKlParetoGofStatistic. Full code: Lequesne_KL_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both shape and scale are unknown. Each call fits

\[ \widehat s=x_{(1)},\qquad \widehat a=\left[\frac1n\sum_i\log(x_i/\widehat s)\right]^{-1}. \]

For ordered data, extend indices outside \(1,\ldots,n\) by the corresponding endpoint. With integer window \(1\le m<n/2\), define

\[ V_{mn}=\frac1n\sum_i\log\left[\frac n{2m}(x_{(i+m)}-x_{(i-m)})\right], \] \[ I_{mn}=-V_{mn}-\log\widehat a+\log\widehat s +(\widehat a+1)\frac1n\sum_i\log(x_i/\widehat s). \]

This equals the negative Vasicek entropy estimate minus the mean fitted log density. It is the raw fixed-window statistic. It does not implement adaptive window selection, the entropy constraint or the bias-corrected p-value procedure in vsgoftest. Negative estimates are retained; reject for large values only.

docs.title: Input and calibration
docs.text:
Require finite real unmasked one-dimensional positive nonconstant data with \(n\ge4\). A constant sample has no finite shape MLE and raises ValueError. A zero window spacing returns positive infinity. The default window is min(int(sqrt(n)), (n - 1) // 2). Pass a different integer m to execute_statistic; booleans, nonintegers and values outside the stated range are rejected. Fits are local to each execution and do not change the declared hypothesis.

The statistic is scale invariant but its finite-sample law depends on shape. External simulation must refit both parameters in every replicate using the same window rule. A plug-in shape bootstrap is approximate. Built-in Pareto simulation is unavailable and generic storage calibration is blocked because its identity does not encode the required shape and execution-time window. No claim of an exact finite-sample test of the whole family is made.

docs.text: Public class: LiaoShimokawaParetoGofStatistic. Full code: LS_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both \(a=\mathrm{shape}>0\) and \(s=\mathrm{scale}>0\) are fixed before observing the sample. Location is zero; \(F(x)=1-(s/x)^a\) for \(x\ge s\). No parameters are estimated.

Here it is applied to a fully specified Pareto CDF; the fitted Weibull/extreme-value critical values in the original paper do not apply. At the lower endpoint the value is positive infinity. Extreme finite penalties can overflow float64.

docs.title: Mathematical verification of Pareto I statistics
docs.text: Audit scope: 21 concrete criteria exported by the pareto package (pareto/pareto_statistics.py): 13 generated EDF criteria, five generated frequency criteria and three composite-hypothesis criteria. The catalog links every public class to its own page, formula, executable example and scientific source.

docs.title: Null hypotheses and transformations
docs.text:
The model has zero location and CDF \(F_{a,s}(x)=1-(s/x)^a\), \(x\ge s>0\), \(a>0\). The generated criteria require both parameters fixed; Obradović requires only scale fixed; Greenwood and KL require neither fixed. These are distinct hypotheses, declared by the concrete classes rather than the family base.

For the specified model, the probability integral transform gives IID \(u_i=F_{a,s}(x_i)\sim U(0,1)\). Applying a fixed-CDF EDF functional is therefore mathematically valid for Pareto without a separate Pareto-specific formula. This argument does not permit estimating parameters and using the same tables. For sorted values define \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\), \(r_i=i-1/2\), and \(W^2=1/(12n)+\sum_i(u_i-r_i/n)^2\).

docs.title: Formula checks
docs.text:
All formulas below agree with the implementations on the checked domain. The source column distinguishes original formulas from adaptations.

Criterion Checked returned value Scientific source Kolmogorov–Smirnov D+ \(D^+\), no scaling Smirnov (1948); Zhang (2002), §2.1 Kolmogorov–Smirnov D− \(D^-\), no scaling Same sources Kolmogorov–Smirnov \(\max(D^+,D^-)\), not squared Zhang (2002), §2.1 Anderson–Darling \(-n-n^{-1}\sum_i(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})]\) Anderson and Darling (1952); Zhang §2.2 Cramér–von Mises \(W^2\) Zhang §2.3 Liao–Shimokawa \(n^{-1/2}\sum_i\max(i/n-u_i,u_i-(i-1)/n)/\sqrt{u_i(1-u_i)}\) Liao and Shimokawa (1999); fixed-CDF adaptation, see qualifications below Watson \(W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2\) Watson (1961); Lemeshko et al. (2014), eq. (6) Kuiper \(D^++D^-\) Kuiper (1960); Lemeshko eq. (1) Scaled Kuiper \(\sqrt n(D^++D^-)\) Lemeshko, discussion before eq. (2) Corrected Kuiper \((\sqrt n+0.155+0.24/\sqrt n)(D^++D^-)\) Lemeshko eq. (3.1) Zhang A \(-\sum_i[\log u_i/(n-r_i)+\log(1-u_i)/r_i]\) Zhang eq. (3.2) Zhang C \(\sum_i[\log((1-u_i)/u_i)-\log((n-i+1/4)/(i-3/4))]^2\) Zhang eq. (3.3) Pearson chi-square \(\sum_j(O_j-E_j)^2/E_j\) Pearson (1900); Cressie and Read (1984), \(\lambda=1\) Freeman–Tukey \(4\sum_j(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j})^2\) Cressie–Read, \(\lambda=-1/2\) Modified log-likelihood \(2\sum_jE_j\log(E_j/O_j)\) Cressie–Read, \(\lambda=-1\) Neyman modified chi-square \(\sum_j(O_j-E_j)^2/O_j\) Cressie–Read, \(\lambda=-2\) Cressie–Read \((9/5)\sum_jO_j[(O_j/E_j)^{2/3}-1]\) Cressie–Read, \(\lambda=2/3\) Obradović \(n^{-1}\sum_i[M_n(z_i)-F_n(z_i)]\), \(z_i=x_i/s\) Obradović et al. (2014), §2, signed integral \(T_n\) Greenwood \(\sum_i\log^2(x_i/x_{(1)})/[\sum_i\log(x_i/x_{(1)})]^2\) Library log-residual adaptation of the concentration functional in Does et al. (1988); derivation below Lequesne KL \(-V_{mn}-n^{-1}\sum_i\log f_{\widehat a,\widehat s}(x_i)\) Lequesne and Regnault (2020); preprint eqs. (5), (8), fixed-window specialization

The frequency kernels require exhaustive cells with positive expected counts and matching totals. With equal-probability binning, \(E_j=n/k\); explicit edges use their null probability differences. The coefficients and zero-count limits were checked independently. For \(O_j=0<E_j\), modified log-likelihood and Neyman are infinite, Freeman–Tukey contributes \(4E_j\), Pearson contributes \(E_j\), and Cressie–Read contributes zero. Returning infinity in these cases is intentional.

docs.title: Obradović
docs.text: The pairwise empirical CDF uses each unordered pair once and denominator \(\binom n2\). Integrating it against \(F_n\) is exactly its average over the sample, which accounts for the additional \(1/n\) factor. The implementation subtracts \(F_n(z_i)\) with inclusive ties, rather than replacing it by a no-tie rank formula. A positive power of all \(z_i\) preserves the pairwise comparisons, so nuisance shape disappears. Known scale is removed by division. The upper-tail convention and signed statistic follow §2; no absolute value or studentization is inserted.

docs.title: Greenwood
docs.text:
This is a direct derivation for the implementation, not an assertion that the cited spacing paper defines a fitted-Pareto test. Since \(\log(X/s)\) is exponential, subtracting its sample minimum leaves one zero and \(k=n-1\) memoryless exponential residuals. Their normalized proportions have a \(k\)-component Dirichlet law. Its moments give

\[ \mathbb EG=\frac2{k+1}=\frac2n,\quad \operatorname{Var}(G)=\frac{4(k-1)}{(k+1)^2(k+2)(k+3)} =\frac{4(n-2)}{n^2(n+1)(n+2)}. \]

Cauchy–Schwarz yields \(1/(n-1)\le G\le1\). The ratio is unchanged by multiplying all observations by a positive constant or raising them to a positive power. At \(n=2\) it is identically one; the implementation requires \(n\ge3\) and a nonconstant sample. Both tails are used. Calibration for ordinary \(n+1\) uniform CDF spacings must not be used without adjusting the number of components.

docs.title: Fixed-window KL
docs.text: Maximizing the Pareto likelihood gives \(\widehat s=x_{(1)}\) and \(\widehat a=1/\bar y\) with \(y_i=\log(x_i/\widehat s)\). Substitution into the fitted mean negative log density gives \(\log\bar y+\log\widehat s+1+\bar y\). Subtracting \(V_{mn}\) gives the implemented expression. Clamped endpoint indices and the factor \(n/(2m)\) match the Vasicek entropy estimator. Scaling the data adds the same logarithm to entropy and negative log density, hence cancels. A power transformation does not cancel in the finite-sample spacing estimator, so shape-dependent calibration remains.

docs.title: Scope, sources and qualifications
docs.text:
This audit verifies statistic calculations and their declared hypotheses. It does not establish exact rejection probabilities, optimality, or power against all alternatives. Built-in Pareto simulation remains unavailable. External calibration must reproduce sample size, the selected statistic normalization, binning, parameter fitting, window selection and any measurement rounding.

Full text was checked for Zhang, Lemeshko et al., Obradović et al., Lequesne and Regnault, and Does et al. The Cressie–Read definition was checked in the article text hosted by NYU. Original Liao–Shimokawa full text could not be retrieved; its expression was checked in Al-Zahrani (2012), eq. (13). The latter studies Topp–Leone distributions. Neither paper supplies calibration for this library's fixed-Pareto adaptation. The criterion uses the shared Liao–Shimokawa kernel through the EDF factory.

The Greenwood source supports the squared-spacing functional, not this exact Pareto construction. Its null derivation is supplied above. KL is the raw fixed-window estimate, not the adaptive-window, entropy-constrained, bias-corrected vsgoftest workflow. Negative KL estimates are possible and are not clipped. The default square-root window does not by itself justify the original paper's asymptotic normal p-value approximation. Plug-in shape bootstrap is approximate; generic stored KL calibration is deliberately rejected.

Small-sample degeneracy is explicit: Watson is \(1/12\) at \(n=1\); raw and scaled Kuiper are one and corrected Kuiper is 1.395. These calculations are defined but uninformative. Corrected Kuiper's asymptotic calibration is not exact at small \(n\).

docs.title: Numerical verification and corrections
docs.text:
The focused checks include:

  • All 13 EDF statistics against independent formulas on four shape/scale pairs; AD, CVM and Watson also against numerical EDF integrals, and KS against SciPy.
  • AD, the weighted Liao–Shimokawa functional and all three Zhang statistics against 240-digit decimal references with upper-tail CDFs rounding to one.
  • All five frequency statistics against SciPy power divergences or their analytic zero-count limits, using explicit and equal-probability cells.
  • Greenwood's exact ratio, scale/power invariance, range and Dirichlet moments in deterministic seeded simulation at \(n=3,7,20\) (6,000 replicates each).
  • Obradović's signed sum against brute-force inclusive indicators and exact rational comparisons, including tied values and overflowing ordinary ratios.
  • KL against independent fitted Pareto log densities and SciPy's Vasicek entropy, across windows; scale invariance, lack of shape invariance, negative values, tied zero spacings and invalid windows.
  • Hypothesis declarations, invalid data, lower endpoints, adjacent large floats, no mutation or retained fits, masked input, public stubs and documentation.

No mathematical formula changes were needed. The audit found and fixed an input validation defect: the three explicit composite criteria silently discarded MaskedArray masks and used hidden observations. They now reject masked input, consistent with the generated criteria. Regression tests cover all 21 classes.

The focused suite passed 527 tests. It includes documentation coverage for all 21 classes, execution of every criterion-page and overview example, local link validation and checks for scientific references and examples in docstrings. Ruff and the pareto/__init__.pyi generator's --check passed. MkDocs built successfully; its warnings concern existing broken links in other families, with no Pareto page warnings.

Ordinary pytest collection is still blocked by the existing import of the removed AbstractChi2Statistic from edf.py in exponentiated_weibull.py. The successful run bypassed only continuous/__init__.py, loading the actual Pareto module, shared kernels, binning and distribution implementation. This does not verify normal package initialization or resolve the unrelated migration errors.

From the repository root, the isolated focused run is reproducible with:

.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import sys
import types
from pathlib import Path
import pytest

name = "pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous"
package = types.ModuleType(name)
package.__path__ = [str(Path("src/pysatl_criterion/statistics/goodness_of_fit/continuous").resolve())]
sys.modules[name] = package
raise SystemExit(pytest.main([
    "-q",
    "tests/distributions/test_pareto.py",
    "tests/distributions/test_pareto_correctness.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_pareto_dynamic.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_pareto_mathematical_validation.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_pareto_documentation.py",
    "tests/statistics/test_pareto_numba.py",
]))
PY
.venv/bin/python scripts/generate_pareto_stub.py --check

After the obsolete imports are migrated, the same six test paths can be supplied to ordinary python -m pytest -q without the bootstrap.

docs.title: Numba optimization
docs.text:
All 21 criteria execute compiled numerical kernels. The 18 generated EDF and frequency criteria reuse the shared Numba kernels. Greenwood and fixed-window KL now have static do_execute_statistic kernels decorated with @jit(nopython=True, cache=True). Stable log-ratio and log-probability evaluation also use cached nopython methods. Validation, hypothesis handling and all helper methods reside inside the Pareto classes; there are no module-level helper functions. No fastmath approximation is enabled.

Obradović uses a compiled pair-counting kernel on unambiguous data. If its logarithmic comparison tolerance detects a potentially ambiguous boundary, the kernel returns an internal NaN sentinel and the public method recomputes using exact Fraction comparisons. The sentinel is never returned as the statistic. This preserves inclusive ties, extreme ratios and the original binary-float semantics. Exact arithmetic remains in Python; the whole public method is not claimed to be nopython. Worst-case complexity and memory bounds are unchanged.

test_pareto_numba.py verifies compiled public execution paths for every class, the class-only helper layout, fast-path execution without the exact fallback, and agreement with rational references when fallback is needed. The existing high-precision, boundary, invariance and documentation checks remain in the suite.

A local warmed benchmark compared the pre-optimization implementation with the new public execute_statistic calls, including validation and sorting. It used seed 2026, samples 1 + rng.pareto(2, n), the minimum of five repeated timings, 1,000 calls per repeat except 10 for Obradović. Compilation was excluded. These are local measurements, not performance guarantees:

Criterion Sample size Before, microseconds/call After, microseconds/call Speedup Greenwood 1,000 40.0 30.3 1.32× Fixed-window KL 1,000 53.0 34.1 1.55× Obradović, ordinary continuous sample 500 10,393.9 4,273.8 2.43× Anderson–Darling 1,000 75.0 61.0 1.23×

First use incurs compilation or cache-loading cost. Samples requiring rational fallback may not obtain the ordinary-sample Obradović speedup.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text:
The implementation follows the continuous/uniform layout:

continuous/pareto/
    __init__.py
    __init__.pyi
    pareto_statistics.py

The package initializer explicitly re-exports all public classes and preserves pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.pareto as their public module path. Existing imports and pickled class references remain valid. Private factory catalogs live in pareto_statistics.py. The stub generator reads that implementation and writes pareto/__init__.pyi; use its --check option to verify freshness. Tests check package/implementation class identity and old pickle references for every exported class, and execute class docstrings using the implementation module's globals.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood for Pareto I
docs.text: Public class: ModifiedLogLikelihoodParetoGofStatistic. Full code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both \(a=\mathrm{shape}>0\) and \(s=\mathrm{scale}>0\) are fixed before observing the sample. Location is zero; \(F(x)=1-(s/x)^a\) for \(x\ge s\). No parameters are estimated.

For full-support edges \(b_0,\ldots,b_k\), let \(O_j\) be the observed counts and \(E_j=n[F(b_j)-F(b_{j-1})]\). Expected counts must be positive and totals must agree.

\[ T=2\sum_j E_j\log(E_j/O_j). \]

Power-divergence parameter \(\lambda=-1\). Any empty observed cell with positive expected count gives positive infinity. This is the reverse likelihood discrepancy, not the usual \(2\sum O_j\log(O_j/E_j)\).

Input is a finite real one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge1\) and \(x_i\ge s\). Masked observations and data below scale are rejected. The method returns one scalar statistic; large values reject. Ties are accepted computationally, but continuous-null calibration does not account for rounding or discrete data.

docs.title: Binning and calibration
docs.text:
The constructor accepts keyword-only binning. The default is EqualProbabilityBins(PowerCount(2.0, 0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000). It counts transformed values in equal-probability cells and sets \(E_j=n/k\). There must be at least two retained cells. See binning. For fixed cells and large expected counts, the usual asymptotic reference is \(\chi^2_{k-1}\); this is not an exact small-sample calibration. Sparse cells, merging and adaptive rules require calibration reproducing the same policy. Binning settings are included in configuration().

Built-in Pareto Monte Carlo generation is unavailable; calibration is external.

docs.text:

    ModifiedLogLikelihoodParetoGofStatistic,

statistic = ModifiedLogLikelihoodParetoGofStatistic(
    Pareto.DEFAULT.parse({"shape": 2, "scale": 1}),
    binning=ExplicitBins((1, 1.5, 3, float("inf"))),
)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([1.1, 1.4, 1.9, 2.7, 4.2, 8.0])
print(value)

docs.title: Neyman modified chi-square for Pareto I
docs.text: Public class: NeymanChi2ParetoGofStatistic. Full code: CHI2_NEYMAN_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both \(a=\mathrm{shape}>0\) and \(s=\mathrm{scale}>0\) are fixed before observing the sample. Location is zero; \(F(x)=1-(s/x)^a\) for \(x\ge s\). No parameters are estimated.

For full-support edges \(b_0,\ldots,b_k\), let \(O_j\) be the observed counts and \(E_j=n[F(b_j)-F(b_{j-1})]\). Expected counts must be positive and totals must agree.

\[ T=\sum_j\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{O_j}. \]

Power-divergence parameter \(\lambda=-2\). Any empty observed cell with positive expected count gives positive infinity.

docs.text:

docs.title: Obradović–Jovanović–Milošević integral statistic
docs.text: Public class: ObradovicParetoGofStatistic. Full code: OJM_Integral_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Scale \(s>0\) is known and shape \(a>0\) is unknown. Put \(z_i=x_i/s\) and define

\[ F_n(t)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbf1\{z_i\le t\},\qquad M_n(t)=\binom n2^{-1}\sum_{j<k}\mathbf1\{\max(z_j/z_k,z_k/z_j)\le t\}. \]

The returned statistic is

\[ T_n=\frac1n\sum_i[M_n(z_i)-F_n(z_i)]. \]

This is the signed empirical integral, without absolute value or \(\sqrt n\) scaling. It is distinct from the paper's supremum statistic \(V_n\). The upper critical tail follows the paper's convention; it is not asserted to be consistent against every alternative.

docs.title: Input and calibration
docs.text:
Require finite real unmasked one-dimensional data, \(n\ge2\) and \(x_i\ge s\). Constants and ties are accepted. Indicators use inclusive comparisons. A cached Numba kernel counts pairs using log ratios to avoid overflow. Numerically ambiguous boundaries trigger recomputation with exact rational comparisons in Python. Cost is \(O(n^2\log n)\) and working memory \(O(n)\).

The paper uses \(s=1\); division by the known scale gives that case. Raising every \(z_i\) to the same positive power preserves each comparison and eliminates the nuisance shape from the continuous IID null law. Estimate neither parameter in this procedure. A scale estimated from the same sample changes the null law and is unsupported. Calibration is external; built-in Pareto simulation is unavailable. Finite-sample calibration must retain the same normalization and inclusive tie convention, and model rounding if present.

docs.title: Watson for Pareto I
docs.text: Public class: WatsonParetoGofStatistic. Full code: WATSON_PARETO_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Both \(a=\mathrm{shape}>0\) and \(s=\mathrm{scale}>0\) are fixed before observing the sample. Location is zero; \(F(x)=1-(s/x)^a\) for \(x\ge s\). No parameters are estimated.

For sorted data set \(u_i=F(x_{(i)})\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\).

\[ U^2=W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2. \]

The implementation evaluates centered squared deviations plus \(1/(12n)\) to avoid cancellation. It applies no small-sample correction. At \(n=1\) the value is always \(1/12\), so the statistic is uninformative.

Input is a finite real one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge1\) and \(x_i\ge s\). Masked observations and data below scale are rejected. The method returns one scalar statistic; large values reject. Ties are accepted computationally, but continuous-null calibration does not account for rounding or discrete data.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
The probability integral transform gives the same finite-sample statistic law as independent uniform observations when both Pareto parameters are truly fixed. Do not substitute estimates from this sample and then use the fixed-null tables. Use critical values for this precise normalization and sample size.

docs.title: Examples and calibration
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import StudentDistributionDescriptor as Student
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.student import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovStudentGofStatistic,
    LequesneRenyiStudentGofStatistic,
)

sample = [-3.2, -1.1, -0.3, 0.2, 0.7, 1.8, 4.1]
fixed = KolmogorovSmirnovStudentGofStatistic(Student.DEFAULT.parse({"df": 5, "loc": 0, "scale": 1}))
composite = LequesneRenyiStudentGofStatistic(Student.DEFAULT.parse({"df": 5}), k=3)
print(fixed.execute_statistic(sample), composite.execute_statistic(sample))

The APIs return statistics, not p-values. Fixed-df composite calibration must recompute the moments/neighbours on every Monte Carlo replicate, keeping df and algorithm settings. Frequency calibration preserves the binning strategy. Lequesne T2 requires external parametric bootstrap at explicitly fitted simulation parameters and refits all parameters on every replicate; the built-in generator and storage lookup reject an unspecified simulation df.

The implementations here are one-dimensional and assume independent observations. The cited multivariate and GARCH research does not imply those models are implemented by this module. Theorem assumptions can be stronger than the computational domain; consult the individual pages before choosing calibration.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Fix all three parameters: df > 0, finite loc, and scale > 0. Use StudentDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({'df': 5, 'loc': 0, 'scale': 1}). Omitted parameters remain unknown and are not supported by this criterion. Write \(u_i=F_{\nu,\mu,s}(X_{(i)})\) for the CDF values of sorted observations.

\[ A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})] \]

No fitted-parameter or finite-sample multiplier is applied.

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample. Ties and constants are allowed. It returns one scalar without changing the input or retaining fitted state. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

The Student implementation evaluates log-CDF and log-survival separately. AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang kernels consume these logarithms directly; other EDF kernels reconstruct the CDF. Unrepresentable standardization or underflow of a required tail probability raises ValueError.

For a continuous fully specified null, the probability integral transform removes the null parameters from the EDF law. Calibrate the same statistic at the same sample size; no parameter estimation is performed. The source below identifies the general discrepancy, not a separate Student-specific derivation.

docs.title: Cadirci kNN Rényi-entropy criterion for Student distributions
docs.text:
All Student criteria · Mathematical verification

CadirciRenyiStudentGofStatistic implements equation (20) of Çadirci, Evans, Leonenko, Makogin and Seleznjev (2025) for dimension one.

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Fix df = ν > 2; location and scale remain unknown. Set q=1-2/(ν+1) and use sample variance with denominator n−1:

\[ \widehat\sigma^2=(1-2/\nu)\frac{\sum_j(X_j-\bar X)^2}{n-1}. \]

Let ρ_i be the distance to observation i's kth nearest neighbour, excluding itself. With C_k=[Γ(k)/Γ(k+1−q)]^{1/(1−q)}, estimate entropy by

\[ \widehat H_q=\frac{1}{1-q}\log\left[ \frac1n\sum_i\{2(n-1)C_k\rho_i\}^{1-q}\right]. \]

The statistic is W=H_q(t_ν(scale=σ̂))−Ĥ_q. The theoretical entropy is evaluated analytically. Calculations use unit sample variance to avoid overflow; in one dimension the two entropy scale terms cancel exactly. This preserves the paper's unscaled statistic and uses the original Euclidean neighbour distances up to a common scale factor.

docs.title: Use and calibration
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import StudentDistributionDescriptor as Student
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.student import (
    CadirciRenyiStudentGofStatistic,
)

criterion = CadirciRenyiStudentGofStatistic(Student.DEFAULT.parse({"df": 5}), k=3)
value = criterion.execute_statistic([-3.2, -1.1, -0.3, 0.2, 0.7, 1.8, 4.1])

k defaults to 3 and must satisfy 1 <= k < n. Samples must be finite, one-dimensional and contain distinct observations; ties raise ValueError. Large values reject. Negative finite-sample values are valid and remain unclipped. No parameter estimates or sample data are retained.

Monte Carlo calibration uses the fixed df, the same k, and recomputes the sample variance and neighbours on every replicate. The built-in sampler chooses location zero and scale one. There is no fitted df or universal chi-square reference distribution. The formula is available for df > 2; the stronger moment conditions for mean-square convergence in Theorem 6 must be checked separately and are not claimed throughout this whole interval.

docs.title: Lequesne Rényi-entropy criterion for Student distributions
docs.text:
All Student criteria · Mathematical verification

LequesneRenyiStudentGofStatistic implements both statistics in Lequesne (2015), AIP Conference Proceedings 1641, 487–494, equations (7)–(10).

docs.title: Hypotheses and formulas
docs.text:
With Student.DEFAULT.parse({'df': nu}), equation (7) gives

\[ T_1=h_q( u,\widehat\sigma^2)-\widehat H_{n,k,q},\qquad q= rac{ u-1}{ u+1},\qquad \widehat\sigma^2= rac{ u-2}{ u}\widehat\Sigma^2. \]

The implementation chooses the unbiased sample variance (denominator n−1) for Σ̂². The article allows a consistent variance estimator without specifying the denominator. With this choice, T1 equals the univariate Çadirci statistic at the same df and k.

With Student.DEFAULT.parse({}), equation (8) gives

\[ T_2=h_{\widehat q}(\widehat u,\widehat\sigma^2) -\widehat H_{n,k,\widehat q},\qquad \widehat q= rac{\widehat u-1}{\widehat u+1}. \]

All three parameters are fitted numerically by maximum likelihood on each call. The theoretical entropy uses the MLE scale, and both entropy terms use the fitted order. The implementation checks optimizer convergence. It rescales the sample before fitting for numerical stability; the common logarithmic scale term cancels from the entropy difference. Estimates are not stored on the instance.

In both cases the sample entropy is the kth-nearest-neighbour estimate (10):

\[ \widehat H_{n,k,q}= rac{1}{1-q}\log\left[ rac1n\sum_i\{2(n-1)G_k ho_i^{(k)}\}^{1-q} ight],\qquad G_k=\left[ rac{\Gamma(k)}{\Gamma(k+1-q)} ight]^{1/(1-q)}. \]

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import StudentDistributionDescriptor as Student
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.student import (
    LequesneRenyiStudentGofStatistic,
)

known_df = LequesneRenyiStudentGofStatistic(Student.DEFAULT.parse({"df": 5}), k=3)
unknown_df = LequesneRenyiStudentGofStatistic(Student.DEFAULT.parse({}), k=3)
value = known_df.execute_statistic([-3.2, -1.1, -0.3, 0.2, 0.7, 1.8, 4.1])

k defaults to 3 and must satisfy 1 <= k < n. Observations must be finite, distinct and one-dimensional. For T2, at least four observations are required. The finite-variance construction requires fixed or fitted df > 2. Fits outside this domain and nonconverged fits raise ValueError; they are not clamped to a boundary. The convergence result in Theorem 2 has the stronger condition df > 4. Negative finite-sample statistics remain unchanged.

docs.title: Rejection direction and calibration
docs.text:
Large entropy deficits reject: the criterion returns RightAlternative(). The lower-tail inequalities printed on page 493 conflict with the positive alternative limit in Theorem 2 and the entropy-deficit construction. This implementation uses the upper tail and does not embed the paper's critical-value table or claim its inequalities are correct as printed.

For T1, the built-in sampler uses standard Student observations at the fixed df. Each simulation must repeat the variance and neighbour calculations and preserve k.

For T2, there is no universal shape-free calibration. External parametric bootstrap must simulate at the observed fitted parameters and repeat the entire fit, including the entropy order, on every replicate. Failed fits must not be silently dropped. The built-in hypothesis sampler and stored-distribution lookup reject this unspecified-df case with an explicit error. The hypothesis remains empty; fitted parameters are not substituted into it.

Code: LEQUESNE_RENYI_STUDENT_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.text: This report covers continuous/student/student_statistics.py: 21 concrete classes, comprising 13 generated EDF criteria, 5 generated frequency criteria and 3 specialized criteria. Lequesne has two hypothesis modes in one class. See the complete catalog for class names, short codes and individual pages.

docs.title: Hypothesis and parameter estimation
docs.text:
The one-dimensional model is

\[ F_{ u,\mu,s}(x)=F_{t_ u}((x-\mu)/s),\qquad u>0,\quad s>0. \]

scale is \(s\), not variance. Where it exists, variance is \(s^2 u/( u-2)\). Every class declares its own supported fixed-parameter sets; AbstractStudentGofStatistic supplies no family-wide hypothesis declaration.

Implementations Hypothesis Estimation performed on each sample 13 EDF and 5 frequency df, loc, scale all fixed None Meintanis ECF Only df > 2 fixed Mean and scatter \(( u-2)S_n/ u\), with \(S_n=n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i- ar X)^2\) Çadirci Rényi Only df > 2 fixed Scatter \(( u-2)\widehat\Sigma^2/ u\), with unbiased sample variance (denominator \(n-1\)) Lequesne T1 Only df > 2 fixed Same unbiased variance choice as Çadirci Lequesne T2 Empty parameter set Numerical MLE of df, location and scale; fitted df must exceed 2

Omitted parameters remain unknown. Fully specified parameters are not accepted by the three specialized criteria. These implementations handle independent one-dimensional data; they do not fit multivariate models or GARCH innovations.

docs.title: Formula checks: generated criteria
docs.text:
For EDF criteria, \(u_i=F_{\nu,\mu,s}(X_{(i)})\), \(r_i=i-1/2\), \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\). For count criteria, \(O_j\) denotes observed counts and \(E_j=np_j>0\) expected counts. The following table enumerates every generated criterion; definitions were compared with its selected shared kernel and the numerical references below.

Criterion Implemented definition Scientific source Kolmogorov–Smirnov D+ \(D^+=\max_{1\le i\le n}(i/n-u_i)\) Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, §2.1. Kolmogorov–Smirnov D− \(D^-=\max_{1\le i\le n}(u_i-(i-1)/n)\) Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, §2.1. Kolmogorov–Smirnov \(D=\max(D^+,D^-),\quad D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i),\quad D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\) Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, §2.1. Anderson–Darling \(A^2=-n-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})]\) Anderson and Darling (1952), Asymptotic Theory of Certain Goodness of Fit Criteria Based on Stochastic Processes; Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, §2.2. Watson \(U^2=W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2,\quad W^2=\frac1{12n}+\sum_i[u_i-(i-1/2)/n]^2\) Watson (1961), Goodness-of-fit tests on a circle. Scaled Kuiper \(V_s=\sqrt n(D^++D^-)\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), Using the Kuiper and Watson tests of goodness-of-fit for composite hypotheses, equations (1)–(3). Corrected Kuiper \(V_c=\left(\sqrt n+0.155+\frac{0.24}{\sqrt n}\right)(D^++D^-)\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), Using the Kuiper and Watson tests of goodness-of-fit for composite hypotheses, equations (1)–(3). Zhang Z_K \(Z_K=\max_i\left[r_i\log\frac{r_i}{nu_i}+(n-r_i)\log\frac{n-r_i}{n(1-u_i)}\right],\quad r_i=i-\tfrac12\) Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, equation (3.1). Zhang Z_A \(Z_A=-\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\frac{\log u_i}{n-i+1/2}+\frac{\log(1-u_i)}{i-1/2}\right]\) Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, equation (3.2). Zhang Z_C \(Z_C=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\log\frac{1-u_i}{u_i}-\log\frac{n-i+1/4}{i-3/4}\right]^2\) Zhang (2002), Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio, equation (3.3). Freeman–Tukey \(FT=4\sum_j(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j})^2\) Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, power-divergence parameter \(\lambda=-1/2\). Modified log-likelihood \(MLL=2\sum_j E_j\log(E_j/O_j)\) Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, \(\lambda=-1\). Neyman chi-squared \(N=\sum_j\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{O_j}\) Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, \(\lambda=-2\). Cressie–Read \(CR=\frac95\sum_j O_j\left[(O_j/E_j)^{2/3}-1\right]\) Cressie and Read (1984), Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests, \(\lambda=2/3\).

The five count statistics correspond to power-divergence parameters \(\lambda=1,-1/2,-1,-2,2/3\). At an empty observed cell with \(E_j>0\), the contributions are respectively \(E_j\), \(4E_j\), infinity, infinity and zero. The default binning is EqualProbabilityBins() with a sample-size-dependent count; explicit counts and other strategies are constructor settings.

docs.title: Meintanis ECF
docs.text:
The criterion page specifies the one-dimensional specialization of Meintanis et al. (2024), equations (2.3)–(2.8), (3.3) and (4.7). Its i.i.d. experiments use moment estimation. The standardized observations are \(Y_i=(X_i- ar X)/\sqrt{( u-2)S_n}\), so their target distribution has Student scale \(1/\sqrt u\), not unit scale. Its CF is

\[ \phi_ u(t)= rac{2^{1- u/2}}{\Gamma( u/2)} |t|^{ u/2}K_{ u/2}(|t|),\qquad \phi_ u(0)=1. \]

The returned value is

\[ rac{n}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R} \left|n^{-1}\sum_i e^{itY_i}-\phi_ u(t) ight|^2\phi_{ u_w}(t)\,dt. \]

weight_df=None selects \( u_w= u\); a different positive value selects the alternative Student weight. The change of variable used for numerical integration retains the Jacobian, \(n\) factor, both frequency half-lines and \(1/(2\pi)\) normalization. A failed quadrature raises an error.

An independent closed-form Fourier-inversion check at \( u=3\) uses \(\phi_3(t)=(1+|t|)e^{-|t|}\), with either the same weight or a Cauchy weight. Separate density integrals check the standard-scale CF at several degrees of freedom, including the large-order Bessel fallback. These checks verify the statistic's normalization, not finite-sample significance levels.

docs.title: Çadirci Rényi kNN
docs.text:
The criterion page follows Çadirci et al. (2025), sections 2.1, 3, 4 and 5.2, with dimension one and \(q=1-2/( u+1)\). With \(\widehat s^2=(1-2/ u)\widehat\Sigma^2\), equation (20) gives \(W=H_q(t_ u(\widehat s))-\widehat H_{n,k,q}\), where

\[ \widehat H_{n,k,q}= rac1{1-q}\log\left[ rac1n\sum_i\{2(n-1)C_k ho_i^{(k)}\}^{1-q} ight],\qquad C_k=\left[ rac{\Gamma(k)}{\Gamma(k+1-q)} ight]^{1/(1-q)}. \]

The unbiased variance, exclusion of each point from its own neighbour set, unit-ball volume 2, factor \(n-1\), and gamma correction were checked independently. Numerical reference calculations use raw pairwise distances and direct integration of the Student density raised to \(q\). Rescaling before calculation cancels in the entropy difference. Large-df calculations were checked against the Gaussian/Shannon limit. Negative finite-sample values remain unclipped. The formula is defined for \( u>2\); stronger convergence moment conditions in Theorem 6 are not asserted over the entire computational domain.

docs.title: Lequesne Rényi T1 and T2
docs.text:
The criterion page follows equations (7)–(10) of Lequesne (2015), checked directly in the user-provided full text, pp. 489–493. T1 fixes \( u\) and estimates variance; choosing the unbiased variance makes its calculation equal to the univariate Çadirci calculation. The paper allows a consistent variance estimator and does not prescribe its denominator.

T2 uses \(h_{\widehat q}(\widehat u,\widehat s^2)-\widehat H_{n,k,\widehat q}\), with both shape and scale from the numerical MLE and \(\widehat q=(\widehat u-1)/(\widehat u+1)\). Tests separately check that the fitted entropy order and MLE scale are used, rather than a fixed order or a moment-matched scale. They also compare an actual fit with a separate SciPy fit. Optimizer convergence is checked; that check is not a proof of a unique global likelihood maximum. Fits with \(\widehat u\le2\) are rejected, not clamped. Theorem 2 uses the stronger condition \( u>4\) (or \(\widehat u>4\)).

The lower-tail critical-region inequalities on p. 493 contradict the positive alternative limit stated in Theorem 2. The implementation uses an upper-tail rejection rule consistent with the entropy deficit. It does not embed Table 1, claim agreement with its tabulated quantiles, or force finite-sample deficits to be nonnegative. The scale notation in the density is used consistently: standardization divides by \(s\), not by \(s^2\).

docs.title: Calibration, numerical boundaries and scope
docs.text:
All 21 criteria return a statistic and use RightAlternative; no automatic p-value follows from executing a statistic. The fixed-null EDF discrepancies are distribution-free under the continuous probability integral transform. This does not extend to substituting estimated parameters into those classes. Liao–Shimokawa here is a fixed-Student application of its EDF functional; original fitted-Weibull/extreme-value critical values do not apply. Kuiper's finite-sample multiplier is not itself a p-value algorithm.

EDF input can contain ties or constants and must be nonempty, finite and one-dimensional. Student log-CDF and log-survival are computed separately; AD, Liao–Shimokawa and Zhang consume logarithms directly. Underflow of a required log probability or unrepresentable standardization raises ValueError. A representable raw observation does not guarantee a representable tail.

Frequency input constraints also depend on the binning strategy. The default CDF-space equal-probability rule includes an internal boundary in the right cell and includes 1 in the last cell. Calibration preserves the selected bins and count rule. The usual chi-square count limit is asymptotic, not an exact finite-sample result; empty-bin infinities are intentional.

Composite criteria recompute estimates on each call and retain no fitted state. Meintanis accepts ties but rejects constants; the entropy criteria require distinct observations and \(n>k\). Lequesne T2 needs at least four observations. For fixed df, location and scale invariance permit standard Student Monte Carlo samples, preserving df, k or the ECF weight and numerical settings. For unknown df, Lequesne T2 requires an external shape-specific parametric bootstrap and refitting on every replicate. The built-in sampler and storage lookup reject that unspecified simulation shape; failed fits must not be silently removed from calibration.

The report distinguishes source attribution from mathematical and executable checks. The Meintanis author PDF, the Çadirci full preprint and the supplied Lequesne PDF were read during implementation. References for generated kernels are inherited from the shared EDF/frequency definitions and existing mathematical reviews. This documentation audit does not claim fresh full-text verification of every historical article: the DOI pages for Zhang, Liao–Shimokawa, Cressie–Read and Lemeshko were inaccessible through the web tool. Formula and numerical checks remain independent of that access limitation. None of these checks establishes nominal test size or power against every alternative.

docs.title: Numerical and documentation verification
docs.text:
Verification on 2026-10-14 includes the following suites:

  • tests/distributions/test_student.py and test_student_correctness.py: SciPy KS references, direct EDF integrals, Zhang equations, tails, sample validation, affine transformations, unchanged input and catalog completeness.
  • tests/statistics/test_student_composite.py: closed-form ECF inversion, entropy density integrals and brute-force neighbours, sample/setting validation, invariance, calibration identity and large-df limits.
  • tests/statistics/test_lequesne_student.py: both entropy formulas, actual and controlled MLE results, fitted order/scale, failed fits, explicit hypotheses, registration and bootstrap restrictions.
  • tests/statistics/test_edf.py and test_frequency.py: independent shared formula references, high-precision Zhang values, SciPy power-divergence comparisons, zero counts and endpoint cases. These exercise common kernels; they are not additional Student-specific scientific derivations.

The documentation audit compares the runtime concrete-class catalog with individual pages, requires scientific URLs and Python examples, checks every catalog/navigation entry and local link, and executes the examples. It also builds MkDocs to verify page rendering and math blocks. The measured results and environment limitations are recorded below.

Results:

  • 21/21 concrete criteria have an individual page, a scientific reference, a Python example, an overview entry and a navigation entry.
  • 22 Python examples executed successfully, including the overview example; local documentation links resolved.
  • 582 tests passed across the six suites listed above.
  • MkDocs built successfully; all 21 criterion pages contain generated arithmatex markup. This checks HTML generation, not browser-side MathJax rendering. Existing build warnings concern other documentation sections; none concern Student pages.

The tests and examples used an isolated continuous package namespace to avoid executing its initializer. Ordinary package initialization currently fails because beta.py imports AbstractChi2Statistic from edf.py, where that class is no longer defined. Thus these results verify Student and shared kernels, but do not certify that ordinary package imports work in the current checkout. The documented examples use ordinary public imports and require that unrelated initialization issue to be resolved when run without isolation.

docs.title: Meintanis ECF criterion for Student distributions
docs.text:
All Student criteria · Mathematical verification

MeintanisStudentGofStatistic implements the univariate i.i.d. specialization of Meintanis, Milošević, Obradović and Veljović (2024), equations (2.3)–(2.8), with the moment estimates in (3.3).

docs.title: Hypothesis and statistic
docs.text:
Only df = ν > 2 is fixed. Location and scale are unknown and re-estimated on every call. Write

\[ S_n= rac1n\sum_j(X_j- ar X)^2,\quad \widehat V= rac{ u-2}{ u}S_n,\quad Y_j= rac{X_j- ar X}{\sqrt{ u\widehat V}}. \]

For the reduced-scale Student characteristic function

\[ \phi_ u(t)= rac{2^{1- u/2}}{\Gamma( u/2)} |t|^{ u/2}K_{ u/2}(|t|),\qquad \phi_ u(0)=1, \]

the returned statistic is

\[ T= rac{n}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R} \left| rac1n\sum_j e^{itY_j}-\phi_ u(t) ight|^2 \phi_{ u_w}(t)\,dt. \]

By default weight_df=None uses ν_w=ν. A positive weight_df selects the alternative Student weight discussed in equation (4.7). The implementation evaluates the one-dimensional integral directly, including its normalization. epsabs=1e-8, epsrel=1e-7 and limit=250 control quadrature; failure to reach the requested accuracy raises ValueError.

docs.title: Use and calibration
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import StudentDistributionDescriptor as Student
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.student import (
    MeintanisStudentGofStatistic,
)

criterion = MeintanisStudentGofStatistic(Student.DEFAULT.parse({"df": 5}))
value = criterion.execute_statistic([-3.2, -1.1, -0.3, 0.2, 0.7, 1.8, 4.1])

Large values reject. Samples must be finite, one-dimensional, nonconstant and contain at least two observations. Ties are allowed. The criterion is invariant to location, nonzero scale and reflection; it leaves input and hypothesis unchanged. The built-in hypothesis sampler uses t(df, loc=0, scale=1). Each Monte Carlo replicate must call execute_statistic to re-estimate the moments. Configuration records the weight and numerical settings, so distinct calibrations remain distinct.

This class uses moment estimation, which requires df > 2. It does not fit unknown degrees of freedom, multivariate scatter matrices or GARCH models.

Code: MEINTANIS_ECF_STUDENT_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood for a specified Student distribution
docs.text:
All Student criteria · Mathematical verification

Class: ModifiedLogLikelihoodStudentGofStatistic. Code: MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_STUDENT_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Hypothesis and formula
docs.text:
Fix all three parameters: df > 0, finite loc, and scale > 0. Use StudentDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({'df': 5, 'loc': 0, 'scale': 1}). Omitted parameters remain unknown and are not supported by this criterion. Write \(O_j\) for observed bin counts and \(E_j=np_j>0\) for expected counts under the specified Student model.

\[ MLL=2\sum_j E_j\log(E_j/O_j) \]

Any \(O_j=0\) with \(E_j>0\) gives positive infinity. This is the reverse log-likelihood statistic, with expected counts as weights.

The keyword-only binning accepts a BinningStrategy. The default EqualProbabilityBins() selects its count from the sample size. Use EqualProbabilityBins(count=4) for four cells of probability ¼. Its CDF-space intervals are left-closed/right-open, except that the last cell also includes 1. n_bins is not a constructor argument.

docs.title: Input, result and calibration
docs.text:
execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a nonempty, finite, one-dimensional real sample. Ties and constants are allowed. It returns one scalar without changing the input or retaining fitted state. Large values reject (RightAlternative). Extra execution keywords are ignored.

The shared binning pipeline constructs observed and expected counts on every call. Infinite empty-cell penalties are valid statistic values, not invalid samples. Additional binning constraints, such as min_expected, can reject small samples. See the formula's zero-count convention above.

Preserve both sample size and binning strategy in Monte Carlo calibration. For fixed equiprobable cells the null counts are multinomial; the usual chi-square limit with number-of-cells minus one degrees of freedom is only asymptotic. No automatic p-value or exact chi-square calibration is provided. Other binning rules need their matching calibration. The source describes a general count discrepancy applied here to Student probabilities.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import StudentDistributionDescriptor as Student
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.student import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodStudentGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Student.DEFAULT.parse({"df": 5, "loc": 0, "scale": 1})
statistic = ModifiedLogLikelihoodStudentGofStatistic(
    parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=4)
)
value = statistic.execute_statistic([-3.2, -1.1, -0.3, 0.2, 0.7, 1.8, 4.1])
print(value)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
AndersonDarlingUniformGofStatistic has algorithm code AD_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. See the uniformity catalog.

Performs the Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The test gives more weight to discrepancies in the tails than the Cramer-von Mises statistic.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

Test Statistic The statistic is computed from the ordered sample using the log cumulative distribution function and log survival function of the reference uniform distribution.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    AndersonDarlingUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = AndersonDarlingUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - explicitly fixed left boundary of the uniform distribution.

b - explicitly fixed right boundary of the uniform distribution.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For the uniform distribution on \([a, b]\),

\[ F_0(x) = \frac{x - a}{b - a}, \quad a \le x \le b. \]

The statistic uses logarithms of the uniform CDF and survival probabilities at the ordered observations. A CDF value of 0 or 1 produces positive infinity. Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform model.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Computes a Bickel-Rosenblatt-type density-based goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic compares a kernel density estimate of the standardized sample with the unit uniform density.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    BickelRosenblattUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = BickelRosenblattUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1}), bandwidth="auto"
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - left boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 0.

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

bandwidth - kernel bandwidth or auto. Default value is auto.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The implementation standardizes observations to \([0, 1]\), uses a Gaussian kernel density estimate, and analytically evaluates

\[ \int_0^1 \left(\hat f(x) - 1\right)^2 dx. \]

The bandwidth is measured in unit-interval coordinates. auto uses \(h=1.06s_n n^{-1/5}\), with population standard deviation \(s_n\). A constant sample requires an explicit positive bandwidth. No asymptotic centering, boundary correction, or \(n\sqrt h\) scaling is applied. Calibration must use this exact statistic and bandwidth rule. Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform density.

docs.title: Author(s)
docs.text: Aleksandr Podmarev, Alexey Mironov

docs.title: References
docs.text: Bickel, P.J. and Rosenblatt, M. (1973): On some global measures of the deviations of density function estimates. - Annals of Statistics, vol. 1, pp. 1071-1095.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs a censored Stein-type U-statistic test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). When no censoring is supplied, the implementation falls back to SteinUniformGofStatistic.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis concerns latent lifetimes \(X\sim U(a,b)\), observed as \(Y=\min(X,C)\) under independent right censoring.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    CensoredSteinUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = CensoredSteinUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic(
    [0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91],
    censoring_indices=[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0],
)
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - left boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 0.

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

censoring_indices - binary array where 1 indicates a censored observation and 0 indicates an uncensored observation.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The implementation standardizes observations to \([0, 1]\). For censored data, the reverse Kaplan–Meier estimator supplies \(\widehat K_c(Y_i-)\), the left limit of censoring survival. Observed events precede censorings at tied times. With \(c_i=1\) for censoring, \(w_i=(1-c_i)/\widehat K_c(Y_i-)\):

\[ \widehat\Delta_c=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}w_iw_jh(U_i,U_j). \]

The denominator uses the full sample size, including censored observations. At least two observations are required. The returned statistic is signed and uses a two-sided alternative. Fewer than two uncensored observations give an empty sum (zero), which alone provides no evidence of fit. Censored-data calibration must reproduce the censoring mechanism; the generic complete-data Monte Carlo resolver is insufficient.

docs.text: Aleksandr Podmarev, Alexey Mironov

docs.text:
Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic has algorithm code CHI2_PEARSON_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. See the uniformity catalog.

Performs Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The implementation bins the sample and compares observed bin counts with equal expected counts.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins, SturgesCount
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = Chi2PearsonUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1}),
    binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=SturgesCount()),
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - explicitly fixed left boundary of the uniform distribution.

b - explicitly fixed right boundary of the uniform distribution.

binning - a binning strategy. The default is EqualProbabilityBins() with PowerCount(2, 0.4), max_bins=1000 and no minimum expected-count constraint.

The old bins and lambda_ options have been removed. Other divergences use separate classes, such as CressieReadUniformGofStatistic. See frequency binning for all strategies and Monte Carlo calibration requirements.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The sample is divided into bins over \([a, b]\). For \(m\) equal-probability bins and sample size \(n\), each bin has expected count \(n / m\). Other strategies calculate each expected count from its null probability. The statistic compares observed and expected counts:

\[ X^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{E_j}. \]

Zero observed counts contribute \(E_j\). Large values indicate disagreement with the null. Calibrations are distinguished by binning configuration; see calibration storage.

docs.title: Author(s)
docs.text: Aleksandr Podmarev, Alexey Mironov

docs.title: References
docs.text: Pearson, K. (1900). On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling. Philosophical Magazine, 50, 157–175.

    parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=SturgesCount())
