docs.title: Description
docs.text: CressieReadUniformGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim U(a,b)\). Its algorithm code is CRESSIE_READ_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    CressieReadUniformGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
criterion = CressieReadUniformGofStatistic(parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=3))
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

binning — keyword-only strategy, default EqualProbabilityBins(): PowerCount(coefficient=2.0, exponent=0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000. Observations must belong to [a, b].

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For observed bin counts \(O_j\) and positive expected counts \(E_j=np_j\), where \(p_j\) is the bin probability under the specified uniform null:

\[ T_{CR}=\frac95\sum_{j=1}^{m}O_j\left[\left(\frac{O_j}{E_j}\right)^{2/3}-1\right]. \]

This class fixes the power-divergence parameter at \(\lambda=2/3\); there is no lambda_ constructor argument. Terms with zero observed counts contribute zero by continuity.

Large values form the right-tail rejection region. Binning is reapplied for every sample. Calibrate with the same rule and sample size; a statistic value alone is not a p-value. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. See binning strategies and calibration storage. configuration() includes the binning policy, while code() identifies the algorithm.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Cressie, N., and Read, T. R. C. (1984). Multinomial Goodness-of-Fit Tests. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 46(3), 440–464.

See the uniformity criterion catalog for the other implementations.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
CrammerVonMisesUniformGofStatistic has algorithm code CVM_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. See the uniformity catalog.

Performs the Cramer-von Mises goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic accumulates squared differences between the empirical distribution function and the theoretical uniform cumulative distribution function.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

Test Statistic The observations are sorted, transformed by the reference uniform cumulative distribution function, and compared with expected uniform plotting positions.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    CrammerVonMisesUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = CrammerVonMisesUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - explicitly fixed left boundary of the uniform distribution.

b - explicitly fixed right boundary of the uniform distribution.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The Cramer-von Mises statistic is

\[ W_n^2 = \frac{1}{12n} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(F_0(X_{(i)}) - \frac{2i - 1}{2n}\right)^2 \]

where \(X_{(i)}\) is the \(i\)-th order statistic and \(F_0\) is the reference uniform cumulative distribution function. Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform model.

docs.text: Aleksandr Podmarev, Alexey Mironov

docs.text:
Cramer, H. (1928): On the composition of elementary errors. Skandinavisk Aktuarietidskrift, 11, 141–180.

von Mises, R. (1931): Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung und ihre Anwendung in der Statistik und theoretischen Physik. Leipzig: Deuticke.

Zhang, J. (2002). Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 64(2), 281–294.

docs.text:

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For observed bin counts \(O_j\) and positive expected counts \(E_j=np_j\), where \(p_j\) is the bin probability under the specified uniform null:

\[ T_{FT}=4\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j}\right)^2. \]

The power-divergence parameter is \(\lambda=-1/2\). An empty observed bin contributes \(4E_j\), so zero observed counts do not make this statistic infinite.

Large values form the right-tail rejection region. Binning is reapplied for every sample. Calibrate with the same rule and sample size; a statistic value alone is not a p-value. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs Greenwood's spacing test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The test is based on the squared spacings between adjacent ordered observations after adding the interval boundaries.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:

    GreenwoodTestUniformGofStatistic,

    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The implementation standardizes the sample to \([0, 1]\), adds boundary points 0 and 1, computes spacings \(D_i\), and returns

\[ G = \sum_i D_i^2. \]

Large values are associated with uneven spacings.

docs.text: KolmogorovSmirnovDMinusUniformGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim U(a,b)\). Its algorithm code is KS_MINUS_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovDMinusUniformGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
criterion = KolmogorovSmirnovDMinusUniformGofStatistic(parameters)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

Values outside [a, b] are mapped by the null CDF to 0 or 1.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ D_n^- = \max_{1\le i\le n}\left(u_i-\frac{i-1}{n}\right). \]

This is the unscaled negative EDF deviation. Large values indicate an empirical CDF below the null CDF, corresponding to observations tending toward larger values. The statistic uses a right-tail rejection region even though the EDF deviation is one-sided.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

Values outside [a, b] are mapped by the null CDF to 0 or 1.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ D_n^+ = \max_{1\le i\le n}\left(\frac{i}{n}-u_i\right). \]

This is the unscaled positive EDF deviation. Large values indicate an empirical CDF above the null CDF, corresponding to observations tending toward smaller values. The statistic uses a right-tail rejection region even though the EDF deviation is one-sided.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
KolmogorovSmirnovUniformGofStatistic has algorithm code KS_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. See the uniformity catalog.

Performs the Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic measures the largest discrepancy between the empirical distribution function and the cumulative distribution function of the reference uniform distribution.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\). Observations must be finite. Values outside the null interval are accepted; the reference CDF is 0 below a and 1 above b.

Test Statistic The statistic is based on the maximum vertical distance between the empirical cumulative distribution function and the theoretical uniform cumulative distribution function.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = KolmogorovSmirnovUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - explicitly fixed left boundary of the uniform distribution.

b - explicitly fixed right boundary of the uniform distribution.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For ordered observations \(X_{(i)}\), the implementation evaluates

\[ F_0(X_{(i)}) = \min\left(1,\max\left(0,\frac{X_{(i)} - a}{b - a}\right)\right). \]

The result is the unscaled \(D_n=\max(D_n^+,D_n^-)\). Directional variants have separate classes: D+ and D−. The constructor takes parameters only. Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform model.

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ V_{n,\mathrm{corrected}}=\left(\sqrt n+0.155+\frac{0.24}{\sqrt n}\right)(D_n^++D_n^-). \]

Here \(D_n^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D_n^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\). This class returns the finite-sample corrected statistic. It does not calculate a p-value. The unscaled, scaled and corrected variants have distinct algorithm codes and require matching critical values.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

docs.text:
KuiperUniformGofStatistic has algorithm code KUIPER_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. See the uniformity catalog.

Performs the Kuiper goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic combines the largest positive and negative deviations between the empirical and theoretical distribution functions.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    KuiperUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = KuiperUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - explicitly fixed left boundary of the uniform distribution.

b - explicitly fixed right boundary of the uniform distribution.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
After standardizing observations to \([0, 1]\), the implementation computes

\[ V = D^+ + D^- \]

where

\[ D^+ = \max_i\left(\frac{i}{n} - U_{(i)}\right), \quad D^- = \max_i\left(U_{(i)} - \frac{i - 1}{n}\right). \]

Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform model.

docs.text: LiaoShimokawaUniformGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim U(a,b)\). Its algorithm code is LIAO_SHIMOKAWA_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    LiaoShimokawaUniformGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
criterion = LiaoShimokawaUniformGofStatistic(parameters)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

Values outside [a, b] are mapped by the null CDF to 0 or 1.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ L_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\max\{i/n-u_i,\;u_i-(i-1)/n\}}{\sqrt{u_i(1-u_i)}}. \]

The statistic divides each local EDF deviation by a tail-dependent weight. A CDF value of 0 or 1 produces positive infinity. The cited paper studies fitted extreme-value and Weibull models; this criterion uses a fully specified uniform CDF. Its calibration must therefore use the specified uniform null, not fitted-model tables from the paper.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

docs.title: Mathematical verification of uniformity statistics
docs.text: The 25 criteria were checked against the formulas and sources below. All bounds are fixed before testing. For EDF statistics, write \(u_i=F_{a,b}(x_{(i)})\); for spacing statistics include \(u_0=0\) and \(u_{n+1}=1\).

docs.title: Formula checks
docs.text: Criteria Checked definition Scientific source Kolmogorov–Smirnov D+, D−, D Maximum positive and negative EDF discrepancies; D is their maximum, without squaring or scaling Zhang (2002), §2.1 Anderson–Darling Weighted logarithmic sum with factor \(1/n\) and subtraction of \(n\) Anderson and Darling (1952); Zhang (2002), §2.2 Cramér–von Mises Squared deviations from \((i-1/2)/n\), plus \(1/(12n)\) Zhang (2002), §2.3 Watson \(W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2\), evaluated through centered deviations Watson (1961); Lemeshko et al. (2014), eq. (6) Kuiper, scaled Kuiper, corrected Kuiper \(V=D^++D^-\); \(\sqrt n V\); \((\sqrt n+0.155+0.24/\sqrt n)V\) Lemeshko et al. (2014), eqs. (1)–(3) Zhang K, A, C Likelihood-ratio expressions with half-ranks and the quarter-rank log-odds correction Zhang (2002), eqs. (3.1)–(3.3) Liao–Shimokawa Sum of local maximum EDF deviations divided by \(\sqrt{u_i(1-u_i)}\) and \(\sqrt n\) Liao and Shimokawa (1999) Pearson, Freeman–Tukey, modified log-likelihood, Neyman chi-squared, Cressie–Read Power divergences at \(\lambda=1,-1/2,-1,-2,2/3\); zero-count limits checked separately Cressie and Read (1984) Greenwood Sum of squares of all \(n+1\) spacings Does, Helmers and Klaassen (1988), eqs. (1)–(2) Sherman Half the sum of absolute spacing deviations from \(1/(n+1)\) Sherman (1950) Quesenberry–Miller Squared spacings plus adjacent-spacing products, with no cyclic product Quesenberry and Miller (1977) Neyman smooth Sum of squared empirical coefficients in the orthonormal shifted Legendre basis, excluding the constant Neyman (1937); Rayner and Rayner (2001), §2 Stein, censored Stein Pairwise signed U-statistic and its inverse-censoring-probability weighted form; denominator \(n(n-1)/2\) Sreedevi and Kattumannil (2023), author preprint, §§2–3 Bickel–Rosenblatt-type Gaussian density estimate integrated squared error over \([0,1]\) Quadratic discrepancy motivated by Bickel and Rosenblatt (1973); the precise integral is a library adaptation

docs.title: Scope and qualifications
docs.text:
No formula changes were needed for the definitions checked. This verifies statistic calculations, not exact finite-sample rejection probabilities or power against every alternative.

Bickel–Rosenblatt returns the raw integral with its specified bandwidth policy, without asymptotic centering or scaling. Liao–Shimokawa uses the specified uniform null here; fitted-model critical values from its original paper do not apply.

Stein statistics are signed and use both tails. Censoring flags use 1 for censored observations, opposite to the paper's event indicator. The censoring estimator uses left limits and an explicit tie convention. The returned statistic omits the paper's variance estimation and studentization.

Where original full text was inaccessible, bibliographic verification was separated from formula verification: Sherman and Quesenberry–Miller formulas were checked in the authors' comparative study in §4.1 of the Stein preprint, and Neyman's polynomial form in Rayner and Rayner (2001). The Liao–Shimokawa expression was additionally compared with its use in a published goodness-of-fit study. The Bickel–Rosenblatt integral was verified directly by quadrature, rather than claimed to reproduce the original asymptotic statistic.

docs.title: Numerical verification
docs.text:
Checks include independent EDF integrals, SciPy reference values, high-precision Zhang examples, published Legendre polynomials, the order-statistic representation of Stein's pairwise sum, hand-calculated censoring weights, and numerical integration of the density discrepancy. Boundary values, empty bins, tied observations and affine changes of fixed uniform bounds are covered.

The focused suite passed 542 tests. The run isolated the pre-existing obsolete imports in continuous/__init__.py; it does not establish that ordinary package initialization works. Every concrete uniform criterion's docstring now includes a scientific reference and a URL.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: ModifiedLogLikelihoodUniformGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim U(a,b)\). Its algorithm code is MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    ModifiedLogLikelihoodUniformGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
criterion = ModifiedLogLikelihoodUniformGofStatistic(
    parameters, binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=3)
)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

binning — keyword-only strategy, default EqualProbabilityBins(): PowerCount(coefficient=2.0, exponent=0.4), min_expected=None, max_bins=1000. Observations must belong to [a, b].

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For observed bin counts \(O_j\) and positive expected counts \(E_j=np_j\), where \(p_j\) is the bin probability under the specified uniform null:

\[ T_{ML}=2\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_j\log\frac{E_j}{O_j}. \]

This is the \(\lambda=-1\) power divergence, with expected counts multiplying the log ratio. It differs from the ordinary likelihood-ratio G statistic (\(\lambda=0\)). Any zero observed count produces positive infinity.

Large values form the right-tail rejection region. Binning is reapplied for every sample. Calibrate with the same rule and sample size; a statistic value alone is not a p-value. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. See binning strategies and calibration storage. configuration() includes the binning policy, while code() identifies the algorithm.

For observed bin counts \(O_j\) and positive expected counts \(E_j=np_j\), where \(p_j\) is the bin probability under the specified uniform null:

\[ T_N=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{O_j}. \]

The power-divergence parameter is \(\lambda=-2\). The denominator contains observed counts, so any empty observed bin produces positive infinity. This is distinct from the Neyman smooth test.

Large values form the right-tail rejection region. Binning is reapplied for every sample. Calibrate with the same rule and sample size; a statistic value alone is not a p-value. The default has no minimum expected-count constraint, so a chi-squared approximation is not automatically justified. docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs Neyman's smooth goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic uses orthonormal polynomial components on the unit interval.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    NeymanSmoothTestUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = NeymanSmoothTestUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1}), k=4
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - left boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 0.

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

k - number of smooth components. Default value is 4.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The implementation standardizes observations to \([0, 1]\) and computes

\[ \sum_{j=1}^{k} V_j^2, \quad V_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_j(U_i). \]

The first components are implemented explicitly, and higher-order components use Legendre polynomials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs the Quesenberry-Miller spacing test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic combines squared spacings and products of consecutive spacings.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    QuesenberryMillerUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = QuesenberryMillerUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - left boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 0.

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(U_i=(X_i-a)/(b-a)\). The implementation adds boundaries 0 and 1 to the ordered transformed sample, computes unit spacings \(D_i\), and returns

\[ Q = \sum_i D_i^2 + \sum_i D_iD_{i+1}. \]

Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform spacing pattern.

docs.title: Author(s)

docs.title: Constructing with ParameterValues
docs.text:
Create ParameterValues with both fixed boundaries, then pass it to the constructor. It validates the supported parameterization and exact fixed parameter set. Omitted bounds are not filled in: a partial mapping such as {"a": 0} raises ValueError in the constructor.

from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    QuesenberryMillerUniformGofStatistic,
)


parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
test_statistic = QuesenberryMillerUniformGofStatistic(parameters)
assert test_statistic.hypothesis().parameters() == {"a": 0, "b": 1}

print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs Sherman's spacing test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The statistic measures absolute deviations of sample spacings from the expected spacing.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    ShermanUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = ShermanUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - left boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 0.

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(U_i=(X_i-a)/(b-a)\). The implementation adds boundaries 0 and 1 to the ordered transformed sample, computes unit spacings \(D_i\), and returns

\[ S = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i \left|D_i - \frac{1}{n + 1}\right|. \]

Large values indicate uneven spacing relative to the uniform model.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Performs a Stein-type U-statistic test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). The implementation standardizes observations to \([0, 1]\) and computes a pairwise kernel statistic.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    SteinUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = SteinUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - left boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 0.

b - right boundary of the uniform distribution. Default value is 1.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For standardized observations, the implementation computes a U-statistic with pairwise kernel

\[ h(x, y) = \frac{1}{2}\left(2\max(x, y) - 2x - 2y + x^2 + y^2\right). \]

The returned statistic is the signed average of this kernel over unordered pairs. At least two observations are required. Both positive and negative departures matter, so the alternative is two-sided.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
WatsonUniformGofStatistic has algorithm code WATSON_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. See the uniformity catalog.

Performs Watson's \(U^2\) goodness-of-fit test for the hypothesis of uniformity on the interval \([a, b]\). Watson's statistic is a rotation-invariant modification of the Cramer-von Mises statistic.

Hypothesis of Uniformity The null hypothesis is that the sample comes from a uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    WatsonUniformGofStatistic,
)


test_statistic = WatsonUniformGofStatistic(
    UniformDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
)
statistic_result = test_statistic.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic_result)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
a - explicitly fixed left boundary of the uniform distribution.

b - explicitly fixed right boundary of the uniform distribution.

rvs - array-like sample data passed to execute_statistic.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
With \(U_{(i)}=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\), the implementation computes

\[ U^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(U_{(i)} - \frac{2i-1}{2n} - \bar U + \frac12\right)^2 + \frac{1}{12n}. \]

Large values indicate stronger deviation from the uniform model.

docs.text: Aleksandr Podmarev, Alexey Mironov

docs.title: References
docs.text: Watson, G. S. (1961). Goodness-of-fit tests on a circle. Biometrika, 48(1–2), 109–114.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: ZhangAUniformGofStatistic tests the fully specified null \(H_0: X \sim U(a,b)\). Its algorithm code is ZHANG_ZA_UNIFORM_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import UniformDistributionDescriptor as Uniform
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.uniform import (
    ZhangAUniformGofStatistic,
)

parameters = Uniform.DEFAULT.parse({"a": 0, "b": 1})
criterion = ZhangAUniformGofStatistic(parameters)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.12, 0.25, 0.41, 0.53, 0.77, 0.91])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

Values outside [a, b] are mapped by the null CDF to 0 or 1.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ Z_A=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{\log u_i}{n-i+1/2}+\frac{\log(1-u_i)}{i-1/2}\right]. \]

This is Zhang (2002), equation (3.2). A CDF value of 0 or 1 produces positive infinity.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Zhang, J. (2002). Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 64(2), 281–294.

See the uniformity criterion catalog for the other implementations.

\[ Z_C=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\log\frac{1-u_i}{u_i}-\log\frac{n-i+1/4}{i-3/4}\right]^2. \]

docs.text:
parameters — ParameterValues with both a and b explicitly fixed and a < b. Bounds are not estimated from the sample; omitted bounds are unsupported.

rvs — a nonempty, one-dimensional sample of finite real observations.

Values outside [a, b] are mapped by the null CDF to 0 or 1.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Let \(u_i=F_{a,b}(X_{(i)})\) for the sorted sample, with \(n\) observations.

\[ Z_K=\max_{1\le i\le n}\left[(i-\tfrac12)\log\frac{(i-\tfrac12)/n}{u_i}+(n-i+\tfrac12)\log\frac{(n-i+\tfrac12)/n}{1-u_i}\right]. \]

This is the maximum likelihood-ratio EDF statistic in Zhang (2002), equation (3.1). A CDF value of 0 or 1 produces positive infinity. Logarithms are evaluated separately in the implementation to avoid overflowing probability ratios.

Large statistic values form the rejection region. execute_statistic returns the statistic only. Use a null distribution calibrated for this class and sample size, for example with MonteCarloLimitDistributionResolver. Parameters remain fixed throughout calibration.

docs.title: Weibull goodness-of-fit criteria
docs.text:
These criteria test the ordinary two-parameter Weibull family with zero location. Both shape and scale are unknown: construct a criterion with WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). The EDF and frequency criteria below fit both parameters by maximum likelihood on every call, including every Monte Carlo replicate. Samples must be finite, strictly positive, nonconstant and contain at least two observations.

The module exports 33 concrete classes: 13 generated EDF criteria, 5 generated frequency criteria and 15 specialized classes.

See mathematical verification for formula checks, scientific sources, source-verification limits and numerical test coverage.

docs.title: EDF criteria
docs.text:
All classes are available from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull. Each class name in the table has the suffix WeibullGofStatistic. All reject for large statistic values.

Criterion Class prefix Short code One-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov D+ KolmogorovSmirnovDPlus KS_PLUS One-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov D− KolmogorovSmirnovDMinus KS_MINUS Kolmogorov–Smirnov KolmogorovSmirnov KS Anderson–Darling AndersonDarling AD Cramér–von Mises CrammerVonMises CVM Liao–Shimokawa LiaoShimokawa LS Watson Watson WATSON Kuiper Kuiper KUIPER Scaled Kuiper KuiperScaled KUIPER_SCALED Corrected Kuiper KuiperCorrected KUIPER_CORRECTED Zhang Z_K ZhangK ZHANG_ZK Zhang Z_A ZhangA ZHANG_ZA Zhang Z_C ZhangC ZHANG_ZC

CDF values are evaluated under the fitted Weibull model. Anderson–Darling, Liao–Shimokawa and the Zhang statistics use logarithmic probabilities to retain tail precision. The definitions of the EDF discrepancies are described in the uniformity catalog; here their null distributions reflect the estimation of Weibull parameters.

docs.text:
These classes also have the suffix WeibullGofStatistic and reject for large values. They accept a keyword-only binning argument; the default is EqualProbabilityBins().

from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (

    Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}),
    binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=4),

value = test.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])

For details of the rules and their settings, see binning. The selected rule is included in configuration().

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For the EDF criteria and frequency criteria with EqualProbabilityBins, affine invariance in log observations permits simulation at shape = scale = 1. Every replicate must re-estimate both parameters. Critical values for a fully specified Weibull or uniform distribution are not applicable.

Other binning rules, including fixed boundaries in observation units, require external calibration with explicit simulation parameters. The built-in Monte Carlo resolver rejects these rules for fitted Weibull, because their null distributions need not share the same invariance. Existing storage-calibration guards remain in place for this family.

The 15 additional Weibull-specific criteria retain their individual definitions and calibration requirements; see their pages in this section.

docs.title: Shapiro–Brain source and calibration
docs.text:
ShapiroBrainWeibullGofStatistic (SB) uses a centered version of the Shapiro–Brain W statistic (1987), with the formula checked through Shell (2003), equation (9). It performs no MLE fit and uses both rejection tails. See its criterion page for the rounded-coefficient centering adjustment and the published-example comparison.

The Öztürk–Korukoğlu criterion implements the standardized \(OK_n^*\) ratio from Öztürk and Korukoğlu (1988), as reproduced in Krit (2014), §3.2.2. It uses two linear scale estimates of log observations and both rejection tails; the centering adjustment is explained on its criterion page.

SmithBainWeibullGofStatistic (RSB) computes \(n(1-R^2)\) using log observations and scores \(\log[-\log(1-i/(n+1))]\). This matches Krit (2014), §3.2.1, (3.12), attributed there to Smith and Bain (1976). It rejects in the right tail, eliminates both parameters without fitting, and requires sample-size-specific calibration. At \(n=2\) it is degenerate; use \(n\ge3\) for testing. See the mathematical verification for the source qualification and rejection-rule correction.

EvansJohnsonGreenWeibullGofStatistic (REJG) returns squared correlation \(R^2\) using log observations and ranks \((i-0.3175)/(n+0.365)\) at every index. The exact formula is checked through Krit (2014), (3.13), which cites Evans, Johnson and Green (1989). It rejects in the left tail, needs no parameter fit and is degenerate at \(n=2\). See the verification for the cancellation of the fitted shape, source limitations and calibration.

ColesWeibullGofStatistic (SPP) uses Blom log-location/log-scale estimates and returns the maximum arcsine-square-root transformed probability distance. The former MLE fit has been replaced. The distance follows Krit (2014), (3.14)–(3.15), with Blom estimation motivated by Coles (1989). It rejects in the right tail and must be recalibrated with Blom on every replicate. See the criterion page for the explicit order-statistic approximation, \(n=2\) degeneracy and source limitations.

TikuSinghWeibullGofStatistic (TS) uses the generalized-spacing functional in Sürücü (2008), (3.4)–(3.5), applied to the log-Weibull family of Tiku and Singh (1981). It requires complete samples with \(n\ge3\), uses approximate expected log-order spacings, performs no parameter fit and rejects in both tails. Calibrate at the observed sample size using this implementation and shape = scale = 1. See verification for the indexing qualification in Krit (2014) and approximation details.

MannScheuerFertigWeibullGofStatistic (MSF) returns the fraction of normalized log spacings above index \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). It matches Krit (2014), (29), attributed to Mann, Scheuer and Fertig (1973), with explicitly approximate expected order statistics. It uses the right tail, requires complete samples with \(n\ge3\), and performs no parameter fit. The former abbreviated class name has been removed without an alias; imports and serialized class references must use the full name. See verification for index checks, range and calibration qualifications.

LockhartOReillyStephensWeibullGofStatistic (LOS) applies the Anderson–Darling functional to \(n-2\) cumulative normalized log spacings, following Lockhart, O’Reilly and Stephens (1986), equations (1)–(3), with approximate expected order statistics. It requires complete samples with \(n\ge3\), eliminates both parameters without fitting, and rejects in the right tail. Endpoint ties give infinity. Ordinary uniform AD tables do not apply. The abbreviated class name has been removed without an alias. See verification.

KullbackLeiblerWeibullGofStatistic (KL) implements the Gumbel entropy test of Pérez-Rodríguez et al. (2009) on log-Weibull data, with the functional checked against EWGoF's WEDF.test KL branch. Both parameters are fitted by MLE; large values reject. The validated local default window differs from EWGoF's piecewise rule, so calibration must match \(n\), \(m\) and the estimator. The finite-sample estimate is not clipped at zero. See verification for source limitations, Gumbel signs and window conventions.

docs.title: Anderson-Darling distance to a maximum-likelihood fitted ordinary Weibull.
docs.text: AndersonDarlingWeibullGofStatistic

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
parameters : ParameterValues
    An empty distribution schema; all distribution parameters are unknown.

docs.title: Hypothesis, formula and calibration
docs.text:
F(x)=1-exp(-(x/eta)**k), x > 0, with location fixed at zero
and unknown positive scale eta and shape k.
Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}) to declare both parameters unknown.
Logarithmic location and scale are eliminated within every call.

A2=-n-sum((2*i-1)*(log(u_i)+log(1-u_(n+1-i))))/n,
where u_i=G(z_i) and z_i are MLE-standardized ordered log observations.
No finite-sample correction factor is applied.

Reject for right tail values.
Calibrate with repeated execute_statistic calls on ordinary Weibull
samples. Affine invariance in log(x) permits eta=k=1 for simulation.
Ordinary fixed-parameter KS tables do not apply to fitted CDFs.
Previously stored unversioned Weibull calibrations must be regenerated.
The cited model-specific comparison includes fitted Anderson-Darling.
Stable log-CDF and log-survival functions retain small tail probabilities;
exp(z) beyond float64 range gives numerical infinity.

docs.title: Calling execute_statistic
docs.text:
Compute the statistic described in the class Notes.

Parameters
----------
rvs : array_like
    One-dimensional finite strictly positive observations, n >= 2.
    Constant samples are invalid; ties are allowed unless stated below.
**kwargs : dict
    Unused common-interface keywords.

Returns
-------
statistic : float
    Scalar discrepancy. Infinite boundary penalties are preserved.

Raises
------
ValueError
    Invalid sample, unsupported settings, or unrepresentable fit.

Notes
-----
The input is never changed and estimated parameters are not retained.

docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Distribution
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    AndersonDarlingWeibullGofStatistic,
)

test = AndersonDarlingWeibullGofStatistic(Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}))
value = test.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(value)

docs.title: Pearson chi-squared test for the Weibull family
Description
docs.text:
Chi2PearsonWeibullGofStatistic has algorithm code CHI2_PEARSON_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. It is generated from the shared frequency kernel.

The null is the ordinary Weibull family with zero location:

\[ F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp\left[-(x/\eta)^k\right],\qquad x>0,\quad k,\eta>0. \]

Both parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood for every sample.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Weibull
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.binning import EqualProbabilityBins
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    Chi2PearsonWeibullGofStatistic,
)

criterion = Chi2PearsonWeibullGofStatistic(
    Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}), binning=EqualProbabilityBins(count=3)
)
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}), declaring both shape and scale unknown. Fixed or partially fixed parameter sets are unsupported.

rvs — a one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant sample with at least two observations. Ties are allowed. Invalid samples raise ValueError. The input is not modified and fitted parameters are not retained on the instance.

binning — keyword-only BinningStrategy, default EqualProbabilityBins(). See binning strategies. The chosen rule is included in configuration(); changing it changes the statistic's calibration.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
After fitting, the selected binning rule constructs observed counts \(O_j\) and strictly positive expected counts \(E_j=n p_j\). For interval bins with boundaries \(b_0,\ldots,b_m\),

\[ p_j=F(b_j;\widehat k,\widehat\eta)-F(b_{j-1};\widehat k,\widehat\eta). \]

The rule must account for all observations. Equal-probability bins use quantiles of the fitted distribution, giving \(E_j=n/m\) before any rule-specific merging.

\[ X^2=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{E_j}. \]

Power divergence with \(\lambda=1\). An empty observed bin contributes \(E_j\).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Large values form the right-tail rejection region. execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. For EqualProbabilityBins, simulate ordinary Weibull samples at shape = scale = 1, refit both parameters, and reconstruct the bins in every replicate. Keep the sample size and binning settings identical.

The built-in Monte Carlo resolver supports this invariant binning rule. Other rules, including fixed boundaries in observation units, require external calibration with explicit simulation parameters. A chi-squared reference with an automatically chosen number of degrees of freedom is not supplied or justified by this implementation. Stored unversioned Weibull critical values are rejected.

docs.text:

The reference describes the frequency discrepancy; the fitted-Weibull binning and calibration procedure above specifies its use in this library.

rvs — a one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant sample with at least two observations. Ties are allowed. Invalid samples raise ValueError. The input is not modified and fitted parameters are not retained on the instance.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For ordered observations, set \(u_i=F(X_{(i)};\widehat k,\widehat\eta)\). The implemented statistic is

\[ V_n=D_n^++D_n^-. \]

This is the unscaled Kuiper discrepancy.

Here \(D_n^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\) and \(D_n^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Large values form the right-tail rejection region. execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. Calibrate at the same sample size by simulating ordinary Weibull samples and re-estimating both parameters for every replicate. Log-location-scale invariance permits shape = scale = 1 for this simulation.

Critical values for a fully specified uniform or Weibull CDF do not apply to the fitted model. The built-in Monte Carlo resolver repeats the fit through execute_statistic; stored unversioned Weibull critical values are rejected.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Kuiper, N. H. (1960). Tests concerning random points on a circle. Proceedings of the Koninklijke Nederlandse Akademie van Wetenschappen, Series A, 63, 38–47.

The references identify the EDF discrepancy. Its application here uses estimated Weibull parameters and therefore requires the fitted-model calibration described above.

See the Weibull criterion catalog for all implementations and shared calibration requirements.

docs.title: Kullback–Leibler information test for log-Weibull
docs.text: KullbackLeiblerWeibullGofStatistic (KL) implements the MLE-based Vasicek-entropy discrepancy for a Gumbel distribution, transferred to Weibull through logarithms. Its functional matches EWGoF's WEDF.test(type="KL") when the effective window and estimation method agree. Defaults differ.

docs.title: Hypothesis and API
docs.text:
The null is the ordinary zero-location Weibull family

\[ F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp[-(x/\eta)^k],\qquad x>0,\quad k,\eta>0. \]

Construct with WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). execute_statistic(rvs, m=None, **kwargs) requires a finite, strictly positive, nonconstant one-dimensional complete sample, \(n\ge3\). Both parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood on every call. The sample is not modified; estimates are not retained. Common-interface keywords are unused.

The entropy window must be an integer \(1\le m<n/2\); booleans are invalid. The default is \(\min(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor,\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor)\). Invalid samples or windows and unrepresentable fits raise ValueError. Zero entropy-window gaps return positive infinity; ties whose window gaps remain positive give finite results. Censoring is not supported.

docs.title: Gumbel transformation and statistic
docs.text:
\(Y=\log X\) is minimum Gumbel, with location \(\mu=\log\eta\) and scale \(\sigma=1/k\). For the ordered MLE-standardized logs

\[ z_i=\widehat k(\log X_{(i)}-\log\widehat\eta), \qquad g(z)=\exp(z-e^z), \]

define the endpoint-repeated Vasicek entropy estimator

\[ H_{m,n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left[\frac{n}{2m} \left(z_{\min(n,i+m)}-z_{\max(1,i-m)}\right)\right]. \]

The returned statistic is

\[ I_{m,n}=-H_{m,n}-\bar z+\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e^{z_i}. \]

The signs follow directly from \(\log g(z)=z-e^z\) and \(D(f\Vert g)=-H(f)-\mathbb E_f\log g\). This is a finite-sample entropy estimate of divergence, not an exact divergence between two known densities; it need not be nonnegative and is not clipped. There is no factor \(n\), no exponentiation and no additional bias correction in the returned value. The MLE location score gives \(n^{-1}\sum_i e^{z_i}=1\) up to numerical error.

Equivalently, applying the entropy estimator to unstandardized \(Y\) gives \(H_{m,n}(z)=H_{m,n}(Y)-\log\widehat\sigma\) and \(I=-H_{m,n}(Y)-n^{-1}\sum_i\log f_Y(Y_i;\widehat\mu,\widehat\sigma)\). For the maximum-Gumbel convention use \(V=-\log X\); reflection reverses the order but preserves the entropy-window sum and gives the same statistic with the appropriately reflected density. Population KL divergence is invariant under the invertible logarithmic change of variable. This does not make a spacing entropy estimate on raw \(X\) identical to one on \(\log X\).

docs.title: Scientific sources and EWGoF correspondence
docs.text:
The Gumbel KL test is due to Pérez-Rodríguez, Vaquera-Huerta and Villaseñor-Alva (2009), using the methodology of Song (2002) and a Vasicek (1976) entropy estimate. The original 2009 full text was not checked directly; exact computational correspondence was checked in the pinned EWGoF 2.2.2 WEDF.test KL branch and MLEst. Although MLEst starts with -log(x), it reflects again when standardizing, so its returned values have the minimum-Gumbel orientation used here.

EWGoF also offers moment and least-squares fits; this class implements MLE only. Our profile-score root solver differs from EWGoF's bounded optimization (shape interval \([0.0001,50]\)), so numerical outputs are not promised to be bit-for-bit equal. More importantly, EWGoF's wrapper overwrites paramKL using a piecewise sample-size rule. For example, at \(n=20\) it chooses \(m=3\), while the local default is \(m=4\). Its rule also contains uncovered boundary sizes which fall through to \(m=14\). This implementation retains its explicit validated window rule and does not copy those boundary behaviours.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text:
Large \(I_{m,n}\) rejects (RightAlternative). Under \(X\mapsto aX^b\), \(a,b>0\), logs undergo a positive affine transformation. MLE location and scale transform accordingly, leaving standardized logs and the statistic unchanged for fixed \(m\). Thus calibration can simulate complete Weibull samples at shape = scale = 1. Every replicate must refit both parameters and use the same window rule.

Use the upper \(1-\alpha\) simulated quantile at the observed \(n\). For explicit m, supply matching external calibration: the generic resolver uses default execution settings. Do not reuse EWGoF defaults or published critical values without matching the window and estimator. No chi-square or unqualified normal limit is asserted. Continuous-null simulation does not model rounding-induced ties. See mathematical verification.

docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Weibull
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    KullbackLeiblerWeibullGofStatistic,
)

test = KullbackLeiblerWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
sample = [0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2]
print(test.execute_statistic(sample))
print(test.execute_statistic(sample, m=2))  # Requires calibration with m=2.

docs.title: Lockhart–O’Reilly–Stephens spacing Anderson–Darling statistic
docs.text:
LockhartOReillyStephensWeibullGofStatistic (LOS) tests the ordinary zero-location Weibull family with unknown positive shape \(k\) and scale \(\eta\):

\[ F(x)=1-\exp[-(x/\eta)^k],\qquad x>0. \]

Use the full class name in imports from continuous.weibull or continuous. The former abbreviated name has been removed without an alias; serialized class references must also be updated. The short code LOS and numerical formula are unchanged.

docs.title: Constructor and observations
docs.text: Construct with WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) requires a finite, strictly positive, nonconstant one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge3\). It returns a float, does not modify the input and performs no parameter fitting. Common-interface keywords are unused. Invalid samples, logarithms indistinguishable at floating-point precision, or nonpositive approximate expected spacings raise ValueError. Only complete samples are supported.

docs.title: Formula and primary-source verification
docs.text:
Let \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}\) and \(m_i=\mathbb E[\log E_{(i)}]\) for independent unit exponential variables \(E_j\). Set

\[ h_i=\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{m_{i+1}-m_i},\quad g_i=\frac{h_i}{\sum_{l=1}^{n-1}h_l},\quad i=1,\ldots,n-1, \qquad q=n-2,\quad z_j=\sum_{i=1}^j g_i,\quad j=1,\ldots,q. \]

The implementation substitutes approximate \(m_i\) as specified below and returns

\[ A_S^2=-q-\frac1q\sum_{j=1}^q(2j-1) \left[\log z_j+\log(1-z_{q+1-j})\right]. \]

The construction and functional were checked directly against equations (1)–(3), pp. 344–345 of Lockhart, O’Reilly and Stephens (1986, JRSS B), using the author-hosted PDF. Their complete-sample indices are \(k=1\), \(r=n-2\); their \(r+1\) normalized spacings correspond to our \(h_i\). The terminal cumulative value 1 is excluded. The paper uses exact expected order statistics, whereas this implementation uses an explicit approximation. There is no additional finite-sample multiplier.

docs.title: Expected-order approximation
docs.text:
For \(Q(p)=\log[-\log(1-p)]\), the exact expectation is

\[ m_i=\frac{1}{B(i,n+1-i)}\int_0^1 Q(u)u^{i-1}(1-u)^{n-i}\,du. \]

GoFNS(1, n, n) instead uses \(p_i=i/(n+1)\), \(q_i=1-p_i\) and

\[ \widetilde m_i=Q(p_i)+\frac{p_iq_i}{2(n+2)}Q''(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{(n+2)^2} \left[\frac{q_i-p_i}{3}Q^{(3)}(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{8}Q^{(4)}(p_i)\right]. \]

This truncates at the fourth derivative and also approximates higher beta central moments: the third-moment denominator \((n+2)(n+3)\) is replaced by \((n+2)^2\), and the fourth moment by \(3p_i^2q_i^2/(n+2)^2\). It is not exact quadrature and is not asserted to reproduce the papers' tables.

docs.title: Mathematical properties and calibration
docs.text:
For the empirical CDF \(H_q\) of \(z_1,\ldots,z_q\), our algebra gives

\[ A_S^2=q\int_0^1\frac{[H_q(u)-u]^2}{u(1-u)}\,du. \]

Thus the statistic is nonnegative in exact arithmetic and unbounded above. Ties in the first or last ordered log gap give \(z_1=0\) or \(z_q=1\) and positive infinity. Interior ties may give repeated interior \(z_j\) and a finite result. Constant samples are rejected before this calculation. For \(n=3\), \(A_S^2=-1-\log[z_1(1-z_1)]\) is nondegenerate.

Under \(X\mapsto aX^b\), \(a,b>0\), every \(h_i\) is multiplied by \(b\); the \(z_j\) and the statistic are unchanged. Hence shape and scale are eliminated without fitting. The implementation computes \(1-z_j\) by reverse cumulative sums of \(g_i\), avoiding subtraction from a value rounded to 1.

Large values reject (RightAlternative). Calibrate the upper \(1-\alpha\) quantile by simulating complete Weibull samples of the observed size with shape = scale = 1 and evaluating this same implementation. As the authors explain on p. 345, the transformed values are not uniform order statistics for a general parent distribution, including log-Weibull. Ordinary uniform Anderson–Darling critical values therefore do not apply. No chi-square limit is asserted. Continuous-null simulation does not model rounding-induced ties.

The companion Weibull article studies critical values and power, including censoring. Its full text was not used for direct formula verification; this API supports complete samples only. See mathematical verification.

docs.title: Mathematical verification of Weibull statistics
docs.text: This review covers the ordinary two-parameter Weibull implementations in continuous/weibull.py: 13 generated EDF classes, 5 generated frequency classes and 15 explicit specialized classes, for a total of 33 concrete classes. Exponentiated Weibull is a separate family. See the criterion catalog for individual pages and public class names.

docs.title: Hypothesis and parameter estimation
docs.text:
The null model has zero location and unknown positive shape \(k\) and scale \(\eta\):

\[ F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp[-(x/\eta)^k],\qquad x>0. \]

Construct criteria with WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). The generated criteria fit both parameters by maximum likelihood on every call. For ordered observations, write \(z_i=\widehat k(\log X_{(i)}-\log\widehat\eta)\) and \(u_i=1-\exp[-\exp(z_i)]\). The implementation solves the profile score in a rescaled log domain rather than forming large powers of the original sample. The Weibull-to-extreme-value transformation and likelihood equations are given in Krit (2014), §2, equations (1)–(7).

Samples for generated criteria must be one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant and have at least two observations. Specialized criteria have additional sample-size, spacing or record requirements. Unknown parameters do not imply that every specialized criterion uses MLE: some eliminate log location and scale through correlations, normalized spacings or moments.

docs.title: Formula checks
docs.text:
The generated definitions below were compared with the shared kernels and numerical references. The citations identify the discrepancy; their fixed-parameter critical values do not automatically apply after Weibull fitting.

Criteria Checked definition Scientific source Kolmogorov–Smirnov D+, D−, D \(D^+=\max_i(i/n-u_i)\), \(D^-=\max_i(u_i-(i-1)/n)\); \(D=\max(D^+,D^-)\), without squaring or scaling Zhang (2002), §2.1 Anderson–Darling \(-n-n^{-1}\sum_i(2i-1)[\log u_i+\log(1-u_{n+1-i})]\); no finite-sample multiplier Anderson and Darling (1952); fitted Weibull context: Liao and Shimokawa (1999) Cramér–von Mises \(W^2=1/(12n)+\sum_i[u_i-(i-1/2)/n]^2\) Zhang (2002), §2.3 Watson \(W^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2\), evaluated using centered deviations Watson (1961) Kuiper, scaled Kuiper, corrected Kuiper \(V=D^++D^-\); \(\sqrt n V\); \((\sqrt n+0.155+0.24/\sqrt n)V\) Lemeshko et al. (2014) Zhang K, A, C Likelihood-ratio discrepancies with half-ranks; Z_C uses the quarter-rank log-odds correction Zhang (2002), equations (3.1)–(3.3) Liao–Shimokawa \(n^{-1/2}\sum_i\max(i/n-u_i,u_i-(i-1)/n)/\sqrt{u_i(1-u_i)}\), using MLEs Liao and Shimokawa (1999) Pearson, Freeman–Tukey, modified log-likelihood, Neyman chi-squared, Cressie–Read Power divergences at \(\lambda=1,-1/2,-1,-2,2/3\), respectively, using fitted bin probabilities Cressie and Read (1984)

For frequency criteria, \(O_j\) is the observed bin count and \(E_j=np_j>0\). The five kernels return, respectively,

\[ \sum_j\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{E_j},\quad 4\sum_j(\sqrt{O_j}-\sqrt{E_j})^2,\quad 2\sum_j E_j\log\frac{E_j}{O_j},\quad \sum_j\frac{(O_j-E_j)^2}{O_j},\quad \frac95\sum_j O_j[(O_j/E_j)^{2/3}-1]. \]

An empty observed bin contributes \(E_j\) to Pearson, \(4E_j\) to Freeman–Tukey and zero to Cressie–Read. It makes modified log-likelihood and Neyman chi-squared infinite. These limits are part of the kernel definitions.

docs.title: Specialized implementations
docs.text:
