docs.title: Scope and qualifications
docs.text:
This document separates checking an implemented formula from establishing its historical attribution or its null distribution. It does not establish finite-sample rejection probabilities, nominal significance levels or power. The Shapiro–Brain numerical formula is unchanged; its rejection region was corrected from the left tail to both tails during the follow-up source review.

Anderson–Darling, Liao–Shimokawa and the Zhang kernels consume log-CDF and log-survival values. This preserves tail information when ordinary CDF values round to zero or one; representable input does not guarantee a finite statistic. LT2/LT3 also use log-domain arithmetic to avoid overflow followed by zero-weight multiplication. The Kuiper correction is the implemented conventional scaling, not a proof of a fitted-Weibull finite-sample p-value approximation.

All generated criteria reject for large values. Specialized exceptions include REJG (left tail), and Shapiro–Brain, OK and TS (both tails).

For generated EDF criteria, Monte Carlo calibration can use shape = scale = 1 because of log-location-scale invariance, but every replicate must refit both parameters. For generated frequency criteria, the built-in resolver permits EqualProbabilityBins and rebuilds the bins after each fit. Other binning rules require external calibration with explicit simulation parameters. No automatic chi-squared law with a parameter-count degrees-of-freedom adjustment is claimed.

MD requires acquisition order or precompressed lower records with counts. Calibration must reproduce record extraction and the requirement of at least two records; the generic unconditional Monte Carlo path is blocked. For other specialized criteria, nondefault execution settings such as m and a must also be preserved during external simulation. Unversioned stored Weibull critical values are rejected by the current storage-calibration guards.

docs.title: Numerical verification
docs.text:
On 2026-10-14, tests/statistics/test_weibull_dynamic.py passed 247 tests with four warnings in an isolated package-loading run. It covers:

  • Registry and pickle identity, per-criterion hypotheses, and completeness of all 13 EDF and 5 frequency exports without explicit class duplicates.
  • Independent SciPy Gumbel fits to log observations and reference KS, AD, Cramér–von Mises and Liao–Shimokawa calculations.
  • Shared-kernel comparisons after an independent fit. These verify integration with the family; they are not independent proofs of the shared formulas.
  • Fitted frequency counts and expected probabilities for explicit and equal-probability bins, including a SciPy Pearson reference.
  • Scale and positive-power transformations, repeated fitting without retained estimates, sample immutability, invalid input, and extreme log probabilities.
  • Monte Carlo refitting, unsupported calibration modes and public stub exports.

The existing tests/distributions/test_weibull.py also contains references for probability-plot correlations, spacing quadrature, moment-covariance integration, Laplace grids, CQ, entropy windows and record likelihood/integration. Its ordinary run failed during collection* on the pre-existing AbstractChi2Statistic import in continuous/beta/beta_statistics.py; those specialized tests are not reported as passing in this review. The isolated 247-test run bypasses continuous/__init__.py and does not establish that normal package initialization works. The test count is a dated execution result, not a claim that every specialized formula has been independently validated.

docs.title: Shapiro–Brain follow-up verification
docs.text:
The formula was checked against Shell (2003), equation (9). The implementation retains an explicit adjustment: centering removes the residual coefficient sum caused by rounding, since \(0.6079\cdot0.4228-0.2570=0.00002012\). Our algebra proves invariance under \(X\mapsto cX^d\) for positive \(c,d\). No MLE is used.

Dedicated checks in tests/statistics/test_shapiro_brain_weibull.py compare the statistic to an independent scalar evaluation, reproduce the published example before centering, check the centered value separately, and test permutation/scale/power invariance, tied samples, the degenerate \(n=2\) case, input validation and the two-tail declaration. These checks establish the implemented calculation, not a finite-sample significance level or power claim.

The follow-up isolated run passed 268 tests: the 247 generated-family checks plus 21 dedicated Shapiro–Brain checks. The package-initialization limitation described above still applies.

docs.title: Öztürk–Korukoğlu follow-up verification
docs.text:
The weights, ratio \(b/S\) and normalization \((b/S-1-0.13/\sqrt n+1.18/n)/(0.49/\sqrt n-0.36/n)\) agree with Krit (2014), equations (3.16), (3.18)–(3.20), which attributes the test to Öztürk and Korukoğlu (1988). The library centers log observations before evaluating the rounded weights: \(b=b_{\mathrm{raw}}-0.00002012\,\overline{\log X}\), as for Shapiro–Brain. This adjustment leaves \(S\) unchanged and makes both estimates scale by \(d\) under \(X\mapsto cX^d\), so their ratio is invariant.

Our algebra also gives \(S=\sum_{i<j}(y_j-y_i)/[n(n-1)\log 2]>0\) for nonconstant samples. The normalization denominator is \((0.49\sqrt n-0.36)/n>0\) for \(n\ge2\). At \(n=2\) the ratio is constant and provides no discrimination. Both tails require calibration for the actual sample size; standardization alone does not establish a standard-normal null law.

Dedicated tests in tests/statistics/test_ozturk_korukoglu_weibull.py use an independent scalar evaluation of the published uncentered numerator, apply the centering correction explicitly, and compute \(S\) from pairwise log differences. They check scale/power/permutation invariance, ties, input immutability, invalid inputs, the two-observation degeneracy and both tails.

The isolated follow-up run passed 288 tests: 247 generated-family, 21 Shapiro–Brain and 20 Öztürk–Korukoğlu checks. The package-initialization limitation described above still applies. Ruff and the documentation build also passed; the latter retains existing broken-link warnings on other pages.

docs.title: Smith–Bain follow-up verification
docs.text:
SmithBainWeibullGofStatistic agrees with the mean ranks and squared centered correlation in Krit (2014), §3.2.1, equation (3.12), p. 47. Krit attributes this definition to Smith and Bain (1976). The original article was not available for direct full-text verification. The implementation is unchanged by this review.

Our algebra establishes the following properties. Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(0\le R^2\le1\), hence \(0\le T=n(1-R^2)\le n\). The ratio \(T/n\) equals the unexplained fraction of variation in an ordinary least-squares regression with an intercept. A right-tail rejection region is therefore appropriate. Krit's phrase “too close to 1” following (3.12) is inconsistent with this transformation and does not define the implemented rejection rule.

For \(X=\eta E^{1/k}\), \(E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), the centered log observations are scaled by \(1/k\), which cancels from the correlation. This proves that the null law depends on \(n\), but not on the two unknown Weibull parameters. It also proves invariance under \(X\mapsto aX^b\) for \(a,b>0\). No MLE is needed. The transformation is given in Krit (2014), §2, equation (3).

The scores are quantiles at mean uniform ranks, not expectations of extreme-value order statistics. Calibration must preserve these scores, sample size and the complete-sample observation scheme. For \(n=2\), \(R^2=1\) for every nonconstant sample, so there is no discriminatory power. Ties are allowed in the calculation, but rounding/censoring cannot be ignored when choosing a null distribution. No universal chi-square limit or finite-sample significance level is established.

On 2026-10-14, the 20 dedicated tests in tests/statistics/test_smith_bain_weibull.py passed with isolated loading of continuous.weibull (bypassing continuous/__init__.py, as in the earlier checks). The reference computes least-squares residuals using SciPy's minimum-Gumbel quantiles and NumPy's linear solver, independently of the correlation helper. Checks cover scale/power/permutation invariance, sample immutability, ties, extreme magnitudes, exact probability-plot samples, the two-observation degeneracy, input validation and the right-tail declaration. The ordinary pytest run still fails during collection because continuous/beta/beta_statistics.py imports the missing AbstractChi2Statistic from edf. Thus these results validate the statistic in isolation, not normal package initialization. Ruff passed and MkDocs built successfully, with existing warnings elsewhere.

docs.title: Evans–Johnson–Green follow-up verification
docs.text:
The squared correlation and ranks in EvansJohnsonGreenWeibullGofStatistic agree with Krit (2014), §3.2.1, equation (3.13), p. 47. Krit attributes it to Evans, Johnson and Green (1989). Their report distinguishes original-scale and log-scale correlations on p. 3; this implementation uses log observations. Its formula images were not directly readable in this review, so the exact rank convention was checked through Krit. The probability-plot background is Filliben (1975); normality tables from that article are not applicable here.

In Krit's formula, \(M_i=c_i/\widehat{k}\), where \(c_i=\log[-\log(1-(i-0.3175)/(n+0.365))]\). Our algebra shows that the factor \(1/\widehat{k}\) cancels, while centering \(M_i\) in the numerator changes nothing because \(\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)=0\). Thus no fit is required. The all-index rank formula includes both endpoints without special replacements.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(0\le R^2\le1\). Since ordered logs and scores are positively correlated, \(R^2\) measures the explained fraction of variation in linear regression with an intercept. Small values indicate departure: the existing left-tail declaration is correct. The result is \(R^2\), not \(R^4\) or \(n(1-R^2)\), and the computation is unchanged by this review.

Writing \(X=\eta E^{1/k}\) with \(E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) proves that the unknown parameters cancel from the correlation. Calibration may therefore use shape = scale = 1, with the same sample size and plotting positions, without refitting. At \(n=2\) all nonconstant samples give \(R^2=1\), so there is no power to discriminate. Tied observations are accepted, but rounded-data calibration must model rounding. Only complete zero-location Weibull samples are covered. This algebra does not establish a chi-square approximation or a finite-sample significance level without calibration.

On 2026-10-14, all 24 dedicated checks in tests/statistics/test_evans_johnson_green_weibull.py passed with isolated loading of continuous.weibull, bypassing continuous/__init__.py. The independent reference uses minimum-Gumbel quantiles and least-squares residuals rather than the implementation's correlation helper. Tests cover scale/power/permutation invariance, input immutability and validation, ties, extreme magnitudes, exact probability-plot samples, the \(n=2\) degeneracy, left-tail declaration, and cancellation of the scale in Krit's uncentered numerator. Regression checks distinguish \(R^2\) from \(R^4\) and the Smith–Bain rank convention.

Ordinary pytest collection still fails because continuous/beta/beta_statistics.py imports the missing AbstractChi2Statistic from edf; these results do not validate normal package initialization. Ruff passed. MkDocs built successfully, with existing warnings elsewhere and no warnings for the updated criterion page.

docs.title: Coles follow-up verification
docs.text:
The implementation now replaces MLE by Blom linear estimates. The maximum stabilized distance matches Krit (2014), (3.14)–(3.15), p. 48. Coles (1989) explicitly studies Blom estimation for this distance; its separate correlation statistic is not used. Michael (1983) introduced the stabilized probability plot. The exact Blom linear-weight construction is checked against EWGoF::BLOMEst, not its MLE-based WPP.test branch. The original Coles full text was unavailable; this is not a claim of exact agreement with its published tables.

The criterion page specifies the least-squares representation of the Blom weights and the fourth-order GoFNS expansion. Its \(1/3\) and \(1/8\) coefficients use real division, whereas the EWGoF C++ source uses integer division. This explicit approximation convention is part of the definition. Expected order statistics are not computed by exact quadrature. The two-column least-squares solve avoids explicit matrix inversion, and normalizing the input logs avoids unnecessary cancellation.

Our algebra proves equivariance of the estimates under positive affine transformations of logs, hence invariance of the statistic to Weibull shape and scale. At fixed \(n\), simulation may use shape = scale = 1, but must repeat the Blom fit. Since \(h(p)\in[0,1]\), the statistic lies in \([0,1]\); large values reject. No \(\sqrt n\) factor, standard-normal or chi-square calibration is asserted. At \(n=2\) it is constant for nonconstant samples. Old MLE calibration is invalid for the revised statistic; unversioned stored critical values remain blocked by the existing guard. Tables based on other estimators, including Kimber (1985), are not used as calibration for this implementation.

The isolated follow-up run on 2026-10-14 passed 269 tests: 22 dedicated Coles checks plus 247 generated-family checks (four existing SciPy warnings). The reference in tests/statistics/test_coles_weibull.py uses explicit Blom linear weights, a scalar 2-by-2 inverse and independently written analytic quantile derivatives, rather than the implementation's least-squares solve and recursive derivative expressions. It checks the distance, ties, extreme log ranges, scale/power/permutation invariance, input immutability, invalid samples, the \(n=2\) degeneracy and the right-tail declaration. A regression check distinguishes Blom from MLE, forbids calls to MLE helpers, verifies re-estimation on repeated calls, and checks that old stored calibration is blocked.

The previous MLE-specific SPP assertion in tests/distributions/test_weibull.py has been replaced by these dedicated Blom checks. That file still fails to collect even with isolated continuous-package loading, because exponentiated_weibull.py imports the missing AbstractChi2Statistic from edf; it is not counted among passing tests. Ordinary package initialization also retains the previously documented beta.py import failure. Ruff passed and MkDocs built successfully, with existing warnings elsewhere.

docs.title: ST1 and ST2 follow-up verification
docs.text:
The descriptive names are BestRaynerThasSkewnessWeibullGofStatistic and BestRaynerThasKurtosisWeibullGofStatistic; ST1/ST2 remain aliases to the same classes with unchanged short codes. EWGoF's source and help page disagree on the ordering. The implementations follow its source: ST1 is the skewness component; ST2 is the kurtosis component with a skewness correction.

The negative-log transform and divisor-n sample moments match the moment conventions in Best, Rayner and Thas (2007). The numerical formulas are checked against EWGoF's source and Krit (2014), §3.2.5. The accessible author PDF contains only printed pages 89–91 and 96–97, so it does not support a direct check of the missing formula pages or appendices.

Independent scalar moment calculations on the 65 Port Pirie observations in Table 1 give skewness 0.7110707539472332 and ST1 0.5966736536522815. ST2 on the same data is 0.37580214526699485. The section 4 values 0.71 for V3 squared and 0.36 for V4 squared are not reproduced by the rounded EWGoF formulas; both numerical results are tested. It is numerically close to the sample skewness, but this is insufficient to conclude that the article has a typo. The formula is not adjusted to fit that single reported number. test_port_pirie_source_formula locks the actual EWGoF formula and distinguishes it from the raw skewness. The same formula applied to the negated glass-fibre observations in Table 2 gives ST1 0.26166084645904814, rather than section 4's 0.19; full source verification is still necessary before attributing either discrepancy to the article.

The implementation uses rounded published coefficients, rather than the previous local delta-method normalization. The algebra of standardized moments proves invariance under positive scaling and powers of the Weibull observations. Both tests use right-tail rejection and finite-sample simulation. Old local calibration is invalid and the existing storage guard remains in force.

Dedicated tests use scalar central-moment calculations, checks of the log sign, scale/power/permutation invariance, input validation, alias identity, the n=2 degeneracy and rejection of old calibration. Normal pytest collection is blocked by the existing beta.py import of missing edf.AbstractChi2Statistic; isolated-module results do not validate normal package initialization.

The follow-up isolated run passed 278 tests (31 dedicated component checks and 247 generated-family checks; four existing SciPy warnings). Ruff and the stub consistency check passed. MkDocs built successfully, with existing broken links elsewhere in the documentation.

docs.title: Tiku–Singh follow-up verification
docs.text:
The implementation's weights and denominator agree with the generalized-spacing \(Z^*\) functional in Sürücü (2008), (3.4)–(3.5). The original sources are Tiku (1980) and Tiku and Singh (1981). Their publisher records were verified; the original full texts were unavailable for direct formula comparison.

Krit (2014), (30) also gives TS, but uses \(E_2,\ldots,E_n\) after defining intervals from \(i\) to \(i+1\). Reading the formula with \(E_i=h_{i-1}\) resolves this indexing mismatch. The code includes all \(n-1\) intervals in the denominator; the final interval has zero numerator weight. No change to the executable formula was needed.

Our algebra gives \(T=2\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}z_j/(n-2)\) with \(z_j=\sum_{i=1}^j g_i\). Nonnegative normalized spacings imply \(0\le T\le2\); positive spacings imply strict inequalities. At \(n=3\), \(T=2g_1\) is still nondegenerate. Zero individual gaps are permitted, including the boundary cases \(T=0\) and \(T=2\); a constant sample is invalid. Both tails are used. Under \(X\mapsto aX^b\), \(h_i\mapsto bh_i\), so the statistic is invariant and its null law depends on \(n\), not the Weibull shape or scale. No MLE is involved.

The criterion page records the exact beta integral and the actual GoFNS approximation. The third- and fourth-central-moment coefficients are approximated as well as truncating the Taylor series. Thus this is an approximation to the expected-order version of the test, not an exact evaluation of its moments. Use fresh two-tail Monte Carlo calibration of this implementation. Neither symmetry around 1 nor the uniform-mean law for ordinary exponential spacings is assumed for generalized log-Weibull spacings.

The follow-up run on 2026-10-14 passed 14 dedicated tests in tests/statistics/test_tiku_singh_weibull.py: an independent analytic-derivative reference combined with the cumulative-spacing identity at four sample sizes, shape/scale invariance, input preservation, both rejection tails, tied boundary samples and invalid inputs. The run isolated the continuous package namespace because its normal initializer fails in beta.py while importing the missing AbstractChi2Statistic from edf. These results validate the TS module but not normal package initialization. Ruff passed for the new tests; MkDocs built successfully with existing warnings about missing documents elsewhere.

docs.title: Mann–Scheuer–Fertig follow-up verification
docs.text:
MannScheuerFertigWeibullGofStatistic replaces the abbreviated class name without a compatibility alias, including exports and type stubs. The MSF short code and executable statistic are unchanged.

The ratio agrees with Krit (2014), equation (29) and Sürücü (2008), equation (4.13). Both attribute it to Mann, Scheuer and Fertig (1973). The original full text was unavailable for direct verification. The criterion page specifies the approximation used for expected log-order spacings and distinguishes it from exact beta integration.

Our indexing check gives \(r=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) lower intervals and \(n-1-r\) upper intervals. The first upper interval is \(h_{r+1}\), corresponding to zero-based g[r]; the final interval is included. In particular, even \(n\) has one fewer upper interval. There is no off-by-one correction to make. Nonnegative gaps give \(0\le S\le1\), with strict bounds for distinct samples; \(n=3\) remains nondegenerate. An equivalent identity is \(S=1-z_r\), where \(z_r=\sum_{i=1}^r h_i/\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}h_i\).

Under \(X\mapsto aX^b\), \(h_i\mapsto bh_i\), proving invariance to the unknown Weibull parameters. The right-tail rule is an explicit one-sided choice, with possible poor power against alternatives producing small ratios. It must not be described as a two-tail omnibus test. Calibrate at fixed \(n\) by simulation at shape = scale = 1, repeating the same approximation. Expected spacings alone do not establish independence or an exact beta law; no exact beta/F distribution or chi-square limit is used. No censoring API or agreement with historical critical-value tables is claimed.

The follow-up run on 2026-10-14 passed 280 isolated tests: 19 dedicated MSF checks, 14 TS checks and 247 generated-family checks (four existing SciPy warnings). tests/statistics/test_mann_scheuer_fertig_weibull.py verifies independent analytic quantile derivatives and the complementary cumulative spacing identity, even/odd splits, endpoint samples, invariance, input preservation, rejection direction, the public name and invalid inputs. The run bypassed continuous/__init__.py, whose normal import still fails in beta.py on the missing AbstractChi2Statistic import from edf. It validates the criterion module, not normal package initialization. Ruff passed for the new tests; MkDocs built with existing missing-document warnings elsewhere and none for the MSF page.

docs.title: Lockhart–O’Reilly–Stephens follow-up verification
docs.text:
The class is now LockhartOReillyStephensWeibullGofStatistic in implementation, exports and type stubs, without an alias for the abbreviated name. The LOS short code and executable formula are unchanged.

We checked equations (1)–(3), pp. 344–345 directly in the author copy of Lockhart, O’Reilly and Stephens (1986, JRSS B). For a complete sample, their \(k=1\) and \(r=n-2\) give \(n-1\) normalized gaps, \(n-2\) interior cumulative values, and precisely the implemented AD sum. There is no off-by-one error or missing finite-sample correction. The companion paper provides Weibull critical-value and power studies; its full text was not checked directly.

The criterion page records the exact beta integral and the explicit fourth-derivative GoFNS approximation. Higher beta central moments are also approximated; this does not reproduce exact expected order statistics or establish agreement with historical tables.

Our integral identity \(A_S^2=q\int_0^1[H_q(u)-u]^2/[u(1-u)]\,du\) verifies nonnegativity and the logarithmic boundary divergence. Ties at either extreme give infinity, while interior ties can remain finite. At \(n=3\), the formula reduces to \(-1-\log[z_1(1-z_1)]\), so it is not degenerate. Reverse cumulative sums retain the small upper-tail mass when direct subtraction would lose it.

Positive affine transformations of logs cancel in the normalized spacings, so complete Weibull shape = scale = 1 samples suffice for calibration at fixed \(n\). No MLE fit is involved. The authors explicitly explain on p. 345 that general normalized spacings do not yield uniform order statistics, even via a naive asymptotic independence argument. Thus ordinary uniform AD tables are inappropriate. Use the right tail of simulations of this same approximate statistic; no chi-square law or censoring calibration is asserted.

The follow-up run on 2026-10-14 passed 300 isolated tests: 20 dedicated LOS checks, 19 MSF checks, 14 TS checks and 247 generated-family checks (four existing SciPy warnings). The LOS reference uses independently written analytic quantile derivatives and numerical quadrature of the weighted EDF integral, rather than the production logarithmic sum. Additional tests cover endpoint/interior ties, preservation of tiny survival mass, invariance, input preservation, invalid samples and removal of the old public name. The runner bypassed continuous/__init__.py because normal initialization fails in beta.py while importing the missing AbstractChi2Statistic from edf; this does not validate normal package initialization. Ruff passed for the new tests. MkDocs built with existing warnings elsewhere and no warning for the LOS page.

docs.title: Kullback–Leibler follow-up verification
docs.text:
The statistic matches the MLE KL functional in the pinned EWGoF 2.2.2 WEDF.test for the same effective entropy window. Its scientific origin is Pérez-Rodríguez, Vaquera-Huerta and Villaseñor-Alva (2009), with Vasicek entropy estimation and Song's KL methodology. The 2009 full text was not available for direct verification; executable formula correspondence uses EWGoF rather than an assertion of identical published tables.

Our change-of-variable calculation gives minimum Gumbel for \(Y=\log X\), \(\mu=\log\eta\), \(\sigma=1/k\). Therefore \(\log g(z)=z-e^z\) and the returned \(-H-\bar z+\overline{e^z}\) has the correct signs. EWGoF's MLEst starts with negative logs but reflects its standardized output again, giving the same orientation. Reflection and endpoint repetition preserve the entropy sum; the maximum-Gumbel formulation on negative logs is equivalent. At the MLE, \(\overline{e^z}=1\). There is no extra factor \(n\), exponentiation or nonnegativity clipping. Estimated entropy can produce negative KL estimates.

The local window is an integer \(1\le m<n/2\), defaulting to \(\min(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor,\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor)\). EWGoF instead overwrites paramKL with a piecewise rule (\(n=20\): 3 versus our 4), with uncovered boundary sizes falling through to 14. These conventions are not equivalent. The local profile-score solver also differs from EWGoF's bounded optimizer. No executable formula or window change was needed; the documented variant now explicitly states these differences.

MLE equivariance under positive affine changes of logs proves invariance to Weibull shape and scale at fixed \(m\). Every Monte Carlo replicate must refit both parameters and preserve the window. Custom execution windows require matching external calibration. Zero window gaps give infinity; individual ties with positive window gaps are allowed. The criterion is right-tailed, with no unqualified normal/chi-square calibration or censoring support.

The follow-up run on 2026-10-14 passed 322 isolated tests, including 22 new KL checks and 300 existing spacing/generated-family checks (four existing SciPy warnings). The new reference fits scipy.stats.gumbel_l to raw logs and evaluates the unstandardized log density with independently padded entropy windows. A separate gumbel_r fit to negative logs verifies reflection; a scalar translation of EWGoF's inner KL branch verifies matched-window algebra, not an execution of R. Tests also check the MLE score identity, default-window differences, invariance, input preservation, ties and invalid inputs. The runner bypasses continuous/__init__.py due to the existing beta.py import of the missing AbstractChi2Statistic from edf; this run does not validate normal package initialization. Ruff passed for the new tests. MkDocs built with existing warnings elsewhere, none for the KL page.

docs.title: Modified log-likelihood ratio test for the Weibull family
Description
docs.text:
ModifiedLogLikelihoodWeibullGofStatistic has algorithm code MODIFIED_LOG_LIKELIHOOD_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. It is generated from the shared frequency kernel.

The null is the ordinary Weibull family with zero location:

\[ F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp\left[-(x/\eta)^k\right],\qquad x>0,\quad k,\eta>0. \]

Both parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood for every sample.

docs.title: Usage

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}), declaring both shape and scale unknown. Fixed or partially fixed parameter sets are unsupported.

rvs — a one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant sample with at least two observations. Ties are allowed. Invalid samples raise ValueError. The input is not modified and fitted parameters are not retained on the instance.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
After fitting, the selected binning rule constructs observed counts \(O_j\) and strictly positive expected counts \(E_j=n p_j\). For interval bins with boundaries \(b_0,\ldots,b_m\),

\[ p_j=F(b_j;\widehat k,\widehat\eta)-F(b_{j-1};\widehat k,\widehat\eta). \]

The rule must account for all observations. Equal-probability bins use quantiles of the fitted distribution, giving \(E_j=n/m\) before any rule-specific merging.

\[ T_{ML}=2\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_j\log\frac{E_j}{O_j}. \]

Power divergence with \(\lambda=-1\), using expected counts as weights. This differs from the ordinary G statistic (\(\lambda=0\)). If any observed count is zero, the result is positive infinity.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Large values form the right-tail rejection region. execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. For EqualProbabilityBins, simulate ordinary Weibull samples at shape = scale = 1, refit both parameters, and reconstruct the bins in every replicate. Keep the sample size and binning settings identical.

The built-in Monte Carlo resolver supports this invariant binning rule. Other rules, including fixed boundaries in observation units, require external calibration with explicit simulation parameters. A chi-squared reference with an automatically chosen number of degrees of freedom is not supplied or justified by this implementation. Stored unversioned Weibull critical values are rejected.

docs.title: Mann–Scheuer–Fertig normalized log-spacing statistic
docs.text:
MannScheuerFertigWeibullGofStatistic (MSF) tests the zero-location Weibull family with unknown positive shape \(k\) and scale \(\eta\):

\[ F(x)=1-\exp[-(x/\eta)^k],\qquad x>0. \]

The public class name is now MannScheuerFertigWeibullGofStatistic in both continuous.weibull and continuous. No alias for the former abbreviated class name is provided. Update imports and serialized class references. The short code MSF and the numerical formula are unchanged.

docs.title: Constructor and observations
docs.text: Pass WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}). execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a finite, strictly positive, nonconstant one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge3\); common-interface keywords are unused. It returns a float, does not modify the input and performs no parameter fitting. Invalid observations, logarithms indistinguishable at floating-point precision, or nonpositive approximate expected spacings raise ValueError. Only complete samples are supported. Ties are accepted computationally; continuous-null simulation does not model measurement rounding.

docs.title: Formula and source correspondence
docs.text:
Write \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}\) and \(m_i=\mathbb E[\log E_{(i)}]\) for independent unit exponential variables \(E_j\). Define \(r=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and

\[ h_i=\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{m_{i+1}-m_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1, \qquad S=\frac{\sum_{i=r+1}^{n-1}h_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}h_i}. \]

The code substitutes approximate \(m_i\) as specified below. The ratio matches Krit (2014), equation (29) and Sürücü (2008), equation (4.13), which attribute it to Mann, Scheuer and Fertig (1973). The original 1973 full text was not checked directly; agreement with its expected-value tables is not asserted.

There are \(r\) lower intervals and \(n-1-r\) upper intervals. The numerator includes the last interval. For \(n=2m\) their counts are \(m\) and \(m-1\); for \(n=2m+1\) both counts are \(m\). Thus the code's zero-based slice g[n // 2:] is correct, including for even sample sizes. At \(n=3\), \(S=h_2/(h_1+h_2)\).

docs.title: Expected-order approximation
docs.text:
For \(Q(p)=\log[-\log(1-p)]\), the exact mean is

\[ m_i=\frac{1}{B(i,n+1-i)}\int_0^1 Q(u)u^{i-1}(1-u)^{n-i}\,du. \]

GoFNS(1, n, n) uses \(p_i=i/(n+1)\), \(q_i=1-p_i\) and

\[ \widetilde m_i=Q(p_i)+\frac{p_iq_i}{2(n+2)}Q''(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{(n+2)^2} \left[\frac{q_i-p_i}{3}Q^{(3)}(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{8}Q^{(4)}(p_i)\right]. \]

Besides truncating at the fourth derivative, this expansion approximates higher beta central moments. The exact third central moment is \(2p_iq_i(q_i-p_i)/[(n+2)(n+3)]\); the code uses \((n+2)^2\) in the denominator and \(3p_i^2q_i^2/(n+2)^2\) for the fourth central moment. This convention is part of the implementation, not exact quadrature of expected order statistics.

docs.title: Range, rejection and calibration
docs.text:
Because all \(h_i\) are nonnegative and their sum is positive, \(0\le S\le1\); for distinct observations \(0<S<1\). Tied samples can attain either endpoint. Under \(X\mapsto aX^b\) with \(a,b>0\), every \(h_i\) is multiplied by \(b\), so \(S\) is invariant. Consequently its null distribution depends on the sample size and expectation approximation, but not on Weibull shape or scale.

The implementation uses RightAlternative: reject for large \(S\), using the upper \(1-\alpha\) Monte Carlo quantile for a level-\(\alpha\) test. It is an explicitly one-sided version; alternatives producing small \(S\) may have poor power. It does not implement a two-tail rule. Simulate complete Weibull samples of the observed size with shape = scale = 1, calling this same implementation in each replicate; no fitting is required.

An exact beta law would require additional assumptions on joint spacing behaviour, not merely their expected values. Neither exact beta/F calibration nor a chi-square limit is asserted here. Historical critical values need not match this expectation approximation. See mathematical verification.

value = test.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(value)

docs.title: Öztürk–Korukoğlu Weibull criterion
docs.text: OzturkKorukogluWeibullGofStatistic, short code OK, computes the standardized \(OK_n^*\) statistic. It compares two linear estimates of the scale of log observations. For Weibull shape \(k\) and scale \(\eta\), \(\log X\) has the smallest-extreme-value distribution with location \(\log\eta\) and scale \(1/k\). The criterion eliminates these unknown parameters without an MLE fit.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
The definition follows Öztürk and Korukoğlu (1988), as reproduced in Krit (2014), §3.2.2, equations (3.16)–(3.20). Write \(\ell_i=\log X_{(i)}\) and \(y_i=\ell_i-\bar\ell\). For \(i<n\) set

\[ w_i=\log\frac{n+1}{n-i+1},\qquad v_i=w_i(1+\log w_i)-1, \]

and complete the weights with

\[ w_n=n-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}w_i,\qquad v_n=0.4228n-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}v_i. \]

The two scale estimates and the returned statistic are

\[ b=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(0.6079v_i-0.2570w_i)y_i, \qquad S=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-n-1)y_i}{n(n-1)\log2}, \] \[ T=\frac{b/S-1-0.13/\sqrt n+1.18/n}{0.49/\sqrt n-0.36/n}. \]

docs.title: Centering adjustment
docs.text: The source evaluates the numerator using uncentered \(\ell_i\). The rounded coefficients satisfy \(0.6079\cdot0.4228-0.2570=0.00002012\), so the implementation uses \(b=b_{\mathrm{raw}}-0.00002012\bar\ell\). This explicitly removes the residual dependence on log location. Under \(X\mapsto cX^d\) with \(c,d>0\), both \(b\) and \(S\) multiply by \(d\); therefore \(T\) is invariant. This is the same adjustment used by Shapiro–Brain.

docs.title: Domain and calibration
docs.text:
Use a complete, finite, strictly positive, one-dimensional sample with \(n\ge2\) and at least two distinct observations. Ties are accepted; invalid samples raise ValueError. The input is not modified.

Since \(\sum_i(2i-n-1)y_i=\sum_{i<j}(y_j-y_i)\), \(S\) is positive for every valid sample. Also \(0.49/\sqrt n-0.36/n>0\) for \(n\ge2\). At \(n=2\) the ratio is sample-independent and cannot discriminate distributions.

Reject for small or large values of \(T\). Use lower and upper Monte Carlo quantiles at the actual sample size, evaluating this centered implementation on every replicate. Invariance permits simulation with shape = scale = 1. The empirical normalization does not imply an exact standard-normal null law; \(T\) is signed and is not a squared discrepancy.

value = criterion.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])

docs.title: Evans–Johnson–Green correlation criterion
docs.text: EvansJohnsonGreenWeibullGofStatistic

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
parameters : ParameterValues
    An empty distribution schema; all distribution parameters are unknown.

docs.title: Hypothesis, formula and calibration
docs.text:
F(x)=1-exp(-(x/eta)**k), x > 0, with location fixed at zero
and unknown positive scale eta and shape k.
Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}) to declare both parameters unknown.
Logarithmic location and scale are eliminated within every call.

R2=corr(log(x_(i)), log(-log(1-p_i)))**2,
p_i=(i-0.3175)/(n+0.365). No fitted shape is needed: it cancels.

Reject for left tail values.
Calibrate with repeated execute_statistic calls on ordinary Weibull
samples. Affine invariance in log(x) permits eta=k=1 for simulation.
The returned statistic is R2, not R4 or n*(1-R2).
The former implementation returned R4; its stored critical values cannot
be reused unchanged.

docs.title: Mathematical verification
docs.text:
Write \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}\), \(p_i=(i-0.3175)/(n+0.365)\) and \(c_i=\log[-\log(1-p_i)]\), for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\), including the endpoints. The implementation computes

\[ R^2=\frac{[\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)(c_i-\bar c)]^2} {\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\sum_i(c_i-\bar c)^2}. \]

The exact formula agrees with Krit (2014), §3.2.1, (3.13), p. 47, which attributes it to Evans, Johnson and Green. Krit uses \(M_i=c_i/\widehat{k}\): the common positive factor cancels from \(R^2\). Also, \(\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)M_i=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)(M_i-\bar M)\). Thus the implementation needs neither a fitted shape nor a fitted scale.

Evans, Johnson and Green (1989), p. 3, equation (3) describe the log-scale correlation statistic for the two-parameter family, distinct from the original-scale statistic in their equation (2). The exact rank formula was checked through Krit; the original report's formula images were not directly readable during this review. Filliben (1975) is the historical probability-plot reference, not a source of Weibull critical values. The ranks here are used at all indices; no special endpoint replacement is made. They differ from Smith–Bain's \(i/(n+1)\), so its calibration cannot be substituted.

Our algebra establishes \(0\le R^2\le1\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. Both sequences are ordered and nonconstant, so their covariance is positive; squaring does not hide negative correlation. In a regression of \(y_i\) on \(c_i\) with an intercept, \(R^2=1-\mathrm{SSE}/\mathrm{SST}\). Poor linear fit lowers \(R^2\), giving a left-tail test. The former fourth-power implementation is not the stated statistic; thresholds would need the corresponding transformation.

For \(X=\eta E^{1/k}\), \(E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), \(\log X=\log\eta+k^{-1}\log E\). Correlation removes the location and positive scale, proving a parameter-free null law at fixed \(n\) and invariance under \(X\mapsto aX^b\) for \(a,b>0\). Simulate complete samples from \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) and recompute \(R^2\) to calibrate its lower tail for the actual sample size. No chi-square or normal approximation is asserted.

At \(n=2\) every nonconstant sample has \(R^2=1\) in exact arithmetic, so testing requires \(n\ge3\) even though the API accepts two observations. Ties are allowed numerically, but rounding must be reproduced during calibration. Constant, nonpositive and nonfinite observations are rejected. This implementation does not support censoring or an unknown location parameter.

docs.title: Smith–Bain correlation criterion
docs.text: SmithBainWeibullGofStatistic

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
parameters : ParameterValues
    An empty distribution schema; all distribution parameters are unknown.

docs.title: Hypothesis, formula and calibration
docs.text:
F(x)=1-exp(-(x/eta)**k), x > 0, with location fixed at zero
and unknown positive scale eta and shape k.
Pass Distribution.DEFAULT.parse({}) to declare both parameters unknown.
Logarithmic location and scale are eliminated within every call.

T=n*(1-r**2), where r=corr(log(x_(i)), log(-log(1-i/(n+1)))).

Reject for right tail values.
Calibrate with repeated execute_statistic calls on ordinary Weibull
samples. Affine invariance in log(x) permits eta=k=1 for simulation.
Ordinary fixed-parameter KS tables do not apply to fitted CDFs.
Previously stored unversioned Weibull calibrations must be regenerated.

docs.title: Mathematical verification
docs.text:
Let \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}\), \(p_i=i/(n+1)\) and \(c_i=\log[-\log(1-p_i)]\). The implementation computes

\[ R^2=\frac{[\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)(c_i-\bar c)]^2} {\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\sum_i(c_i-\bar c)^2},\qquad T=n(1-R^2). \]

This agrees with Krit (2014), §3.2.1, equation (3.12), p. 47, which attributes the test to Smith and Bain (1976). The original article's full text was not checked directly. The scores are quantiles at mean uniform ranks, not exact expected log order statistics: in general \(G^{-1}(E[U_{(i)}])\ne E[G^{-1}(U_{(i)})]\). Changing the ranks changes the test and requires new calibration.

Our algebra gives \(0\le T\le n\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. In a regression of \(y_i\) on \(c_i\) with an intercept, \(T/n\) is the residual sum of squares divided by the total centered sum of squares. Thus a poor fit gives large \(T\). Krit's accompanying phrase “too close to 1” is inconsistent with the stated \(Z_2=n(1-R^2)\); it must not be used as a rejection rule or a fixed threshold.

For \(X=\eta E^{1/k}\) with \(E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), \(\log X=\log\eta+k^{-1}\log E\). Correlation eliminates both parameters; no MLE is performed. More generally, \(X\mapsto aX^b\), \(a,b>0\), preserves \(T\). The log-Weibull transformation and probability-plot construction are also explained in Krit (2014), §2, equations (3), (8).

Calibrate the right tail for the actual sample size using independent complete samples from \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) (Weibull shape = scale = 1), recomputing \(T\) in every replicate. No chi-square or standard-normal null law is assumed. At \(n=2\), every nonconstant sample has \(R^2=1\) and \(T=0\) in exact arithmetic: the API accepts it, but a nondegenerate test requires \(n\ge3\). Constant or nonpositive samples are rejected. Ties are accepted numerically; rounded-data calibration must reproduce the observation/rounding mechanism. Censoring is not supported by this implementation, despite the original article's title.

docs.title: Shapiro–Brain W test for the Weibull family
docs.text: ShapiroBrainWeibullGofStatistic uses code SB_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. It tests the ordinary Weibull family with zero location and unknown positive shape and scale. It uses ordered log observations, without an MLE fit.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Weibull
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    ShapiroBrainWeibullGofStatistic,
)

criterion = ShapiroBrainWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(statistic)

parameters must declare both parameters unknown; fixed or partially fixed parameters are unsupported. rvs must contain at least two finite, strictly positive, nonconstant observations in one dimension. Ties are accepted. The sample is sorted internally without modifying the caller's array.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}-\overline{\log X}\), in ascending order. Define

\[ w_i=\log\frac{n+1}{n-i+1},\quad v_i=w_i(1+\log w_i)-1,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1, \] \[ w_n=n-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}w_i,\qquad v_n=0.4228n-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}v_i, \] \[ b=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(0.6079v_i-0.2570w_i)y_i,\qquad W=\frac{nb^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2}. \]

The coefficients and normalization agree with the Shapiro–Brain formula reproduced in Shell (2003), equation (9). The original article is Shapiro and Brain (1987).

docs.title: Centering and mathematical checks
docs.text:
Centering is an explicit adjustment to the formula with rounded coefficients. Our algebraic check gives

\[ \delta=0.6079\cdot0.4228-0.2570=0.00002012,\qquad \sum_i(0.6079v_i-0.2570w_i)=n\delta. \]

Consequently, evaluating the same weights on uncentered logs gives \(b_{\rm raw}=b+\delta\overline{\log X}\). Without the subtraction, changing the units of observation changes the statistic. This implementation centers first and therefore has \(W(cX^d)=W(X)\) for \(c,d>0\), up to floating-point error: centered logs and \(b\) scale by \(d\), so numerator and denominator scale by \(d^2\). The denominator is positive for accepted nonconstant log samples and \(W\ge0\). This ratio is not normalized as a squared correlation, so a bound of one is not assumed. At \(n=2\) it is constant over nonconstant samples and has no discriminatory power, although the numerical formula is defined.

Shell's Table 1 sample reproduces the report's rounded \(W=0.4930\) with the uncentered equation: our calculation gives \(0.4930407980\). The centered library variant gives \(0.4929256593\). Tests distinguish these values rather than claiming bit-for-bit equality to the uncentered expression.

docs.title: Rejection region and calibration
docs.text:
Both small and large values reject, following the two-quantile comparison in Shell (2003), Section VI. alternative() returns TwoSidedAlternative; execute_statistic returns only the statistic. This corrects the former left-tail-only declaration.

Calibrate the centered variant at the same sample size. Log-location-scale invariance permits simulation at Weibull shape = scale = 1. Every replicate recomputes the ordered-log statistic; there is no parameter-fitting stage. Use matching two-tail critical values, not fully specified KS tables or a chi-squared approximation. Existing unversioned storage calibrations remain blocked; the tail correction also changes interpretation of old decisions.

docs.text:

docs.title: Coles stabilized probability-plot criterion
docs.text:
ColesWeibullGofStatistic (short code SPP) uses Blom estimates, replacing the previous MLE implementation. It tests the complete, uncensored two-parameter Weibull family with zero location and unknown positive shape \(k\) and scale \(\eta\):

\[F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp[-(x/\eta)^k],\qquad x>0.\]

Construct with WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}).

docs.title: Statistic and rejection region
docs.text:
For sorted \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}\), let \(z_i=(y_i-\widehat\mu_B)/\widehat\sigma_B\) and \(u_i=1-\exp[-\exp(z_i)]\). With \(h(p)=2\arcsin\sqrt p/\pi\), return

\[T=\max_{1\le i\le n}\left|h\!\left(\frac{i-1/2}{n}\right)-h(u_i)\right|.\]

The transform and maximum distance match Krit (2014), (3.14)–(3.15). Coles (1989) studies Michael's maximum distance using Blom estimates and also a separate correlation statistic. This implementation returns the unscaled maximum distance, not that correlation or a normalizing transformation of it. Large distances reject: the critical region is the right tail, despite the absolute value measuring discrepancies in both directions. There is no additional \(\sqrt n\) multiplier.

docs.title: Blom estimates and approximation convention
docs.text:
The linear estimator follows EWGoF::BLOMEst. Let \(p_i=i/(n+1)\), \(\theta_i=-(1-p_i)\log(1-p_i)\), and let \(m_i\) approximate the expected \(i\)th order statistic of the standard minimum-Gumbel distribution. Pad \(\theta\), \(\theta m\), and \(\theta y\) with zero endpoints. For \(j=0,\ldots,n\), form

\[ A_j=(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1},\ \theta_jm_j-\theta_{j+1}m_{j+1}),\qquad b_j=\theta_jy_j-\theta_{j+1}y_{j+1}. \]

Then \((\widehat\mu_B,\widehat\sigma_B)\) minimizes \(\|A(\mu,\sigma)^T-b\|^2\). This is algebraically equivalent to the explicit linear weights in BLOMEst; the implementation uses a least-squares solver instead of explicitly inverting \(A^TA\). The corresponding Weibull estimates would be \(\widehat\eta=\exp(\widehat\mu_B)\) and \(\widehat k=1/\widehat\sigma_B\); only standardized logs are needed, avoiding exponentiation of the location.

The library reuses its GoFNS(1,n,n) approximation. For \(Q(p)=\log[-\log(1-p)]\), \(q=1-p\), it uses

\[ m_i=Q(p_i)+\frac{p_iq_i}{2(n+2)}Q''(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{(n+2)^2} \left[\frac{q_i-p_i}{3}Q^{(3)}(p_i)+\frac{p_iq_i}{8}Q^{(4)}(p_i)\right]. \]

This is a fourth-order Taylor approximation, not exact quadrature of expected order statistics. The fractions \(1/3\) and \(1/8\) are evaluated as real numbers. The EWGoF C++ source uses integer division at those two coefficients, so its compiled output is not an exact numerical oracle for this convention. Also, EWGoF::WPP.test itself uses MLE in its SPP branch: only BLOMEst supplies our estimator reference. The Coles abstract confirms Blom estimation; the full original article was not directly available. Exact reproduction of its critical-value tables is therefore not claimed.

docs.title: Mathematical properties and calibration
docs.text:
Since \(h\) maps \([0,1]\) into \([0,1]\), \(0\le T\le1\). Under \(X\mapsto aX^d\), \(a,d>0\), the response becomes \(b'=\log(a)A_{:,1}+d b\). Consequently \(\widehat\mu'_B=\log(a)+d\widehat\mu_B\) and \(\widehat\sigma'_B=d\widehat\sigma_B\), leaving every \(z_i\) and \(T\) unchanged. The code shifts and rescales logs before solving for numerical stability; this is the same fit in different coordinates.

For \(X=\eta E^{1/k}\), \(E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), this invariance eliminates the two unknown parameters. Calibrate at shape = scale = 1, re-estimating with Blom on every replicate, at the actual sample size and with this approximation convention. Old MLE critical values must be regenerated. The existing storage guard rejects unversioned Weibull critical values. Neither standard KS tables, a chi-square law, nor a standard-normal null law applies automatically. Kimber's tables use a different estimator, as noted by Krit, and are not substituted here.

For \(n=2\), any two nonconstant ordered log samples are related by a positive affine transformation, so \(T\) is constant and has no discriminatory power. Use \(n\ge3\) for testing. This does not imply that the two-observation value is zero.

docs.title: Input and numerical behavior
docs.text: execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) accepts a one-dimensional finite, strictly positive, nonconstant sample of at least two observations. It does not mutate the sample or retain estimates. Additional common-interface keywords are unused. Invalid samples, indistinguishable logs, nonpositive fitted log-scale or an unrepresentable fit raise ValueError. Ties are accepted; when observations are rounded, calibration must reproduce rounding. Censoring and unknown location are not supported. CDF saturation at zero or one gives a finite endpoint value of \(h\).

test = ColesWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
print(test.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2]))

docs.title: Best–Rayner–Thas skewness component for Weibull fit
docs.text: BestRaynerThasSkewnessWeibullGofStatistic is also available as ST1WeibullGofStatistic. The alias refers to the same class; its code remains ST1_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a zero-location Weibull sample with unknown shape \(k\) and scale \(\eta\), use \(Y_i=-\log X_i\). Under the null, \(Y\) is maximum Gumbel with location \(-\log\eta\) and scale \(1/k\). Define

\[ m_j=\frac1n\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^j,\qquad g_n=\frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}},\qquad b_n=\frac{m_4}{m_2^2}. \]

All moments use divisor \(n\); \(b_n\) denotes Pearson kurtosis (not excess). The implementation returns

\[ V_3^2=\frac{n(g_n-1.139547)^2}{20}. \]

These are the rounded coefficients used by EWGoF 2.2.2 source and reproduced in Krit (2014), §3.2.5, (3.33)–(3.36). The fourth component includes a correction for skewness. No maximum-likelihood fit is used in either component.

docs.title: Names and compatibility
docs.text:
EWGoF's executable code defines ST1 as skewness and ST2 as kurtosis. Its help page reverses these labels. The descriptive Python names remove this ambiguity; the historical aliases follow the executable source.

The previous local delta-method discrepancies have been replaced. In particular, ST1 no longer divides by the asymptotic variance of sample skewness, and ST2 no longer uses a covariance-based regression correction. Old critical values must be regenerated despite the preserved short codes.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Weibull
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    BestRaynerThasSkewnessWeibullGofStatistic,
)

criterion = BestRaynerThasSkewnessWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
value = criterion.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])

Both parameters must be unknown. Input must be one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive and nonconstant, with at least two observations. Ties are accepted. Invalid input raises ValueError; input arrays are not modified.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Large values reject. At fixed sample size, invariance under \(X\mapsto aX^b\) for \(a,b>0\) permits simulation with Weibull shape = scale = 1. Every replicate must undergo the same negative-log transformation and moment standardization. At \(n=2\) the statistic is constant and cannot discriminate alternatives. Rounded or censored observations require calibration for that observation scheme.

The return value is a statistic, not a p-value. The denominators are smooth polynomial normalizations, not delta-method variances after estimating location and scale. An unqualified \(\chi^2_1\) approximation is not justified for these rounded implementations. Use finite-sample Monte Carlo calibration. Unversioned stored Weibull calibrations remain blocked.

docs.title: Scientific reference and verification scope
docs.text:
Best, D. J., Rayner, J. C. W., & Thas, O. (2007). Comparison of Five Tests of Fit for the Extreme Value Distribution. Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice, 1(1), 89–99. Author-uploaded copy.

The accessible author PDF contains printed pages 89–91 and 96–97 only; pages 92–95 and the appendices needed for direct formula verification are missing. Exact implementation coefficients were checked against EWGoF and Krit, not against the missing pages. Agreement with every example in the original article has therefore not been established.

See the mathematical validation for reproducible numerical checks and the unresolved Port Pirie discrepancy.

For the 65 observations in the article's Table 1 (Port Pirie), treating them as \(Y\) and passing \(X=\exp(-Y)\) gives \(g_n=0.7110707539472332\) and \(V_3^2=0.5966736536522815\). Section 4 reports \(V_3^2=0.71\). The reported number is close to the sample skewness, but this alone does not establish a typographical error. Replacing the statistic by sample skewness or changing its denominator merely to reproduce 0.71 would change the test without scientific justification. The discrepancy remains unresolved.

docs.title: Tiku–Singh normalized log-spacing statistic
docs.text:
TikuSinghWeibullGofStatistic (TS) tests the ordinary two-parameter Weibull family with zero location and unknown shape and scale:

\[ F(x)=1-\exp[-(x/\eta)^k],\qquad x>0,\quad k,\eta>0. \]

docs.title: Construction and sample requirements
docs.text: Pass WeibullDistributionDescriptor.DEFAULT.parse({}) to the constructor. execute_statistic(rvs, **kwargs) returns a scalar statistic; common-interface keywords are unused. The sample must be one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant and have \(n\ge3\) observations. Invalid samples, logarithms indistinguishable at floating-point precision, or nonpositive approximate expected spacings raise ValueError. The input is not modified. No parameters are fitted. Only complete samples are supported. Ties are accepted computationally; continuous-null simulation does not account for a measurement-rounding mechanism.

docs.title: Statistic
docs.text:
Let \(y_i=\log X_{(i)}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\). For independent unit exponential variables \(E_j\), let \(m_i=\mathbb E[\log E_{(i)}]\). Define

\[ h_i=\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{m_{i+1}-m_i},\quad g_i=\frac{h_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}h_j},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1, \] \[ T=\frac{2}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-2}(n-1-i)g_i. \]

The implementation replaces \(m_i\) by the explicit approximation below. This functional is \(Z^*\) in Sürücü (2008), (3.4)–(3.5), applied to log observations. Its Weibull attribution is Tiku and Singh (1981), building on Tiku (1980).

Krit (2014), (30) reproduces TS, but its preceding definition of \(E_i\) uses observations \(i,i+1\) while (30) sums over \(i=2,\ldots,n\). These indices are inconsistent. Interpreting \(E_i=h_{i-1}\) in (30) gives the formula above. The original 1981 full text was not checked directly; exact agreement with its tables or expectation approximations is not asserted.

docs.title: Expected-order approximation
docs.text:
For \(U_{(i)}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(i,n+1-i)\) and \(Q(p)=\log[-\log(1-p)]\), the exact mean is

\[ m_i=\frac{1}{B(i,n+1-i)}\int_0^1 Q(u)u^{i-1}(1-u)^{n-i}\,du. \]

GoFNS(1, n, n) instead uses \(p_i=i/(n+1)\), \(q_i=1-p_i\) and

\[ \widetilde m_i=Q(p_i)+\frac{p_iq_i}{2(n+2)}Q''(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{(n+2)^2} \left[\frac{q_i-p_i}{3}Q^{(3)}(p_i) +\frac{p_iq_i}{8}Q^{(4)}(p_i)\right]. \]

This is a fourth-derivative Taylor expansion with approximate higher beta central moments, not an exact fourth-order moment calculation. In particular, the exact third central moment is \(2p_iq_i(q_i-p_i)/[(n+2)(n+3)]\); the code replaces \((n+2)(n+3)\) by \((n+2)^2\) and uses \(3p_i^2q_i^2/(n+2)^2\) for the fourth central moment. This approximation is part of the implemented definition and can affect finite-sample critical values, particularly through extreme order statistics.

docs.title: Rejection and calibration
docs.text:
Both small and large values reject (TwoSidedAlternative). Use sample-size-specific Monte Carlo quantiles of this same implementation, for example lower \(\alpha/2\) and upper \(1-\alpha/2\) quantiles for an equal-tail level-\(\alpha\) test. Do not assume that these quantiles are symmetric around 1.

Under \(X\mapsto aX^b\) with \(a,b>0\), log spacings are multiplied by \(b\), so \(g_i\) and \(T\) are unchanged. Therefore simulation can use shape = scale = 1 without fitting parameters in any replicate.

Since \(g_i\ge0\) and \(\sum g_i=1\), \(T\) is a weighted average of numbers in \([0,2]\). Thus \(0\le T\le2\) in exact arithmetic, and \(0<T<2\) for distinct observations. With \(z_j=\sum_{i=1}^j g_i\), \(T=2\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}z_j/(n-2)\). These \(z_j\) are not assumed to be independent uniform variables under a log-Weibull null. In particular, the exact uniform-mean law for ordinary exponential spacings does not supply a calibration for this generalized log-spacing statistic.

Historical critical values need not match the approximation used here. Generate fresh calibration with execute_statistic; no chi-square limit or censored-data calibration is supplied. See the mathematical verification.

docs.text:

    TikuSinghWeibullGofStatistic,
)

test = TikuSinghWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
value = test.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(value)

docs.title: Watson test for the Weibull family
Description
docs.text:
WatsonWeibullGofStatistic has algorithm code WATSON_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. It is generated from the shared EDF kernel.

The null is the ordinary Weibull family with zero location:

\[ F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp\left[-(x/\eta)^k\right],\qquad x>0,\quad k,\eta>0. \]

Both parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood for every sample.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Weibull
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    WatsonWeibullGofStatistic,
)

criterion = WatsonWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}), declaring both shape and scale unknown. Fixed or partially fixed parameter sets are unsupported.

rvs — a one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant sample with at least two observations. Ties are allowed. Invalid samples raise ValueError. The input is not modified and fitted parameters are not retained on the instance.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For ordered observations, set \(u_i=F(X_{(i)};\widehat k,\widehat\eta)\). The implemented statistic is

\[ U_n^2=W_n^2-n(\bar u-1/2)^2,\qquad \bar u=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n u_i. \]

Here \(W_n^2\) is the Cramér–von Mises statistic. The implementation uses centered deviations to reduce cancellation.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Large values form the right-tail rejection region. execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. Calibrate at the same sample size by simulating ordinary Weibull samples and re-estimating both parameters for every replicate. Log-location-scale invariance permits shape = scale = 1 for this simulation.

Critical values for a fully specified uniform or Weibull CDF do not apply to the fitted model. The built-in Monte Carlo resolver repeats the fit through execute_statistic; stored unversioned Weibull critical values are rejected.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Watson, G. S. (1961). Goodness-of-fit tests on a circle. Biometrika, 48(1–2), 109–114.

The references identify the EDF discrepancy. Its application here uses estimated Weibull parameters and therefore requires the fitted-model calibration described above.

See the Weibull criterion catalog for all implementations and shared calibration requirements.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Large values form the right-tail rejection region. execute_statistic returns a statistic, not a p-value. Calibrate at the same sample size by simulating ordinary Weibull samples and re-estimating both parameters for every replicate. Log-location-scale invariance permits shape = scale = 1 for this simulation.

Critical values for a fully specified uniform or Weibull CDF do not apply to the fitted model. The built-in Monte Carlo resolver repeats the fit through execute_statistic; stored unversioned Weibull critical values are rejected.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Zhang, J. (2002). Powerful goodness-of-fit tests based on the likelihood ratio. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 64(2), 281–294.

The references identify the EDF discrepancy. Its application here uses estimated Weibull parameters and therefore requires the fitted-model calibration described above.

See the Weibull criterion catalog for all implementations and shared calibration requirements.

docs.title: Zhang Z_K test for the Weibull family
Description
docs.text:
ZhangKWeibullGofStatistic has algorithm code ZHANG_ZK_WEIBULL_GOODNESS_OF_FIT. It is generated from the shared EDF kernel.

The null is the ordinary Weibull family with zero location:

\[ F(x;k,\eta)=1-\exp\left[-(x/\eta)^k\right],\qquad x>0,\quad k,\eta>0. \]

Both parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood for every sample.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from pysatl_criterion.distribution import WeibullDistributionDescriptor as Weibull
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous.weibull import (
    ZhangKWeibullGofStatistic,
)

criterion = ZhangKWeibullGofStatistic(Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}))
statistic = criterion.execute_statistic([0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 2.2])
print(statistic)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text:
parameters — Weibull.DEFAULT.parse({}), declaring both shape and scale unknown. Fixed or partially fixed parameter sets are unsupported.

rvs — a one-dimensional, finite, strictly positive, nonconstant sample with at least two observations. Ties are allowed. Invalid samples raise ValueError. The input is not modified and fitted parameters are not retained on the instance.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
For ordered observations, set \(u_i=F(X_{(i)};\widehat k,\widehat\eta)\). The implemented statistic is

\[ Z_K=\max_{1\le i\le n}\left[(i-\tfrac12)\log\frac{(i-\tfrac12)/n}{u_i}+(n-i+\tfrac12)\log\frac{(n-i+\tfrac12)/n}{1-u_i}\right]. \]

This is the discrepancy in Zhang (2002), equation (3.1), evaluated at Weibull MLEs.

The kernel uses fitted log-CDF and log-survival probabilities to preserve tail precision when the CDF rounds to 0 or 1. Extreme penalties may still overflow to positive infinity.
