docs.title: Loading distributions
docs.text:
Use DistributionLoader to copy stored limit distributions and their cached critical values into a local database. This lets an application reuse simulation results already available in another PySATL database. Loading transfers existing records; it does not run simulations or calculate missing critical values.

Start with the guide below, try the runnable examples, or see custom loaders and adapters to connect your own data source.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
With pysatl-criterion installed, create a loader and choose a local database:

from pysatl_criterion.loader import DistributionLoader


loader = DistributionLoader(local="sqlite:///local.db")
result = loader.load()
print(result.saved_count)

This copies all available distributions and their current cached critical values from the configured remote database. The loader creates missing tables in local.db. The source must already contain the PySATL tables and the records you want to load.

When remote is omitted, the loader uses pysatl_criterion.utils.constants.REMOTE_PYSATL_URL. To configure it, set PYSATL_REMOTE_DB_URL before importing the library, for example before starting Python:

export PYSATL_REMOTE_DB_URL='sqlite:///shared.db'

You can also pass the source explicitly:

loader = DistributionLoader(
    remote="sqlite:///shared.db",
    local="sqlite:///local.db",
)
result = loader.load(batch_size=50)

Both arguments accept a SQLAlchemy connection URL or an AlchemyDatabase object. local is required; PYSATL_LOCAL_DB_URL is not used as its default. An explicit remote takes precedence over the environment configuration. A URL using another database engine requires its Python driver and a reachable database. See connection ownership if your application already manages database objects.

docs.title: Selecting distributions
docs.text:
Pass a LimitDistributionFilter to load(). All its fields are optional:

Field Default Meaning criteria None Select any criterion, or supply a sequence of CriterionFilter objects. min_sample_size None Inclusive lower sample-size bound; no lower bound when omitted. max_sample_size None Inclusive upper sample-size bound; no upper bound when omitted. min_monte_carlo_count None Inclusive minimum number of simulations; no minimum when omitted.

sample_size is the number of observations in each simulated sample. monte_carlo_count is the number of simulations used to produce a stored distribution. batch_size controls how many database records are transferred in one batch; it is separate from both quantities.

docs.title: Bind each code to its parameters
docs.text:
Each CriterionFilter contains a required criterion_code and optional criterion_parameters. Obtain these from the statistic you use so that they agree with the stored distribution identity:

from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.limit_distribution import (
    CriterionFilter,
    LimitDistributionFilter,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovGammaGofStatistic,
)


statistic = KolmogorovSmirnovGammaGofStatistic(alpha=2.0, beta=1.0)
query = LimitDistributionFilter(
    criteria=[
        CriterionFilter(
            criterion_code=statistic.code(),
            criterion_parameters=statistic.hypothesis().parameters(),
        ),
    ],
    min_sample_size=20,
    max_sample_size=100,
    min_monte_carlo_count=10_000,
)
result = loader.load(query, batch_size=50)

This example reuses loader from the quick start. It selects sample sizes from 20 through 100 for the specified code and complete parameter dictionary, with at least 10,000 simulations. The result may be empty if the source has no matching records.

A record must match at least one entry in criteria, as well as all size and simulation-count bounds. Each entry's parameters apply only to that entry's code. You can repeat a code to select several parameter sets, as shown in the examples.

Selection Meaning LimitDistributionFilter() or criteria=None All criteria and parameter variants. criteria=[] No distributions. CriterionFilter(code) or CriterionFilter(code, None) All parameter variants of this code. CriterionFilter(code, {}) Only the parameterless variant of this code. CriterionFilter(code, {"alpha": 2.0, "beta": 1.0}) Exactly this complete parameter set for this code.

Parameter matching is not a partial dictionary match: specifying only alpha does not match a stored dictionary containing both alpha and beta. Dictionary order is ignored and numeric values such as 2 and 2.0 match the same parameter value.

docs.title: Use either size bound independently
docs.text:
# Every size at or above 100; no upper bound.
query = LimitDistributionFilter(min_sample_size=100)

# Every size at or below 100; no lower bound.
query = LimitDistributionFilter(max_sample_size=100)

# Exactly sample size 100.
query = LimitDistributionFilter(min_sample_size=100, max_sample_size=100)

Pass the desired query to loader.load(query). Omitted bounds and explicit None have the same meaning. Specified size/count bounds must be positive, and the minimum sample size must not exceed the maximum. Invalid bounds raise ValueError when the filter is constructed.

docs.title: Selecting cached critical values
docs.text:
A plain LimitDistributionFilter copies all current cached levels and alternatives for the selected distributions. Use CriticalValueFilter to restrict those values:

from decimal import Decimal

from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.critical_value import CriticalValueFilter
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.alternative import AlternativeType


query = CriticalValueFilter(
    min_sample_size=20,
    max_sample_size=100,
    significance_levels=[Decimal("0.05"), Decimal("0.01")],
    alternative_types=[AlternativeType.RIGHT],
)
result = loader.load(query)

CriticalValueFilter inherits criteria and all size/count bounds. Those fields select the distributions in both transfer stages. significance_levels and alternative_types affect only the critical-value stage: the distributions are still copied even when no cached values match. For either extra field, None means unrestricted and [] means no critical values.

Use Decimal levels strictly between zero and one, with at most ten decimal places. Alternatives are AlternativeType.LEFT, AlternativeType.RIGHT, and AlternativeType.TWO_TAILED. Only existing current cache entries are transferred. Requesting a level that is absent from the source does not calculate it.

docs.title: Understanding the result
docs.text:
load() returns DistributionLoadResult. Its limit_distributions and critical_values attributes are separate LoadResult objects:

print(result.limit_distributions.saved_count)
print(result.critical_values.saved_count)
print(result.fetched_count, result.saved_count, result.skipped_count)
print(result.limit_distributions.not_found_codes)
print(result.critical_values.not_found_codes)
Attribute Meaning fetched_count Number of matching records read from the source. saved_count Number of records that changed the destination. skipped_count fetched_count - saved_count. not_found_codes Requested codes with no matching source records in this stage; available on each LoadResult.

The three counts on DistributionLoadResult are sums across both stages. One distribution and its one cached critical-value record therefore count as two records.

Missing codes are tracked after applying the complete filter, not by checking whether a code exists anywhere in the source. They are deduplicated in request order. If several entries request one code, any matching record for that code removes it from not_found_codes; this field does not report individual missing parameter sets. With criteria=None, there are no explicitly requested codes, so the lists are empty.

The facade prints one summary after a successful load. To disable summaries, use the component loaders with print_summary=False, as described in custom loaders.

docs.title: Repeated loads and failures
docs.text:
A distribution is identified by its code, complete parameter dictionary, and sample size. For that identity, the destination keeps the record with the larger monte_carlo_count. Equal or smaller counts are skipped. Updating a distribution also invalidates its local cached critical values in the same transaction.

The loader finishes all selected distributions before starting the critical-value stage. Cached values are accepted only when their simulation count matches the destination distribution; missing distributions, mismatched versions, and already stored equal versions are skipped. A repeat load can still fill missing cached values even when no distribution changes.

Each destination batch is committed separately. If reading or writing raises an exception, it propagates to the caller and earlier completed batches remain saved. A failure during distribution loading prevents the critical-value stage from starting. There is no automatic retry or saved resume cursor; calling load() again rereads the selection and applies the same rules for keeping existing records.

batch_size defaults to 100 and must be positive. It limits records per batch, not the number of statistics inside each distribution. The built-in readers release each source transaction before yielding a batch. Reads across multiple batches do not form a single database snapshot.

docs.title: Custom loaders and storage adapters
docs.text:
Use the built-in DistributionLoader for transfers between supported databases. To read distributions from a file, an API, or another storage system, implement a reader and pass it to LimitDistributionLoader. To change where records are saved, implement a writer. The existing loaders already handle batch iteration and result counts.

See Usage examples for transfers that use the standard database adapters.

docs.title: Share a storage across pipeline threads
docs.text:
Use DistributionStorage and CriticalValueStorage from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.storage when pipeline stages need to read, calculate, write, and read again. Create one AlchemyDatabase per database configuration in each process, initialize it before starting workers, and pass the same storage objects between stages. Each method creates its own short-lived unit of work. Neither storage keeps an active session between calls.

Both storages implement the reader/writer interfaces below and can be passed directly to LimitDistributionLoader or CriticalValueLoader as either source or destination. They also expose get_batch for cursor-based reads; CriticalValueStorage exposes save_if_current and delete_for_distribution.

This example uses illustrative simulated values to demonstrate ownership and threading; replace the calculation with your calibration algorithm:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from dataclasses import replace

from pysatl_criterion.persistence.models.limit_distribution import LimitDistributionModel
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.config import StorageConfig
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.database import AlchemyDatabase
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.storage import (
    CriticalValueStorage,
    DistributionStorage,
)


config = StorageConfig(max_workers=30)
database = AlchemyDatabase("sqlite:///calibrations.db", config=config)
try:
    database.init()
    distributions = DistributionStorage(database)
    critical_values = CriticalValueStorage(database)
    initial = [LimitDistributionModel(f"example_{i}", {}, 20, 2, [1.0, 2.0]) for i in range(30)]
    distributions.bulk_insert(initial)

    def process(key):
        source = distributions.get(key)
        if source is None:
            raise LookupError(key)
        # No session or connection is held during this calculation.
        values = source.results_statistics + [3.0, 4.0]
        updated = replace(source, monte_carlo_count=len(values), results_statistics=values)
        distributions.insert(updated)  # Returns after commit and cache invalidation.
        return distributions.get(key)

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=config.max_workers) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(process, [item.key for item in initial]))
finally:
    database.dispose()  # Wait for accepted public operations and stop the SQLite writer.

get returns a plain model, independent of the closed session. Each iter_batches page releases its transaction and connection before yielding; the complete iteration does not promise one database snapshot. Do not mutate input models, filter dictionaries, or sequences concurrently with an operation, and do not advance the same iterator from multiple threads.

DistributionStorage.insert and bulk_insert save improvements and invalidate derived critical values in one transaction through DistributionService. CriticalValueStorage accepts writes only for the matching local source version. save_if_current returns true for an unchanged but still-current entry; insert reports actual changes. A read/calculate/write pipeline is not one transaction: the source may change during calculation, so a rejected stale write must be recomputed from a fresh source when required.

docs.title: Configure connection pools and the SQLite writer
docs.text:
StorageConfig separates pipeline concurrency from connection limits:

Setting Default Meaning max_workers 30 Suggested executor size; pass it to your executor explicitly. Storage does not start a compute pool. pool_size None Resolves to 5 for file SQLite, or max_workers for server databases. max_overflow 0 Extra connections above pool_size; the pool is bounded by default. pool_timeout 30 seconds Maximum wait to check out a connection; exhaustion raises SQLAlchemy TimeoutError. pool_pre_ping True Validate a pooled connection at checkout; does not recover a failed transaction. pool_recycle -1 No age-based recycling; set a nonnegative lifetime when required by the server. sqlite_timeout 30 seconds SQLite driver lock timeout. write_queue_size 30 Pending SQLite writes, in addition to one running write. write_queue_timeout 30 seconds Maximum wait for queue capacity; raises built-in TimeoutError before submitting the write. retry_attempts 3 Total attempts for recognized lock, deadlock, and serialization failures. retry_backoff 0.05 seconds Initial delay between attempts, doubled on each retry.

For PostgreSQL/MySQL, writes execute in the calling workers using separate sessions from the shared pool. For example, pass StorageConfig(max_workers=30, pool_size=10, max_overflow=0) to allow 30 compute workers while limiting that engine to 10 simultaneous database connections. Database URLs select the driver; install the corresponding driver separately. Existing AlchemyDatabase(..., **engine_options) arguments remain supported and override configuration-derived engine options. Explicit pool/poolclass options retain responsibility for their own concurrency behavior.

For file SQLite, all public storage instances sharing one AlchemyDatabase submit writes to its single writer thread. The bounded queue applies backpressure, and the caller waits for commit or receives the transaction's exception. Reads continue in their calling threads with independent sessions. The queue limit is a task count, not a byte limit; choose batch sizes with the size of compressed arrays in mind. Other database objects or processes have their own writers and still contend for SQLite's database-wide write lock. WAL is not enabled automatically.

Ordinary in-memory SQLite retains single-thread behavior. Public storages reject calls from another thread rather than silently opening a separate empty database. Use file SQLite for threaded pipelines. A shared StaticPool alone does not make simultaneous use of one SQLite connection safe.

Connection pools open connections on demand. A fresh Session does not imply a new physical connection: completed operations return connections to the pool. Inspect database.engine.pool.status() and measure checkout waits, transaction durations, throughput, and lock/retry rates on representative workloads before increasing limits. A larger pool does not provide additional SQLite writers.

docs.title: Transactions, retries, and shutdown
docs.text:
Retries reopen the entire operation in a fresh unit of work after rollback. Validation/integrity errors, queue/pool exhaustion, and invalidated connections are not retried automatically. A disconnected commit may have an uncertain outcome and requires application-level handling. Do not add external side effects to retryable transaction operations.

Keep the existing AlchemyLimitDistributionStorage(session) and AlchemyCriticalValueStorage(session) for advanced operations requiring an explicit shared transaction. The existing Reader/Writer adapters also remain available. Direct session/UoW access and those adapters bypass the new public storage dispatcher: callers own their retries, concurrency limits, and shutdown.

Stop pipeline workers before database.dispose(). Disposal rejects new public operations, waits for accepted ones, stops the writer, and releases the engine's pool; it is terminal for that database object. Exhausted iterators should be discarded, and subsequent calls must use a new database object. Storages do not dispose caller-owned databases. Finish direct sessions/UoWs yourself before disposing the database.

The default example uses one process. For multiprocessing, create the database, pool, storages, and worker threads inside each process; never pass them through a process pool or reuse them after fork. Public operations detect use from a different process and raise an error. Budget the sum of pool_size + max_overflow across all engines and processes against the server's connection limit. The SQLite writer is process-local.

DistributionLoader(remote=..., local=..., config=config) uses the public storages internally. Its configuration applies to databases created from URLs; passed AlchemyDatabase instances retain their own settings and remain caller-owned. Transfers still finish distributions before critical values and commit each batch independently.

docs.title: Choose an extension point
docs.text:
Task Extension point Read limit distributions from a custom source IBulkStoreReader with LimitDistributionLoader Read cached critical values from a custom source IBulkStoreReader with CriticalValueLoader Save either model type to a custom destination IBulkStoreWriter with the corresponding loader Transfer a different model with criterion-based filtering A subclass of AbstractLoader plus suitable adapters

DistributionLoader accepts database URLs or AlchemyDatabase objects. It does not accept custom readers or writers. Use LimitDistributionLoader and CriticalValueLoader directly when supplying your own adapters. If you transfer both kinds of records, finish loading distributions before loading their cached critical values.

docs.title: Reader and writer interfaces
docs.text:
The interfaces are defined in pysatl_criterion.persistence.stores.base.

Interface Required method Contract IBulkStoreReader[M, Q, F] get(query: Q) -> M \| None Return one model by its identity, or None when absent. IBulkStoreReader[M, Q, F] iter_batches(query: F, *, batch_size: int = 100) -> Iterator[list[M]] Apply the filter and yield nonempty batches of at most batch_size models. Reject nonpositive batch sizes. IBulkStoreWriter[M] insert(model: M) -> bool Save one model according to the destination policy; return whether it changed stored data. IBulkStoreWriter[M] bulk_insert(models: Sequence[M]) -> list[M] Save a batch and return the accepted model for each identity that changed.

get and insert are inherited abstract methods and must be implemented even though the loaders call only iter_batches and bulk_insert during a transfer. Readers need no writing methods, and writers need no reading methods.

The built-in loaders use these types:

Loader Model (M) Single-record query (Q) Batch filter (F) LimitDistributionLoader LimitDistributionModel DistributionKey LimitDistributionFilter CriticalValueLoader CriticalValueModel CriticalValueLookupQuery CriticalValueFilter

docs.title: Reader responsibilities
docs.text:
Filtering happens in the reader. The loader passes the query through without filtering the returned models again. Apply every relevant field of the filter, including these distinctions:

  • criteria=None leaves criterion selection unrestricted; criteria=[] matches nothing.
  • Each CriterionFilter binds a code to its own parameters. Match at least one complete code/parameter pair, not independent lists of codes and parameters.
  • criterion_parameters=None matches all parameter variants of that code; {} matches only the parameterless variant. A supplied dictionary must match the entire parameter set.
  • Sample-size and Monte Carlo count bounds are inclusive. An omitted bound (None) imposes no restriction.

For a critical-value reader, also apply the significance-level and alternative filters and return only values that match the source distribution's current Monte Carlo count.

Release any source transaction before yielding a batch. A database reader can use a stable identity cursor to fetch one bounded page at a time; the standard readers use this approach. The interface does not promise a single snapshot across batches. Avoid fetching the complete source into memory merely to split it into batches.

docs.title: Writer responsibilities
docs.text:
The writer owns transaction boundaries, conflict handling, and cache consistency. The batch loader does not open transactions, commit changes, or retry failed reads and writes. Exceptions propagate, and previously committed batches remain saved. To retain the standard behavior, commit each batch atomically before bulk_insert returns and roll back that batch on failure.

The returned list controls LoadResult.saved_count. Return only changed identities, not all attempted rows; an unchanged batch returns []. fetched_count counts source rows, while skipped_count is the difference between fetched and saved counts.

For the library's distribution database, prefer the existing LimitDistributionWriter(DistributionService(uow_factory)). It saves new distributions or improvements with a higher Monte Carlo count and invalidates their cached critical values in the same transaction. CriticalValueWriter(uow_factory) commits cached values only when their Monte Carlo count matches the destination distribution. A custom writer should preserve these rules when maintaining the same data model.

docs.title: Example: read distributions from an in-memory collection
docs.text:
This runnable example adapts a collection of already decoded models. It uses the standard transactional writer with a temporary, in-memory SQLite database. The sample criterion code and statistics are illustrative.

from collections.abc import Iterator, Sequence
from functools import partial

from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.distribution_service import DistributionService
from pysatl_criterion.loader.limit_distribution_loader import LimitDistributionLoader
from pysatl_criterion.loader.store_adapters import LimitDistributionWriter
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.models.distribution_key import DistributionKey
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.models.limit_distribution import LimitDistributionModel
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.limit_distribution import (
    CriterionFilter,
    LimitDistributionFilter,
)
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.database import AlchemyDatabase
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.unit_of_work import AlchemyUnitOfWork
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.stores.base import IBulkStoreReader


class SequenceDistributionReader(
    IBulkStoreReader[LimitDistributionModel, DistributionKey, LimitDistributionFilter]
):
    def __init__(self, models: Sequence[LimitDistributionModel]):
        self._models = models

    def get(self, query: DistributionKey) -> LimitDistributionModel | None:
        return next((model for model in self._models if model.key == query), None)

    @staticmethod
    def _matches(model: LimitDistributionModel, query: LimitDistributionFilter) -> bool:
        if query.criteria is not None and not any(
            model.criterion_code == criterion.criterion_code
            and (
                criterion.criterion_parameters is None
                or model.criterion_parameters == criterion.criterion_parameters
            )
            for criterion in query.criteria
        ):
            return False
        if query.min_sample_size is not None and model.sample_size < query.min_sample_size:
            return False
        if query.max_sample_size is not None and model.sample_size > query.max_sample_size:
            return False
        if (
            query.min_monte_carlo_count is not None
            and model.monte_carlo_count < query.min_monte_carlo_count
        ):
            return False
        return True

    def iter_batches(
        self, query: LimitDistributionFilter, *, batch_size: int = 100
    ) -> Iterator[list[LimitDistributionModel]]:
        if batch_size <= 0:
            raise ValueError("batch_size must be positive")
        batch: list[LimitDistributionModel] = []
        for model in self._models:
            if self._matches(model, query):
                batch.append(model)
                if len(batch) == batch_size:
                    yield batch
                    batch = []
        if batch:
            yield batch


source = SequenceDistributionReader(
    [
        LimitDistributionModel("example", {"shape": 2.0}, 40, 4, [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]),
        LimitDistributionModel("example", {"shape": 3.0}, 40, 4, [0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5]),
        LimitDistributionModel("example", {"shape": 2.0}, 80, 4, [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6]),
    ]
)
query = LimitDistributionFilter(
    criteria=[CriterionFilter("example", {"shape": 2.0})],
    max_sample_size=40,
    min_monte_carlo_count=4,
)

database = AlchemyDatabase("sqlite:///:memory:")
try:
    database.init()
    uow_factory = partial(AlchemyUnitOfWork, database.session_factory)
    destination = LimitDistributionWriter(DistributionService(uow_factory))
    loader = LimitDistributionLoader(source, destination, print_summary=False)

    result = loader.load(query, batch_size=1)
    assert (result.fetched_count, result.saved_count, result.skipped_count) == (1, 1, 0)

    repeated = loader.load(query, batch_size=1)
    assert (repeated.fetched_count, repeated.saved_count, repeated.skipped_count) == (1, 0, 1)
finally:
    database.dispose()

Keep the input collection stable during iteration and supply one current model per distribution identity. For a file or API reader, replace the collection scan with streaming reads or pagination while preserving the same filtering and batch-size contracts.

docs.title: Extending AbstractLoader
docs.text:
AbstractLoader[M, Q, F], from pysatl_criterion.loader.abstract_loader, is the shared transfer implementation. F must be LimitDistributionFilter or a subclass, because the loader reads query.criteria to report missing codes. The only abstract loader method is:

@staticmethod
def _criterion_code(model: M) -> str: ...

Implement it to return the criterion code associated with your model. The inherited constructor accepts source, destination, and the keyword argument print_summary=True; load(query, *, batch_size=100) returns LoadResult.

For each batch, the base implementation counts fetched rows, records which requested codes were seen, calls the destination's bulk_insert, and counts the returned models. It writes the current batch before requesting the next one. not_found_codes reports requested codes with no source matches; it does not report missing individual parameter variants or rejected destination rows.

Use the supplied concrete loaders for LimitDistributionModel and CriticalValueModel: their specializations already extract the code from model.criterion_code and model.distribution_key.criterion_code, respectively.

docs.title: Distribution loader examples
docs.text: These examples use the public loader API described in the loading guide. The first example is self-contained and needs no remote server. The later examples assume that shared.db already contains PySATL distributions.

docs.title: Run a complete transfer locally
docs.text:
This script creates two temporary SQLite databases, stores one demonstration distribution, caches a critical value, and copies both records. It then repeats the load to show that existing equal-version records are skipped. The small synthetic statistics are only demonstration data.

from decimal import Decimal
from functools import partial
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from pysatl_criterion.hypothesis_testing.distribution_service import DistributionService
from pysatl_criterion.loader import DistributionLoader
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.models.limit_distribution import LimitDistributionModel
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.critical_value import CriticalValueLookupQuery
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.limit_distribution import (
    CriterionFilter,
    LimitDistributionFilter,
)
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.database import AlchemyDatabase
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.unit_of_work import AlchemyUnitOfWork
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.alternative import AlternativeType


with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    remote = AlchemyDatabase(f"sqlite:///{Path(directory) / 'source.db'}")
    local = AlchemyDatabase(f"sqlite:///{Path(directory) / 'destination.db'}")
    try:
        remote.init()
        remote_uow = partial(AlchemyUnitOfWork, remote.session_factory)
        local_uow = partial(AlchemyUnitOfWork, local.session_factory)
        source = DistributionService(remote_uow)

        distribution = LimitDistributionModel(
            criterion_code="demo",
            criterion_parameters={"shape": 2.0},
            sample_size=20,
            monte_carlo_count=4,
            results_statistics=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0],
        )
        source.save_distribution(distribution)
        cached = source.get_critical_value(
            distribution.key,
            Decimal("0.05"),
            AlternativeType.RIGHT,
        )

        query = LimitDistributionFilter(
            criteria=[CriterionFilter("demo", {"shape": 2.0})],
            min_sample_size=20,
            max_sample_size=20,
        )
        loader = DistributionLoader(remote=remote, local=local)
        first = loader.load(query, batch_size=1)
        assert first.limit_distributions.saved_count == 1
        assert first.critical_values.saved_count == 1

        # The destination tables are initialized by DistributionLoader.load().
        with local_uow() as uow:
            stored = uow.limit_distributions.get(distribution.key)
            value = uow.critical_values.get(
                CriticalValueLookupQuery(
                    distribution.key,
                    distribution.monte_carlo_count,
                    Decimal("0.05"),
                    AlternativeType.RIGHT,
                )
            )
        assert stored == distribution
        assert value == cached

        repeated = loader.load(query, batch_size=1)
        assert repeated.fetched_count == 2
        assert repeated.saved_count == 0
        assert repeated.skipped_count == 2
    finally:
        remote.dispose()
        local.dispose()

Expected output:

Loaded 2 records (limit distributions: 1, critical values: 1; fetched: 2, skipped: 0).
Loaded 0 records (limit distributions: 0, critical values: 0; fetched: 2, skipped: 2).

The call to source.get_critical_value() prepares the source cache for the demonstration. DistributionLoader itself only transfers that cached record.

docs.title: Selecting several parameter sets
docs.text:
Construct one CriterionFilter per code and parameter combination. The same code may appear more than once. This example loads gamma criteria for two different shapes while leaving sample sizes unrestricted:

from pysatl_criterion.loader import DistributionLoader
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.queries.limit_distribution import (
    CriterionFilter,
    LimitDistributionFilter,
)
from pysatl_criterion.statistics.goodness_of_fit.continuous import (
    KolmogorovSmirnovGammaGofStatistic,
)


statistics = [
    KolmogorovSmirnovGammaGofStatistic(alpha=2.0, beta=1.0),
    KolmogorovSmirnovGammaGofStatistic(alpha=3.0, beta=1.0),
]
query = LimitDistributionFilter(
    criteria=[
        CriterionFilter(statistic.code(), statistic.hypothesis().parameters())
        for statistic in statistics
    ],
    min_monte_carlo_count=10_000,
)
loader = DistributionLoader(remote="sqlite:///shared.db", local="sqlite:///local.db")
result = loader.load(query)
print(result.limit_distributions.not_found_codes)

To select every parameter variant of one statistic instead, use CriterionFilter(statistics[0].code()). To select exactly one sample size, add equal min_sample_size and max_sample_size bounds to the query.

docs.title: Reusing database objects
docs.text:
Passing AlchemyDatabase objects lets your application control connection options and reuse the connections after loading:

from pysatl_criterion.loader import DistributionLoader
from pysatl_criterion.persistence.sqlalchemy.database import AlchemyDatabase


remote = AlchemyDatabase("sqlite:///shared.db")
local = AlchemyDatabase("sqlite:///local.db")
try:
    loader = DistributionLoader(remote=remote, local=local)
    result = loader.load()
    # Both objects remain available for subsequent application operations here.
finally:
    remote.dispose()
    local.dispose()

The caller owns database objects passed to the loader. When you pass URL strings instead, each load() call creates and disposes its own database objects, including when loading fails. You can mix a URL for one side with a database object for the other. In all cases, the loader initializes the local tables and expects the remote tables to exist already.

For loading only distributions, copying only cached values, or reading from an application API, see custom loaders and adapters.

docs.title: Multiple Hypothesis Testing
docs.text: Testing many hypotheses at an unadjusted 5% level can produce false discoveries even when every null is true. Choose a family of hypotheses before examining its results, then apply one procedure to all raw p-values in that family.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
• m: number of hypotheses; R: number rejected; V: rejected true nulls.
  • FWER: \(P(V>0)\), the chance of at least one false rejection. Strong control applies to every true/false configuration; weak control applies only to the global null.
  • FDR: \(E[V/\max(R,1)]\), the expected false discovery proportion. Under the global null FDR equals FWER, but generally an FDR guarantee is less restrictive.
  • Raw p-value: a single-test measure satisfying \(P(p_i\le t)\le t\) under its null.
  • Adjusted p-value: the smallest error level at which a fixed adjustment rejects a hypothesis. Ordinary adjusted values can be compared to different alpha levels. The reported adaptive values here are an exception: they apply only at the supplied alpha and must be recomputed when it changes.
  • q-value: in Storey's framework, the minimum positive FDR associated with a rejection region containing the observation (estimated in applications using pi0). It is not a universal synonym for every FDR-adjusted value. Storey estimation is deferred. See Storey (2002), A direct approach to false discovery rates.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Statistic -> PValueCalculator / p-value resolver -> PValues
          -> AbstractMultipleTesting[PValues].test -> MultipleTestingResult
             |- AbstractPValueAdjustment.adjust (alpha-independent)
             |- AbstractAlphaDependentPValueProcedure (alpha required)

Joint resampling preserving dependence
  -> ResamplingStatistics (observed statistics, joint statistics; larger is extreme)
     -> AbstractResamplingMultipleTesting -> MultipleTestingResult
  -> ResamplingPValues (observed raw p-values, jointly resampled raw p-values)
     -> AbstractResamplingPValueTesting -> MultipleTestingResult

The last two paths implement Westfall–Young maxT and minP. Simes uses a separate GlobalTestResult, because it tests one intersection rather than individual nulls. Tests of generic annotations ensure mypy rejects the wrong input type. No GOF-statistic registry or distribution-calibration responsibility is mixed into multiple testing. The dedicated immutable P_VALUE_PROCEDURES mapping exposes classes by short_code(); code() prefixes these identifiers with MULTIPLE_TESTING_.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text: The common contract, inputs, result and metadata live in base.py, inputs.py, result.py and metadata.py. Each p-value procedure is implemented in its own module under pvalue/, with family contracts in pvalue/base.py. Joint-resampling contracts and explicit design assumptions live in resampling/base.py. Separate Westfall–Young modules implement maxT and minP with exact and Monte Carlo modes. The root package and api.testing export the same typed classes. Compatibility modules have been removed.

docs.title: Implemented methods
docs.text:
All procedures require valid raw null p-values; none repairs invalid calibration.

Method Error criterion Input Alpha-dependent Dependence / guarantee Bonferroni FWER PValues No Super-uniform null p-values: \(P(p_i \le t) \le t\). Arbitrary dependence is allowed. Šidák FWER PValues No Super-uniform null p-values and mutual independence of the p-values. No arbitrary-dependence guarantee is asserted. Holm–Bonferroni FWER PValues No Super-uniform null p-values: \(P(p_i \le t) \le t\). Arbitrary dependence is allowed. Holm–Šidák FWER PValues No Super-uniform null p-values and mutual independence of the p-values. No arbitrary-dependence guarantee is asserted. Hochberg (Simes–Hochberg) FWER PValues No Every intersection of true null hypotheses must admit a valid Simes local test. Independence suffices. Arbitrary dependence does not; a generic statement that correlations are positive is insufficient. Hommel FWER PValues No Every intersection of true null hypotheses must admit a valid Simes local test. Independence suffices. Arbitrary dependence does not; a generic statement that correlations are positive is insufficient. Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) FDR PValues No Valid null p-values; independence or PRDS (positive regression dependency on each member of the true null subset). PRDS is a distributional condition, not simply positive pairwise correlation. Benjamini–Yekutieli (BY) FDR PValues No Super-uniform null p-values: \(P(p_i \le t) \le t\). Arbitrary dependence is allowed. Two-stage Benjamini–Hochberg FDR target PValues Yes Exploratory uncorrected variant: nominal FDR control is not guaranteed even under independence. Use BKY when relying on the proved independent-case guarantee. Two-stage Benjamini–Krieger–Yekutieli (BKY) FDR PValues Yes Super-uniform null p-values and mutual independence of the p-values. No arbitrary-dependence guarantee is asserted. Simes Global Type I PValues No Valid Simes inequality; independent uniform nulls suffice. One global result. Rom FWER PValues No Independence; step-up critical values, inverted for adjusted p-values. Holland–Copenhaver FWER PValues No Independence or the paper's positive orthant dependence condition; optional justified logical bounds. Westfall–Young maxT FWER ResamplingStatistics No Valid joint exchangeable resampling, subset pivotality, comparable statistics. Westfall–Young minP FWER ResamplingPValues No Valid joint exchangeable resampling, subset pivotality, calibrated raw p-values.

Single-step methods apply a common correction. Step-down methods examine small p-values first and stop at a failure; step-up methods locate the largest passing rank. Closed testing requires rejection of every intersection containing a null. Adaptive methods estimate the number of true nulls from the same family. Resampling methods use a joint null distribution rather than just raw p-values.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import BenjaminiHochberg, Holm, PValues

p = PValues(np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02]))
bh = BenjaminiHochberg().test(p, alpha=0.05)
holm = Holm().test(p, alpha=0.05)
assert bh.rejected.tolist() == [True, True, False, True, True]
assert holm.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False, False, False]
np.testing.assert_allclose(holm.adjusted_p_values, [0.08, 0.005, 0.7, 0.08, 0.08])

import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import PValues, BenjaminiKriegerYekutieli

procedure = BenjaminiKriegerYekutieli()
result = procedure.test(PValues(np.array([0.001, 0.02, 0.2])), alpha=0.10)
assert result.alpha_dependent
# To use another alpha, run test again. decisions_at(0.05) would raise ValueError.
recomputed = procedure.test(PValues(np.array([0.001, 0.02, 0.2])), alpha=0.05)
assert recomputed.alpha == 0.05

docs.title: Choosing a method
docs.text: For strong FWER control without dependence restrictions, use Holm or Bonferroni. For FDR under arbitrary dependence, BY is available, often conservatively. BH is appropriate when independence or PRDS is justified. Independence permits Šidák procedures and the two-stage BKY guarantee. Hochberg and Hommel require valid Simes local tests. The uncorrected two-stage BH option is for reproducibility, without a claimed nominal FDR guarantee. Positive correlation alone is not PRDS.

docs.title: Limitations and common mistakes
docs.text:
Typed APIs require 0 < alpha < 1. Inputs are finite real vectors in [0, 1]; empty families produce empty results. Stored arrays are defensive read-only copies. Do not change the family after inspecting significance, pass rejection thresholds as p-values, or interpret non-rejection as acceptance of the null. Adjustment cannot fix invalid single-test p-values, optional stopping or unmodeled selection. A global Simes test is distinct from a procedure making individual decisions.

Adaptive output arrays are inspectable but alpha-specific: the result's decisions_at() guard rejects reuse at a different level. A frozen dataclass and read-only NumPy flags protect against accidental mutation, not deliberate circumvention of array flags. Hommel is quadratic in the number of hypotheses.

Legacy classmethod calls are no longer supported. See the migration guide below for the replacement API and boundary behavior.

docs.title: Deferred extensions
docs.text: Storey/q-values are not implemented. Westfall–Young requires explicit JointResamplingAssumptions; these caller declarations do not establish the statistical validity of the supplied arrays. Its exact mode requires a complete equally weighted orbit, and its Monte Carlo mode uses the identity correction. Iterated and multistage BKY are also deferred; the implemented BKY is exactly two-stage.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
See the implementation report for the file manifest, method inventory, measured simulation rates and actual validation outcomes.

Every method has its own page above, primary references, attribution evidence, independent worked example and executable Python example. Unit tests execute all Python fences on these pages and check local links. Fixed fixtures are generated with statsmodels 0.14.6 (a development dependency only), with seeded live comparisons. Hommel also has an exhaustive closed-Simes oracle, and BKY a direct two-stage oracle. Rom has a high-precision polynomial oracle and analytic inversion checks; Holland–Copenhaver has logical-bound examples and independent software comparisons. Westfall–Young is checked against exhaustive closed testing and exact sign-flip FWER calculations. Simes has scalar hand-calculated examples.

P_VALUE_PROCEDURES contains twelve per-hypothesis p-value procedures. Simes is in GLOBAL_TESTS; the two Westfall–Young classes have separate typed resampling registries. All concrete classes are exported from the package root and api.testing.

python -m pytest tests/multiple_testing
PYSATL_MULTIPLE_TESTING_MONTE_CARLO=1 python -m pytest tests/multiple_testing/test_validation.py -k monte_carlo -s
python -m mkdocs build --strict

Monte Carlo validation uses seed 62173, 5,000 independent families of 20 hypotheses, alpha 0.05, both the global null and five false nulls fixed at zero. It measures FWER or FDR as appropriate, using a six-standard-error upper tolerance. Simulations are skipped unless explicitly enabled and do not replace mathematical guarantees.

docs.title: Migration from the removed API
docs.text:
The abstract_multiple_testing.py, fdr.py and fwer.py adapters have been removed. This intentionally breaks old classmethod/list calls. All three public entry points (pysatl_criterion, pysatl_criterion.api.testing, and pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing) now expose the same typed procedure classes.

Old name New name BonferroniMultipleTesting Bonferroni SidakMultipleTesting Sidak SidakHolm HolmSidak

Instantiate the procedure, wrap a NumPy vector in PValues, replace threshold with alpha, and read result fields instead of unpacking lists:

import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion import Holm, PValues

result = Holm().test(PValues(np.array([0.01, 0.03, 0.04])), alpha=0.05)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [True, False, False]
np.testing.assert_allclose(result.adjusted_p_values, [0.03, 0.06, 0.06])

The new API compares with <= alpha and requires 0 < alpha < 1. The former API used strict < threshold and allowed endpoint thresholds. Empty families still produce empty outputs. External subclasses should use the generic contract in base.py or family contracts in pvalue/base.py and resampling/base.py. The corrected Holm and Holm–Šidák algorithms intentionally change old numerical results. For reproducing the former incorrect recurrences, explicitly select Hochberg or single-step Sidak, respectively.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: BenjaminiHochberg is a step-up procedure for FDR. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text:
Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg (1995). Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 57(1), 289–300. Primary publication.

Yoav Benjamini and Daniel Yekutieli (2001). The Control of the False Discovery Rate in Multiple Testing under Dependency. Annals of Statistics 29(4), 1165–1188. Primary publication.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Implementation authors: not individually documented. Maintained by the PySATL project; see overview.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: FDR is bounded by alpha under the stated conditions, including mixtures of true and false null hypotheses.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Valid null p-values; independence or PRDS (positive regression dependency on each member of the true null subset). PRDS is a distributional condition, not simply positive pairwise correlation.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.
  2. Compute \(a_{(i)}=\min(1,\min_{j\ge i}mp_{(j)}/j)\). Find the largest rank k satisfying \(p_{(k)}\le k\alpha/m\) and reject ranks 1 through k.
  3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
PValues(values) owns a read-only copy of a finite real NumPy vector of shape (m,), with values in [0, 1]. test(data, alpha=0.05) requires 0 < alpha < 1. MultipleTestingResult contains boolean rejected, float alpha, and adjusted_p_values in original order, each array of shape (m,).

adjust(p) accepts a float NumPy vector and returns adjusted p-values independent of alpha. result.decisions_at(other_alpha) can reuse them.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import BenjaminiHochberg, PValues

p = np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02])
procedure = BenjaminiHochberg()
result = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.05)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    result.adjusted_p_values, [0.05, 0.005, 0.7, 0.033333333333, 0.033333333333], atol=1e-11
)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [True, True, False, True, True]
# True means reject that null hypothesis, not proof that its alternative is true.
other = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.10)
assert other.alpha == 0.10

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: For the unsorted input [0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02] (including ties) at alpha 0.05, the adjusted values are [0.05, 0.005, 0.7, 0.033333333333, 0.033333333333] and decisions are [True, True, False, True, True]. These numbers were obtained independently with statsmodels 0.14.6, multipletests(..., method="fdr_bh", maxiter=1), not from the PySATL implementation. The committed reference fixture retains full precision and tests both values and decisions.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: FDR control does not bound the chance of any false discovery when some nulls are false. BH adjusted p-values are not automatically Storey estimates of q-values. Complexity \(O(m\log m)\). Ties are handled without changing the input hypothesis order. Invalid p-values, non-finite entries and multidimensional arrays raise ValueError. No constructor tuning parameters are needed for this fixed procedure.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: BenjaminiYekutieli is a step-up procedure for FDR. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Yoav Benjamini and Daniel Yekutieli (2001). The Control of the False Discovery Rate in Multiple Testing under Dependency. Annals of Statistics 29(4), 1165–1188. Primary publication.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Original PySATL implementation: AxelF23, verified in commit 27953e2. Refactor authors: not individually documented. See attribution evidence.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: FDR is bounded by alpha under the stated conditions, including mixtures of true and false null hypotheses.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Super-uniform null p-values: \(P(p_i \le t) \le t\). Arbitrary dependence is allowed.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.
  2. Compute \(H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m1/j\), then \(a_{(i)}=\min(1,\min_{j\ge i}mH_mp_{(j)}/j)\). The step-up critical values are \(i\alpha/(mH_m)\).
  3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
PValues(values) owns a read-only copy of a finite real NumPy vector of shape (m,), with values in [0, 1]. test(data, alpha=0.05) requires 0 < alpha < 1. MultipleTestingResult contains boolean rejected, float alpha, and adjusted_p_values in original order, each array of shape (m,).

adjust(p) accepts a float NumPy vector and returns adjusted p-values independent of alpha. result.decisions_at(other_alpha) can reuse them.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import BenjaminiYekutieli, PValues

p = np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02])
procedure = BenjaminiYekutieli()
result = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.05)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    result.adjusted_p_values,
    [0.114166666667, 0.011416666667, 1.0, 0.076111111111, 0.076111111111],
    atol=1e-11,
)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False, False, False]
# True means reject that null hypothesis, not proof that its alternative is true.
other = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.10)
assert other.alpha == 0.10

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: BenjaminiKriegerYekutieli is a adaptive procedure for FDR. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Yoav Benjamini, Abba M. Krieger and Daniel Yekutieli (2006). Adaptive Linear Step-up Procedures That Control the False Discovery Rate. Biometrika 93(3), 491–507. Primary publication; authors’ manuscript.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Implementation authors: not individually documented. Maintained by the PySATL project; see overview.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: FDR is bounded by alpha under the stated conditions, including mixtures of true and false null hypotheses.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Super-uniform null p-values and mutual independence of the p-values. No arbitrary-dependence guarantee is asserted.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.
  2. Use the two-stage construction below with \(f=1+\alpha\), hence \(q_1=\alpha/(1+\alpha)\). This is Definition 6 (TST) and Theorem 1 in the authors’ manuscript.
  3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

The shared two-stage construction is:

  1. Calculate BH adjusted values b and the first-stage rejection count \(r_1=\#\{i:b_i\le q_1\}\).
  2. If \(r_1=0\) or \(r_1=m\), stop and report \(a_i=\min(1,fb_i)\).
  3. Otherwise estimate \(\widehat m_0=m-r_1\) and run BH at \(q_2=q_1m/\widehat m_0\). Report \(a_i=\min(1,fb_i\widehat m_0/m)\).
  4. These reported values support \(a_i\le\alpha\) only at this run's alpha; they are not alpha-independent adjusted p-values or Storey q-values.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
PValues(values) owns a read-only copy of a finite real NumPy vector of shape (m,), with values in [0, 1]. test(data, alpha=0.05) requires 0 < alpha < 1. MultipleTestingResult contains boolean rejected, float alpha, and adjusted_p_values in original order, each array of shape (m,).

This procedure has no adjust(p) method. alpha_dependent=True; result.decisions_at(other_alpha) raises ValueError. NumPy arrays remain inspectable, so callers must not manually reuse adaptive values at another level.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import BenjaminiKriegerYekutieli, PValues

p = np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02])
procedure = BenjaminiKriegerYekutieli()
result = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.05)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    result.adjusted_p_values, [0.021, 0.0021, 0.294, 0.014, 0.014], atol=1e-11
)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [True, True, False, True, True]
# True means reject that null hypothesis, not proof that its alternative is true.
other = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.10)
assert other.alpha == 0.10

These numbers were obtained independently with statsmodels 0.14.6, multipletests(..., method="fdr_tsbky", maxiter=1), not from the PySATL implementation. No constructor tuning parameters are needed for this fixed procedure.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: Bonferroni is a single-step procedure for FWER. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text:
Olive Jean Dunn (1961). Multiple Comparisons among Means. Journal of the American Statistical Association 56(293), 52–64. Primary publication. The inequality is traditionally attributed to Carlo Emilio Bonferroni; Dunn is the primary multiple-comparisons reference used here.

Historical origin: Carlo Emilio Bonferroni (1936), Teoria statistica delle classi e calcolo delle probabilità, Pubblicazioni del R. Istituto Superiore di Scienze Economiche e Commerciali di Firenze, 8, 3–62. No DOI for that work is asserted here. The implemented multiple-testing rule is justified directly by the union bound and the Dunn reference above.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Original PySATL implementation: Ksenia Nigmatulina, verified in commit 0eb6cfa. Refactor authors: not individually documented. See attribution evidence.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER control under the stated conditions, for every configuration of true and false nulls.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Super-uniform null p-values: \(P(p_i \le t) \le t\). Arbitrary dependence is allowed.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.
  2. Compute \(a_i=\min(1,mp_i)\) for each hypothesis. Reject when \(a_i\le\alpha\), equivalently \(p_i\le\alpha/m\).
  3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

docs.text:
PValues(values) owns a read-only copy of a finite real NumPy vector of shape (m,), with values in [0, 1]. test(data, alpha=0.05) requires 0 < alpha < 1. MultipleTestingResult contains boolean rejected, float alpha, and adjusted_p_values in original order, each array of shape (m,).

adjust(p) accepts a float NumPy vector and returns adjusted p-values independent of alpha. result.decisions_at(other_alpha) can reuse them.

import numpy as np

result = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.05)

assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False, False, False]

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: HollandCopenhaver is a step-down Šidák-type procedure. Without logical bounds it gives the same results as Holm–Šidák.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Burt S. Holland and Margaret DiPonzio Copenhaver (1987), An improved sequentially rejective Bonferroni test procedure, Biometrics 43(2), 417–423. Primary publication.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER, provided both the dependence condition and any supplied logical bounds are justified.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Valid null p-values and independence suffice. The paper also permits a specific positive orthant dependence condition on the test statistics. Positive pairwise correlations alone do not establish this condition. A custom bound at each rank must dominate the possible number of true nulls after earlier rejections, for every possible ordering of hypotheses.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text: Sort p-values increasingly. With bounds \(t_i\), reject sequentially while \(p_{(i)}\le 1-(1-\alpha)^{1/t_i}\), stopping at the first failure. The adjusted values are \(\min(1,\max_{j\le i}[1-(1-p_{(j)})^{t_j}])\). Restore original order. The default is \(t_i=m-i+1\).

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text: HollandCopenhaver(true_null_bounds=None) accepts an optional fixed tuple of positive integers, one per rank, nonincreasing and no larger than m-i at zero-based rank i. test(PValues(p), alpha) returns MultipleTestingResult; adjust(p) returns alpha-independent adjusted values. The tuple is not inferred from data.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import HollandCopenhaver, PValues

# Three pairwise equality nulls: if one is false, at most one can remain true.
# Dependence assumptions still need separate justification for the actual tests.
procedure = HollandCopenhaver(true_null_bounds=(3, 1, 1))
result = procedure.test(PValues(np.array([0.8, 0.01, 0.04])))
np.testing.assert_allclose(result.adjusted_p_values, [0.8, 0.029701, 0.04])
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, True]

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: Sorted values are .01, .04, .8. Applying exponents 3, 1, 1 produces 1-.99**3 = .029701, .04, .8; the prefix maximum leaves them unchanged.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: Structural validation cannot prove that custom bounds are scientifically valid. The API supports fixed rank bounds, not hypothesis-specific dynamic constraints. Default bounds coincide with Holm–Šidák and are tested against statsmodels. Complexity is \(O(m\log m)\). Empty input is supported; mismatched bound counts, invalid probabilities or alpha raise errors. Numerical evaluation uses log1p and expm1 to preserve precision near zero.

docs.title: References
docs.text: See Holland and Copenhaver (1987), especially Theorem 3.1, and the author paper scan.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: Hommel is a closed testing procedure for FWER. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Gerhard Hommel (1988). A Stagewise Rejective Multiple Test Procedure Based on a Modified Bonferroni Test. Biometrika 75(2), 383–386. Primary publication.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Implementation authors: not individually documented. Maintained by the PySATL project; see overview.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER control under the stated conditions, for every configuration of true and false nulls.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Every intersection of true null hypotheses must admit a valid Simes local test. Independence suffices. Arbitrary dependence does not; a generic statement that correlations are positive is insufficient.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.

  2. Initialize \(a_{(i)}=p_{(i)}\). For \(s=m,m-1,\ldots,2\), compute

    $\(c_s=\min_{k=1,\ldots,s}\frac{s\,p_{(m-s+k)}}{k}.\)$

    Replace the last s entries by \(\max(a_{(i)},c_s)\) and each earlier entry by \(\max(a_{(i)},\min(sp_{(i)},c_s))\). Clip to one. This is the shortcut for closed Simes testing: each individual adjusted value is the maximum local Simes p-value over all intersections containing it. 3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False, False, False]

docs.title: Architectural decisions
docs.text:
The new generic contract is pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing.AbstractMultipleTesting[InputT]. It uses mathematical input objects and a common MultipleTestingResult, without optional context dictionaries or generic keyword payloads. Ten ordinary procedures share AbstractPValueAdjustment.adjust; two adaptive procedures have only an alpha-explicit test and mark their results alpha-dependent. decisions_at prevents accidental reuse at another alpha. Holland–Copenhaver optionally accepts logical true-null bounds. Simes returns a separate scalar GlobalTestResult. Resampling procedures require explicit design assumptions and expose single-step/step-down and exact/Monte Carlo settings.

The legacy abstract class and five adapters have been removed at the user's request. Root and api.testing exports now refer to the typed classes. This intentionally breaks the classmethod/list API; see migration. The typed API uses <= alpha, requires 0 < alpha < 1, and returns named fields.

Joint statistic and raw-p-value matrices are separate validated containers because maxT and minP need different mathematical information. Westfall–Young maxT and minP implement these contracts. Strong FWER is conditional on valid joint exchangeability and subset pivotality, declared by the caller. The implementation cannot infer these properties from numeric arrays.

docs.title: Method inventory
docs.text:
There are twelve per-hypothesis p-value procedures in P_VALUE_PROCEDURES, one global test in GLOBAL_TESTS, and two procedures in separate typed resampling registries. The original ten procedures have independent statsmodels fixtures and live comparisons. Rom has a high-precision recurrence oracle and analytic inversion checks. Holland–Copenhaver has independent Holm–Šidák comparisons and logical-bound examples. Simes has hand-calculated scalar examples. Westfall–Young is checked against exhaustive closed testing, hand-counted matrices, and a complete sign-flip orbit under global and partial null configurations.

All procedures have executable documentation examples and public-export checks. Tests live in test_procedures.py, test_extended.py, and test_validation.py under tests/multiple_testing. Hommel additionally uses exhaustive Simes closure; BKY uses an independent critical-value decision oracle.

docs.title: Monte Carlo observations
docs.text:
Each cell uses 5,000 families, 20 hypotheses, seed 62173, alpha 0.05. The mixture has five false-null p-values fixed at zero. All true-null p-values are independent uniform draws. The acceptance upper bound is alpha plus six binomial standard errors (approximately 0.0685). This is a reproducible diagnostic, not a proof.

Method Global null Mixture Quantity Bonferroni 0.04480 0.04340 FWER Holm 0.04480 0.05400 FWER BH 0.04640 0.03765 FDR BY 0.01100 0.01160 FDR Two-stage BKY 0.04440 0.04920 FDR

docs.title: Statistical verification and limits
docs.text:
Formulas were checked using primary publications/manuscripts or authoritative software documentation, plus independent numerical tests. The original Holm, Šidák, BH, BY and BKY sources and publisher abstracts for Hochberg and Hommel were consulted; full publisher PDFs were not available for every method. The R documentation and independent exhaustive closure supply additional checks for Hommel. No claim is made that inaccessible full papers were read. Original scientific authors and verified historical PySATL contributors are separate fields on every method page.

Guarantees require valid single-test p-values. Holm/Bonferroni and BY permit arbitrary dependence; Šidák methods and the BKY guarantee here assume independence. BH permits PRDS on true nulls, while Hochberg/Hommel need valid intersection Simes tests. Uncorrected two-stage BH is explicitly exploratory without nominal FDR control asserted. Only two-stage BKY is implemented; its iterated/multistage variants are deferred. Storey needs a specified and tested pi0 estimator. Westfall–Young now provides the algorithms and independent permutation checks; the experimental resampling design, calibration and subset pivotality remain the caller's responsibility. Rom's recurrence was checked against the authors' academic supplement and independently evaluated using 70-digit arithmetic; its full original publisher paper was unavailable. Inverse critical values, not alpha-specific multipliers, define its adjusted p-values.

docs.title: Final module layout and API
docs.text: All production code lives in src/pysatl_criterion/multiple_testing. The generic contract is in base.py, result types in result.py, p-value contracts in pvalue/base.py, and joint-resampling contracts in resampling/base.py. Each concrete procedure has its own named module in pvalue/ or resampling/. Legacy abstract_multiple_testing.py, fdr.py, fwer.py and the former directory under hypothesis_testing have been removed. Root and api.testing exports use the typed classes. The previously deleted audit page remains deleted.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: Rom is a step-up FWER procedure using improved Bonferroni critical values.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Dror M. Rom (1990), A sequentially rejective test procedure based on a modified Bonferroni inequality, Biometrika 77(3), 663–665. Primary publication.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER under independence and valid null p-values.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Mutual independence is required for the guarantee claimed here. Do not use the power improvement as a justification for arbitrary dependence.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
For level \(q\), define \(c_1(q)=q\), \(c_2(q)=q/2\) and

\[c_k(q)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}q^j- \sum_{j=1}^{k-2}{k\choose j}c_{j+1}(q)^{k-j}}{k}.\]

Sort increasingly. Find the largest rank \(i\) with \(p_{(i)}\le c_{m-i+1}(\alpha)\) and reject all ranks through \(i\). For adjusted values, numerically invert each critical function and take a suffix minimum. If a critical function never reaches the raw p-value below level one, its inverse is set to one. Restore original order.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text: test(PValues(p), alpha) returns MultipleTestingResult. adjust(p) returns alpha-independent adjusted values. critical_values(m, alpha) returns rank-ordered thresholds, not p-values. Alpha is in (0, 1) and m is a nonnegative Python integer.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import Rom, PValues

procedure = Rom()
np.testing.assert_allclose(procedure.critical_values(3), [0.016875, 0.025, 0.05])
result = procedure.test(PValues(np.array([0.8, 0.01, 0.03])))
expected = [0.8, 6 * 0.01 / (np.sqrt(1 + 3 * 0.01) + 1), 0.06]
np.testing.assert_allclose(result.adjusted_p_values, expected)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False]

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: For three hypotheses, \(c_3(q)=q/3+q^2/12\). Its inverse at .01 is \(6(.01)/(\sqrt{1+3(.01)}+1)\), approximately .0297783. The second sorted p-value .03 requires level .06; the last .8 requires .8. These analytic values independently check the numerical inversion.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: The implementation uses 60 bisection steps per inverse and a quadratic recurrence: worst-case adjustment cost is \(O(60m^3)\), intended for modest family sizes. Threshold generation alone is \(O(m^2)\). Empty, singleton, zero, one and tied values are supported. Finite-precision arithmetic applies near rejection boundaries; non-finite or negative recurrence results raise ArithmeticError. Multiplying p-values by alpha / critical gives alpha-specific quantities; this implementation instead inverts the whole critical function for reusable adjustments.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The recurrence is also documented in the authors' supplementary material for García et al.. The tests independently evaluate it with 70-digit Decimal arithmetic, and compare step-up decisions across several levels and family sizes.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: Sidak is a single-step procedure for FWER. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Zbyněk Šidák (1967). Rectangular Confidence Regions for the Means of Multivariate Normal Distributions. Journal of the American Statistical Association 62(318), 626–633. Primary publication.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Original PySATL implementation: Ksenia Nigmatulina, verified in commit 0eb6cfa. Refactor authors: not individually documented. See attribution evidence.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER control under the stated conditions, for every configuration of true and false nulls.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Super-uniform null p-values and mutual independence of the p-values. No arbitrary-dependence guarantee is asserted.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.
  2. Compute \(a_i=1-(1-p_i)^m\). Reject when \(p_i\le 1-(1-\alpha)^{1/m}\). Evaluation uses -expm1(m * log1p(-p)), including the limit \(a_i=1\) at \(p_i=1\).
  3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
PValues(values) owns a read-only copy of a finite real NumPy vector of shape (m,), with values in [0, 1]. test(data, alpha=0.05) requires 0 < alpha < 1. MultipleTestingResult contains boolean rejected, float alpha, and adjusted_p_values in original order, each array of shape (m,).

adjust(p) accepts a float NumPy vector and returns adjusted p-values independent of alpha. result.decisions_at(other_alpha) can reuse them.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import Sidak, PValues

p = np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02])
procedure = Sidak()
result = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.05)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    result.adjusted_p_values,
    [0.1846273024, 0.004990009995, 0.99757, 0.0960792032, 0.0960792032],
    atol=1e-11,
)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False, False, False]
# True means reject that null hypothesis, not proof that its alternative is true.
other = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.10)
assert other.alpha == 0.10

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: For the unsorted input [0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02] (including ties) at alpha 0.05, the adjusted values are [0.1846273024, 0.004990009995, 0.99757, 0.0960792032, 0.0960792032] and decisions are [False, True, False, False, False]. These numbers were obtained independently with statsmodels 0.14.6, multipletests(..., method="sidak", maxiter=1), not from the PySATL implementation. The committed reference fixture retains full precision and tests both values and decisions.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: Independence is sufficient. The original paper also treats symmetric normal rectangles, which does not justify arbitrary dependent p-values. Stable evaluation preserves tiny positive values. Ties are handled without changing the input hypothesis order. Invalid p-values, non-finite entries and multidimensional arrays raise ValueError. No constructor tuning parameters are needed for this fixed procedure.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: Simes tests the intersection of all supplied null hypotheses. Rejection means there is evidence against their joint truth; it does not identify individual false nulls.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: R. John Simes (1986), An improved Bonferroni procedure for multiple tests of significance, Biometrika 73(3), 751–754. Primary publication.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Type I error for the global intersection, at the requested alpha.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: The intersection-null distribution must satisfy the Simes inequality. Independent uniform null p-values suffice. Arbitrary dependence is not supported by this guarantee.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text: Sort increasingly and calculate \(p_{global}=\min(1,\min_{i=1}^m m p_{(i)}/i)\). Reject the intersection exactly when \(p_{global}\le\alpha\).

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text: test(PValues(p), alpha) returns GlobalTestResult(p_value, alpha) with scalar boolean property rejected. combine(p) returns the scalar global p-value. There is no individual adjust() API. Alpha must be strictly between zero and one.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import Simes, PValues

result = Simes().test(PValues(np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02])))
assert result.p_value == 0.005
assert result.rejected

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: For this sorted family [.001, .02, .02, .04, .7], the five candidates are .005, .05, .033333..., .05, .7; their minimum is .005. This calculation checks the example without another multiple-testing implementation.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: Complexity is \(O(m\log m)\). The empty intersection returns p-value one and is never rejected. Ties are allowed. Non-finite, out-of-range or non-vector input is rejected. A significant global result must not be turned into five individual rejections.

docs.title: References
docs.text: See Simes (1986) above. Hommel uses Simes local tests within closed testing.
