docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: TwoStageBenjaminiHochberg is a adaptive procedure for FDR target. It returns one decision for each input hypothesis.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Yoav Benjamini, Abba M. Krieger and Daniel Yekutieli (2006). Adaptive Linear Step-up Procedures That Control the False Discovery Rate. Biometrika 93(3), 491–507. Primary publication; authors’ manuscript.

docs.title: Implementation authors / maintainers
docs.text: Implementation authors: not individually documented. Maintained by the PySATL project; see overview.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: FDR is the target, not an asserted nominal-level guarantee for this uncorrected variant.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Exploratory uncorrected variant: nominal FDR control is not guaranteed even under independence. Use BKY when relying on the proved independent-case guarantee.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Let m denote the family size and alpha the requested error level.

  1. Sort p-values increasingly as \(p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}\), retaining their original indices.
  2. Use the two-stage construction below with \(f=1\), hence \(q_1=\alpha\). This is the software convention fdr_tsbh, not the BKY paper’s proved corrected procedure and not the different adaptive BH (2000) estimator.
  3. Restore original hypothesis order and compare adjusted values to the supplied alpha. Empty input returns empty arrays.

The shared two-stage construction is:

  1. Calculate BH adjusted values b and the first-stage rejection count \(r_1=\#\{i:b_i\le q_1\}\).
  2. If \(r_1=0\) or \(r_1=m\), stop and report \(a_i=\min(1,fb_i)\).
  3. Otherwise estimate \(\widehat m_0=m-r_1\) and run BH at \(q_2=q_1m/\widehat m_0\). Report \(a_i=\min(1,fb_i\widehat m_0/m)\).
  4. These reported values support \(a_i\le\alpha\) only at this run's alpha; they are not alpha-independent adjusted p-values or Storey q-values.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
PValues(values) owns a read-only copy of a finite real NumPy vector of shape (m,), with values in [0, 1]. test(data, alpha=0.05) requires 0 < alpha < 1. MultipleTestingResult contains boolean rejected, float alpha, and adjusted_p_values in original order, each array of shape (m,).

This procedure has no adjust(p) method. alpha_dependent=True; result.decisions_at(other_alpha) raises ValueError. NumPy arrays remain inspectable, so callers must not manually reuse adaptive values at another level.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import TwoStageBenjaminiHochberg, PValues

p = np.array([0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02])
procedure = TwoStageBenjaminiHochberg()
result = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.05)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    result.adjusted_p_values, [0.01, 0.001, 0.14, 0.006666666667, 0.006666666667], atol=1e-11
)
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [True, True, False, True, True]
# True means reject that null hypothesis, not proof that its alternative is true.
other = procedure.test(PValues(p), alpha=0.10)
assert other.alpha == 0.10

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: For the unsorted input [0.04, 0.001, 0.7, 0.02, 0.02] (including ties) at alpha 0.05, the adjusted values are [0.01, 0.001, 0.14, 0.006666666667, 0.006666666667] and decisions are [True, True, False, True, True]. These numbers were obtained independently with statsmodels 0.14.6, multipletests(..., method="fdr_tsbh", maxiter=1), not from the PySATL implementation. The committed reference fixture retains full precision and tests both values and decisions.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: Do not attach the BKY theorem to this uncorrected variant. Values depend on alpha; comparisons at another alpha require recomputing the entire procedure. Ties are handled without changing the input hypothesis order. Invalid p-values, non-finite entries and multidimensional arrays raise ValueError. No constructor tuning parameters are needed for this fixed procedure.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: WestfallYoungMaxT adjusts a family using its joint resampling distribution, with single-step and step-down modes.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Peter H. Westfall and S. Stanley Young (1993), Resampling-Based Multiple Testing: Examples and Methods for p-Value Adjustment, Wiley. The computational reference is Ge, Dudoit and Speed (2003), Resampling-based multiple testing for microarray data analysis, technical report, Box 2.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER under a valid exchangeable joint randomization scheme and subset pivotality. The numeric arrays alone cannot establish either condition.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
Each row must come from one shared null resampling operation across all columns. Subset pivotality requires that true-null subvectors have the same distribution under partial and complete nulls. Construct JointResamplingAssumptions explicitly only after justifying these properties for the experimental design.

Statistics must be comparable across hypotheses (for example, studentized). tail="greater" is the default; "less" negates both arrays and "two-sided" applies absolute value to both. Supply signed, zero-centered statistics when absolute value represents the intended two-sided test. Calibration/studentization is the caller’s responsibility.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Sort observed statistics decreasingly after the selected tail transformation. For each rank, take the maximum statistic over all remaining columns in each resampled row; count how often it is at least the observed statistic. In step-down mode, take the prefix maximum of these tail probabilities and restore original order. Single-step mode uses the entire family for every rank.

With sampling="monte_carlo", use (count + 1)/(B + 1): the B rows are uniform random draws with replacement from the valid joint null randomization orbit. The observed configuration supplies the extra identity contribution. Random draws may happen to equal it; do not append an extra identity row manually in this mode. With sampling="exact", enumerate the complete equally weighted orbit, including the identity, and use count/B. The implementation checks that an observed row is present; it cannot verify completeness or uniform weighting.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text: ResamplingStatistics(observed, resampled) holds (m,) and (B, m) read-only copies; B > 0. The constructor takes assumptions, step_down=True, and sampling="monte_carlo". test(data, alpha) returns MultipleTestingResult with alpha-independent adjusted p-values and decisions in original column order. Alpha must lie strictly between zero and one.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import (
    WestfallYoungMaxT,
    ResamplingStatistics,
    JointResamplingAssumptions,
)

# Numerical illustration only: a real analysis must justify its resampling design.
observed = np.array([3.0, 4.0, 2.0])
draws = np.array([[3.0, 1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 5.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], [2.0, 3.0, 1.0]])
assumptions = JointResamplingAssumptions(exchangeable=True, subset_pivotal=True)
procedure = WestfallYoungMaxT(assumptions, step_down=True, sampling="monte_carlo")
result = procedure.test(ResamplingStatistics(observed, draws), alpha=0.5)
np.testing.assert_allclose(result.adjusted_p_values, [0.6, 0.4, 0.6])
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False]

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: The ordered family has extreme-count totals 1, 2, 2 among four joint draws. Adding the identity yields 2/5, 3/5, 3/5. The prefix maximum is unchanged; restoring input order gives .6, .4, .6. Single-step adjustment gives 1, .4, 1.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: Independent shuffling of columns destroys dependence information. The assertion object records caller declarations; it does not certify the design. The smallest Monte Carlo value is 1/(B+1), so too few draws limit resolution. Ties use inclusive comparisons. Empty families return empty results. Complexity is \(O(m\log m + Bm)\) with \(O(Bm)\) intermediate memory.

docs.title: References
docs.text: For random sampling and the identity correction, see Phipson and Smyth (2010), Permutation P-values Should Never Be Zero, primary publication. Tests compare step-down results to exhaustive closed intersection tests and check FWER over a complete sign-flip orbit under global and partial null configurations.

docs.title: Name and purpose
docs.text: WestfallYoungMinP adjusts a family using its joint resampling distribution, with single-step and step-down modes.

docs.title: Original authors and publication
docs.text: Peter H. Westfall and S. Stanley Young (1993), Resampling-Based Multiple Testing: Examples and Methods for p-Value Adjustment, Wiley. The computational reference is Ge, Dudoit and Speed (2003), Resampling-based multiple testing for microarray data analysis, technical report, Box 3.

docs.title: Error rate controlled
docs.text: Strong FWER under a valid exchangeable joint randomization scheme and subset pivotality. The numeric arrays alone cannot establish either condition.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
Each row must come from one shared null resampling operation across all columns. Subset pivotality requires that true-null subvectors have the same distribution under partial and complete nulls. Construct JointResamplingAssumptions explicitly only after justifying these properties for the experimental design.

All entries must be calibrated raw p-values in [0, 1], computed using a consistent null calibration for observed and resampled data. Marginal p-values must reflect the intended tail already. The class neither computes marginal p-values nor accepts a vector of statistics in their place.

docs.title: Mathematical algorithm
docs.text:
Sort observed p-values increasingly. For each rank, take the minimum raw p-value over all remaining columns in each resampled row; count how often it is at most the observed p-value. In step-down mode, take the prefix maximum of these tail probabilities and restore original order. Single-step mode uses the entire family for every rank.

With sampling="monte_carlo", use (count + 1)/(B + 1): the B rows are uniform random draws with replacement from the valid joint null randomization orbit. The observed configuration supplies the extra identity contribution. Random draws may happen to equal it; do not append an extra identity row manually in this mode. With sampling="exact", enumerate the complete equally weighted orbit, including the identity, and use count/B. The implementation checks that an observed row is present; it cannot verify completeness or uniform weighting.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text: ResamplingPValues(observed, resampled) holds (m,) and (B, m) read-only copies; B > 0. The constructor takes assumptions, step_down=True, and sampling="monte_carlo". test(data, alpha) returns MultipleTestingResult with alpha-independent adjusted p-values and decisions in original column order. Alpha must lie strictly between zero and one.

docs.title: Usage example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pysatl_criterion.multiple_testing import (
    WestfallYoungMinP,
    ResamplingPValues,
    JointResamplingAssumptions,
)

# Numerical illustration only: a real analysis must justify its resampling design.
observed = np.array([0.3, 0.2, 0.4])
draws = np.array([[0.3, 0.5, 0.6], [0.6, 0.1, 0.4], [0.5, 0.4, 0.3], [0.4, 0.3, 0.5]])
assumptions = JointResamplingAssumptions(exchangeable=True, subset_pivotal=True)
procedure = WestfallYoungMinP(assumptions, step_down=True, sampling="monte_carlo")
result = procedure.test(ResamplingPValues(observed, draws), alpha=0.5)
np.testing.assert_allclose(result.adjusted_p_values, [0.6, 0.4, 0.6])
assert result.rejected.tolist() == [False, True, False]

docs.title: Worked numerical example
docs.text: The ordered family has extreme-count totals 1, 2, 2 among four joint draws. Adding the identity yields 2/5, 3/5, 3/5. The prefix maximum is unchanged; restoring input order gives .6, .4, .6. Single-step adjustment gives 1, .4, 1.

docs.title: Limitations and pitfalls
docs.text: Independent shuffling of columns destroys dependence information. The assertion object records caller declarations; it does not certify the design. The smallest Monte Carlo value is 1/(B+1), so too few draws limit resolution. Ties use inclusive comparisons. Empty families return empty results. Complexity is \(O(m\log m + Bm)\) with \(O(Bm)\) intermediate memory.

docs.title: References
docs.text: For random sampling and the identity correction, see Phipson and Smyth (2010), Permutation P-values Should Never Be Zero, primary publication. Tests compare step-down results to exhaustive closed intersection tests and check FWER over a complete sign-flip orbit under global and partial null configurations.
